lessons.label: Prokaryotic vs Eukaryotic Cells

sections.heading: The cell as the unit every hypothesis perturbs
sections.body: Cell theory, formalized by Theodor Schwann and Matthias Schleiden in 1838-1839 and extended by Rudolf Virchow's 1855 dictum that every cell arises from a preexisting cell, sets the working boundary for MCB: the cell is the smallest unit that is alive, and every experiment in this field is really a perturbation of one — knock down a gene, add a drug, change the media — then read out what the cell does. That means before you touch a bench technique, you have to know which kind of cell you are perturbing, because prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells differ enough in architecture that the same word 'cell' hides two very different machines.

sections.heading: Size, compartmentalization, and ribosomes
sections.body: Bacterial and archaeal cells are prokaryotes (from Greek for 'before nucleus'): typically 1-2 um long, with a single circular chromosome sitting free in the cytoplasm, no membrane-bound organelles, and 70S ribosomes (a 30S small subunit plus a 50S large subunit, named for their sedimentation coefficients in a centrifuge, not their mass). Eukaryotic cells — protists, fungi, plants, animals — run 10-100 um across, roughly 5 to 100 times the linear dimension of a bacterium, and package their DNA inside a double-membraned nucleus alongside a set of membrane-bound organelles (ER, Golgi, mitochondria, lysosomes) that let different chemical reactions run in separate compartments simultaneously. Eukaryotic cytoplasmic ribosomes are larger, 80S (40S + 60S), which is why the antibiotic streptomycin can jam a bacterial 30S subunit and stop an infection without stopping your own translation.

sections.heading: Why the split decides your model system
sections.body: This split is not trivia — it decides which organism a project even can use. A question about DNA replication speed, gene regulation logic, or antibiotic mechanism is naturally asked in Escherichia coli, which divides every 20 minutes under optimal lab conditions and has a genome of about 4.6 million base pairs. A question about protein trafficking through the ER-Golgi pathway, or about a mitochondrial process, has no prokaryotic analog and needs a eukaryote — often Saccharomyces cerevisiae (budding yeast), which is eukaryotic but still single-celled and fast (dividing roughly every 90 minutes), or a mammalian cell line when the question is specifically about human biology. Picking the wrong kingdom for your question is a fixable-before-you-start error; picking it after you have already ordered cells is expensive.

lessons.workedExample: A student wants to study how a candidate antibiotic affects ribosome function. If they culture human cells (80S ribosomes, membrane-bound nucleus) and see no effect, that is not evidence the drug fails as an antibiotic — it may simply be selective for the 70S bacterial ribosome, the entire point of a good antibiotic. The correct design uses E. coli (or another bacterium) as the target organism and a human cell line only as a counter-screen for toxicity, because the drug's job is to hit 70S without touching 80S.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'why this organism?' to see whether the student chose their cell type on purpose or by default. A weak answer says 'we used E. coli because it's easy to grow.' A strong answer names the structural reason the question requires that domain of life — no nucleus and 70S ribosomes for a translation/antibiotic question, or ER-Golgi trafficking and organelle compartmentalization for a secretion question — and can say what result in the wrong cell type would have been meaningless.

questions.prompt: A drug is designed to jam the bacterial ribosome without affecting human cells. Which structural difference makes this selectivity possible?

options.text: Bacteria have 70S ribosomes while eukaryotic cytoplasmic ribosomes are 80S
Bacteria lack ribosomes entirely
Human cells have circular chromosomes while bacteria have linear ones
Bacterial cells are larger than human cells, so the drug can't fit inside

explanations.a: Correct — the 70S (30S+50S) bacterial ribosome is structurally distinct from the eukaryotic cytoplasmic 80S (40S+60S) ribosome, which is exactly the difference streptomycin-class drugs exploit.
explanations.b: All cells, prokaryotic and eukaryotic, need ribosomes to translate mRNA into protein.
explanations.c: It is the reverse: bacteria typically have a single circular chromosome, while eukaryotes have linear chromosomes.
explanations.d: Bacterial cells (1-2 um) are far smaller than eukaryotic cells (10-100 um), and size is irrelevant to a molecular-scale drug target anyway.

questions.prompt: Match each research question to the model organism best suited to answer it.

left.text: How fast can a bacterial genome replicate?
How does a protein get modified as it moves through the Golgi?
What is the fastest-dividing eukaryotic single-celled model?

right.text: E. coli
A eukaryotic cell (has ER/Golgi; bacteria don't)
Saccharomyces cerevisiae

questions.explanation: E. coli is the standard fast-dividing prokaryote for genome/replication questions; Golgi processing only exists in eukaryotes, which compartmentalize their cytoplasm; and among eukaryotes, budding yeast divides fastest (about every 90 minutes) while still being a full eukaryotic cell.

questions.prompt: Order these cell types from smallest to largest typical linear dimension.

items.text: Bacterial cell (E. coli)
Typical animal cell
Large plant cell

questions.explanation: Bacteria run about 1-2 um, typical animal cells run roughly 10-30 um, and large eukaryotic cells (some plant cells) can reach the higher end of the 10-100 um eukaryotic range or beyond.

questions.prompt: Rudolf Virchow's 1855 contribution to cell theory is best summarized as which claim?

options.text: Every cell arises from a preexisting cell
All organisms are made of one or more cells
Cells contain a nucleus that stores genetic information
Ribosomes synthesize protein

explanations.a: Correct — Virchow's 1855 principle, 'omnis cellula e cellula,' established that new cells come only from division of existing cells, not spontaneous generation.
explanations.b: That claim belongs to Schwann and Schleiden's 1838-1839 formulation of cell theory, not specifically to Virchow's addition.
explanations.c: This is a structural fact about eukaryotic cells, not Virchow's historical contribution.
explanations.d: Ribosome function was established a century later through biochemistry, unrelated to Virchow's 19th-century claim.

lessons.label: Organelles and Their Jobs

sections.heading: The nucleus and the secretory pathway
sections.body: The nucleus stores the genome behind a double membrane (the nuclear envelope) perforated by nuclear pores that let mRNA out and regulatory proteins in; it is also where transcription and pre-mRNA splicing happen before a transcript is ready for translation. Two ER domains lead into a coordinated pipeline: the rough ER, studded with ribosomes, translates and folds proteins destined for secretion or membranes, while the smooth ER (no ribosomes) synthesizes lipids and, in liver cells, detoxifies drugs. Proteins leaving the rough ER are packaged into vesicles and sent to the Golgi apparatus, a stack of flattened membranes that further modifies them — trimming and adding sugar groups (glycosylation) — and sorts each protein to its final address: the plasma membrane, a lysosome, or secretion outside the cell. This ER-to-Golgi-to-membrane route is called the secretory pathway, and it is the reason a single misfolded protein early in the chain can derail everything downstream of it.

sections.heading: Power, breakdown, and cleanup
sections.body: Mitochondria run oxidative phosphorylation, using the electron transport chain across their folded inner membrane (cristae) to generate most of a cell's ATP — commonly cited as up to roughly 30-36 ATP per glucose molecule, versus just 2 net ATP from glycolysis alone. Free ribosomes in the cytoplasm (not attached to the ER) make proteins that stay in the cytosol or go to the nucleus, mitochondria, or peroxisomes. Lysosomes are membrane-bound sacs of acid hydrolases, enzymes that work best near pH 5, used to digest worn-out organelles, engulfed pathogens, and macromolecules; a genetic defect in a single lysosomal enzyme causes a class of Tay-Sachs-like storage diseases where undigested material piles up inside the cell. Peroxisomes handle a different oxidative job: breaking down very-long-chain fatty acids and detoxifying hydrogen peroxide with the enzyme catalase, converting it to water and oxygen.

sections.heading: Endosymbiotic origin: an organelle that was once free-living
sections.body: Mitochondria (and chloroplasts, in plants) did not evolve from scratch inside the eukaryotic cell — the endosymbiotic theory, most influentially argued by Lynn Margulis (published as Lynn Sagan in 1967), holds that they descend from free-living bacteria engulfed by an ancestral host cell roughly 1.5-2 billion years ago in a relationship that became permanent. The evidence is structural and genetic at once: mitochondria carry their own small circular DNA genome separate from the nuclear genome, are wrapped in a double membrane (an inner membrane from the original bacterium, an outer one from the engulfing host), and translate their own genes on 70S ribosomes — the bacterial size, not the 80S size used by the rest of the eukaryotic cell.

lessons.workedExample: A protein destined for secretion (say, an antibody made by an immune cell) is translated by a ribosome on the rough ER, folded and checked for quality inside the ER lumen, packaged into a vesicle that buds off and fuses with the Golgi, modified there by sequential enzymes across the Golgi stack, then packaged into a secretory vesicle that fuses with the plasma membrane and releases the antibody outside the cell. If a mutation blocks vesicle budding from the ER, the protein backs up and never reaches the Golgi — a phenotype a student can directly test by fluorescently tagging the protein and watching where it accumulates.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe organelle function to check whether a student understands mechanism or has just memorized a labeled diagram. A weak answer says 'the mitochondria is the powerhouse of the cell.' A strong answer explains what evidence supports a specific claim — for instance, citing the mitochondrion's own DNA, double membrane, and 70S ribosomes as the three lines of evidence for endosymbiotic origin, or tracing a secreted protein correctly from rough ER through Golgi to the membrane rather than naming organelles in no particular order.

questions.prompt: Order the stops of the secretory pathway for a protein destined to leave the cell.

items.text: Rough ER (translation and folding)
Golgi apparatus (modification and sorting)
Secretory vesicle fuses with plasma membrane

questions.explanation: Secreted proteins are made and folded on the rough ER, sent by vesicle to the Golgi for modification and sorting, then packaged into vesicles that fuse with the plasma membrane to release the cargo.

questions.prompt: Which piece of evidence LEAST supports the endosymbiotic origin of mitochondria?

options.text: Mitochondria have their own circular DNA genome
Mitochondria are enclosed by a double membrane
Mitochondria use 70S ribosomes to translate their own genes
Mitochondria are found in nearly all eukaryotic cells

explanations.a: A separate circular genome, resembling a bacterial chromosome, is one of the three core lines of evidence Margulis's 1967 argument relied on.
explanations.b: The double membrane (host-derived outer, bacterium-derived inner) is structural evidence directly predicted by engulfment.
explanations.c: 70S ribosomes match the bacterial ribosome size, not the eukaryotic 80S cytoplasmic size, supporting a bacterial ancestor.
explanations.d: Correct — how widespread mitochondria are says nothing about their evolutionary origin; it only reflects that the endosymbiotic event became essential and was inherited broadly, not a mechanism-level piece of evidence.

questions.prompt: Match each organelle to its primary job.

right.text: Digests worn organelles and pathogens with acid hydrolases
Breaks down long-chain fatty acids and detoxifies peroxide
Synthesizes lipids; detoxifies drugs in liver cells
Generates most cellular ATP via oxidative phosphorylation

questions.explanation: Each organelle has a distinct chemistry: lysosomes use acid hydrolases for digestion, peroxisomes handle fatty-acid oxidation and peroxide breakdown via catalase, smooth ER builds lipids and detoxifies, and mitochondria run the electron transport chain for ATP.

questions.prompt: A cell's rough ER is experimentally destroyed but the smooth ER, Golgi, and nucleus remain functional. Which process is most directly disrupted?

options.text: Translation of proteins destined for secretion or the plasma membrane
Transcription of DNA into mRNA
Lipid synthesis
ATP generation via oxidative phosphorylation

explanations.a: Correct — the rough ER is where ribosomes translate and begin folding secretory and membrane-bound proteins; without it, this step in the pathway has no site to occur.
explanations.b: Transcription happens in the nucleus, which the scenario states is still functional.
explanations.c: Lipid synthesis is largely a smooth ER job, which is unaffected in this scenario.
explanations.d: ATP generation is a mitochondrial function, unrelated to rough ER integrity.

lessons.label: Membrane Structure

sections.heading: Amphipathic lipids that assemble themselves
sections.body: A phospholipid has a hydrophilic phosphate-containing head and two hydrophobic fatty-acid tails, making it amphipathic — part water-loving, part water-fearing. Drop phospholipids into water and they do not need instructions to organize: driven purely by the thermodynamics of minimizing contact between the hydrophobic tails and surrounding water, they spontaneously self-assemble into a bilayer, tails facing inward toward each other, heads facing outward toward the aqueous cytoplasm and extracellular fluid. This self-assembly is why membranes are described as a stable but non-covalent structure — no bonds hold the sheet together, just the collective hydrophobic effect, which is also why a torn membrane reseals itself rather than staying open.

sections.heading: The fluid-mosaic model
sections.body: S. Jonathan Singer and Garth Nicolson proposed the fluid-mosaic model in 1972: the membrane is not a static wall but a two-dimensional fluid in which proteins float and drift laterally, like icebergs in a lipid sea. Integral membrane proteins are embedded through the bilayer (many spanning it entirely as transmembrane proteins), while peripheral proteins attach loosely to one face without penetrating the hydrophobic core, and can often be washed off with a change in salt concentration. Cholesterol, wedged between phospholipid tails in animal cell membranes, acts as a fluidity buffer: at high temperature it restrains excess movement and packs lipids more tightly, while at low temperature it prevents the tails from locking into a rigid, gel-like state — keeping the membrane in a workable fluid range across a wider temperature window than pure phospholipid would allow.

sections.heading: Selective permeability: what gets through unaided
sections.body: The hydrophobic fatty-acid core of the bilayer is the actual gatekeeper. Small nonpolar molecules like O2 and CO2, and small uncharged polar molecules like water and ethanol, can diffuse directly through that oily interior at an appreciable rate. Ions (Na+, K+, Cl-, Ca2+, H+) and large polar molecules like glucose are effectively blocked — an ion's charge makes it energetically very costly to strip away its shell of water molecules and cross the hydrophobic interior, so even a concentration gradient thousands-fold steep will not push it through unassisted. This is not an accident of the bilayer; it is the entire reason cells can maintain internal ion concentrations wildly different from the outside world, and it is why any regulated transport of an ion or glucose requires a dedicated protein — the subject of the next lesson.

lessons.workedExample: A student purifies pure phospholipid vesicles (liposomes, no protein) and tests how fast glucose versus ethanol crosses the membrane. Ethanol, small and only weakly polar, crosses readily and equilibrates within minutes. Glucose, a larger polar molecule, barely crosses at all over the same timescale — its permeability coefficient through a pure lipid bilayer is roughly six orders of magnitude lower than water's. This single side-by-side comparison is exactly the evidence that the bilayer itself, not some added machinery, is what discriminates between molecules by size and polarity, and it sets up why real cells need glucose transporter proteins to move sugar across their membranes at a biologically useful rate.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'why can't glucose (or an ion) just diffuse through the membrane?' to test whether a student understands the hydrophobic core as a physical barrier, not a rule to memorize. A weak answer says 'the membrane blocks big things.' A strong answer explains the mechanism: charged or polar molecules cannot shed their hydration shell cheaply enough to pass through a nonpolar interior, while small nonpolar molecules can dissolve directly into that same interior — and can connect this to why a specific transporter protein is needed for the molecule they are studying.

questions.prompt: Why do phospholipids spontaneously form a bilayer in water without any cellular machinery directing them?

options.text: Covalent bonds form between adjacent phospholipid heads
Minimizing contact between hydrophobic tails and water is thermodynamically favorable
Enzymes catalyze the bilayer assembly reaction
Phospholipids are electrically charged and attract each other like ions in a crystal

explanations.a: No covalent bonds hold a bilayer together; it is a non-covalent, self-assembled structure, which is why it can reseal after being torn.
explanations.b: Correct — amphipathic phospholipids arrange tails-inward, heads-outward because this minimizes unfavorable contact between hydrophobic tails and surrounding water, a purely thermodynamic driving force.
explanations.c: No enzyme is required; the assembly happens spontaneously even in a test tube with no biological catalyst present.
explanations.d: Phospholipid self-assembly is driven by the hydrophobic effect on the tails, not electrostatic attraction between charged heads.

questions.prompt: Match each membrane component to its role in the fluid-mosaic model.

right.text: Spans the bilayer, embedded through the hydrophobic core
Attaches loosely to one membrane face without penetrating the core
Buffers fluidity across a range of temperatures

questions.explanation: Singer and Nicolson's 1972 model distinguishes proteins fully embedded through the bilayer from those loosely bound to a surface, while cholesterol sits between lipid tails to keep fluidity workable at both high and low temperature.

questions.prompt: In a liposome permeability experiment, glucose crosses the pure lipid bilayer far more slowly than ethanol does. What best explains this difference?

options.text: Glucose is polar and too large to dissolve readily into the hydrophobic core, while ethanol is small enough to pass through
Glucose has a stronger positive charge than ethanol
Ethanol is broken down by enzymes in the liposome before it can be measured
Glucose molecules are chemically identical to ions and are actively pumped out

explanations.a: Correct — ethanol is small and only weakly polar, letting it dissolve into the nonpolar interior, while glucose is larger and polar enough that direct diffusion through the bilayer is very slow.
explanations.b: Glucose is an uncharged polar molecule, not charged; the barrier here is about polarity and size, not charge.
explanations.c: Pure liposomes made only of lipid have no enzymes; the experiment specifically has no protein to catalyze anything.
explanations.d: Glucose is neutral, not an ion, and this liposome experiment has no transport proteins present at all — there is nothing to pump it.

lessons.label: Transport Across Membranes

sections.heading: Diffusion, osmosis, and tonicity
sections.body: Passive diffusion moves a substance down its concentration gradient, from high to low concentration, with no energy input, and it applies to the small nonpolar/uncharged molecules the bilayer already lets through directly. Osmosis is diffusion of water specifically, across a selectively permeable membrane, from a region of lower solute concentration to higher solute concentration. Tonicity describes how a solution's solute concentration compares to a cell's interior: in a hypotonic solution (lower external solute than inside), water rushes in and the cell swells, potentially bursting (lysing) if unchecked; in a hypertonic solution (higher external solute), water leaves and the cell shrinks (crenates in a red blood cell, or plasmolyzes in a plant cell where the wall keeps the cell from collapsing entirely); in an isotonic solution, water moves in and out at equal rates and cell volume stays stable. This is why IV fluids are formulated near-isotonic to blood plasma, and why a plant wilts in salted soil.

sections.heading: Facilitated diffusion: passive but protein-assisted
sections.body: Facilitated diffusion still moves a substance down its gradient with no ATP cost, but it uses a protein to get a molecule across that the bilayer alone would block. Channel proteins form a continuous, often highly selective pore — potassium channels, for instance, use a selectivity filter of backbone carbonyl oxygens spaced to mimic K+'s hydration shell, letting K+ through roughly 1,000-fold faster than the very slightly smaller Na+. Carrier proteins instead bind their substrate (as GLUT transporters do for glucose), then undergo a conformational change that shuttles it to the other side, which makes carriers slower than channels but able to move substrates too large or too polar for a simple pore.

sections.heading: Primary active transport: spending ATP to go uphill
sections.body: Active transport moves a substance against its concentration gradient, which costs energy because it fights diffusion rather than following it. The Na+/K+ ATPase, present in essentially every animal cell, is the textbook example of primary active transport: each cycle hydrolyzes one ATP to pump 3 Na+ ions out of the cell and 2 K+ ions in, both against their gradients, using the phosphate released by ATP hydrolysis to drive a conformational change in the pump. Because this pump runs continuously, it builds and maintains steep electrochemical gradients for both ions — high extracellular Na+, high intracellular K+ — and those stored gradients are themselves a form of potential energy the cell later spends on other jobs: firing an action potential, or driving secondary active transport, where a solute is moved uphill by coupling its movement to Na+ flowing back downhill through a separate carrier.

lessons.workedExample: A student places red blood cells into three test solutions: distilled water, 0.9% saline (isotonic to blood), and 5% saline. Under a microscope, the distilled-water cells swell and several burst (hypotonic — water rushed in), the 0.9% saline cells look normal and stable (isotonic), and the 5% saline cells shrivel with a crenated, spiky outline (hypertonic — water left the cells). This one experiment demonstrates all three tonicity outcomes side by side and is the standard way to show osmosis is happening without needing to measure it directly — cell shape alone reports the direction water moved.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe transport mechanism to see if a student can distinguish passive from active and explain why each costs (or doesn't cost) energy. A weak answer says 'active transport uses energy, passive doesn't' with no mechanism. A strong answer names the specific gradient being fought — for the Na+/K+ ATPase, both Na+ and K+ move against their gradients simultaneously, at a fixed 3:2 stoichiometry per ATP — and can explain that the resulting gradient itself stores usable energy, which is why a poisoned Na+/K+ ATPase (e.g., by ouabain) collapses far more than ion balance alone.

questions.prompt: A red blood cell placed in distilled water swells and eventually bursts. What tonicity is the distilled water relative to the cell's interior, and why?

options.text: Hypertonic — solute concentration outside is higher, so water leaves the cell
Hypotonic — solute concentration outside is lower, so water enters the cell
Isotonic — solute concentrations are equal, so no net water movement occurs
Hypotonic, but water leaves the cell to dilute the surrounding solution

explanations.a: This describes the opposite outcome (shrinking), not swelling and bursting.
explanations.b: Correct — distilled water has essentially no solute, so relative to the cell's interior it is hypotonic; osmosis pulls water into the cell, causing it to swell and potentially lyse.
explanations.c: An isotonic solution would keep the cell's volume stable, not cause swelling and bursting.
explanations.d: Water moves toward the higher-solute side (into the cell here), not away from it; this option has the direction backward.

questions.prompt: Match each transport mechanism to its defining feature.

left.text: Facilitated diffusion via a channel protein
Facilitated diffusion via a carrier protein

right.text: Forms a continuous selective pore; no conformational cycling of the whole protein needed
Binds substrate then changes shape to shuttle it across; no ATP used
Hydrolyzes ATP to move ions against their gradients

questions.explanation: Channels provide a fast selective pore, carriers bind-and-flip their cargo without spending ATP, and only primary active transport like the Na+/K+ ATPase spends ATP to move substances uphill against their gradient.

questions.prompt: Each cycle of the Na+/K+ ATPase, per ATP hydrolyzed, moves which ions in which direction?

options.text: 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in, both against their concentration gradients
2 Na+ out and 3 K+ in, both down their concentration gradients
3 Na+ in and 2 K+ out, both against their concentration gradients
Equal numbers of Na+ and K+ moved in opposite directions, down their gradients

explanations.a: Correct — the pump moves 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in per ATP hydrolyzed, both moves working against each ion's own concentration gradient, which is exactly why the process requires energy.
explanations.b: The stoichiometry is reversed here, and moving ions 'down' their gradient would not require ATP at all.
explanations.c: The direction of each ion is reversed; Na+ is pumped out of the cell and K+ into the cell, not the other way around.
explanations.d: The stoichiometry is not equal (it's 3:2), and both ions move against their gradients, which is why ATP is spent rather than moving passively downhill.

questions.prompt: Which grouping of these three transport types by direct ATP cost is correct: passive diffusion, facilitated diffusion, primary active transport?

options.text: Passive diffusion and facilitated diffusion have no direct ATP cost; primary active transport does
All three cost ATP directly, just at different rates
Only passive diffusion has no ATP cost; facilitated diffusion and active transport both cost ATP
Facilitated diffusion costs more ATP than primary active transport

explanations.a: Correct — passive diffusion and facilitated diffusion both move a substance down its gradient with no direct ATP cost (facilitated diffusion just needs a protein to enable the crossing), while primary active transport uniquely spends ATP to move a substance against its gradient.
explanations.b: Passive and facilitated diffusion move substances downhill and require no direct ATP spend; only active transport does.
explanations.c: Facilitated diffusion, like passive diffusion, moves substances downhill with no direct ATP cost — the protein enables the crossing but doesn't spend ATP to do it.
explanations.d: Facilitated diffusion has no direct ATP cost at all, so it cannot cost more ATP than active transport, which is the only one of the three that spends ATP.

lessons.label: The Cell Cycle and Its Control

sections.heading: Interphase and mitosis: the four phases
sections.body: The cell cycle has two acts: interphase, where the cell spends most of its time growing and preparing, and mitosis, the actual division. Interphase splits into three phases — G1 (first gap, general growth and organelle production), S (synthesis, where the entire genome is replicated so each chromosome now has two sister chromatids), and G2 (second gap, final growth and error-checking before division). A typical cultured mammalian cell completes one full cycle in roughly 24 hours, with G1 usually the longest and most variable phase, S taking around 6-8 hours, and G2 plus M together taking a few more hours. Mitosis (M phase) then physically separates the duplicated chromosomes into two daughter nuclei, followed by cytokinesis splitting the cytoplasm in two.

sections.heading: Checkpoints: where the cell decides whether to proceed
sections.body: The cycle is not a fixed timer — it is monitored at checkpoints where the cell tests whether conditions justify continuing. The most consequential is the G1 restriction point (identified by Arthur Pardee in 1974), the point late in G1 past which a cell is committed to complete the cycle even if growth factors are later withdrawn; before the restriction point, a cell can pause or exit into a non-dividing resting state called G0. The G2/M checkpoint confirms DNA replication finished correctly and DNA damage is repaired before mitosis begins, and a separate spindle-assembly checkpoint during M phase holds the cell in metaphase until every chromosome's kinetochore is properly attached to spindle microtubules from opposite poles — a single unattached kinetochore is enough to delay anaphase, because attaching it wrong risks a daughter cell with the wrong chromosome number.

sections.heading: Cyclins and CDKs as the drivers
sections.body: The molecular engine behind these transitions is a family of cyclin-CDK complexes: cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) are enzymes that stay present at roughly constant levels through the cycle but are inactive alone, while cyclins are regulatory partners whose concentration rises and falls in a specific pattern (built up, then abruptly destroyed) that gives each phase transition its trigger. Tim Hunt discovered cyclins in 1983 studying sea urchin embryos, watching a protein accumulate steadily then vanish abruptly right at each division; Paul Nurse's parallel work identifying the CDK gene (cdc2) in fission yeast showed the same kinase core is conserved from yeast to humans. Hunt, Nurse, and Leland Hartwell shared the 2001 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for this work. In culture, cells stop dividing and a growth curve plateaus once they run out of space or growth factors and drop out of the cycle into G0 — which is exactly what a proliferation assay measures: not how fast a single cell divides, but what fraction of a population is actively cycling under the tested condition.

lessons.workedExample: A student treats cultured cells with a drug and wants to know if it blocks proliferation. A simple cell-count growth curve over several days shows the treated population plateaus earlier and at a lower density than untreated controls. That alone does not say why — the drug could be killing cells, or just holding them at a checkpoint. Adding a specific readout (e.g., staining for DNA content by flow cytometry) can show cells piling up with a single genome's worth of DNA (arrested in G1, before the restriction point) versus a doubled genome's worth (arrested in G2/M) — distinguishing a G1 arrest from a G2/M arrest tells the student which checkpoint the drug is acting on.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'what does your proliferation assay actually measure?' because a plateauing growth curve is often over-read as 'the drug killed the cells' when it may only have paused them at a checkpoint. A weak answer treats a flat growth curve as self-explanatory. A strong answer names the specific checkpoint framework — G1 restriction point vs G2/M vs spindle-assembly checkpoint — and proposes a way to tell arrest from death (e.g., a viability stain) rather than assuming the simplest explanation.

questions.prompt: Order the phases of the cell cycle starting from G1.

items.text: G1 (growth)
S (DNA synthesis)
G2 (growth, error-checking)
M (mitosis)

questions.explanation: The cycle runs G1 (growth) to S (genome replication) to G2 (final growth and checking) to M (division), after which daughter cells can re-enter G1 or exit to G0.

questions.prompt: A cell has just passed the G1 restriction point. What happens if growth factors are withdrawn immediately afterward?

options.text: The cell reverses back into G0 regardless of the restriction point
The cell is committed and will complete the cycle through division even without further growth-factor signaling
The cell immediately arrests in mitosis
The restriction point has no effect on the cell's later behavior

explanations.a: This describes what happens BEFORE the restriction point, not after — the whole significance of the restriction point is that this option becomes impossible once it's passed.
explanations.b: Correct — Arthur Pardee's 1974 restriction-point concept is exactly this commitment: once past it, the cell no longer needs continued growth-factor signaling to finish the cycle.
explanations.c: The restriction point is a G1 event; it doesn't cause an automatic mitotic arrest, and the scenario describes normal progression, not arrest.
explanations.d: The restriction point is specifically defined by this later behavior — calling it 'no effect' contradicts what makes it a checkpoint at all.

questions.prompt: Match each scientist to their key contribution to cell-cycle control.

right.text: Identified the G1 restriction point (1974)
Discovered cyclins in sea urchin embryos (1983)
Identified the CDK gene cdc2 in fission yeast

questions.explanation: Pardee defined the G1 restriction point, Hunt discovered cyclins by watching a protein rise and abruptly vanish each division cycle in sea urchin embryos, and Nurse identified the conserved CDK core using fission yeast; the three shared the 2001 Nobel Prize for this combined work.

questions.prompt: In a proliferation assay, a treated cell population's growth curve plateaus earlier than untreated controls. What is the most careful conclusion?

options.text: The drug definitely killed the cells
A smaller fraction of the population is actively cycling, but arrest vs death cannot be distinguished by cell count alone
The drug had no biological effect
The cells have permanently lost the ability to ever divide again

explanations.a: Cell count alone cannot distinguish checkpoint arrest from cell death; assuming death overstates what the data shows.
explanations.b: Correct — a plateauing growth curve reflects fewer cells actively completing the cycle, but a raw count can't tell you whether cells are arrested at a checkpoint (reversible) or dying (irreversible) without an additional assay like a viability stain.
explanations.c: A visibly lower, earlier plateau versus controls is itself evidence of a biological effect on proliferation, even if the exact cause isn't yet known.
explanations.d: Checkpoint arrest (e.g., at G1 or G2/M) is often reversible once the triggering condition is removed, so 'permanent' is an unsupported leap from a growth curve alone.

lessons.label: Choosing a Model System

sections.heading: Speed and genetic tractability vs biological relevance
sections.body: Every model system trades biological relevance for speed and ease of manipulation. E. coli divides roughly every 20 minutes, is genetically simple to edit, and costs almost nothing to culture, but it cannot answer a question about a human-specific pathway. Saccharomyces cerevisiae (budding yeast) is eukaryotic, dividing about every 90 minutes, with a genome that is comparatively easy to knock genes out of one at a time — a large fraction of its roughly 6,000 genes have a recognizable human counterpart, which is why yeast has been a workhorse for cell-cycle and DNA-repair discoveries (including the cyclin/CDK work covered in the previous lesson). Immortalized mammalian cell lines sit further along the relevance axis: HeLa cells, derived in 1951 by George Gey from a cervical cancer biopsy taken from Henrietta Lacks without her knowledge or consent, were the first human cell line capable of dividing indefinitely in culture, and remain widely used today despite this troubling origin, which is itself now a standard case study in research ethics.

sections.heading: Other standard lines and what they're used for
sections.body: HEK293 cells (human embryonic kidney), generated by Frank Graham in 1973 by transforming human embryonic kidney cells with sheared adenovirus 5 DNA, are prized for how efficiently foreign DNA can be introduced into them, making them a default for producing recombinant proteins and for testing gene constructs before moving to a more specialized system. CHO cells (Chinese hamster ovary), first cultured by Theodore Puck in 1957, are the standard workhorse of industrial biotechnology, most notably for manufacturing therapeutic antibodies at scale, because they grow robustly in suspension and glycosylate proteins in a way regulators accept as close enough to human. All three are immortalized lines, meaning they have acquired mutations (often in cell-cycle checkpoint genes) that let them bypass the normal proliferative limit and divide indefinitely — convenient for reproducibility, but a real caveat: an immortalized line's checkpoint biology is already broken in ways a normal cell's isn't, so it is not a perfect stand-in for a checkpoint experiment.

sections.heading: Primary cells, cost, and biosafety
sections.body: Primary cells — taken directly from an organism and cultured without immortalizing them — avoid that caveat because their checkpoint and signaling machinery is intact, but they divide only a limited number of times before senescence, vary donor to donor, and are far more expensive and technically demanding to maintain than an immortalized line. Biosafety level (BSL) is a practical constraint that often gets skipped until it's too late: standard laboratory E. coli strains (like K-12) are BSL-1, requiring only basic precautions, while essentially all human- and other mammalian-derived cell lines, including HeLa, HEK293, and primary human cells, are handled at BSL-2 because they can carry bloodborne pathogens, which means dedicated biosafety cabinets, specific waste disposal, and often institutional review before a student project can even begin culturing them — so check that clearance timeline before committing to a BSL-2 model system, not after.

lessons.workedExample: A student wants to test whether a candidate compound affects normal cell-cycle checkpoint arrest. Using HeLa cells alone is a real risk: HeLa's checkpoint genes are already altered by the immortalization process (and further disrupted by the HPV oncoproteins that originally transformed the cells), so an apparent 'failure to arrest' could reflect pre-existing checkpoint damage, not the compound. A stronger design pairs the immortalized line with a comparison in a line known to retain closer-to-normal checkpoint behavior (or explicitly caveats the result as line-specific), rather than presenting a HeLa-only result as if it generalizes to normal human cells.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask 'why this model system?' to separate a student who chose an organism because it was available from one who matched it to the question. A weak answer says 'we used HeLa cells because they're famous and easy to get.' A strong answer weighs the actual tradeoffs — genetic tractability against biological relevance, cost against biosafety level, and specifically flags when an immortalized line's altered checkpoint biology could bias a cell-cycle result, rather than treating any human cell line as an interchangeable stand-in for 'human biology.'

questions.prompt: Match each model system to how it was established or its defining origin.

right.text: Derived in 1951 from a cervical cancer biopsy (George Gey)
Transformed with adenovirus 5 DNA by Frank Graham in 1973
First cultured by Theodore Puck in 1957, now the industrial antibody-production standard

questions.explanation: Each line has a distinct, well-documented origin: HeLa from Henrietta Lacks's 1951 biopsy taken without consent, HEK293 from Frank Graham's 1973 adenoviral transformation, and CHO from Theodore Puck's 1957 culture, now central to biotech antibody manufacturing.

questions.prompt: A student's project needs to study a checkpoint-arrest response and wants a cell line where checkpoint machinery is as close to unaltered as possible. Which choice best fits, and why?

options.text: HeLa cells, because they are the most widely available human cell line
Primary cells, because they have not been immortalized and their checkpoint genes are intact
CHO cells, because they grow robustly in suspension
E. coli, because it divides fastest

explanations.a: HeLa cells are immortalized (and further altered by HPV oncoproteins), meaning their checkpoint biology is already disrupted — the opposite of what this question needs.
explanations.b: Correct — primary cells are not immortalized, so their checkpoint and signaling machinery has not acquired the mutations that let cell lines bypass normal proliferative limits, making them the closer stand-in for intact checkpoint behavior, at the cost of limited division and higher cost.
explanations.c: CHO cells are chosen for industrial protein production, not because they preserve normal checkpoint biology — they are also immortalized.
explanations.d: E. coli is prokaryotic and has no eukaryotic cell-cycle checkpoint machinery (no G1/S/G2/M cycle) at all, so it cannot answer this question.

questions.prompt: Why are human-derived cell lines like HeLa and HEK293 handled at biosafety level 2 (BSL-2) rather than BSL-1?

options.text: Because they grow too fast to be handled safely at BSL-1
Because they can carry bloodborne pathogens, requiring biosafety cabinets and specific waste handling
Because BSL-2 status is only about the cost of the reagents used
Because they are prokaryotic and therefore riskier than eukaryotic cells

explanations.a: Growth rate is not the criterion for biosafety classification; the concern is biological hazard, not culture speed.
explanations.b: Correct — human- and mammalian-derived material can carry bloodborne pathogens, so essentially all such lines require BSL-2 precautions: dedicated biosafety cabinets, controlled waste disposal, and often institutional review.
explanations.c: Biosafety level reflects hazard classification, not reagent cost.
explanations.d: Human and mammalian cell lines are eukaryotic, not prokaryotic; standard lab E. coli strains are actually the lower-risk BSL-1 category by contrast.

units.label: Molecules of Life & the Central Dogma

lessons.label: The Four Biomolecules

sections.heading: Four classes, one monomer-polymer logic
sections.body: Living cells build almost everything from four families of organic molecules: carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids. Three of the four are polymers — long chains of repeating monomer units linked by dehydration synthesis, the same condensation reaction that releases a water molecule at every bond and gets reversed by hydrolysis during digestion or degradation. Carbohydrates chain simple sugars (glucose, fructose) into starch, glycogen, or cellulose depending on the bond geometry — alpha versus beta linkages that human enzymes can or cannot cleave. Proteins chain 20 different amino acids into polypeptides. Nucleic acids chain nucleotides into DNA and RNA. Lipids are the exception: fats, phospholipids, and steroids are built from fatty acids and glycerol or a ring backbone, not a repeating monomer-polymer chain, which is why they don't dissolve in water and instead form the membranes that wall off every cell and organelle.

sections.heading: Why two of the four dominate MCB research
sections.body: Molecular and cell biology experiments overwhelmingly manipulate and measure two of these four classes: nucleic acids and proteins. Carbohydrates and lipids are mostly structural and metabolic — glycogen stores energy, phospholipids form membranes — but they don't carry heritable instructions or catalyze reactions with the specificity biology needs. Nucleic acids carry information: the linear order of four nucleotide bases in DNA encodes instructions with the same logic as letters in a sentence, and that sequence can be copied, transmitted to offspring, and read out. Proteins carry function: a polypeptide's specific sequence of amino acids folds into a three-dimensional shape that acts as an enzyme, a structural fiber, a receptor, or a motor. This sequence-to-structure-to-function chain — DNA sequence specifies protein sequence, protein sequence specifies protein fold, protein fold specifies what the protein does — is the throughline of nearly every hypothesis in this unit and the two after it: change the sequence, predict the functional consequence.

sections.heading: The 20 amino acids and their side chains
sections.body: All 20 standard amino acids share a backbone (an amino group, a carboxyl group, and a central carbon) but differ in one variable side chain, the R group, which is what gives each protein its personality. Side chains range from nonpolar and hydrophobic (leucine, valine — they cluster in a folded protein's water-avoiding core) to polar (serine, threonine) to charged, acidic (aspartate, glutamate) or basic (lysine, arginine). This chemical diversity is why swapping even one amino acid — a single point mutation — can change how a protein folds or functions, the mechanistic basis for the sequence-to-function argument this whole unit builds toward.

lessons.workedExample: A student hypothesizes that a plant's drought tolerance comes from a specific enzyme, not from generic sugar storage. To test the sequence-to-function claim, they would not measure total carbohydrate content (that's downstream metabolism, not the causal driver they're claiming) — they would identify the gene encoding the enzyme, compare its DNA sequence between drought-tolerant and drought-sensitive plant lines, and check whether a sequence difference predicts a measurable difference in the enzyme's protein structure or activity. This is the DNA-sequence-to-protein-function logic in miniature, and it is why a project proposal that only measures carbohydrate or lipid levels, without tracing back to a gene or protein, reads as descriptive rather than mechanistic.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe the four-biomolecule framework to check whether a student can say WHY their project measures DNA, RNA, or protein instead of carbohydrate or lipid content, when the hypothesis is about a causal mechanism. A weak answer lists the four classes like a vocabulary quiz. A strong answer explains that nucleic acids carry the heritable instruction and proteins carry out the function, so a mechanistic hypothesis about causation almost always has to trace back to a gene or its protein product — carbohydrates and lipids are usually downstream readouts, not the mechanism itself.

questions.prompt: Which biomolecule class is the exception to the monomer-polymer chain pattern followed by the other three?

options.text: Carbohydrates
Lipids
Proteins
Nucleic acids

explanations.a: Carbohydrates are polymers of sugar monomers linked by dehydration synthesis, following the standard pattern.
explanations.b: Correct — lipids are built from fatty acids and glycerol or a ring backbone, not a repeating monomer chain, which is also why they are hydrophobic and form membranes.
explanations.c: Proteins are polymers of amino acid monomers, following the standard pattern.
explanations.d: Nucleic acids are polymers of nucleotide monomers, following the standard pattern.

questions.prompt: In the sequence-to-structure-to-function logic of this unit, what role do nucleic acids play that proteins do not?

options.text: They catalyze most metabolic reactions
They store and transmit heritable information
They form the cell membrane
They store short-term chemical energy

explanations.a: Catalysis is overwhelmingly a protein (enzyme) function, not a nucleic acid one.
explanations.b: Correct — the linear order of bases in DNA (and RNA) encodes instructions that can be copied and inherited, which is the informational role proteins don't fill.
explanations.c: Membranes are built from lipids (phospholipids), not nucleic acids.
explanations.d: Short-term energy storage is a carbohydrate role (e.g., glycogen), not a nucleic acid one.

questions.prompt: Match each biomolecule class to its monomer unit.

right.text: Amino acids
Simple sugars
Nucleotides

questions.explanation: Carbohydrates chain simple sugars, proteins chain amino acids, and nucleic acids chain nucleotides — each via dehydration synthesis.

questions.prompt: What property of amino acid side chains (R groups) explains why a single point mutation can change a protein's function?

options.text: All side chains are chemically identical, so mutations rarely matter
Side chains vary in polarity and charge, so swapping one can change folding or activity
Side chains only affect the protein's color
Side chains are added after translation and are unrelated to the gene sequence

explanations.a: Side chains are highly variable, not identical — that variability is exactly why single swaps matter.
explanations.b: Correct — because side chains differ in hydrophobicity, polarity, and charge, replacing one amino acid can disrupt folding or an active site, changing function.
explanations.c: Side chains determine chemical behavior and folding, not pigmentation.
explanations.d: Side chains are specified by the amino acid encoded at that position, which comes directly from the gene's codon sequence.

lessons.label: DNA and RNA Structure

sections.heading: The nucleotide: three parts, one code
sections.body: Every nucleic acid is built from nucleotides, each with three parts: a five-carbon sugar, a phosphate group, and a nitrogenous base. In DNA the sugar is deoxyribose; in RNA it is ribose, which carries one extra hydroxyl group at the 2' carbon. That single oxygen makes RNA chemically less stable and more reactive than DNA — a difference that matters later when this unit contrasts DNA's long-term storage role with RNA's disposable, working-copy role. The phosphate and sugar alternate to form the backbone of a strand, with the base projecting off each sugar. Because the backbone has a chemical direction — a free phosphate at the 5' carbon on one end and a free hydroxyl at the 3' carbon on the other — every strand of DNA or RNA has a 5' end and a 3' end, and enzymes that build or read these strands work in a fixed direction, always 5' to 3'.

sections.heading: Base pairing and Chargaff's rules
sections.body: DNA carries four bases: adenine (A), thymine (T), guanine (G), and cytosine (C). Biochemist Erwin Chargaff found in the late 1940s and early 1950s that in any DNA sample, the amount of A always equals the amount of T, and G always equals C — a pattern later explained structurally: A pairs with T using two hydrogen bonds, and G pairs with C using three hydrogen bonds, so the pairing is fixed and complementary. Because G-C pairs have one more hydrogen bond, DNA regions richer in G-C content are more thermally stable and require more heat to separate than A-T-rich regions — the same principle exploited when choosing PCR primer melting temperatures. RNA replaces thymine with uracil (U), which pairs with A the same way but lacks thymine's extra methyl group, making it cheaper for the cell to synthesize disposable RNA.

sections.heading: The double helix: Watson, Crick, Franklin, and Photo 51
sections.body: James Watson and Francis Crick published the double-helix structure of DNA in Nature in 1953, proposing two strands wound around each other, running antiparallel — one strand oriented 5' to 3', the other 3' to 5' — with the sugar-phosphate backbones on the outside and the base pairs stacked like rungs on the inside. Their model depended critically on X-ray diffraction data collected by Rosalind Franklin and her student Raymond Gosling, especially the image known as Photo 51, which revealed the helical geometry, and on Chargaff's base-equivalence rule, which told them A must pair with T and G with C. Franklin's data was shown to Watson without her knowledge, by colleague Maurice Wilkins, a fact that has shaped how the discovery is now credited. RNA, by contrast, is typically single-stranded and folds back on itself into local hairpins rather than forming a stable double helix across its full length.

lessons.workedExample: A student is given an unknown nucleic acid sample and told it is 30% adenine. Using Chargaff's rule, if it is double-stranded DNA, thymine must also be 30% (A=T), leaving 40% split evenly between G and C, so 20% each. If instead the sample turns out to be 30% adenine but only 20% of a pairing partner base with no consistent A=T pattern, that mismatch signals the sample is single-stranded RNA (or single-stranded DNA), where Chargaff's equivalence rule does not have to hold because there is no complementary strand enforcing it.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about DNA/RNA structure to see if a student understands why the double helix's chemistry — not just its shape — makes DNA a stable long-term archive while RNA is a disposable working copy. A weak answer recites 'DNA is a double helix, RNA is single-stranded' without explanation. A strong answer connects deoxyribose's missing 2'-OH and thymine's extra methyl group to DNA's greater chemical stability, and can trace the base-pairing logic (A-T two bonds, G-C three bonds) back to Chargaff's data and Franklin's diffraction images that constrained the Watson-Crick model.

questions.prompt: A DNA sample is 24% guanine. What percentage is cytosine, and why?

options.text: 24%, because Chargaff's rule requires G to equal C
76%, because all remaining bases must be cytosine
12%, because C is always half of G
Cannot be determined without knowing the adenine content

explanations.a: Correct — Chargaff's rule states G always equals C in double-stranded DNA, since each G on one strand pairs with a C on the other.
explanations.b: This ignores Chargaff's rule and assumes no adenine or thymine are present.
explanations.c: There is no rule making C half of G; the rule is G equals C.
explanations.d: The G=C relationship holds independent of the A/T content; it doesn't require knowing adenine first.

questions.prompt: What structural difference between deoxyribose and ribose helps explain why RNA is less chemically stable than DNA?

options.text: Ribose lacks a phosphate group
Ribose has an extra hydroxyl group at the 2' carbon
Deoxyribose has an extra nitrogen atom
Ribose is missing the 3' carbon needed for bonding

explanations.a: Both sugars are attached to a phosphate group in the nucleotide; this is not the distinguishing feature.
explanations.b: Correct — the extra 2'-OH in ribose makes RNA's backbone more chemically reactive and prone to breakdown compared to DNA's deoxyribose.
explanations.c: The sugars differ in oxygen content at the 2' position, not nitrogen content.
explanations.d: Both sugars retain a 3' carbon; that is what allows the 5'-to-3' backbone linkage in both DNA and RNA.

questions.prompt: Match each historical contributor to their key contribution to the DNA structure discovery.

right.text: Published the double-helix model in Nature, 1953
Captured Photo 51, the X-ray diffraction image showing helical geometry
Established that A equals T and G equals C in DNA

questions.explanation: Watson and Crick built the model; Franklin and Gosling's diffraction data (Photo 51) revealed the helical shape; Chargaff's base-equivalence rule supplied the pairing logic — together these three lines of evidence converged on the 1953 structure.

questions.prompt: Order these from smallest to largest structural unit of a DNA strand.

items.text: A single nitrogenous base
A single nucleotide (sugar + phosphate + base)
A full single strand of DNA
The double helix (two paired strands)

questions.explanation: A base is one component of a nucleotide; nucleotides link into a single strand via the sugar-phosphate backbone; two complementary antiparallel strands wind together to form the double helix.

lessons.label: DNA Replication

sections.heading: Semiconservative copying
sections.body: When a cell divides, it must copy its entire genome so each daughter cell gets a complete set. Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl showed in 1958, using density-labeled nitrogen isotopes, that DNA replicates semiconservatively: each of the two original strands serves as a template, and each new double helix ends up with one old strand and one newly synthesized strand. This ruled out the competing conservative model (the whole original helix stays intact while an entirely new copy is made) and the dispersive model (both strands end up as patchworks of old and new). Semiconservative replication works because the two strands are already complementary — Chargaff's A-T, G-C pairing means each strand alone contains enough information to specify its partner.

sections.heading: The replication machinery
sections.body: Replication starts at an origin, a specific DNA sequence where the enzyme helicase unwinds and separates the two strands, creating a replication fork. Because DNA polymerase, the enzyme that builds new strands, can only add nucleotides to an existing 3' end, it cannot start a strand from scratch — primase first lays down a short RNA primer to give it a starting point. DNA polymerase then extends the new strand by reading the template 3' to 5' and synthesizing the new strand 5' to 3', continuously on the leading strand (which runs toward the fork) but discontinuously on the lagging strand (which runs away from the fork), producing short Okazaki fragments that DNA ligase later seals together into one continuous strand. This leading/lagging asymmetry is a direct consequence of DNA polymerase's fixed directionality combined with the strands' antiparallel orientation.

sections.heading: Fidelity, proofreading, and why it matters for PCR
sections.body: DNA polymerase makes a raw copying error roughly once per 10^5 nucleotides, but most polymerases have a built-in proofreading function — a 3'-to-5' exonuclease activity that detects a mismatched base and removes it before continuing — which combined with post-replication mismatch repair pushes the overall error rate down to roughly one mistake per 10^9 base pairs copied. That fidelity is what keeps a genome stable across billions of cell divisions in a human lifetime, while still leaving enough rare mutation for evolution to act on. This same enzymatic logic is what a PCR machine exploits in the lab: a heat-stable DNA polymerase (commonly Taq, isolated from a bacterium that lives in hot springs) repeatedly primes and extends copies of a target DNA sequence through dozens of heating-and-cooling cycles, doubling the amount of target DNA each cycle.

lessons.workedExample: Meselson and Stahl grew E. coli in a medium with heavy nitrogen (15N) so all its DNA became heavy, then switched the bacteria to normal 14N medium and let them divide. After one round of replication, they spun the DNA in a density gradient and found a single band at an intermediate density — not two bands (one heavy, one light) as the conservative model would predict. That single intermediate band ruled out the conservative model, but it was not yet enough to distinguish semiconservative from dispersive replication, since a dispersive model (every strand an even patchwork of old and new DNA) would also average out to intermediate density after one round. The deciding test came from a second round of replication: the bacteria were allowed to divide once more in 14N medium, and the DNA now formed two bands — one intermediate, one fully light — exactly as the semiconservative model predicts (one old hybrid strand paired with a new light strand, and one all-new light duplex). A dispersive model would instead have produced a single band, just lighter than before. That two-band result was the direct evidence for semiconservative replication.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe replication mechanics because 'how do you know your DNA was copied faithfully' is a real question behind any project using PCR, sequencing, or genotyping. A weak answer says 'DNA polymerase copies the DNA.' A strong answer names the proofreading step, gives a rough error-rate figure, and can explain why a heat-stable polymerase (and the leading/lagging asymmetry it inherits from replication biology) is what makes PCR possible at all — connecting a textbook mechanism to a bench technique they may have actually used.

questions.prompt: What result from the Meselson-Stahl experiment ruled out the conservative model of DNA replication?

options.text: After one replication round, all DNA was heavy density
After one replication round, DNA formed a single intermediate-density band
After one replication round, DNA formed two bands: one heavy, one light
DNA density did not change at all after replication

explanations.a: This would suggest no new synthesis occurred, which contradicts the observed data.
explanations.b: Correct — a single intermediate band is incompatible with the conservative model, which predicts two separate bands (fully heavy and fully light). It doesn't yet rule out the dispersive model on its own; a second round of replication was needed to do that.
explanations.c: Two separate bands (heavy and light) is what the conservative model predicts, but that is not what Meselson and Stahl observed.
explanations.d: Density did shift to an intermediate value, showing new light-nitrogen strands had been incorporated.

questions.prompt: Why does the lagging strand require Okazaki fragments while the leading strand does not?

options.text: The lagging strand has no primase activity
DNA polymerase can only synthesize 5' to 3', so the strand running away from the fork must be made in discontinuous pieces
The lagging strand uses a different, error-prone polymerase
The lagging strand is copied after the leading strand is fully complete

explanations.a: Primase still lays down RNA primers on the lagging strand — multiple times, in fact, once per Okazaki fragment.
explanations.b: Correct — because polymerase only extends 3' ends and the strands are antiparallel, the strand oriented away from the fork can only be synthesized in short, repeatedly re-primed fragments.
explanations.c: The same DNA polymerase performs both strands' synthesis; fidelity is not the reason for fragmentation.
explanations.d: Leading and lagging strand synthesis happen concurrently at the same replication fork, not sequentially.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of DNA replication at a single origin, from first to last.

items.text: Helicase unwinds the double helix at the origin
Primase lays down a short RNA primer
DNA polymerase extends new strands from the primer
DNA ligase joins Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand

questions.explanation: Helicase must open the helix before primase can act; primase must lay a primer before polymerase has a 3' end to extend from; ligase's sealing of fragments is the final step, after extension has produced the fragments to be joined.

questions.prompt: Roughly what is the overall error rate of DNA replication after proofreading and mismatch repair are included?

options.text: About 1 error per 100 base pairs
About 1 error per 10^5 base pairs
About 1 error per 10^9 base pairs
Essentially zero errors, ever

explanations.a: This is far too high; such an error rate would make stable genomes impossible across generations.
explanations.b: This is roughly the raw polymerase error rate before proofreading is applied, not the final rate.
explanations.c: Correct — proofreading exonuclease activity plus mismatch repair brings the combined error rate down to about one mistake per billion base pairs.
explanations.d: Some errors do slip through even with proofreading and repair, which is part of how mutations arise.

lessons.label: Transcription and RNA Processing

sections.heading: Reading DNA to build RNA
sections.body: Transcription is the process of copying a gene's DNA sequence into a complementary RNA strand. RNA polymerase binds a promoter, a specific DNA sequence upstream of a gene that marks where transcription should begin, then unwinds the double helix locally and reads one strand — the template strand — in the 3'-to-5' direction, synthesizing a new RNA strand 5' to 3' that is complementary to the template and therefore identical in sequence to the other DNA strand (the coding strand), except with uracil replacing thymine. Transcription proceeds through three phases: initiation, where polymerase and associated factors assemble at the promoter; elongation, where polymerase moves along the gene synthesizing RNA; and termination, where polymerase reaches a terminator sequence and releases both the DNA and the finished RNA transcript.

sections.heading: Eukaryotic mRNA gets processed before it can be used
sections.body: In eukaryotes, the RNA transcript made in the nucleus is not yet ready to be translated — it must be processed into mature messenger RNA (mRNA) first. Three modifications happen: a 5' cap, a modified guanine nucleotide added to the transcript's 5' end, protects the RNA from degradation and helps the ribosome recognize it later; a poly-A tail, a stretch of roughly 100-250 adenine nucleotides added to the 3' end, similarly stabilizes the transcript and aids its export from the nucleus; and splicing removes introns, the non-coding stretches interspersed within the gene, while joining the exons, the coding stretches, into a continuous reading sequence. Splicing is carried out by the spliceosome, a complex of proteins and small nuclear RNAs that recognizes specific sequences at intron-exon boundaries. Alternative splicing, in which different combinations of exons are joined in different cell types or conditions, lets a single gene produce multiple distinct protein products.

sections.heading: Prokaryotes skip the processing step entirely
sections.body: Bacteria have no nucleus, so transcription and translation are physically coupled: a ribosome can begin translating an mRNA while RNA polymerase is still transcribing further downstream on the same molecule. Prokaryotic mRNA also has no introns to splice, no 5' cap, and typically no poly-A tail, so it is used essentially as soon as it is made and is generally far shorter-lived than eukaryotic mRNA. This is a structural consequence of compartmentalization, not just a simpler organism having simpler biochemistry: eukaryotic cells physically separate transcription (nucleus) from translation (cytoplasm) with a nuclear envelope, which is exactly what necessitates processing steps like capping and splicing to protect and prepare the transcript for export and makes the coupled prokaryotic mode impossible.

lessons.workedExample: A eukaryotic gene contains three exons separated by two introns: Exon1-Intron1-Exon2-Intron2-Exon3. RNA polymerase transcribes the entire stretch into a pre-mRNA that still contains both introns. The spliceosome then recognizes the boundary sequences flanking each intron, excises Intron1 and Intron2, and joins Exon1 directly to Exon2 directly to Exon3, producing a mature mRNA of only the exon sequence. If a mutation disrupts one splice-site boundary, the spliceosome may skip that exon entirely or retain an intron, producing a different final protein — the molecular basis of several disease-causing splicing mutations.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about transcription and processing to check whether a student understands mRNA is not simply 'the DNA sequence in RNA form' in eukaryotes — it is a processed, edited molecule. A weak answer treats transcription as a one-step copy. A strong answer can name the cap, tail, and splicing separately, explain what each does functionally (protection, export, exon-joining), and connects the nucleus/cytoplasm separation in eukaryotes to why that processing is necessary at all, while bacteria transcribe and translate in the same coupled step.

questions.prompt: RNA polymerase reads the template strand in which direction, and synthesizes the new RNA strand in which direction?

options.text: Reads 5' to 3'; synthesizes 3' to 5'
Reads 3' to 5'; synthesizes 5' to 3'
Reads and synthesizes both 5' to 3'
Reads and synthesizes both 3' to 5'

explanations.a: This reverses the actual directionality of both processes.
explanations.b: Correct — RNA polymerase reads the template strand 3' to 5' while building the new complementary RNA strand 5' to 3', the same directional rule DNA polymerase follows during replication.
explanations.c: Reading and synthesis happen in opposite directions relative to each other, not the same direction.
explanations.d: New RNA is always synthesized 5' to 3', never 3' to 5'.

questions.prompt: Match each eukaryotic mRNA processing step to its primary function.

right.text: Protects the 5' end and aids ribosome recognition
Stabilizes the transcript and aids nuclear export
Removes introns and joins exons into a continuous sequence

questions.explanation: The 5' cap protects the transcript's start and helps ribosomes find it; the poly-A tail stabilizes the 3' end and assists export from the nucleus; splicing, done by the spliceosome, removes introns and joins exons into the final coding sequence.

questions.prompt: Why can bacterial ribosomes begin translating an mRNA before transcription of that mRNA is even finished?

options.text: Bacterial ribosomes translate faster than eukaryotic ones
Bacteria lack a nucleus, so transcription and translation occur in the same compartment without a physical barrier
Bacterial mRNA does not need to be accurate before translation
Bacterial RNA polymerase transcribes the whole gene instantly

explanations.a: Relative ribosome speed is not what enables coupling; the physical arrangement of the cell is.
explanations.b: Correct — without a nuclear envelope separating DNA from ribosomes, translation can start on the leading end of an mRNA while polymerase is still transcribing further downstream.
explanations.c: Bacterial mRNA still needs to be accurate; coupling is about physical access, not accuracy requirements.
explanations.d: Transcription still takes time in bacteria; it is not instantaneous, which is exactly why coupling with translation is possible mid-transcript.

questions.prompt: Order these events in eukaryotic gene expression from earliest to latest.

items.text: RNA polymerase binds the promoter
A pre-mRNA transcript containing introns is produced
The spliceosome removes introns, producing mature mRNA
Mature mRNA is exported to the cytoplasm for translation

questions.explanation: Transcription must initiate at the promoter before any transcript exists; the initial transcript still contains introns until the spliceosome acts; only after splicing produces mature mRNA can it be exported from the nucleus for translation.

lessons.label: The Genetic Code and Translation

sections.heading: Cracking the code: Nirenberg, Matthaei, and Khorana
sections.body: By the late 1950s, biologists knew mRNA sequence somehow specified protein sequence, but not the rule connecting them. In 1961, Marshall Nirenberg and Heinrich Matthaei made the first breakthrough: they synthesized an artificial mRNA made entirely of uracil (poly-U) and added it to a cell-free translation system, which produced a protein made entirely of the amino acid phenylalanine — polyphenylalanine. This showed that the codon UUU specifies phenylalanine and proved the code could be experimentally decoded rather than merely theorized. Har Gobind Khorana extended the approach through the 1960s by chemically synthesizing RNA molecules with defined, repeating sequences (such as alternating UC or UCU triplets), which let researchers work out most of the remaining codon assignments. By 1966 the full genetic code table was essentially complete.

sections.heading: Triplet codons: redundant but unambiguous
sections.body: The genetic code reads mRNA in non-overlapping triplets called codons, each specifying one amino acid or a stop signal. With four possible bases at each of three positions, there are 4^3 = 64 possible codons, but only 20 standard amino acids, so the code is degenerate (also called redundant): most amino acids are specified by more than one codon — leucine and serine each have six. This redundancy is not random; codons for the same amino acid often differ only in the third position (the 'wobble' position), which buffers many mutations at that position from changing the resulting protein at all. One codon, AUG, doubles as both the start codon (specifying methionine) and the signal that sets the reading frame — the grouping of subsequent bases into triplets from that point on. Three codons (UAA, UAG, UGA) specify no amino acid and instead signal translation to stop.

sections.heading: Translation: ribosomes, tRNA, and matching codon to amino acid
sections.body: Translation happens on the ribosome, a complex of ribosomal RNA and protein that reads mRNA codons and assembles the corresponding amino acid chain. The physical link between a codon and its amino acid is transfer RNA (tRNA): each tRNA molecule carries a three-base anticodon that base-pairs with a complementary mRNA codon, and is charged with the matching amino acid by an enzyme called an aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase — one synthetase per amino acid, each responsible for correctly pairing that amino acid with every tRNA that carries its anticodon. The ribosome moves along the mRNA one codon at a time, and at each step a matching charged tRNA enters, the ribosome catalyzes a peptide bond between the new amino acid and the growing chain, and the tRNA is released, until a stop codon is reached and the finished polypeptide is released.

lessons.workedExample: Given the mRNA sequence 5'-AUG-GCU-UUC-UAA-3', a ribosome reads it in that reading frame. AUG is the start codon, specifying methionine and setting the frame. GCU specifies alanine. UUC specifies phenylalanine. UAA is a stop codon, so translation halts and the finished tripeptide is methionine-alanine-phenylalanine. If a single base were inserted right after the start codon, every downstream triplet grouping would shift by one base — a frameshift mutation — scrambling every codon that follows and almost certainly producing a nonfunctional protein, even though not a single original base was changed, only its position relative to the reading frame.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe the genetic code to test whether a student grasps that DNA/RNA sequence and protein sequence are related by a specific, discoverable rule, not by magic — and that the rule was worked out experimentally, not just assumed. A weak answer says 'codons code for amino acids' with no mechanism. A strong answer can walk through how Nirenberg and Matthaei's poly-U experiment established the first codon assignment, explain why the code is described as degenerate, and reason correctly about what a frameshift versus a point mutation does to a reading frame.

questions.prompt: What did Nirenberg and Matthaei's 1961 poly-U experiment demonstrate?

options.text: That DNA replicates semiconservatively
That the codon UUU specifies the amino acid phenylalanine
That introns must be spliced out of pre-mRNA
That RNA polymerase reads DNA 3' to 5'

explanations.a: Semiconservative replication was demonstrated by Meselson and Stahl, a different experiment entirely.
explanations.b: Correct — an artificial poly-U mRNA produced a protein made entirely of phenylalanine, establishing that UUU codes for phenylalanine and proving the code was experimentally crackable.
explanations.c: Splicing was not investigated by this experiment, and the poly-U mRNA had no introns to remove.
explanations.d: This experiment was about codon-to-amino-acid assignment in translation, not about RNA polymerase's reading direction in transcription.

questions.prompt: Why is the genetic code described as degenerate (redundant)?

options.text: Because most of the 64 codons do not code for anything
Because most amino acids are specified by more than one codon
Because the code differs between every species
Because a single codon can specify multiple different amino acids at once

explanations.a: 61 of the 64 codons do code for an amino acid; only 3 are stop codons, so the vast majority are used.
explanations.b: Correct — with 64 codons but only 20 amino acids, most amino acids have multiple codons assigned to them, often differing only in the third (wobble) position.
explanations.c: The genetic code is nearly universal across species, which is part of why it could be worked out using bacterial cell-free systems and applied broadly.
explanations.d: Each codon specifies exactly one amino acid or a stop signal, never multiple amino acids at once — that would make translation ambiguous.

questions.prompt: Match each translation component to its role.

right.text: Base-pairs its anticodon to the mRNA codon and delivers the matching amino acid
Reads codons and catalyzes peptide bond formation between amino acids
Attaches the correct amino acid onto its corresponding tRNA

questions.explanation: The ribosome reads codons and assembles the polypeptide; tRNA physically links a codon to its amino acid via anticodon pairing; the synthetase is the enzyme that charges each tRNA with the correct amino acid in the first place.

questions.prompt: In the mRNA 5'-AUG-GCU-UUC-UAA-3', what happens if one base is inserted immediately after the AUG start codon?

options.text: Nothing changes, because only the inserted base is affected
Every downstream codon shifts by one base, scrambling the reading frame (a frameshift)
The ribosome automatically skips the inserted base and reads normally
Translation stops immediately at the point of insertion

explanations.a: A single insertion changes the grouping of every base downstream of it, not just the inserted base itself.
explanations.b: Correct — because translation reads non-overlapping triplets from a fixed starting point, inserting one base shifts every subsequent triplet grouping, scrambling the rest of the protein sequence.
explanations.c: Ribosomes do not detect or skip erroneous insertions; they simply read three bases at a time from wherever the frame currently sits.
explanations.d: Translation does not necessarily stop at the insertion point; it continues reading the now-shifted frame until it happens to hit a stop codon, often much later or with a different result than expected.

lessons.label: Gene to Protein: The Whole Flow

sections.heading: Assembling the pipeline
sections.body: The central dogma, a term Francis Crick introduced in 1958, describes the directional flow of sequence information in a cell: DNA is transcribed into RNA, and RNA is translated into protein.
