sections.body: Because a fold-change number is easy to compute and easy to get wrong, the MIQE guidelines from Bustin and colleagues (2009) set out what must be reported for a qPCR result to be trusted: primer efficiency and the R-squared of its standard curve, validation that the reference gene is actually stable under the tested conditions, technical replicates for each sample, and no-template controls to rule out contamination. A fold-change claim without this supporting information -- efficiency near 100%, a validated reference gene, and replicated Ct values -- is not something a careful reviewer, or a science-fair judge, should accept at face value.

lessons.workedExample: A student compares gene X expression between treated and control cells, using GAPDH as the reference. Treatment: Ct(X) = 22, Ct(GAPDH) = 18, so delta-Ct(treatment) = 22 - 18 = 4. Control: Ct(X) = 25, Ct(GAPDH) = 18, so delta-Ct(control) = 25 - 18 = 7. Delta-delta-Ct = 4 - 7 = -3. Fold change = 2^(-(-3)) = 2^3 = 8, meaning gene X is expressed about eightfold higher in the treated sample -- but only trustworthy if the student first confirmed GAPDH's Ct did not itself shift between conditions and that both primer pairs had validated efficiency near 100%.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes delta-delta-Ct because it is the step where a raw instrument readout becomes a biological claim, and it is easy to compute correctly while still being scientifically unjustified. A weak answer states the fold-change number without mentioning the reference gene or efficiency. A strong answer walks through delta-Ct then delta-delta-Ct, names the equal-efficiency assumption explicitly, and describes how they checked it -- for instance confirming the reference gene's Ct was stable across conditions and that primer efficiencies fell in the acceptable range before trusting an 8-fold claim.

questions.prompt: In a treated sample, Ct(target) = 22 and Ct(reference) = 18. In the paired control, Ct(target) = 25 and Ct(reference) = 18. What is the fold change in target expression (treatment vs. control)?

options.text: 2-fold
3-fold
8-fold
16-fold

explanations.a: This would follow only if delta-delta-Ct were -1, not -3.
explanations.b: 3 is the delta-delta-Ct magnitude itself, not the fold change -- it still needs to be exponentiated as 2^3.
explanations.c: Correct -- delta-Ct(treatment) = 22-18 = 4, delta-Ct(control) = 25-18 = 7, delta-delta-Ct = 4-7 = -3, fold change = 2^3 = 8.
explanations.d: 16-fold would require a delta-delta-Ct of -4, one more cycle of difference than these Ct values give.

questions.prompt: Why is a reference (housekeeping) gene included in a delta-delta-Ct experiment?

options.text: To amplify the target gene more efficiently
To correct for differences in total RNA/cDNA input between samples
To replace the need for a no-template control
To set the annealing temperature for the target primers

explanations.a: The reference gene is a separate, independent reaction; it does not influence amplification of the target gene.
explanations.b: Correct -- normalizing target Ct to a stably-expressed reference gene's Ct cancels out sample-to-sample differences in loading and reverse-transcription efficiency.
explanations.c: A no-template control checks for reagent contamination and serves a different purpose than normalization.
explanations.d: Annealing temperature is set by primer Tm, unrelated to the reference gene's role.

questions.prompt: The 2^(-delta-delta-Ct) formula assumes what about primer efficiency?

options.text: Both target and reference primers amplify at 100% efficiency
Only the reference primer needs to be efficient
Efficiency does not matter for this calculation
Target primers must be twice as efficient as reference primers

explanations.a: Correct -- the formula's base of 2 assumes perfect doubling (100% efficiency) for both the target and reference amplicons; the Pfaffl method is used when this assumption fails.
explanations.b: Both primer pairs, not just the reference, must meet the equal-efficiency assumption for the shortcut to hold.
explanations.c: Efficiency is central to the formula -- it is precisely what justifies using 2 as the exponent base.
explanations.d: The assumption is that the two efficiencies are equal to each other (and to 100%), not that one is double the other.

questions.prompt: Match each MIQE reporting element to what it establishes.

right.text: Confirms the equal-efficiency assumption behind fold-change math
Confirms the normalizer itself is not changing with treatment
Rules out reagent contamination producing false signal

questions.explanation: Reported efficiency justifies the 2^x math, reference-gene validation confirms the normalizer is a fair baseline, and a no-template control rules out contamination as the source of any signal.

lessons.label: Reverse Transcription and Gene Expression

sections.heading: Reverse transcriptase: the central-dogma exception
sections.body: The central dogma describes information flowing DNA to RNA to protein, but Howard Temin and David Baltimore independently discovered in 1970 that retroviruses run part of that flow backward, using an enzyme called reverse transcriptase to build a DNA copy from an RNA genome -- a finding recognized with the 1975 Nobel Prize. That same enzymatic activity, isolated from retroviruses such as Moloney murine leukemia virus (MMLV) or avian myeloblastosis virus (AMV), is now a standard lab tool: given an RNA template and a short primer, reverse transcriptase synthesizes a complementary DNA (cDNA) strand, letting researchers convert any RNA sample into a stable DNA copy for downstream analysis.

sections.heading: The RT-qPCR workflow
sections.body: Measuring gene expression means measuring how much messenger RNA a gene is producing, but qPCR runs on Taq polymerase, which only extends from a DNA template and cannot use RNA directly, and RNA itself is far more chemically fragile and vulnerable to ubiquitous RNases than DNA. The workflow therefore extracts total RNA, reverse-transcribes it into cDNA using oligo-dT, random hexamer, or gene-specific primers, and then runs qPCR on that cDNA exactly as with any DNA template. This is why 'gene expression' data is really cDNA abundance data one enzymatic step removed from the RNA that was actually present in the cell. The primer choice for that reverse-transcription step is a real tradeoff, not a formality. Oligo-dT primers anneal only to the poly-A tail found on mature mRNA, giving mRNA-specific priming, but because reverse transcriptase's processivity is limited, they leave long transcripts under-represented at their 5' end (3' bias). Random hexamers prime everywhere along any RNA species, including the far more abundant rRNA, so they give more even coverage across a transcript's length at the cost of some specificity and sensitivity for a single gene of interest. Gene-specific primers target only the transcript of interest, giving the highest specificity and sensitivity for single-target RT-qPCR, but they must be redesigned for every new gene and cannot be reused for genome-wide work.

sections.heading: Controls that rule out genomic DNA contamination
sections.body: The biggest threat to an RT-qPCR result is genomic DNA (gDNA) left over from RNA extraction, since gDNA carries the same sequence as the mature mRNA's exons and can amplify right alongside true cDNA signal, inflating the apparent expression level. Two controls guard against this. A DNase treatment step, applied to the RNA before reverse transcription, enzymatically digests contaminating gDNA. A no-RT control -- an aliquot of the same RNA carried through the entire protocol but with reverse transcriptase omitted -- should produce no product, since without an RNA-to-DNA conversion step there is no template for Taq polymerase except leftover gDNA; if the no-RT control still amplifies, that signal is gDNA contamination, not real transcript.

lessons.workedExample: A student measures expression of gene Y by RT-qPCR and gets Ct = 24 in the +RT sample. Their no-RT control, run alongside it using the same RNA but without reverse transcriptase added, gives Ct = 26 -- almost as strong as the real signal. Because a clean no-RT control should show no amplification (or a Ct at least 5-10 cycles higher, reflecting only trace contamination), this result means most of the apparent gene Y signal is coming from residual genomic DNA, not true mRNA-derived cDNA. The fix is a more thorough DNase treatment before reverse transcription, or redesigning primers to span an exon-exon junction so they cannot amplify genomic DNA at all.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about the no-RT control because it is the single check that separates a real gene-expression measurement from an artifact of DNA contamination, and it is often the first thing omitted by students in a hurry. A weak answer reports a Ct value and calls it 'gene expression' with no mention of controls. A strong answer explains that Taq cannot use an RNA template directly, states why reverse transcription is necessary, and describes running a no-RT control (and ideally DNase treatment) to confirm the measured signal came from mRNA and not contaminating genomic DNA.

questions.prompt: Why must RNA be reverse-transcribed into cDNA before qPCR, rather than running qPCR directly on RNA?

options.text: RNA is negatively charged and cannot enter a PCR tube
Taq polymerase cannot extend from an RNA template, and RNA is far more prone to degradation
cDNA fluoresces more brightly under SYBR Green
Reverse transcription is required to add a reference gene

explanations.a: Charge is not the issue -- DNA is also negatively charged and works fine in PCR.
explanations.b: Correct -- Taq polymerase requires a DNA template it can extend, and RNA's chemical instability and vulnerability to ubiquitous RNases make it a poor direct substrate for the multi-hour qPCR workflow.
explanations.c: SYBR Green fluoresces based on double-strandedness, not on whether the strand originated as DNA or cDNA.
explanations.d: A reference gene is a separate primer pair for normalization, unrelated to why reverse transcription itself is needed.

questions.prompt: A no-RT control (RNA carried through the protocol with reverse transcriptase omitted) shows strong amplification, nearly matching the +RT sample. What does this most likely indicate?

options.text: The gene is highly expressed
Genomic DNA contamination in the RNA sample
The reference gene was chosen incorrectly
The reaction efficiency is above 100%

explanations.a: High expression would explain signal in the +RT sample, but the no-RT sample has no cDNA template to amplify unless something else is present.
explanations.b: Correct -- without reverse transcriptase there is no RNA-to-cDNA conversion, so any amplification in this control must come from leftover genomic DNA carrying the same sequence.
explanations.c: Reference gene choice affects normalization calculations, not whether the no-RT control itself amplifies.
explanations.d: Reaction efficiency describes how well an existing template doubles each cycle, not why a template exists in a control that should have none.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a properly controlled RT-qPCR workflow.

items.text: Extract total RNA
Treat RNA with DNase to remove genomic DNA
Reverse-transcribe RNA into cDNA (plus a paired no-RT control)
Run qPCR on the cDNA

questions.explanation: RNA is extracted first, treated with DNase to remove contaminating genomic DNA, reverse-transcribed into cDNA with a no-RT control run in parallel, and only then amplified and measured by qPCR.

questions.prompt: Match each historical figure or reagent to its role in reverse transcription.

right.text: Discovered that retroviruses copy RNA into DNA, overturning strict unidirectional central dogma
Retrovirus-derived enzyme used in labs to synthesize cDNA from an RNA template
Digests contaminating genomic DNA before reverse transcription

questions.explanation: Temin and Baltimore's 1970 discovery established reverse transcription as biology; MMLV/AMV reverse transcriptase is the lab enzyme built on that discovery; DNase treatment is the control step that prevents genomic DNA from masquerading as transcript signal.

lessons.label: Gel Electrophoresis

sections.heading: How agarose separates DNA by size
sections.body: Agarose, a polysaccharide extracted from seaweed, forms a porous matrix when melted and cooled into a gel, and the concentration used sets the pore size: a low percentage like 0.8% resolves large fragments above 10 kb, while a higher percentage like 2% is needed to resolve small fragments under 500 bp. DNA's phosphate backbone carries a negative charge at neutral pH, so when the gel is placed in an electric field, every fragment migrates toward the positive electrode (the anode). Because the matrix acts as a molecular sieve, smaller fragments thread through the pores faster than larger ones, and over most of a gel's useful range migration distance is inversely related to the logarithm of fragment size -- a general empirical property of agarose electrophoresis that Southern himself characterized in his 1979 study of measuring DNA length by gel electrophoresis (distinct from his 1975 Southern-blot paper, whose contribution was the transfer-and-hybridization technique, not this sizing relationship).

sections.heading: Reading the gel: ladders and calibration
sections.body: A DNA size ladder -- a commercially prepared mixture of fragments of known, predetermined lengths -- is loaded into its own lane alongside experimental samples on every gel. After the run, comparing how far an unknown band has migrated relative to the ladder's bands lets a researcher estimate that fragment's size, typically by plotting the ladder's known sizes against migration distance (log-linear over most of the gel's range) and reading the unknown off that curve. Without a ladder, a band's position is meaningless -- it is only interpretable relative to fragments of known size run under identical conditions.

sections.heading: Staining and visualization
sections.body: DNA itself is colorless, so it must be stained to be seen. Ethidium bromide, in use since the 1970s, intercalates between DNA base pairs and fluoresces brightly under UV light, but it is a potent mutagen and suspected carcinogen that requires careful handling and disposal. SYBR Safe was developed as a safer alternative: it fluoresces under blue-light rather than UV illumination and carries substantially lower mutagenic risk, making it the more common choice in modern teaching and research labs, even though ethidium bromide remains in wide use for its sensitivity and low cost.

sections.heading: What bands, smears, and dimers tell you
sections.body: A clean single band at the expected size confirms a specific, correctly sized PCR product. Extra bands at unexpected sizes indicate the primers bound off-target sequences somewhere else in the template, producing nonspecific amplification. A small, bright band well under 100 bp, running near the bottom of the gel, is the signature of primer-dimers -- primers that annealed to each other instead of the template and were extended into a short spurious product, usually a sign that primer concentration was too high or annealing temperature too low. A smear rather than a discrete band points to degraded starting template or an overloaded, nonspecific reaction rather than a single clean amplicon.

lessons.workedExample: A student runs their 350 bp PCR product on a 2% agarose gel next to a 100 bp ladder and sees a bright band aligning between the ladder's 300 bp and 400 bp marks, confirming the expected amplicon size. They also notice a small, bright band below the ladder's smallest 100 bp marker, at roughly 40-50 bp. Because this band is far smaller than any real target and runs near the dye front, they correctly identify it as a primer-dimer rather than genuine product, and redesign their primers with a smaller 3' overlap and slightly lower concentration to eliminate it in the next run.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who points at a gel image on a poster is testing whether the student can read it, not just show it. A weak answer says 'this band shows our gene was amplified.' A strong answer names the ladder, states the expected size and where the band actually falls, and proactively explains any extra bands, smearing, or a small dimer band near the bottom -- showing they understand migration is by size, that a ladder is required to interpret position, and that a gel is a specificity check, not just a presence/absence check.

questions.prompt: Why does DNA migrate toward the positive electrode (anode) during gel electrophoresis?

options.text: DNA's phosphate backbone is negatively charged
DNA is naturally attracted to heat generated at the anode
The agarose matrix pulls DNA toward the anode
DNA has no charge and simply diffuses toward the anode

explanations.a: Correct -- the phosphate groups in the DNA backbone carry a negative charge at neutral pH, so DNA is drawn toward the positively charged anode in an electric field.
explanations.b: Migration is driven by electrostatic charge, not heat generated by the current.
explanations.c: The agarose matrix is a passive sieve that affects speed by pore size; it does not itself pull DNA in any direction.
explanations.d: DNA is charged, not neutral, and its movement is directed migration in an electric field, not random diffusion.

questions.prompt: A gel shows an extra small, bright band under 100 bp in a PCR reaction expected to produce a 350 bp product. What does this most likely represent?

options.text: A second, longer isoform of the target gene
A primer-dimer from primers annealing to each other
Residual genomic DNA contamination
An overloaded ladder lane

explanations.a: A longer isoform would run above, not below, the 350 bp expected band.
explanations.b: Correct -- a small, bright band well under 100 bp is the classic signature of primer-dimer, where primers extended off each other instead of the template.
explanations.c: Genomic DNA contamination would typically appear as a larger or off-target band reflecting real genomic sequence length, not a sub-100 bp fragment.
explanations.d: An overloaded ladder lane is a separate loading issue in the ladder's own lane, not an extra band in the sample lane.

questions.prompt: Match each gel observation to what it indicates.

left.text: Single clean band at expected size
Extra band at an unexpected size
Smear instead of a discrete band

right.text: Specific, correctly sized product
Nonspecific primer binding elsewhere in the template
Degraded template or overloaded, nonspecific reaction

questions.explanation: A single band at the expected size confirms specific amplification; an unexpected extra band points to off-target primer binding; a smear points to degraded template or a nonspecific, overloaded reaction.

questions.prompt: Order these fragments from fastest to slowest migration through an agarose gel (all else equal).

items.text: 100 bp fragment
500 bp fragment
2000 bp fragment

questions.explanation: Smaller fragments thread through the agarose pores faster than larger ones, so the 100 bp fragment migrates farthest and fastest, followed by 500 bp, then the 2000 bp fragment migrates least.

lessons.label: Spectrophotometry and Beer-Lambert

sections.heading: Absorbance, transmittance, and the law that links them
sections.body: A spectrophotometer shines a chosen wavelength of light through a sample and measures how much comes out the other side. Transmittance T is the ratio of transmitted to incident light intensity (I/I0); absorbance A is defined as -log10(T), so a solution that transmits 10% of the light has A = 1. The Beer-Lambert law, built from Pierre Bouguer's 1729 work on light attenuation through a medium and Johann Heinrich Lambert's 1760 formalization, plus August Beer's 1852 extension relating attenuation to solute concentration, states A = epsilon * c * l: absorbance equals the molar absorptivity (epsilon, a wavelength-specific constant for the absorbing molecule), times concentration (c), times the path length of light through the sample (l, usually 1 cm in a standard cuvette). Because A is linear in c, absorbance readings translate directly into concentration once epsilon and l are fixed. Molar absorptivity carries units of M^-1 cm^-1 (equivalently L mol^-1 cm^-1), chosen so that A -- a unitless ratio of intensities -- comes out consistent when c is in mol/L and l is in cm. NADH, a common biochemical assay target, has an epsilon340 of about 6,220 M^-1 cm^-1 at 340 nm; rearranging Beer-Lambert to solve for concentration, c = A / (epsilon * l), a reading of A340 = 0.622 in a standard 1 cm cuvette gives c = 0.622 / (6220 x 1) = 1.0 x 10^-4 M, or 100 uM NADH.

sections.heading: Blanking, the linear range, and why wavelength choice matters
sections.body: Before reading any sample, the instrument is zeroed against a blank -- a cuvette holding only the solvent or buffer -- so that A = 0 represents the sample matrix itself, not the analyte. Skipping this step means every later reading is inflated by background absorbance from the buffer, the cuvette material, or dust. Beer-Lambert holds only within a linear range, typically A below about 1.0-2.0 depending on the instrument; at higher concentrations, stray light inside the monochromator and intermolecular interactions (aggregation, shifted ionization) cause absorbance to plateau below what the law predicts, so concentrated samples must be diluted back into the linear range rather than trusted at face value. Wavelength choice exploits which molecules absorb where: nucleic acids absorb maximally near 260 nm because of the purine and pyrimidine rings in their bases, while proteins absorb near 280 nm mainly through the aromatic side chains of tryptophan and tyrosine. Reading both wavelengths and taking the A260/A280 ratio is a quick purity check -- pure DNA sits near 1.8, pure RNA near 2.0, and a lower ratio flags residual protein contamination.

lessons.workedExample: A student purifies plasmid DNA and reads A260 = 0.42 on a spectrophotometer blanked against elution buffer. Using the standard conversion that an A260 of 1.0 corresponds to about 50 ug/mL of double-stranded DNA, the concentration is 0.42 x 50 = 21 ug/mL. To check this factor rather than trust it blindly, the student runs a calibration curve: five known dilutions of a DNA standard (5, 10, 20, 40, 80 ug/mL) are measured at A260, plotted against concentration, and fit with a line through the origin. The fitted slope's reciprocal closely matches 50 ug/mL per absorbance unit, confirming the conversion is valid in this linear range before it is applied to the unknown sample.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'how do you know that number is real concentration and not just a reading?' to test whether the student understands spectrophotometry as an indirect measurement resting on an assumed constant (epsilon) and a linear range, not a direct scale. A weak answer just quotes the A260 number. A strong answer explains what the blank subtracted out, states the A260/280 ratio as evidence of purity, and describes diluting a sample that read above the linear range instead of trusting the raw absorbance.

questions.prompt: A purified RNA sample has an A260/A280 ratio of 1.5 instead of the expected ~2.0. What does this most likely indicate?

options.text: The sample is unusually concentrated
Residual protein contamination
The cuvette path length is too short
The RNA has degraded into smaller fragments

explanations.a: Concentration changes A260 and A280 together and does not by itself shift their ratio.
explanations.b: Correct -- protein absorbs strongly near 280 nm through aromatic residues, so contaminating protein pulls A280 up and lowers the 260/280 ratio below the pure-RNA value of about 2.0.
explanations.c: Path length is a fixed property of the cuvette and affects both wavelengths proportionally, not their ratio.
explanations.d: Fragmentation changes the total absorbing bases very little and is not what the 260/280 ratio is designed to detect.

questions.prompt: Why must a spectrophotometer be blanked with pure solvent/buffer before reading samples?

options.text: To warm up the light source
To zero out absorbance from the cuvette and solvent so only the analyte's absorbance is measured
To convert transmittance into molar absorptivity
To extend the linear range of the instrument

explanations.a: Blanking is a measurement step, not an instrument warm-up procedure.
explanations.b: Correct -- without subtracting the solvent and cuvette's own background absorbance, every sample reading is inflated by a constant offset unrelated to the analyte.
explanations.c: Molar absorptivity is a property of the molecule at a given wavelength, not something blanking calculates.
explanations.d: The linear range is set by the chemistry and optics of the assay, not by blanking.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for building and using a calibration curve to find an unknown concentration.

items.text: Prepare a dilution series of known standard concentrations
Measure absorbance of each standard
Plot absorbance vs. concentration and fit a line
Measure absorbance of the unknown sample
Use the fitted equation to back-calculate the unknown's concentration

questions.explanation: Standards must exist and be measured before a line can be fit; the fitted equation is only then applied to convert the unknown's absorbance into a concentration.

questions.prompt: Match each term in the Beer-Lambert law (A = epsilon * c * l) to what it represents.

right.text: Absorbance, -log10 of transmittance
Molar absorptivity, a constant specific to the molecule and wavelength
Concentration of the absorbing species
Path length of light through the sample

questions.explanation: Beer-Lambert states absorbance is the product of a molecule-specific constant, the concentration of that molecule, and how far the light travels through the solution.

lessons.label: Optical Density and Turbidity

sections.heading: OD600 is scattering, not true absorbance
sections.body: Optical density at 600 nm (OD600) is the standard proxy for bacterial or yeast culture density, but it is not measuring the same physical process as A260 or A280. Cells do not have a chromophore that absorbs strongly at 600 nm; instead, whole cells scatter light out of the detector's path (Rayleigh and Mie scattering, depending on cell size relative to the wavelength), and the spectrophotometer reports that lost light as if it were absorbance. This distinction matters because scattering depends on cell size, shape, and refractive index as well as number, so an OD600 reading is only a reliable stand-in for cell density within one organism and one instrument -- it is not a universal absolute unit the way a molar absorptivity is.

sections.heading: Nonlinearity, dilution, and calibrating OD to real cell counts
sections.body: At low density, OD600 rises roughly linearly with cell number, but as a culture gets dense, light scattered by one cell is re-scattered by neighboring cells before reaching the detector -- a multiple-scattering effect that makes the instrument systematically undercount how crowded the culture really is. Most benchtop spectrophotometers stay reasonably linear only up to roughly OD 0.3-0.6, so any reading above that range must be diluted into the linear range and multiplied back by the dilution factor rather than trusted directly. Because OD600 is only a proxy, it must be periodically calibrated against a ground-truth cell count -- a hemocytometer count or a colony-forming-unit (CFU) plate count -- to establish a conversion factor for a given strain and instrument; for common lab E. coli, OD600 = 1.0 is often cited as roughly 8 x 10^8 cells/mL, though this figure shifts with strain, growth phase, and cuvette geometry. Once calibrated, OD600 measured repeatedly over time produces a growth curve: an initial lag phase while cells adjust, exponential (log) phase as cell number doubles at a constant rate, a stationary phase as nutrients deplete or waste accumulates, and eventual decline -- the same lag-log-stationary-death framework formalized in Jacques Monod's 1949 work on bacterial growth kinetics. During log phase, two OD600 readings taken at different times let you calculate the specific growth rate mu = ln(OD_t2 / OD_t1) / (t2 - t1) and, from it, the doubling time = ln(2) / mu; a culture rising from OD600 0.10 to OD600 0.40 over 2 hours, for example, gives mu = ln(4)/2 = 0.693 hr^-1 and a doubling time of about 1 hour.

lessons.workedExample: A yeast culture read straight from the flask gives OD600 = 1.8, well above the instrument's linear range of about 0.3-0.6. The student dilutes it 1:10 into fresh media, re-reads, and gets OD600 = 0.21. Multiplying back by the dilution factor gives a true OD600 of 0.21 x 10 = 2.1 -- notably higher than the undiluted 1.8 reading, which was compressed below the true value by multiple scattering. The student then counts the same diluted sample on a hemocytometer, finds it corresponds to 6 x 10^7 cells/mL, and uses that pairing to build a strain-specific OD-to-cell-count conversion factor for future growth-curve experiments.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe OD600 because it is easy to treat as a plug-and-play number without understanding what it physically represents. A weak answer reports raw OD readings above 1.0 without comment. A strong answer explains that OD600 reflects light scattering rather than true absorbance, states that it diluted any high readings back into the linear range before multiplying by the dilution factor, and describes calibrating OD against an independent cell count rather than assuming a textbook conversion applies to its specific strain and instrument.

questions.prompt: Physically, what does an OD600 reading of a bacterial culture primarily measure?

options.text: True chromophore absorbance by a pigment in the cells
Light scattered away from the detector by whole cells
Fluorescence emitted by the growth media
pH-dependent color change in the media

explanations.a: Bacterial cells lack a strong 600 nm chromophore; the signal is not true molecular absorbance.
explanations.b: Correct -- cells scatter light out of the detector's path, and the instrument reports that scattering loss as if it were absorbance.
explanations.c: OD600 is a scattering measurement, not a fluorescence measurement.
explanations.d: Standard OD600 readings do not depend on media pH indicators.

questions.prompt: Why must a culture reading OD600 = 1.8 be diluted before it can be trusted as a growth measurement?

options.text: Because the spectrophotometer cannot read values above 1.0 at all
Because at high density, multiple scattering between cells makes the reading underestimate true density
Because 600 nm light degrades cells at high concentration
Because the blank becomes invalid above OD 1.0

explanations.a: Most instruments can produce a numeric reading above 1.0; the problem is accuracy, not an inability to read it.
explanations.b: Correct -- once cells are crowded, light scattered by one cell is re-scattered by another before reaching the detector, so the reading rises more slowly than true density and understates it.
explanations.c: Standard OD600 measurement light intensity does not meaningfully damage cells during a brief reading.
explanations.d: The blank subtracts media background and remains valid regardless of the sample's own OD.

questions.prompt: Match each bacterial growth phase to its description.

right.text: Cells adjust to new conditions; little increase in number yet
Cell number doubles at a constant rate
Growth rate roughly balances death rate as nutrients deplete
Cell number declines as conditions become unsustainable

questions.explanation: The classic bacterial growth curve moves from adjustment (lag), to constant-rate doubling (log), to a nutrient-limited plateau (stationary), to decline (death).

questions.prompt: Order the steps for building an OD600-to-cell-count calibration.

items.text: Prepare a dilution series from a culture
Measure OD600 for each dilution
Independently count cells (hemocytometer or CFU plate) for each dilution
Plot cell count against OD600 and fit a line
Use the fitted relationship to convert future OD600 readings into cell counts

questions.explanation: Calibration requires paired OD and independent count data across a dilution series before a conversion factor can be fit and reused.

lessons.label: Colorimetric and Antibody Assays

sections.heading: Total protein: Bradford and BCA
sections.body: Two dye-based assays dominate total-protein quantification. The Bradford assay, published by Marion Bradford in 1976, uses Coomassie Brilliant Blue G-250 dye, which shifts its absorbance peak from 465 nm to 595 nm when it binds protein, mainly through arginine and aromatic residues; it is fast (minutes) but sensitive to detergents in the sample, which can interfere with dye binding. The BCA (bicinchoninic acid) assay, described by Paul Smith and coworkers in 1985, instead relies on the biuret reaction: peptide bonds reduce Cu2+ to Cu+ in alkaline solution, and bicinchoninic acid then chelates the Cu+ to form a purple product read at 562 nm. BCA tolerates detergents better than Bradford but needs a longer incubation (often 30-60 minutes at 37 C) before reading. Both assays are compared against a standard curve built from known dilutions of a reference protein, usually bovine serum albumin (BSA). Because both dyes respond to specific amino-acid side chains rather than to peptide bonds uniformly, their color yield per milligram of protein varies with amino-acid composition; a sample protein whose arginine/aromatic content (Bradford) or overall composition (BCA) differs substantially from BSA will read as systematically over- or under-concentrated relative to its true value, even though the standard curve itself is accurate for BSA.

sections.heading: Viability dyes and the ELISA principle
sections.body: Metabolic-activity assays estimate live cell number indirectly. The MTT assay, described by Tim Mosmann in 1983, uses a yellow tetrazolium salt that mitochondrial dehydrogenases in living cells reduce to purple formazan crystals; the crystals are solubilized and read near 570 nm, so signal is proportional to mitochondrial activity, not a direct cell count. Resazurin-based assays (commercially, alamarBlue) work on a related idea but stay soluble: live cells reduce blue, weakly fluorescent resazurin to pink, strongly fluorescent resorufin, which allows repeated non-destructive readings over a time course rather than the single endpoint MTT requires. ELISA (enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay), first described by Eva Engvall and Peter Perlmann in 1971, detects a specific antigen rather than bulk protein or activity: in the common sandwich format, a capture antibody bound to the plate grabs the antigen from the sample, then an enzyme-linked detection antibody binds the captured antigen, and adding the enzyme's substrate produces a colored product whose intensity is proportional to antigen amount. All of these colorimetric and fluorescent endpoints are read on a microplate reader, which shines light through each well of a 96- or 384-well plate and records absorbance, fluorescence, or luminescence per well, giving far higher throughput than reading samples one at a time in a cuvette.

lessons.workedExample: A student treats cultured cells with a candidate drug at several doses, runs an MTT assay, and reads absorbance at 570 nm on a plate reader: untreated control wells average 0.80, and drug-treated wells average 0.32. Percent viability is calculated as (treated absorbance / control absorbance) x 100 = (0.32/0.80) x 100 = 40%. The student notes this number reflects mitochondrial dehydrogenase activity relative to control, not a literal cell count -- a drug that suppresses mitochondrial enzymes directly, without killing cells, would lower this number even though the cells are technically still alive, which is a limitation worth stating alongside the result.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe these assays because it is easy to report a colorimetric number as if it were a direct cell count. A weak answer says 'the MTT assay measures how many cells survived.' A strong answer states precisely what is being measured -- mitochondrial dehydrogenase activity as a proxy for viable cell number -- and flags the confound that a drug acting directly on mitochondrial enzymes would depress the readout independent of actual cell death, which is why a second, orthogonal viability check strengthens the claim.

questions.prompt: What chemical event produces the color shift measured in a Bradford assay?

options.text: Cu2+ is reduced to Cu+ by peptide bonds
Coomassie dye shifts its absorbance peak upon binding protein
A tetrazolium salt is reduced to formazan by mitochondrial enzymes
An enzyme-substrate reaction generates a chromogenic product

explanations.a: That is the biuret chemistry underlying the BCA assay, not Bradford.
explanations.b: Correct -- Coomassie Brilliant Blue G-250 shifts from 465 nm to 595 nm absorbance when it binds arginine and aromatic residues on proteins.
explanations.c: That describes the MTT viability assay, which measures metabolic activity, not total protein.
explanations.d: That describes the enzyme-substrate step of an ELISA, not a dye-binding protein assay.

questions.prompt: An MTT assay absorbance readout is best described as directly proportional to which quantity?

options.text: Total protein content of the well
Mitochondrial dehydrogenase activity, used as a proxy for viable cell number
The exact number of dead cells present
Antigen concentration bound by a capture antibody

explanations.a: MTT does not react with total protein; that is what Bradford or BCA measure.
explanations.b: Correct -- living cells' mitochondrial enzymes reduce the tetrazolium salt to colored formazan, so the signal tracks metabolic activity, a proxy for live cell number, not a direct count.
explanations.c: MTT signal comes from living, metabolically active cells, not dead ones.
explanations.d: Antigen-proportional signal describes ELISA, not MTT.

questions.prompt: Match each assay to what it primarily reports.

right.text: Total protein via Coomassie dye binding
Total protein via copper reduction and BCA chelation
Live-cell metabolic (mitochondrial) activity
Concentration of one specific antigen via antibody capture

questions.explanation: Bradford and BCA both quantify bulk protein through different chemistries; MTT reports metabolic activity as a viability proxy; ELISA is antigen-specific because it relies on antibody recognition rather than a generic chemical reaction.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a sandwich ELISA.

items.text: Coat the plate with capture antibody
Block remaining nonspecific binding sites
Add sample so antigen binds the capture antibody
Add enzyme-linked detection antibody, which binds the captured antigen
Add substrate and measure the resulting colored product

questions.explanation: The plate must be coated and blocked before sample is added, and the detection antibody can only bind after antigen has been captured, so substrate is added last to generate the measurable signal.

lessons.label: Light Microscopy

sections.heading: Magnification is not resolution
sections.body: Magnification describes how much bigger an image appears; resolution describes the smallest distance between two points that can still be told apart as separate. A microscope can magnify an image indefinitely with extra lenses, but once the underlying resolution limit is reached, additional magnification only enlarges blur -- a phenomenon called empty magnification. Ernst Abbe worked out the physical limit in 1873: the smallest resolvable distance d is approximately lambda / (2 x NA), where lambda is the wavelength of light used and NA is the numerical aperture of the objective lens (NA = n sin(theta), the refractive index of the medium times the half-angle of light the lens can collect). For visible light around 500 nm and a high-end oil-immersion objective with NA near 1.4, this works out to a resolution limit near 200 nm -- two structures closer together than that will blur into one no matter how much the image is magnified afterward. Reaching that rated resolution also requires the condenser's own numerical aperture to match or exceed the objective's NA: an under-filled condenser -- one set below the objective's NA -- caps the usable NA of the whole optical path, so even a 1.4 NA oil-immersion objective performs no better than a poorly adjusted or low-NA condenser allows.

sections.heading: Seeing unstained, live cells: phase-contrast and DIC
sections.body: Most living cells are nearly transparent under ordinary brightfield illumination because they absorb very little visible light; what varies is their refractive index, not their color, so brightfield alone shows almost no contrast without killing and staining the cells first. Frits Zernike solved this in the 1930s with phase-contrast microscopy (work that earned him the 1953 Nobel Prize in Physics): it converts the small phase shifts light undergoes passing through different cell structures into visible differences in brightness, at the cost of a characteristic bright halo artifact around edges. Georges Nomarski developed differential interference contrast (DIC) in the 1950s, using polarized light split by Wollaston prisms to generate a pseudo-3D, shadow-relief image with higher resolution and no halo, though DIC requires a birefringence-free optical path and so does not work through standard plastic culture dishes. Reproducible imaging in any of these modes also depends on Kohler illumination, a lamp-alignment method August Kohler introduced in 1893 that focuses the light source at the condenser aperture rather than the specimen plane, giving even, glare-free lighting across the field of view. Common stains -- hematoxylin and eosin for tissue sections, Gram stain for bacterial cell walls, crystal violet, Giemsa -- restore contrast in brightfield but require fixing or killing the sample first.

lessons.workedExample: A student switches from a 10x objective to a 100x objective on the same brightfield microscope without adding immersion oil, expecting a sharper view of bacterial cells. The image instead looks blurrier, not clearer. The 100x dry objective typically caps out around NA 0.95 versus roughly 1.4 for a comparable oil-immersion objective, so by Abbe's formula the resolvable detail barely improves even though the image is magnified far more -- the extra magnification just enlarges the same blur (empty magnification). Adding immersion oil to match the objective's design raises the effective NA and genuinely improves resolution, which is the fix, not simply cranking up magnification further.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'why didn't you just use higher magnification to see more detail?' is testing whether the student conflates enlarging an image with resolving finer structure. A weak answer treats magnification numbers as the whole story. A strong answer names the diffraction limit, states that resolution depends on wavelength and numerical aperture rather than magnification alone, and explains why phase-contrast or DIC -- not brightfield -- was chosen for unstained live cells.

questions.prompt: For visible light with a high-NA oil-immersion objective, the Abbe diffraction limit puts the smallest resolvable distance near what value?

options.text: 200 nm
2 nm
2 micrometers
20 micrometers

explanations.a: Correct -- with lambda around 500 nm and NA near 1.4, d = lambda/(2NA) works out to roughly 200 nm.
explanations.b: 2 nm is far below what visible-light optics can resolve; that scale requires electron microscopy.
explanations.c: 2 micrometers is an order of magnitude worse than the actual diffraction limit for a good objective.
explanations.d: 20 micrometers is far coarser than the diffraction-limited resolution of light microscopy.

questions.prompt: Why is phase-contrast or DIC microscopy preferred over brightfield for imaging live, unstained cells?

options.text: They magnify the sample far more than brightfield
They convert refractive-index/phase differences into visible contrast without staining or killing the cells
They eliminate the diffraction limit entirely
They require no light source, reducing phototoxicity

explanations.a: Magnification power is a property of the objective, not of switching to phase-contrast or DIC.
explanations.b: Correct -- live unstained cells barely absorb light, so these techniques exploit phase/refractive differences to create contrast that brightfield cannot show.
explanations.c: Diffraction still limits resolution in phase-contrast and DIC; they solve the contrast problem, not the resolution limit.
explanations.d: Both techniques still require illumination; they just process the light differently.

questions.prompt: Match each imaging technique to its underlying principle.

right.text: Contrast from direct light absorption by the sample
Converts phase shifts into brightness differences
Polarized light and Wollaston prisms create a relief-like image
Lamp alignment method giving even, glare-free illumination

questions.explanation: Brightfield relies on absorption, phase-contrast and DIC both exploit phase/refractive differences (via different optical tricks) to see unstained samples, and Kohler illumination is a setup method for even lighting rather than a contrast technique itself.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for setting up Kohler illumination.

items.text: Focus the specimen under the objective
Close the field diaphragm
Raise or lower the condenser until the diaphragm edges are sharp
Center the diaphragm image in the field of view
Open the field diaphragm until its edge just leaves the field of view

questions.explanation: The specimen must be in focus first; closing the field diaphragm makes its edges visible so the condenser height and centering can be adjusted against them, and only then is the diaphragm opened back out to fill the field evenly.

lessons.label: Fluorescence Microscopy and Reporters

sections.heading: Excitation, emission, and the filter cube that separates them
sections.body: A fluorophore absorbs a photon at a specific excitation wavelength, jumps to a higher-energy electronic state, loses a fraction of that energy as heat and molecular vibration, then emits a photon at a longer wavelength as it relaxes back down. Because emitted light always carries less energy than the light that excited it, its wavelength is shifted longer -- the Stokes shift, named for George Stokes, who described the effect in 1852. A fluorescence microscope isolates this weak emitted signal from the much brighter excitation light using a three-part filter cube: an excitation filter that passes only a narrow band of wavelengths tuned to the fluorophore, a dichroic mirror that reflects that excitation light up toward the sample but transmits the longer emission wavelengths back down, and an emission filter that blocks any leftover excitation light while passing the fluorophore's emission to the detector. Without all three working together, the excitation light -- orders of magnitude brighter than the emission -- would swamp the image.

sections.heading: Genetic and antibody-based reporters, and their limits
sections.body: Green fluorescent protein (GFP) was first isolated from the jellyfish Aequorea victoria by Osamu Shimomura in 1962; Martin Chalfie showed in 1994 that GFP could be expressed as a genetic tag in living organisms such as C. elegans, and Roger Tsien engineered a palette of brighter and spectrally shifted variants (CFP, YFP, enhanced GFP). All three shared the 2008 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Because GFP can be fused to a gene of interest, it reports where and when that protein is expressed in a living cell without killing it. Immunofluorescence instead labels a target after fixation: an unlabeled primary antibody binds the specific target antigen, and a fluorophore-conjugated secondary antibody then binds the primary's constant region -- since several secondary molecules can bind each primary, this amplifies the signal, and the same fluorescent secondary can be reused with any primary raised in the same host species. DAPI (4',6-diamidino-2-phenylindole) is a common companion stain that binds AT-rich DNA in the minor groove and fluoresces blue, marking the nucleus in almost any fixed-cell image. A key practical limit on all of this is photobleaching: repeated excitation eventually destroys a fluorophore's ability to fluoresce, through reactive byproducts generated during excitation, which caps how long or how brightly a sample can be imaged and motivates minimizing light exposure or adding antifade reagents.

lessons.workedExample: A student wants to know whether a specific protein localizes to the actin cytoskeleton in fixed cells. They apply an unlabeled primary antibody raised against that protein, then a secondary antibody conjugated to a green-emitting fluorophore (such as Alexa Fluor 488) that binds the primary, plus DAPI to mark nuclei. Imaging with a green-fluorescence filter cube shows the protein's distribution, and imaging the same field with a DAPI filter cube shows nuclear position; overlaying the two channels lets the student judge whether the protein signal traces the same filamentous, cytoplasmic pattern expected of actin or instead concentrates in the nucleus, without needing a second stain for actin itself.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe fluorescence setups because a lot of students can name 'GFP' or 'antibody staining' without explaining the optics or the logic of amplification. A weak answer says 'we used a fluorescent antibody to see the protein.' A strong answer explains why both an excitation and an emission filter are needed (to separate a bright excitation beam from a much dimmer emission signal), why an unlabeled primary plus a labeled secondary amplifies signal instead of labeling every primary directly, and acknowledges photobleaching as a real constraint on exposure time and imaging duration.

questions.prompt: What causes the Stokes shift between a fluorophore's excitation and emission wavelengths?

options.text: Some absorbed energy is lost as heat/vibration before the photon is re-emitted
The dichroic mirror adds energy to the emitted light
Emission always occurs at a shorter wavelength than excitation
Photobleaching converts excitation photons directly into emission photons

explanations.a: Correct -- energy lost to vibrational relaxation means the emitted photon carries less energy, hence a longer wavelength, than the absorbed photon.
explanations.b: The dichroic mirror only redirects and filters light by wavelength; it does not add energy.
explanations.c: The Stokes shift is toward longer wavelengths (lower energy), not shorter.
explanations.d: Photobleaching is fluorophore destruction over repeated cycles, not the mechanism producing each shift.

questions.prompt: Why use an unlabeled primary antibody plus a fluorophore-conjugated secondary antibody, rather than directly conjugating a fluorophore to every primary antibody?

options.text: Because primary antibodies cannot bind antigens once fixed
Because multiple secondary antibodies can bind one primary, amplifying signal, and one labeled secondary works with any primary from that host species
Because secondary antibodies do not photobleach
Because primary antibodies emit their own background fluorescence

explanations.a: Fixation preserves antigen structure well enough for primary antibody binding; that is the basis of immunofluorescence.
explanations.b: Correct -- several fluorescent secondaries can bind each primary for signal amplification, and the same labeled secondary is reusable across many different unlabeled primaries.
explanations.c: Secondary antibody fluorophores are just as subject to photobleaching as any other conjugated dye.
explanations.d: Unconjugated primary antibodies are not themselves fluorescent.

questions.prompt: Match each component or reagent to its role in a fluorescence experiment.

right.text: Passes only the narrow wavelength band that excites the fluorophore
Reflects excitation light to the sample, transmits longer emission wavelengths back
Blocks residual excitation light, passes emission to the detector
Binds AT-rich DNA to mark the nucleus

questions.explanation: The three filter-cube components work together to isolate weak emission from strong excitation, while DAPI is a separate reagent used as a standard nuclear counterstain.

questions.prompt: Order the physical steps of the fluorescence process, from light striking the fluorophore to detection.

items.text: Photon is absorbed, exciting an electron to a higher energy state
Some energy is lost as heat/vibration during relaxation
A lower-energy, longer-wavelength photon is emitted
The emission filter passes that photon to the detector

questions.explanation: Absorption precedes relaxation, relaxation precedes emission at a shifted wavelength, and only after emission can the filtered light reach the detector.

lessons.label: Cell Culture and Aseptic Technique

sections.heading: Keeping the culture sterile
sections.body: Mammalian cell culture is done in a laminar-flow biosafety cabinet, which pulls room air through a HEPA filter and pushes a steady, particle-free stream across the work surface so airborne contaminants are swept away from open flasks and dishes. Surfaces and gloved hands are wiped with 70% ethanol before and during work, tools are flame- or autoclave-sterilized, and time spent with caps off or dishes uncovered is minimized. Media itself is a buffered nutrient solution -- commonly DMEM (Dulbecco's Modified Eagle Medium, an elaboration of Harry Eagle's 1959 basal medium formulation) or RPMI-1640 (developed at the Roswell Park Memorial Institute in 1966) -- typically supplemented with about 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) to supply growth factors, hormones, and attachment proteins, and sometimes antibiotics such as penicillin-streptomycin. Cultures are kept in a humidified incubator at 37 C with 5% CO2, which maintains the bicarbonate buffering system in the media near physiological pH; phenol red in the media serves as a built-in indicator, turning yellow if the media becomes acidic (often from overgrowth or contamination) and magenta/purple if it becomes too alkaline.

sections.heading: Growth formats, passaging, and what can go wrong
sections.body: Adherent cell lines, such as HeLa or fibroblasts, grow attached to the flask surface and must be enzymatically released to passage them; suspension lines, such as many blood- and immune-lineage cell types, grow floating freely in media and are passaged simply by diluting into fresh media. Passaging an adherent line at confluency involves washing away the serum-containing media with PBS (serum carries protease inhibitors that would blunt the next step), adding trypsin-EDTA to enzymatically cleave the surface adhesion proteins holding cells to the flask and to each other, then adding fresh serum-containing media to neutralize the trypsin before diluting the cells into a new vessel at a defined split ratio. Contamination is the recurring hazard: bacteria and fungi typically show up within hours to days as visible turbidity, a sudden pH shift, or floating debris under the scope. Mycoplasma is the more dangerous risk precisely because it is not obvious -- these cell-wall-less bacteria are roughly 0.1-0.3 micrometers, below the resolving power of standard light microscopy and invisible as turbidity, yet surveys of cultured cell lines have repeatedly found a substantial fraction, often cited in the range of roughly one-fifth to one-third, silently mycoplasma-positive; detecting it requires PCR-based testing or a DNA stain such as DAPI/Hoechst rather than a visual check. This lesson covers the shared basics every lab needs; deeper culture-specific protocols and imaging analysis live in a separate, more specialized branch.

lessons.workedExample: A flask of HeLa cells reaches roughly 90% confluency under the scope. The student aspirates the old media, washes once with PBS to remove residual serum, adds a small volume of trypsin-EDTA, and incubates at 37 C for 3-5 minutes until the cells round up and detach when the flask is gently tapped. Fresh serum-containing media is added to neutralize the trypsin, the suspension is counted, and the cells are split 1:10 into a new flask with fresh media before returning to the 37 C, 5% CO2 incubator -- each step exists to either free the cells from the surface (trypsin) or stop that same enzyme before it damages the freed cells (serum neutralization).
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'why that specific sequence, not just sterile technique in general?' to see whether a student understands the biochemical reason behind each step rather than reciting a memorized protocol. A weak answer says 'we kept everything sterile and split the cells.' A strong answer explains that the PBS wash removes trypsin-inhibiting serum before enzymatic detachment, that serum is added back afterward specifically to neutralize the trypsin, and can name mycoplasma -- not bacteria or fungi -- as the contaminant that would go undetected without a dedicated test.

questions.prompt: Why is a PBS wash performed before adding trypsin during passaging of adherent cells?

options.text: To lower the pH of the flask before enzyme addition
To remove residual serum, which contains protease inhibitors that would blunt trypsin's action
To pre-cool the cells for detachment
To sterilize the flask surface

explanations.a: PBS is a neutral, isotonic buffer and is not used to shift pH.
explanations.b: Correct -- serum carries protease inhibitors, and leaving residual serum in the flask would interfere with trypsin's ability to cleave adhesion proteins.
explanations.c: The wash is not a temperature step; incubation for detachment happens at 37 C.
explanations.d: Sterility is maintained by aseptic technique throughout, not specifically by the PBS wash step.

questions.prompt: Which contaminant is hardest to detect by eye or standard light microscopy, requiring PCR or a DNA stain instead?

options.text: Bacteria
Fungi
Mycoplasma
Yeast

explanations.a: Bacterial contamination usually produces visible turbidity or a pH shift within hours to days.
explanations.b: Fungal contamination is typically visible as filaments or floating clumps under the scope.
explanations.c: Correct -- mycoplasma cells are far smaller than standard resolving power and produce no obvious turbidity, so dedicated PCR testing or a DNA stain is needed to catch them.
explanations.d: Yeast contamination is generally visible as budding cells under brightfield.

questions.prompt: Match each culture format to how it is passaged.

right.text: Enzymatically detach with trypsin, neutralize, then reseed
Dilute directly into fresh media

questions.explanation: Adherent cells are physically attached and require enzymatic release before reseeding, while suspension cells float freely and only need dilution to passage.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of passaging an adherent cell line.

items.text: Aspirate old media
Wash with PBS
Add trypsin-EDTA and incubate until cells detach
Add serum-containing media to neutralize trypsin
Count cells and reseed at a defined split ratio

questions.explanation: Old media and residual serum must be cleared before trypsin can act efficiently, and the enzyme must be neutralized before cells are counted and reseeded into a new flask.

lessons.label: Counting Cells and Viability

sections.heading: The hemocytometer and the dilution math behind it
sections.body: A hemocytometer is a thick glass slide etched with a precise counting grid, typically the Neubauer ruling: nine large 1 mm x 1 mm squares, with a coverslip held a fixed 0.1 mm above the grid. Each large square therefore covers a known chamber volume of 1 mm x 1 mm x 0.1 mm = 0.1 mm^3, which equals 1 x 10^-4 mL. To count, a cell suspension is loaded into the chamber by capillary action, cells within the four corner squares are counted under a microscope, following the standard edge convention: a cell is counted if it touches the top or left boundary line of a square, but excluded if it touches only the bottom or right line. This convention keeps a cell straddling a shared boundary from being counted in both adjacent squares (inflating the count) or missed by both (deflating it), which matters because that systematic bias would otherwise compound with every subsequent dilution and seeding calculation. The four counts are then averaged. Because that average represents the concentration in a volume of 1 x 10^-4 mL, multiplying it by 10^4 converts it to cells/mL, and multiplying further by whatever dilution factor was used when the sample was mixed with dye gives the concentration of the original, undiluted suspension.

sections.heading: Trypan blue, automated counters, and why counts matter downstream
sections.body: Trypan blue dye-exclusion is the standard viability check paired with hemocytometer counting: cells with an intact plasma membrane exclude the dye and appear clear, while dead or membrane-compromised cells let the dye in and appear blue under brightfield, giving a simple live/dead classification rather than the graded metabolic signal of an assay like MTT. Viability is reported as the fraction of unstained cells among the total counted. Automated cell counters -- image-based instruments or ones using the Coulter principle, in which cells passing through a small aperture disrupt an electrical current in proportion to their volume (a method Wallace Coulter patented in 1953) -- reduce the subjectivity and tedium of manual counting and are increasingly standard alongside the hemocytometer. Whatever method is used, the resulting number matters beyond the count itself: seeding density (cells plated per cm^2 or per well) determines how quickly a culture reaches confluency and strongly affects the reproducibility of downstream assays, and both raw cell counts over time and viability fractions at each condition are the direct inputs to growth curves and dose-response experiments, where a drug's effect is read out as the viable fraction remaining at each tested concentration.

lessons.workedExample: A student mixes a cell suspension 1:1 with trypan blue (dilution factor 2) and loads a hemocytometer. The four corner squares give counts of 42, 38, 45, and 40 cells, for a total of 165 cells across the four squares and an average of 165/4 = 41.25 cells per square. Concentration = 41.25 x 2 (dilution factor) x 10^4 = 8.25 x 10^5 cells/mL. Of the 165 cells counted, 15 stained blue (dead), so viability = (165-15)/165 = 90.9%. This concentration and viability fraction are exactly what the student then uses to calculate how much suspension to add for a target seeding density in a new dose-response plate.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe hemocytometer counting because the arithmetic (dilution factor, the 10^4 conversion) is a common place for silent errors that inflate or deflate every downstream number. A weak answer reports a cell concentration without showing the conversion or mentions 'we checked viability' without saying how. A strong answer walks through the square-average-times-dilution-times-10^4 calculation explicitly and explains that trypan blue gives a binary live/dead classification based on membrane integrity, distinct from a metabolic-activity assay like MTT.

questions.prompt: Why do dead cells stain blue in a trypan blue exclusion test?

options.text: Dead cells actively pump the dye into themselves
A compromised plasma membrane no longer excludes the dye, letting it enter
Trypan blue binds specifically to DNA released from dead cells
Dead cells reduce trypan blue chemically, changing its color

explanations.a: Dye entry into dead cells is passive, not an active transport process.
explanations.b: Correct -- an intact membrane excludes the dye in live cells; once membrane integrity is lost, the dye diffuses in freely and the cell appears blue.
explanations.c: Trypan blue exclusion depends on membrane permeability, not DNA binding.
explanations.d: Unlike MTT's tetrazolium chemistry, trypan blue does not undergo a reduction reaction here; it simply enters or is excluded.

questions.prompt: A student averages 30 cells per corner square and used a 1:5 dilution with trypan blue. What is the concentration of the original suspension?

options.text: 3 x 10^5 cells/mL
1.5 x 10^6 cells/mL
3 x 10^6 cells/mL
1.5 x 10^5 cells/mL

explanations.a: This omits the dilution factor entirely (30 x 10^4 without multiplying by 5).
explanations.b: Correct -- 30 (average count) x 5 (dilution factor) x 10^4 = 1.5 x 10^6 cells/mL.
explanations.c: This double-counts the dilution factor (multiplying by 10 instead of 5).
explanations.d: This divides by the dilution factor instead of multiplying by it.

questions.prompt: Match each counting-related term to its role.

right.text: Etched grid slide for manual microscope-based counting
Dye that marks dead cells via membrane permeability
Counts and sizes cells via electrical impedance as they pass an aperture
Cells plated per unit area, set before an experiment begins

questions.explanation: The hemocytometer is the physical counting device, trypan blue is the viability dye used with it, automated counters offer an electrical or image-based alternative, and seeding density is a planning parameter set before cells are ever counted post-experiment.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a trypan blue hemocytometer cell count.

items.text: Mix cell suspension with trypan blue
Load the mixture into the hemocytometer chamber
Count clear (live) and blue (dead) cells in the four corner squares
Average the four square counts
Multiply by the dilution factor and by 10^4 to get cells/mL

questions.explanation: The dye must be mixed in and the chamber loaded before counting can happen, and the conversion to cells/mL only makes sense after the raw counts are averaged.

lessons.label: Positive, Negative, and Vehicle Controls

sections.heading: A control is a claim about what could have gone wrong
sections.body: Every control exists to rule out one specific alternative explanation for a result, not to make an experiment look more rigorous. A positive control is a sample known to give the expected result, run alongside the unknowns so a blank plate or a dead reagent shows up as a failure of the positive control rather than a false 'no effect' in the real samples. A negative control is a sample expected to give no signal, so any signal that appears there tells you the assay itself is generating false positives. In PCR the standard negative control is the no-template control (NTC): a reaction with every reagent — primers, polymerase, buffer, dNTPs — but water instead of template DNA. If the NTC amplifies, the problem is contamination of a reagent or primer-dimer formation, and every 'positive' result in that run is now suspect until the source is found and the run repeated.

sections.heading: Vehicle controls isolate the drug from its delivery
sections.body: In dose-response work, the compound being tested is almost never soluble in water; it is usually dissolved in a solvent like DMSO or ethanol at a stock concentration, then diluted in so a tiny volume delivers the dose. That solvent is not biologically inert — DMSO above roughly 0.1-1% can itself slow growth or alter membrane permeability. An untreated control (media only) shows baseline behavior, but it cannot distinguish 'the drug did this' from 'the DMSO did this,' because the untreated well never saw any solvent. The vehicle control — media plus the same volume of pure solvent used in the highest treatment dose, with no active compound — is what makes that separation possible. A dose-response curve without a vehicle control is only valid if the solvent's own effect happens to be zero, which is an assumption, not a fact.

sections.heading: Loading controls make band or lane intensity comparable
sections.body: A Western blot or qPCR plate does not load exactly equal amounts of protein or RNA into every lane by hand-pipetting alone; small pipetting and transfer differences of even 10-20% are routine. A loading control — a housekeeping gene like GAPDH or beta-actin by Western blot, or total protein stain (e.g., Ponceau S or a stain-free gel) — measures that lane-to-lane input, so the band of interest can be expressed as a ratio to it rather than as raw intensity. Skip the loading control and a 'stronger band' in the treated lane could simply mean more total protein went into that well.

lessons.workedExample: A student runs a qPCR assay to test whether a plant extract induces a stress-response gene in yeast, alongside three DMSO-only wells and three untreated wells, plus a no-template control on the same plate. The NTC shows a faint amplification curve crossing threshold at cycle 34 versus cycle 22 for real samples — evidence of trace primer-dimer, not contamination, since it is 12 cycles later and the melt curve confirms a non-specific product, so the real data stands. The DMSO wells show a small (Ct shift of 0.3) but real increase over untreated, meaning the 1% DMSO vehicle itself mildly induces the gene. Reporting fold-change against the DMSO control rather than the untreated control removes that solvent artifact from the extract's apparent effect.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'what did you use as your negative control?' is testing whether the student can distinguish a real effect from an assay artifact or a solvent effect. A weak answer says 'we didn't really need one' or describes only an untreated group. A strong answer names the specific alternative explanation each control rules out — an NTC for reagent contamination, a vehicle control for solvent effects, a loading control for pipetting variance — and can say what result in that control would have invalidated the data.

questions.prompt: A PCR no-template control (water instead of DNA) produces a visible amplification product. What does this most directly indicate?

options.text: The target gene is expressed at very low levels
A reagent is contaminated or primers are forming dimers, and other results in the run are now suspect
The positive control was too concentrated
The thermocycler's annealing temperature was set too high

explanations.a: The NTC has no template at all, so any signal cannot reflect expression level — there is no RNA/DNA source for a real target.
explanations.b: Correct — the NTC should never amplify since there is no template; a signal there means contamination or primer-dimer, and it puts every other result on that plate in doubt.
explanations.c: The positive control's concentration doesn't affect what happens in a separate, template-free well.
explanations.d: A too-high annealing temperature would suppress amplification everywhere, including real samples, not create a false signal in an empty well.

questions.prompt: Why is an untreated (media-only) well not sufficient on its own to interpret a dose-response experiment with a drug dissolved in DMSO?

options.text: Untreated wells always have more cells than treated wells
It cannot separate the drug's effect from an effect of the DMSO solvent itself
Untreated wells cannot be measured with the same assay
DMSO is always biologically inert, so this is not actually a problem

explanations.a: Cell number differences aren't the core issue here — the issue is which variable produced any observed difference.
explanations.b: Correct — since the untreated well never receives DMSO, any difference between it and a drug-treated well could be caused by the drug, the solvent, or both, and there is no way to tell them apart.
explanations.c: Untreated wells are measured with the exact same assay as treated ones; that is the point of a control.
explanations.d: DMSO is not inert at typical working concentrations (roughly 0.1-1% and up) — it can itself affect cell behavior, which is exactly why a vehicle control is needed.

questions.prompt: Match each control to the specific problem it is designed to catch.

right.text: Reagent contamination or primer-dimer producing false signal
The solvent itself, not the drug, causing the observed change
Unequal amount of sample loaded per lane or well

questions.explanation: Each control targets one specific confound: the NTC catches contamination/primer-dimer, the vehicle control catches solvent effects, and the loading control catches unequal input between lanes.

questions.prompt: Order these steps for interpreting a dose-response Western blot correctly, from sample prep to final claim.

items.text: Load equal target volumes plus vehicle-only and untreated lanes
Probe for both the target protein and a housekeeping loading control
Normalize each lane's target band to its own loading-control band
Compare normalized (not raw) band intensities across drug doses

questions.explanation: You must first load the right set of samples including controls, then probe for both target and loading control, then normalize each lane to its own loading control before any dose comparison is valid — comparing raw intensities skips the step that removes lane-to-lane loading variation.

lessons.label: Replicates and Reproducibility

sections.heading: Technical replicates measure the assay; biological replicates measure the biology
sections.body: A technical replicate is the same biological sample measured multiple times — three qPCR wells loaded from one cDNA tube, or three absorbance readings of one culture. It tells you how noisy your pipetting and instrument are, nothing more. A biological replicate is an independent biological unit: a separate flask started from a separate colony, a separate animal, a separate donor. Only biological replicates let you ask whether an effect generalizes beyond the one flask or organism you happened to grow that day. The two are not interchangeable, and averaging technical replicates first (to get one number per biological unit) before any statistics are run is standard practice — otherwise the technical noise gets treated as if it were biological variation.

sections.heading: Pseudoreplication: the trap of inflated n
sections.body: Pseudoreplication is treating non-independent measurements as if they were independent samples, which artificially inflates the sample size and the apparent statistical confidence. The term and its diagnosis were formalized by Stuart Hurlbert in a widely cited 1984 paper, which found the error common enough in published field experiments to warrant a name. The classic cell-biology version: one flask of treated cells and one flask of untreated cells, each split into three wells before an assay, reported as 'n=3' per group. Those three wells share every source of biological variation in that single flask — the same passage number, the same media lot, the same incubator position — so they are three technical measurements of n=1 biological unit, not three independent biological replicates. Statistics computed on n=3 wells will report tighter confidence intervals and smaller p-values than the real biological uncertainty justifies, because the math assumes independence that does not exist.

sections.heading: Batch effects and how many replicates are enough
sections.body: A batch effect is systematic variation introduced by when or how a set of samples was processed — a different reagent lot, a different day, a different person pipetting — that can masquerade as a treatment effect if treatment and control groups are not processed together. Randomizing which group gets processed first, and running paired conditions on the same day with the same reagent lot, limits this. As for sample size, cell-culture experiments commonly use n=3 biological replicates as a practical floor, chiefly because it is the minimum needed to compute a standard deviation and detect a wildly divergent outlier, not because three is statistically powerful — a bigger, more variable effect needs more replicates to detect reliably, and a formal power calculation before the experiment is the rigorous way to set n rather than defaulting to three out of habit.

lessons.workedExample: A student treats one flask of E. coli with a candidate antimicrobial extract and one flask with buffer only, then plates each onto three agar plates and counts colonies, reporting 'n=3, p<0.05' for reduced colony count. This is pseudoreplication: both flasks were each grown once, so there is only one biological replicate per condition, and the three plates just resample the same culture. To fix it, the student instead starts three independent overnight cultures per condition, from three separate colonies, treats each independently, and plates each once — now n=3 refers to three truly independent biological trials, and a difference that holds up across all three flasks is far more convincing than one flask split three ways.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask 'what does your n refer to?' because pseudoreplication is one of the most common and easiest-to-catch errors in a student poster, and catching it instantly separates a real understanding of experimental design from a plausible-looking but invalid statistic. A weak answer treats wells, plates, or lanes from one sample as the n. A strong answer states explicitly that n counts independent biological units — separate cultures, animals, or donors — and can explain what confound (shared media, shared passage, shared incubator) the technical replicates fail to control for.

questions.prompt: A researcher grows one flask of treated cells and one flask of untreated cells, then measures each flask in triplicate wells, reporting n=3. What is the actual number of independent biological replicates per condition?

options.text: 3, because there are three wells
1, because there is only one flask per condition
6, combining both conditions
0, because wells cannot be measured this way

explanations.a: The three wells all come from the same flask, so they share every source of biological variation in that flask — they are technical, not biological, replicates.
explanations.b: Correct — each condition has exactly one independent biological unit (one flask), so n=1 per condition regardless of how many wells were measured from it.
explanations.c: Combining conditions doesn't change the count within each condition, and biological replicates aren't pooled across treatment groups this way.
explanations.d: Wells can absolutely be measured this way — the issue is what the resulting number of wells is allowed to represent statistically, not whether the measurement is valid.

questions.prompt: What is the main practical purpose of running treatment and control samples on the same day with the same reagent lot?

options.text: To reduce the number of biological replicates needed
To prevent a batch effect from being mistaken for a treatment effect
To make the experiment finish faster
To eliminate the need for a vehicle control

explanations.a: Same-day processing doesn't change how many independent biological units you need — that is set by the biology, not the schedule.
explanations.b: Correct — if treatment and control are processed on different days or with different reagent lots, day-to-day or lot-to-lot variation can look exactly like a treatment effect.
explanations.c: Speed isn't the reason; the reason is controlling for a specific confound.
