Presenting a hypothesis found by exploring the data as if it had been predicted in advance
Refusing to publish a study with a non-significant result
Repeating an experiment multiple times to confirm a result

explanations.a: This describes p-hacking, a related but distinct practice, not HARKing.
explanations.b: Correct — HARKing (Hypothesizing After the Results are Known) means treating a data-derived hypothesis as if it were the original prediction, hiding that it emerged from exploring the data rather than testing a clean prior hypothesis.
explanations.c: This describes publication bias against null results, a separate phenomenon from HARKing.
explanations.d: Repeating an experiment for confirmation is good practice and the opposite of what HARKing describes.

questions.prompt: What was the core warning of the American Statistical Association's 2016 statement on p-values?

options.text: P-values should never be calculated or reported
A p-value below 0.05 should not be treated as a bright-line proof that a result is real or important
Only p-values below 0.001 should ever be published
P-values are more reliable than replication for establishing a finding

explanations.a: The statement did not call for abandoning p-values, only for not misusing them as an automatic pass/fail line.
explanations.b: Correct — the ASA statement, led by Wasserstein and Lazar, warned that a p-value measures how surprising data would be under no true effect, not how large or important an effect is, and that treating p<0.05 as decisive proof is a misuse of the statistic.
explanations.c: The statement did not propose a stricter fixed threshold; it argued against relying on any single bright-line cutoff.
explanations.d: The statement's point runs the other way: replication and effect size matter alongside, not beneath, a p-value.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the reproducibility crisis narrative.

items.text: Kerr's paper introduces the term HARKing
Prinz and colleagues report Bayer's low internal reproducibility of preclinical findings
Begley and Ellis report only 6 of 53 landmark cancer studies replicated
The American Statistical Association issues its 2016 statement on p-values

questions.explanation: Kerr named HARKing in 1998, Bayer's internal reproducibility review was published in 2011, Begley and Ellis's Amgen-based report followed in 2012, and the ASA's formal statistical guidance came in 2016 partly in response to this accumulating evidence.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

right.text: Trying many analyses until one crosses a significance threshold, then reporting only that one
Presenting a data-derived hypothesis as if it were predicted before the data were seen
Whether an independent attempt to repeat a study finds the same result

questions.explanation: P-hacking is about selectively reporting favorable analyses, HARKing is about misrepresenting when a hypothesis was formed, and reproducibility is the broader outcome both practices erode — whether independent replication confirms a published result.

units.label: From Bench to Fair: Applying the Core

lessons.label: Framing a Tractable MCB Question

sections.heading: From curiosity to a testable claim
sections.body: "Does stress affect gene expression?" is a topic, not a hypothesis — it names no manipulated variable, no measured outcome, and no mechanism. A tractable molecular-biology hypothesis takes the if-then-because shape: IF you change one thing (the independent variable, IV), THEN one specific, numerically measurable thing should change (the dependent variable, DV), BECAUSE of a stated mechanism. "If E. coli K-12 is grown at 42 degC instead of 37 degC, then relative hsp70 mRNA expression measured by RT-qPCR will increase, because heat activates the heat-shock transcription factor sigma-32." Everything else in the project — the culture conditions, the media, the incubation time — has to be held constant so that the IV is the only thing that plausibly explains a change in the DV. Students who skip this step usually discover the gap only at the poster, when a judge asks what exactly they changed and what exactly they measured, and the honest answer is "a lot of things, sort of."

sections.heading: The tractability filter
sections.body: A question can be scientifically interesting and still be a bad school-lab project. Clinical researcher Hulley and coauthors' FINER framework — Feasible, Interesting, Novel, Ethical, Relevant, from their textbook on clinical research design — is a useful filter here even though it was written for human-subjects trials. Feasibility is the one that kills the most ambitious student ideas: does the school have a thermocycler and a qPCR machine, or only a gel box and a -20 degC freezer? Can the assay's timeline fit inside a semester of once- or twice-weekly lab periods, or does it need daily sampling a school schedule cannot support? A CRISPR knock-in project is novel and relevant but rarely feasible; a growth-curve comparison of two E. coli strains under two temperatures is unglamorous but finishable with equipment most school labs already own.

sections.heading: Safety sets the ceiling before design starts
sections.body: Biosafety narrows the menu before a single reagent is chosen. Under the Society for Science's International Rules for pre-college research, student projects are restricted to Biosafety Level 1 (BSL-1) organisms — either purchased from a reputable vendor with documented BSL-1 status or unknown microbes sampled from an environment with low probability of containing BSL-2+ agents — and even BSL-1 culturing is prohibited in a home setting; it must happen in a school or institutional lab with a Designated Supervisor. Any project touching a potentially hazardous biological agent needs prior Scientific Review Committee (SRC) approval, before experimentation, not after. Framing the question with these limits in view — E. coli K-12, S. cerevisiae, and B. subtilis are common BSL-1 workhorses — saves a rewrite in week six.

lessons.workedExample: A student starts with "I want to see how antibiotics affect bacteria." Run through the filter: IV must be specific (ampicillin concentration: 0, 10, 50, 100 micrograms/mL), DV must be measurable (zone of inhibition diameter in mm via Kirby-Bauer disk diffusion), organism must be BSL-1 (E. coli K-12, ordered from a vendor, not swabbed from a doorknob), and timeline must fit the schedule (plate on day one of a lab period, read the next class after 24 h at 37 degC). The rewritten hypothesis: "If ampicillin concentration on a disk increases from 0 to 100 micrograms/mL, then the zone of inhibition around E. coli K-12 will increase, because higher local drug concentration diffuses further before falling below the minimum inhibitory concentration."
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask "what exactly did you change, and what exactly did you measure?" first because it is the fastest way to tell a scoped experiment from a exploratory poke. A weak answer restates the topic ("I looked at how bacteria respond to antibiotics") with no units, no levels, no held-constant conditions. A strong answer names the IV with its levels, the DV with its units and instrument, and states in one sentence why holding everything else constant lets the result be attributed to the IV alone. Judges also listen for the safety trail — vendor-sourced BSL-1 organism, SRC approval on file — because a project that skipped that step is disqualified regardless of its data.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a properly scoped molecular-biology hypothesis?

options.text: Bacteria are affected by temperature.
If E. coli K-12 is incubated at 42 degC instead of 37 degC, then relative hsp70 mRNA (RT-qPCR) will increase, because heat activates the heat-shock response.
I want to study how gene expression changes under stress.
Temperature might do something interesting to cells.

explanations.a: No specific IV level, no measured DV, no mechanism — this is a topic, not a hypothesis.
explanations.b: Correct — it names a specific IV (42 vs 37 degC), a specific measurable DV (relative hsp70 mRNA by RT-qPCR), and a mechanism (sigma-32 heat-shock activation).
explanations.c: "Want to study" describes an intention, not a testable if-then-because claim.
explanations.d: "Might do something interesting" has no IV, no DV, and no predicted direction of effect.

questions.prompt: Under the Society for Science's International Rules, what must happen before a student begins culturing a potentially hazardous biological agent, even one that is BSL-1?

options.text: Nothing extra — BSL-1 organisms are exempt from all review.
The Scientific Review Committee (SRC) must approve the project in advance, and culturing must happen at school under a Designated Supervisor, not at home.
The student's teacher can verbally approve it after the fact.
Only projects with vertebrate animals need SRC approval.

explanations.a: BSL-1 status lowers risk but does not exempt the project from SRC pre-approval or the ban on home culturing.
explanations.b: Correct — SRC approval must come before experimentation starts, and even BSL-1 culturing is barred from home settings under Society for Science rules.
explanations.c: Approval must be documented through the SRC process, not an informal verbal sign-off, and it must come before the work begins.
explanations.d: Potentially hazardous biological agents require SRC review independent of whether vertebrate animals are also involved.

questions.prompt: Order the steps in narrowing a broad curiosity into a tractable, safety-cleared hypothesis.

items.text: State a broad topic of interest
Check feasibility against school equipment, timeline, and budget (FINER-style filter)
Confirm the organism/agent is BSL-1 and gets SRC approval if required
Write the if-then-because hypothesis with a specific IV and measurable DV

questions.explanation: You start broad, filter for what the school lab can actually pull off, clear the safety/approval gate for the specific organism, and only then lock in the precise IV and DV — writing the hypothesis before the safety and feasibility checks risks designing something you are not allowed or able to run.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its role in the ampicillin disk-diffusion example.

right.text: Ampicillin concentration on the disk (0-100 micrograms/mL)
Incubation temperature and time (37 degC, 24 h)
Zone of inhibition diameter in mm

questions.explanation: The IV is the thing deliberately manipulated (drug concentration); the DV is the measured outcome (zone size); temperature and incubation time are held constant so they cannot explain any difference between conditions.

lessons.label: Designing Controls and Replicates for Your Experiment

sections.heading: Three controls, three different jobs
sections.body: A positive control confirms the assay can detect the effect at all — a sample already known to give the expected signal, run alongside your unknowns. A negative control confirms the assay is not producing false signal on its own — for PCR, a no-template control (NTC) with water instead of cDNA; a band there means contamination, not a real result. A vehicle control is the one students most often skip: if a drug is dissolved in DMSO, the comparison group is not "no treatment" but "DMSO alone at the same volume," because DMSO itself can alter membrane permeability and gene expression at even 0.1-1% concentrations. Without it, an observed effect could be the drug, the solvent, or both, and there is no way to tell which from the data alone.

sections.heading: Technical vs biological replicates — and why n=3 is a floor, not a target
sections.body: Blainey, Krzywinski, and Altman's 2014 Nature Methods primer on replication draws the line precisely: a technical replicate measures the same biological sample more than once (three qPCR wells loaded from one cDNA prep), while a biological replicate is an independent sample subjected to the whole procedure separately (three separate cell cultures, each individually treated and harvested). Technical replicates estimate measurement noise; only biological replicates estimate whether the effect is real across biology, not just across pipetting. A common molecular-biology convention is a minimum of n=3 biological replicates per condition — enough to compute a standard deviation, not enough to call an effect statistically robust. A project with three technical replicates of one flask and zero biological replicates has an n of 1, no matter how many numbers are on the plot.

sections.heading: Blinding and randomization at student scale
sections.body: Full double-blinding is often impractical in a school lab, but the core idea scales down: whoever measures the outcome should not know which tube is which. A simple version is to have a partner relabel tubes A/B/C/D before the person doing the plate reading or the gel-band scoring sees them, then reveal the key afterward — this prevents an unconscious "I expected this well to be brighter" bias when eyeballing a gel or a color-change assay. Randomizing which plate position or which incubator shelf each condition sits on likewise controls for confounds like uneven heat distribution or edge effects on a 96-well plate, which are real and well documented sources of systematic error in plate-based assays.

lessons.workedExample: A student is testing whether a plant extract lowers E. coli growth (OD600 after 8 h). Design: positive control = ampicillin-treated culture (known to suppress growth); negative control = untreated culture; vehicle control = culture with the same volume of extract solvent (ethanol) alone, since the extract is dissolved in ethanol; three independent overnight starter cultures are each split into all four conditions (n=3 biological replicates), and each condition is read in triplicate wells on the plate reader (technical replicates within each biological replicate). A labmate assigns plate positions randomly and covers the condition labels until after OD600 readings are recorded.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about controls before they ask about results because a result without the right controls cannot be interpreted at all — it is not weaker evidence, it is no evidence. A weak answer says "we had a control group" without specifying which kind or why; a strong answer names the positive, negative, and (if relevant) vehicle control individually, states what each one rules out, and reports n as biological replicates rather than technical ones. Judges are also quick to catch when a student reports n=9 by counting technical replicates from three wells times three plates of the same single culture — that is measurement precision, not biological evidence.

questions.prompt: A student dissolves a candidate drug in DMSO and treats cells, comparing them to untreated cells. What is missing from this design?

options.text: A positive control showing the assay can detect an effect
A vehicle control: cells treated with DMSO alone at the same volume
Nothing — untreated cells are a sufficient comparison
A no-template control

explanations.a: A positive control is good practice but is not the specific gap created by using a solvent — the missing piece here is isolating the solvent's own effect.
explanations.b: Correct — DMSO can itself affect cells at the concentrations used to deliver a drug, so "untreated" does not isolate the drug's effect from the solvent's.
explanations.c: Untreated cells confound drug effect with solvent effect; they are not sufficient once a solvent is introduced.
explanations.d: No-template controls are specific to PCR-type assays, not a cell-treatment comparison.

questions.prompt: A student runs one flask of treated cells and reads its OD600 in three separate wells. What is their biological replicate count (n)?

options.text: n=3, because there are three readings
n=1, because all three readings come from the same single culture
n=9, because you can combine wells and days
It cannot be determined without a control group

explanations.a: Three readings from one flask are technical replicates, which estimate measurement noise, not biological variation.
explanations.b: Correct — n counts independent biological samples; one flask measured three times is still n=1 biologically.
explanations.c: Multiplying technical replicates does not create biological replicates; it inflates n without adding independent evidence.
explanations.d: n is a property of the sampling design (how many independent cultures), independent of whether a control group exists.

questions.prompt: Order these steps in setting up a controlled, blinded plate-based assay.

items.text: Grow independent biological replicate cultures for each condition
Randomize which plate position each condition/replicate occupies
Relabel or code tubes so the person reading results cannot see condition identity
Read and record results, then reveal the coding key

questions.explanation: You need independent biological samples before you can randomize their layout; randomization has to happen before blinding is set, since blinding hides the layout's meaning from the reader; only after both are in place should the reader collect data, with the key revealed afterward.

questions.prompt: Match each control type to what it rules out.

right.text: That the assay simply cannot detect a real effect
That an observed effect comes from the solvent, not the treatment
That a positive-looking signal is contamination or assay artifact rather than a real template

questions.explanation: A positive control shows the assay works at all; a negative control (like an NTC) catches false signal from contamination; a vehicle control isolates the treatment's effect from the solvent used to deliver it.

lessons.label: Choosing the Right Readout and Assay

sections.heading: Match the assay to the noun in your hypothesis
sections.body: Every hypothesis has a noun the DV must measure directly — expression, growth, viability, or shape — and picking an assay that measures something merely correlated with that noun is the single most common design mistake in student molecular biology projects. RT-qPCR measures relative mRNA abundance: it amplifies a target transcript over cycles and compares its threshold cycle (Ct) to a reference gene using the 2^(-ddCt) method Livak and Schmittgen formalized in 2001, so it can support a claim about gene expression but says nothing about whether the corresponding protein was made or whether cells behaved differently. An OD600 growth curve measures optical density, a proxy for how much light-scattering material is in the culture — it tracks population size over time but cannot tell a dense culture of live cells from a dense culture of dead ones, because dead cells and debris scatter light too.

sections.heading: Viability and toxicity need a viability assay, not a proxy
sections.body: If the hypothesis is about toxicity or cell death, the readout has to test membrane integrity or metabolic activity directly. Trypan blue exclusion is the simplest: the dye crosses a compromised membrane and stains dead cells blue while live cells with intact membranes exclude it, and a hemocytometer count gives a direct percent-viable figure. The MTT assay, developed by Mosmann in 1983, instead measures metabolic activity — living cells' mitochondrial reductase enzymes convert the yellow MTT reagent into purple formazan crystals, and the absorbance is roughly proportional to the number of metabolically active cells. Neither assay is interchangeable with OD600: a culture can hit a normal OD600 while a large fraction of its cells are non-viable, which is exactly the failure mode a toxicity project needs to catch.

sections.heading: Microscopy answers 'what shape,' not 'how much'
sections.body: Brightfield or fluorescence microscopy is the right tool for a morphology hypothesis — cell shape, size, aggregation, or the presence/absence of a labeled structure — but a handful of representative images is not quantitative data on its own. A judge will ask how many cells were scored, from how many fields, chosen how (randomly, not just the prettiest field), because eyeballing one photogenic image and reporting it as "the effect" is the microscopy equivalent of n=1. Turning microscopy into real evidence means counting a defined feature across a blinded, randomly sampled set of fields and reporting a proportion or measurement with a sample size, not a single illustrative picture.

lessons.workedExample: A student hypothesizes that a plant extract is toxic to E. coli and supports it with a growth curve showing lower OD600 in the treated flask at 8 h. A judge points out this only shows fewer light-scattering particles, not death — clumped or filamented stressed cells can lower OD600 without dying, and lysed dead cells can even raise apparent turbidity from debris. The fix is to add a trypan blue count or a colony-forming-unit (CFU) plate count alongside the OD600 curve: CFU counts only live, culturable cells, so a genuine drop in CFU/mL alongside the OD600 drop is real evidence of killing, while a CFU count that tracks OD600 exactly would instead suggest slowed growth, not toxicity.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe assay choice because it exposes whether a student understands what their own data can and cannot prove — a mismatched readout is a fatal flaw dressed up as a result. A weak answer treats OD600, viability, and expression data as interchangeable evidence for "the treatment worked." A strong answer states precisely what the chosen assay measures at the molecular or cellular level, names one thing it cannot distinguish (e.g., OD600 cannot separate live from dead), and explains why that gap did or did not matter for this specific hypothesis.

questions.prompt: A student claims a compound is toxic to bacteria based solely on a lower OD600 in the treated flask. What is the flaw?

options.text: OD600 cannot be measured on a standard plate reader
OD600 measures turbidity/light scattering, which does not distinguish live cells from dead cells or debris
OD600 only works for eukaryotic cells
There is no flaw; OD600 is a direct viability measurement

explanations.a: OD600 is routinely read on standard spectrophotometers and plate readers; that is not the issue.
explanations.b: Correct — a lower OD600 could reflect fewer cells, stressed/altered cell morphology, or lysis debris rather than confirmed cell death; a viability assay (trypan blue, MTT) or CFU count is needed to support a toxicity claim.
explanations.c: OD600 is used for bacterial cultures routinely (E. coli growth curves are a standard use case).
explanations.d: OD600 is a density/turbidity proxy, not a direct measure of viability.

questions.prompt: The MTT assay determines viability by measuring:

options.text: Direct counting of blue-stained dead cells under a microscope
Relative mRNA abundance of a viability-associated gene
Conversion of MTT reagent to purple formazan by mitochondrial reductase activity in living cells, read as absorbance
Optical density of the whole culture at 600 nm

explanations.a: That description is trypan blue exclusion, a different viability method, not MTT.
explanations.b: MTT is a colorimetric metabolic assay, not a gene-expression measurement.
explanations.c: Correct — Mosmann's 1983 MTT assay relies on active mitochondrial reductase in living cells converting the reagent to formazan, with absorbance roughly proportional to metabolically active cell number.
explanations.d: OD600 measures culture turbidity generally, not the MTT-specific formazan conversion.

questions.prompt: Match each hypothesis type to the assay that actually tests it.

left.text: "Gene X expression increases under heat stress"
"Compound Y kills a defined fraction of cells"

right.text: RT-qPCR (2^-ddCt relative to a reference gene)
Trypan blue exclusion or MTT viability assay
Microscopy with blinded, randomly sampled field counts

questions.explanation: Expression claims need a transcript-level readout (RT-qPCR); death/toxicity claims need a viability assay that tests membrane integrity or metabolic activity directly; shape or aggregation claims need quantified microscopy, not a proxy measurement like OD600.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for turning microscopy into quantitative evidence rather than a single illustrative photo.

items.text: Define the feature to be scored (e.g., percent cells showing aggregation)
Randomly sample multiple fields rather than choosing the most striking one
Blind the scorer to condition where possible
Count the feature across all sampled fields and report a proportion with sample size

questions.explanation: You must first know what you are counting, then sample fields without cherry-picking, then remove scorer bias, and only then tally the counts into a reportable, sample-size-backed proportion.

lessons.label: Troubleshooting and Failure Modes

sections.heading: Contamination often hides in plain sight
sections.body: Bacterial or fungal contamination in a cell culture usually announces itself — cloudy media, a sudden pH shift turning the phenol red indicator yellow, visible clumps. Mycoplasma contamination does neither: it causes no turbidity, no obvious morphology change, and can quietly alter growth rate, gene expression, and metabolism for weeks while a culture looks completely normal under the scope. Large surveys of cell lines have repeatedly reported contamination rates in the range of roughly 15% or higher, which is why serious cell-culture labs run a dedicated PCR-based mycoplasma test on a schedule rather than trusting a visual check. The lesson for a school project: a normal-looking culture is not proof of a clean one, and any result that seems inexplicably drifted from a known baseline is worth treating as a contamination suspect before it is treated as a real biological finding.

sections.heading: Reading a failed gel like a diagnosis
sections.body: A PCR gel with no band at all usually points to one of a short list: the template was omitted or degraded, the annealing temperature was set above the primers' effective melting range so they never bound, or the Mg2+ concentration was off enough to block the polymerase. A faint low-molecular-weight band or smear under about 100 bp, especially strongest in reactions with no template control (NTC) too, is a primer-dimer — primers annealing to each other instead of the target, common when primer concentration is too high or cycling ran too long. A smeared, unfocused band spanning many sizes usually means the annealing temperature was too low, letting primers bind nonspecifically across the genome. A band appearing in the NTC lane at the expected size is the most serious sign: contamination of a reagent, not a real result, and every reaction run alongside it is now suspect.

sections.heading: Pipetting error and out-of-range signal
sections.body: Random pipetting error (day-to-day hand variability) is why replicates exist; systematic pipetting error — a consistently mis-calibrated volume, or always pipetting from the bottom of the tip — shows up as one condition's replicates all shifted the same direction, which a quick pipette-calibration check against a known volume on a balance can catch. A signal that reads as "undetermined" on a qPCR run, or an OD reading pinned at an instrument's ceiling (many plate readers saturate and stop being linear above roughly OD 3-4), is not evidence of "very high" or "very low" — it means the sample is outside the instrument's valid range and needs to be diluted and re-read against a standard curve before the number means anything.

sections.heading: The notebook is what makes a failure diagnosable
sections.body: None of this troubleshooting works without a contemporaneous record. Data-integrity practice across real labs and regulated science follows something close to the ALCOA principle — records should be Attributable (who did it), Legible, Contemporaneous (written at the time, not reconstructed from memory the night before the poster is due), Original, and Accurate — because a notebook entry made two days late has already lost the exact volumes, timings, and reagent lots that would let a judge, or the student, figure out what actually went wrong.

lessons.workedExample: A student expects a 500 bp band and gets nothing. Diagnostic order: check the NTC lane first — it is blank, so contamination is ruled out. Check for a primer-dimer smear at the bottom — none, so primer concentration is not the issue. Check the notebook: the annealing temperature was logged as 68 degC, but the primers' calculated melting temperatures were 58-60 degC — the reaction never let the primers anneal. Re-running at 53 degC (5 degC below the lower primer Tm, a standard rule of thumb) produces the expected band. Because the notebook recorded the exact temperature used, the fix took one re-run instead of re-testing every reagent.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe failed runs because troubleshooting reveals whether a student understands the mechanism behind their assay or just followed a protocol. A weak answer says "the PCR didn't work, so we tried again and it worked the second time" with no diagnosis. A strong answer names the specific failure mode from the gel or trace (no band vs primer-dimer vs smear vs NTC contamination), states the most likely cause, and explains how the notebook record let them identify and fix it rather than guess. A student who can diagnose their own failed run is, to a judge, more convincing than one who never reports a failure at all.

questions.prompt: A cell culture looks clear and healthy under the microscope with no turbidity, but downstream RT-qPCR results drift inexplicably from baseline over several weeks. What should be suspected first?

options.text: Fungal contamination, since it always causes visible cloudiness
Mycoplasma contamination, which typically causes no visible turbidity or morphology change
A broken microscope
Nothing — normal appearance rules out contamination

explanations.a: Fungal contamination is usually visually obvious (cloudiness, filaments); this scenario describes a culture that looks normal.
explanations.b: Correct — mycoplasma contamination is notorious for being invisible under standard culture checks (large surveys of cell lines have reported contamination rates of roughly 15% or higher) while still altering growth and gene expression.
explanations.c: The microscope working normally is consistent with mycoplasma contamination, which does not produce visible morphology changes.
explanations.d: A normal appearance does not rule out mycoplasma, which specifically evades visual detection.

questions.prompt: A PCR gel shows a faint band under 100 bp, present even in the no-template control (NTC) lane. What does this most likely indicate?

options.text: A successful amplification of the target gene
A primer-dimer artifact, since primers can anneal to each other and amplify even without template
The annealing temperature was too high
The Mg2+ concentration was too low to support any amplification

explanations.a: A 500+ bp target would not appear as a sub-100 bp band; this size is characteristic of primer-dimers, not the real product.
explanations.b: Correct — a small band appearing even in the NTC (no template present) is the signature of primers annealing to each other rather than to a target sequence.
explanations.c: Too-high annealing temperature typically produces no band at all, not a primer-dimer band.
explanations.d: Too-low Mg2+ would suppress amplification generally; it would not selectively produce a primer-dimer band in the NTC.

questions.prompt: Order the diagnostic steps for a PCR reaction that produced no visible band.

items.text: Check the no-template control (NTC) lane for contamination
Check for a primer-dimer smear near the bottom of the gel
Check the notebook record of annealing temperature against primer melting temperatures
Re-run with a corrected parameter and compare

questions.explanation: Rule out contamination first via the NTC, then check for primer-dimer artifacts, then check the recorded run conditions against the primers' known properties, and only then re-run with the corrected parameter to confirm the diagnosis.

questions.prompt: Match each notebook principle from the ALCOA framework to its meaning.

right.text: Recorded at the time the work was done, not reconstructed later from memory
Clearly tied to who performed the step
The first, unedited record of the observation, not a cleaned-up rewrite

questions.explanation: Contemporaneous means written at the time; attributable means the record identifies who did it; original means the raw first record is kept, not a later polished version — all three are part of why a notebook can actually reconstruct what went wrong.

lessons.label: Defending Your Claim to Judges

sections.heading: Controls first, effect second
sections.body: The order a result is presented in is itself an argument. Leading with the treatment effect and mentioning controls later, if at all, invites the question every judge is trained to ask: how do you know the assay was even working? Leading with the positive control (confirming the assay can detect a real effect) and the negative or vehicle control (confirming no false signal) establishes that the measurement system is trustworthy before a single treatment number is shown. Only then does the treatment-vs-control comparison mean anything, because the audience already knows the yardstick is calibrated. Students who present results in discovery order — 'first we tried this, then we noticed that' — usually bury the controls in the middle of a slide instead of using them to open the argument.

sections.heading: Effect size and spread, not a bare p-value
sections.body: The American Statistical Association's 2016 statement on p-values, authored by Wasserstein and Lazar, makes a point every science-fair presenter should internalize: a p-value tells you how surprising a result would be if there were truly no effect, but it does not by itself say how large or important that effect is. A p-value of 0.001 attached to a 2% difference is not more impressive than p=0.04 attached to a 40% difference — the second is the bigger biological effect. A strong results slide reports the effect size (e.g., percent change, fold-change, or a standardized measure like Cohen's d), the spread (explicitly labeled as standard deviation or standard error — the two look identical as error bars but mean different things, and judges routinely ask which one is shown), and the sample size n, with the p-value as one supporting number, not the headline.

sections.heading: Name your own limitations before the Q&A does
sections.body: Every school-lab project has at least one real confound — small n, one strain instead of a species-wide claim, a single experimenter doing all the pipetting, a short timeline that only captured one time point. Stating it plainly in the presentation, along with what a follow-up experiment would need to address it, converts a weakness a judge would otherwise have to extract through cross-examination into evidence that the student understands the boundaries of their own claim. The rehearsal that pays off most is a specific one: for each major result, ask 'how do you know it wasn't X?' for every plausible alternative explanation (contamination, an unblinded observer, a confound in temperature or timing) and have a one-sentence answer ready that points to the specific control or design choice that rules it out.

lessons.workedExample: A student's results slide claims their extract 'significantly reduced' E. coli growth, citing p=0.03, with no error bars and no mention of the vehicle control. In a mock Q&A, a coach asks: 'How do you know the ethanol solvent wasn't doing this?' The student has no ready answer, because the vehicle control was run but never shown. The fix: reorder the slide to show the vehicle control (ethanol alone, no significant change vs untreated) before the treatment result, add SD error bars labeled as such, and report the actual effect ("CFU/mL dropped by 62% (n=3 biological replicates, p=0.03) versus a vehicle control showing no significant change"). Now the same p-value sits inside an argument a judge cannot immediately puncture.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe presentation order and statistics because a student who can only recite "it was significant" has usually memorized a conclusion rather than understood the evidence for it. A weak defense repeats the p-value under pressure and cannot say whether the error bars are SD or SEM, or what the vehicle control showed. A strong defense walks a judge through the controls first, states the effect size in real units alongside n, and has a specific, control-backed answer ready for the leading alternative explanation — signaling that the limitation was anticipated during the design, not discovered during questioning.

questions.prompt: According to the American Statistical Association's 2016 statement on p-values (Wasserstein and Lazar), what is the key limitation of a p-value?

options.text: It directly measures the size or importance of an effect
It measures how surprising a result would be under no true effect, but does not by itself indicate the size or importance of the effect
It can only be calculated with n greater than 30
It replaces the need for a control group

explanations.a: This is the exact misconception the ASA statement warns against — p-values do not measure effect size.
explanations.b: Correct — a small p-value can accompany a small effect and a larger p-value can accompany a large effect; effect size needs to be reported separately.
explanations.c: P-values can be calculated for small samples; there is no such n threshold requirement.
explanations.d: A p-value evaluates a comparison but does not substitute for having a valid control group to compare against.

questions.prompt: Why should a presentation show controls before the treatment result?

options.text: It is simply the order the experiments were run in
It establishes that the assay is working and trustworthy before the treatment comparison is presented, so the comparison means something
Judges are not interested in controls
It is required by ISEF rules regardless of content

explanations.a: Discovery order is not the same as argument order; presenting in the order things happened often buries the controls.
explanations.b: Correct — a treatment effect is only interpretable once the audience knows the measurement system can detect a real signal and does not produce false positives.
explanations.c: Judges specifically probe controls, often before anything else, precisely because they are the foundation of the result's validity.
explanations.d: This is a scientific-argument convention, not a stated ISEF procedural rule.

questions.prompt: Order these elements as they should appear when defending a result to a judge.

items.text: Show the positive and negative/vehicle controls worked as expected
Present the treatment-vs-control comparison with effect size, labeled error bars, and n
State the study's main limitation and what it would take to address it
Answer 'how do you know it wasn't X?' with the specific control or design choice that rules X out

questions.explanation: Controls establish that the assay can be trusted; only then does the effect-size comparison mean something; naming the limitation preempts obvious follow-up questions; and the rehearsed alternative-explanation answer closes the loop by pointing back to the specific design choice that addresses it.

questions.prompt: Match each reporting practice to what it protects against in a judge's cross-examination.

left.text: Explicitly labeling error bars as SD or SEM
Reporting effect size alongside the p-value
Stating the study's known limitation up front

right.text: A judge asking 'is that difference actually large, or just statistically detectable?'
A judge asking 'what do those error bars even represent?'
A judge extracting an unacknowledged weakness through pointed questioning

questions.explanation: Labeled error bars answer the SD-vs-SEM question directly; reporting effect size alongside p answers whether a significant result is also a meaningfully large one; naming the limitation yourself turns a potential gotcha into evidence of understanding.

lessons.label: The Logic of Bacterial Gene Regulation

sections.heading: The cost of making protein you don't need
sections.body: Every gene an E. coli cell transcribes and translates costs ATP, amino acids, and ribosome time that could go toward growth. A cell that made every enzyme constitutively — all the time, regardless of need — would carry that cost permanently. Dekel and Alon (2005) measured this directly: E. coli strains engineered to constitutively express the lac operon's proteins, even when growing on glucose where lactose enzymes are useless, grew roughly 3% slower than strains that kept the operon off. That 3% is not trivial; bacterial populations compete on doubling time, and a growth deficit that size compounds over hundreds of generations into extinction relative to a faster competitor. The same study showed wild-type E. coli tunes its induction threshold to roughly the point where the benefit of the lac enzymes first exceeds this cost, evidence that natural selection has fitted the regulatory switch itself, not just the genes it controls.

sections.heading: Four logical ways to gate a gene
sections.body: Bacterial operons are built from two design choices that combine into four control logics. First: is the regulatory protein a repressor (negative control, DNA-bound by default, must be removed to permit transcription) or an activator (positive control, transcription needs it to be recruited)? Second: does the small-molecule effector switch the gene on (an inducer) or off (a corepressor, producing a repressible system)? Crossing these gives negative-inducible (a repressor is knocked off DNA by an inducer, as in the lac operon), negative-repressible (a repressor is only activated once a corepressor binds it, as in the trp operon), positive-inducible (an activator only works once bound to an inducer, as CAP does once cAMP binds it), and positive-repressible (an activator is switched off by a corepressor) — the rarest of the four in real operons, but a useful boundary case for reasoning about any new system.

sections.heading: cis-acting sites vs trans-acting regulators
sections.body: A second axis separates the DNA sequences a regulator acts on (cis-acting: promoters, operators — they only affect genes physically linked to them on the same DNA molecule) from the proteins that bind those sequences (trans-acting: repressors and activators — they diffuse through the cytoplasm and can act on any copy of their target sequence). Jacob and Monod established this distinction genetically in the early 1960s using partial diploid ('merodiploid') E. coli carrying two copies of the lac region, one on the chromosome and one on an F' plasmid. A lacI- mutation (broken repressor) was rescued in trans by a wild-type lacI+ copy elsewhere in the cell — one working repressor gene sufficed for both operons. But an operator-constitutive (Oc) mutation, which prevents the repressor from binding, only derepressed the lacZ gene physically linked to it in cis; the operator sequence itself could not diffuse to help the other copy.

lessons.workedExample: Consider an E. coli merodiploid with genotype lacI+ O+ Z+ / lacI- Oc Z+, one wild-type operon on the chromosome and one on an F' plasmid carrying a repressor-null mutation and an operator-constitutive mutation. Which lacZ copies make beta-galactosidase without inducer? The chromosomal copy (lacI+ O+ Z+) stays off: it has a working operator, and functional repressor protein is diffusing through the shared cytoplasm to bind it, supplied in trans by the chromosomal lacI+ gene. The plasmid copy (lacI- Oc Z+) is constitutively on: even though repressor protein is available (from the chromosomal lacI+), it cannot bind the plasmid copy's mutant Oc operator, so that lacZ transcribes regardless of lactose. One gene off, one on, in the same cytoplasm, is only explicable if lacI acts in trans and O acts only in cis.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks why a gene is regulated this way, and not always on, is testing whether a student can name the specific cost of unregulated expression rather than gesture at 'efficiency.' A weak answer says regulation 'saves energy.' A strong answer cites a number, even an approximate one like the roughly 3% growth cost Dekel and Alon measured for needless lac expression, and explains what that cost buys: a repressor or activator system that turns the gene on only when its product is needed. Judges also probe cis/trans distinctions directly, asking whether a mutated sequence needs to be on the same DNA molecule to matter.

questions.prompt: In a negative-inducible operon, what is the default state of transcription with no effector present, and what turns it on?

options.text: Default OFF; an inducer binds and removes a bound repressor
Default ON; a corepressor binds and activates a repressor
Default OFF; an inducer binds and activates a bound activator protein
Default ON; an inducer removes a bound activator

explanations.a: Correct — negative control means a repressor is the default-bound regulator; inducible means the effector removes it, turning transcription on.
explanations.b: This describes a negative-repressible system like trp, not negative-inducible.
explanations.c: This mixes positive-control language ('activator') into a system defined as negative control.
explanations.d: This describes positive-control off logic, not negative-inducible.

questions.prompt: Dekel and Alon (2005) found that forcing E. coli to constitutively express the lac operon's proteins while growing on glucose, where those proteins are useless, reduced growth rate by roughly how much?

explanations.a: This overstates the measured cost by an order of magnitude.
explanations.b: Correct — the study measured roughly a 3% growth-rate reduction from needless constitutive expression.
explanations.c: This understates the cost; the effect was large enough to be selectable, not negligible.
explanations.d: A cost above 100% is not a meaningful growth-rate reduction.

questions.prompt: Match each control logic to its description.

right.text: Repressor bound by default; an inducer removes it to permit transcription (e.g., lac)
Repressor inactive by default; a corepressor activates it to block transcription (e.g., trp)
Activator only functions once bound by an inducer (e.g., CAP-cAMP)
Activator active by default; a corepressor inactivates it, turning transcription off

questions.explanation: The two axes, repressor-vs-activator and inducer-vs-corepressor, cross to give exactly these four logics; lac and trp are the concrete anchors for the two negative-control cases.

questions.prompt: Order the logical steps of a cis/trans complementation test used to classify a regulatory mutation.

items.text: Construct a merodiploid carrying a wild-type allele and a mutant allele of the regulatory element on two separate DNA molecules in the same cell
Let both copies of the linked reporter gene be expressed in the shared cytoplasm
Score the phenotype of the reporter gene linked to each copy separately
If both linked reporters show the wild-type phenotype the mutation is trans-acting; if only the physically linked copy is affected it is cis-acting

questions.explanation: The test requires building the merodiploid first, letting both DNA copies share one cytoplasm, then scoring each linked reporter independently before drawing the cis/trans conclusion from the pattern.

lessons.label: The lac Operon: Negative Control

sections.heading: A tetrameric clamp on the operator
sections.body: The lac repressor, LacI, is a homotetramer, functionally two DNA-binding dimers joined at a tetramerization domain, each dimer capable of gripping a separate operator sequence. Its primary binding site, O1, overlaps the transcription start site immediately downstream of the promoter; when LacI occupies O1, its bulk physically blocks RNA polymerase from initiating transcription of the three downstream structural genes. Because LacI has two DNA-binding heads, it can simultaneously grip O1 and one of two weaker auxiliary operators (O2, inside lacZ, or O3, upstream of the promoter), looping the intervening DNA. Oehler and colleagues (1990) showed this looping is not decorative: deleting both auxiliary operators drops repression by more than 50-fold, showing the loop meaningfully stabilizes repressor occupancy on top of O1 binding alone.

sections.heading: Three structural genes, one function each
sections.body: Three structural genes lie downstream of the promoter-operator region, transcribed as one polycistronic mRNA. lacZ encodes beta-galactosidase, a large homotetrameric enzyme that hydrolyzes lactose into glucose and galactose, and, as a minor side reaction, converts a small fraction of lactose into allolactose, the operon's own inducer. lacY encodes lactose permease, a membrane symporter that pumps lactose into the cell against its concentration gradient using the proton motive force; without LacY, external lactose cannot accumulate fast enough to induce the operon at physiological concentrations. lacA encodes thiogalactoside transacetylase, which acetylates non-metabolizable thiogalactoside sugars that LacY imports by accident, tagging them for export, a detoxification role rather than a role in lactose catabolism itself.

sections.heading: Bootstrapping induction, and why cells never do it halfway
sections.body: Induction begins from a bootstrap: a fully repressed operon is not perfectly silent, because LacI dissociates from O1 transiently, and basal 'leaky' transcription produces a handful of LacZ and LacY molecules per cell. When lactose is present, that trace LacY imports it and trace LacZ converts a fraction to allolactose, which binds LacI, distorts its DNA-binding domain, and drops operator affinity by roughly a thousandfold, enough to release the operon and let expression climb to full induction. Laboratories bypass this loop using IPTG, a synthetic allolactose mimic that inactivates LacI just as well but cannot be hydrolyzed by beta-galactosidase, so it stays stable for hours. Novick and Weiner (1957) showed this induction is not a smooth population dial: at intermediate inducer levels, individual cells are fully on or fully off, never partial, because LacY import creates a positive feedback loop, more permease imports more inducer, which represses less LacI, which makes more permease.

lessons.workedExample: A student grows two E. coli cultures in minimal medium with lactose as the sole carbon source, one wild-type and one lacY-null, both carrying functional lacI and lacZ. After a lag, the wild-type culture's beta-galactosidase activity, measured colorimetrically with ONPG, rises roughly a thousandfold over the uninduced baseline as internal allolactose accumulates and inactivates LacI. The lacY-null culture, lacking permease, cannot import enough lactose to reach the intracellular allolactose concentration needed to inactivate LacI's tetramers, so beta-galactosidase stays near the uninduced basal level and the culture barely grows on lactose at all, direct evidence that LacY import, not LacZ catalysis, is the rate-limiting step in triggering induction.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probing the lac operon almost always ask what happens to induction if one gene is knocked out, because the answer separates memorized diagrams from mechanistic understanding. A weak answer treats lacZ, lacY, and lacA as interchangeable 'lactose genes.' A strong answer explains that a lacY-null strain cannot self-induce on lactose because the bootstrap depends on permease importing enough substrate for basal LacZ to make allolactose, while a lacZ-null strain can still import lactose but never converts it to inducer or breaks it down. Naming the operator, including looping to O2/O3, versus the repressor as distinct cis/trans components is the other common probe.

questions.prompt: LacI represses transcription primarily by...

options.text: Binding O1 near the transcription start site and physically blocking RNA polymerase
Degrading lac mRNA after it is made
Methylating the promoter DNA
Sequestering CAP protein away from its binding site

explanations.a: Correct — LacI is a DNA-binding protein that physically occupies the operator, blocking polymerase from initiating transcription.
explanations.b: LacI acts at the DNA level before transcription, not by degrading finished mRNA.
explanations.c: LacI represses through direct protein-DNA binding, not DNA methylation.
explanations.d: LacI and CAP are independent regulators; LacI does not act by sequestering CAP.

questions.prompt: Which lac gene, if deleted, most directly prevents the operon from self-inducing on physiological concentrations of external lactose, even though LacI and LacZ are both intact?

options.text: lacA
lacY
lacI
None; induction does not depend on any transporter

explanations.a: lacA handles detoxification of accidental substrates and is not needed to import lactose or trigger induction.
explanations.b: Correct — without LacY permease, external lactose cannot accumulate intracellularly fast enough to generate enough allolactose to inactivate LacI.
explanations.c: Deleting lacI removes the repressor, which would make the operon constitutively on, not blocked.
explanations.d: Physiological lactose concentrations are too low for passive diffusion alone to induce the operon; active import via LacY is required.

questions.prompt: Match each lac gene product to its function.

right.text: Hydrolyzes lactose to glucose and galactose, and makes trace allolactose
Imports lactose into the cell using the proton motive force
Acetylates and detoxifies non-metabolizable thiogalactosides
Homotetrameric repressor that binds the operator to block RNA polymerase

questions.explanation: Each of the three structural genes has a distinct catalytic or transport role, while lacI encodes the separate regulatory protein that controls their transcription.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the lac induction bootstrap, from repressed operon to full induction.

items.text: Basal leaky transcription produces a few LacZ and LacY molecules despite LacI bound at O1
Trace LacY imports external lactose into the cell
Trace LacZ converts a small fraction of imported lactose into allolactose
Allolactose binds LacI, lowering its operator affinity roughly a thousandfold and releasing the operon

questions.explanation: Induction cannot start from zero gene product, so leaky basal expression must supply the first permease and enzyme molecules that generate the inducer that then removes the repressor.

lessons.label: The lac Operon: Positive Control and Catabolite Repression

sections.heading: CAP-cAMP: recruiting a reluctant polymerase
sections.body: The lac promoter is intrinsically weak; RNA polymerase binds it poorly even with LacI fully released from the operator. Full-strength transcription needs a second, positive signal: the catabolite activator protein (CAP, also called CRP), a homodimer that binds DNA tightly only once each subunit has bound a molecule of cyclic AMP (cAMP). The cAMP-CAP complex binds a specific site upstream of the transcription start, bending the DNA by roughly 90 degrees and making direct contact with the C-terminal domain of RNA polymerase's alpha subunit, which helps recruit and stabilize polymerase at the promoter. This single contact accounts for roughly a 50-fold activation of transcription, a substantial slice of the operon's overall dynamic range, which reaches roughly 50,000-fold once LacI repression and CAP activation are combined, illustrating that lac control is not one switch but two, wired together.

sections.heading: Glucose lowers cAMP and blocks lactose entry
sections.body: Glucose suppresses the lac operon through two mechanisms that share a single sensor: Enzyme IIA of the glucose phosphotransferase system (EIIAGlc). While glucose is being actively transported into the cell, EIIAGlc stays dephosphorylated, having donated its phosphate down the relay to the incoming sugar. Dephospho-EIIAGlc fails to activate adenylate cyclase, so cAMP stays low and cAMP-CAP cannot form; this is catabolite repression proper. The same dephospho-EIIAGlc also binds LacY directly and blocks its transport activity, a separate mechanism called inducer exclusion, which prevents lactose from even entering the cell while glucose is present. Once glucose is exhausted, EIIAGlc reverts to its phosphorylated form, adenylate cyclase resumes, cAMP rises, cAMP-CAP forms, and inducer exclusion lifts, all governed by the same phosphorylation state. The swing is large: intracellular cAMP is commonly measured at roughly an order of magnitude lower while glucose is being transported than after it is exhausted, which is why cAMP-CAP formation tracks glucose availability so tightly. Inducer exclusion itself was established as a mechanism distinct from transcriptional catabolite repression by Saier and Roseman's work in the 1970s, which traced the PTS relay's direct block of sugar permeases like LacY.

sections.heading: An AND gate written in growth curves
sections.body: Monod's classic 1941-42 growth curves gave the first physiological evidence for this dual control. E. coli grown in a medium containing both glucose and lactose does not grow smoothly; it shows a diauxic, two-phase growth curve: rapid growth while glucose lasts, then a lag as the population pauses to induce lac gene expression, then a second, slower growth phase fueled by lactose. That lag is the visible signature of an AND gate: full lac expression requires lactose present (to inactivate LacI) and glucose absent (to permit cAMP-CAP formation); either condition alone yields only partial or no induction, which is exactly why cells cannot switch substrates instantaneously.

lessons.workedExample: Predict lac operon output in four E. coli cultures differing only in glucose and lactose availability. No glucose, no lactose: LacI bound, no allolactose, cAMP high but nothing to bind — operon off. Glucose only: LacI bound and cAMP low — operon off, doubly repressed. Lactose only: LacI released by allolactose, cAMP high because no glucose suppresses adenylate cyclase, cAMP-CAP bound — operon fully on. Both glucose and lactose: allolactose is present so LacI is released, but dephospho-EIIAGlc keeps cAMP low, so CAP cannot activate, and it also blocks LacY-mediated entry via inducer exclusion, so expression stays near basal, matching the glucose-only case until glucose runs out.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks what happens when bacteria grow on both sugars at once is testing whether a student understands that lac control has two independent inputs, not one. A weak answer says 'lactose turns it on.' A strong answer names both the derepression event (allolactose releasing LacI) and the activation event (low glucose raising cAMP for CAP) and predicts that glucose plus lactose together still yields low expression until glucose is depleted, pointing to the diauxic lag as the observable consequence. Tracing inducer exclusion as a second, faster-acting glucose effect beyond just lowering cAMP is what separates the strongest answers.

questions.prompt: What directly enables cAMP-CAP to activate transcription at the lac promoter?

options.text: It removes LacI from O1
It bends the DNA and contacts RNA polymerase's alpha subunit near the intrinsically weak lac promoter
It phosphorylates RNA polymerase
It degrades the operator DNA sequence

explanations.a: CAP and LacI act at different sites and independently of each other; CAP does not remove LacI.
explanations.b: Correct — cAMP-CAP bends the DNA and makes a direct protein contact with RNA polymerase's alpha subunit, recruiting it to a weak promoter.
explanations.c: CAP is not a kinase and does not phosphorylate RNA polymerase.
explanations.d: CAP is a DNA-binding activator, not a nuclease.

questions.prompt: A cell is growing with both glucose and lactose in the medium. Which best describes the lac operon's state before glucose is exhausted?

options.text: LacI is released by allolactose, but cAMP is low and inducer exclusion blocks lactose entry, so expression stays near basal
LacI stays bound because glucose blocks allolactose formation entirely
cAMP-CAP is bound and active, giving full induction
The operon is fully off because no lactose is present

explanations.a: Correct — allolactose can still form and release LacI, but low cAMP prevents CAP activation and inducer exclusion limits further lactose entry, keeping expression near basal.
explanations.b: Some lactose still enters and is converted to allolactose even with glucose present; LacI is not permanently locked on.
explanations.c: cAMP stays low while glucose is transported, so CAP cannot form and activate transcription.
explanations.d: Lactose is present in this scenario, so the operon is not simply off from absence of substrate.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its role in glucose/lactose signaling.

right.text: PTS relay protein whose phosphorylation state senses glucose transport
Activator complex that bends DNA and recruits RNA polymerase
Enzyme that synthesizes cAMP, inhibited when EIIAGlc is dephosphorylated
Direct block of LacY transport activity by dephosphorylated EIIAGlc

questions.explanation: EIIAGlc's phosphorylation state is the shared sensor that both sets adenylate cyclase activity (controlling cAMP-CAP formation) and directly gates LacY (inducer exclusion).

questions.prompt: Order the phases of the classic diauxic growth curve on glucose plus lactose.

items.text: Rapid exponential growth consuming glucose
Growth lag as cAMP rises and the lac operon begins inducing
cAMP-CAP forms and activates full lac transcription
Second growth phase fueled by lactose catabolism

questions.explanation: Glucose is consumed first while it keeps cAMP low; only after it is depleted does cAMP rise, CAP activate the operon, and growth resume on lactose after the lag.

lessons.label: The trp Operon: Repressible Biosynthesis

sections.heading: TrpR: an inactive repressor until tryptophan says stop
sections.body: The trp operon (trpE, trpD, trpC, trpB, trpA) encodes five enzymes that build tryptophan from chorismate. Its repressor, TrpR, is unusual precisely because on its own it cannot bind the operator at all; the apo-repressor's DNA-binding helices are held in the wrong conformation. Only when tryptophan itself binds TrpR as a corepressor does the protein's two DNA-binding domains swing into the shape that fits the operator, letting the tryptophan-loaded repressor clamp down over the promoter and block RNA polymerase. This makes tryptophan a direct sensor of its own abundance: when intracellular tryptophan is scarce, TrpR stays inactive and the operon transcribes; when tryptophan is abundant, TrpR-tryptophan represses transcription roughly 80-fold relative to the derepressed state. The operon is never fully silent even when repressed, leaving a low basal synthesis rate so a cell that runs out of environmental tryptophan is never caught with zero biosynthetic capacity.

sections.heading: Two layers of end-product feedback
sections.body: TrpR-mediated repression is the slow, transcriptional layer of a two-layer feedback system. A faster layer acts within seconds: tryptophan also allosterically inhibits TrpE (anthranilate synthase), the first enzyme of the pathway, directly shutting off flux through already-made protein without waiting for transcription and translation to change enzyme levels. The two layers serve different timescales; allosteric feedback inhibition corrects for a transient spike in tryptophan within seconds, while TrpR repression conserves the far larger cost of continuing to build enzyme that isn't currently needed, adjusting over minutes as mRNA and protein pools turn over. Both are instances of end-product feedback, the concept Jacob and Monod folded into their 1961 operon model when they proposed that gene expression itself, not only enzyme activity, could be a target of feedback control.

sections.heading: Repressible anabolic vs inducible catabolic operons
sections.body: Comparing trp to lac reveals why anabolic and catabolic operons default to opposite states. lac is a catabolic operon: its substrate, lactose, is only sometimes present, so the cell defaults to off and switches on only when the substrate itself signals its presence, wasting nothing on enzymes for a sugar that isn't there. trp is an anabolic operon: tryptophan is always needed for protein synthesis, so the cell defaults to on and switches off only once the product becomes abundant enough that making more is wasteful, whether from internal synthesis or from tryptophan scavenged out of the environment. The shared principle is economy; regulation tracks whichever direction, presence of substrate or sufficiency of product, actually predicts whether the enzymes are worth their cost.

lessons.workedExample: A strain with a trpR-null mutation, no functional repressor, is grown in rich medium with abundant free tryptophan. Predict trp operon output relative to wild-type. In wild-type cells, abundant tryptophan binds TrpR, activates it, and represses transcription roughly 80-fold; trp enzyme levels drop close to their basal floor. In the trpR-null strain, no functional repressor can ever form regardless of tryptophan concentration, so the operon transcribes at its high, derepressed rate continuously, even though the cell has more than enough tryptophan and no biosynthetic need. The strain wastes ribosomes and ATP making trpE through trpA nonstop, a direct, testable version of the same metabolic cost problem: a knockout that decouples gene expression from the environmental signal it evolved to track.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges use the trp operon to test whether a student understands regulation as tracking cost, not just mechanism. A weak answer states that tryptophan turns the operon off without saying why that's adaptive. A strong answer explains that trp defaults ON because the amino acid is constantly needed, and is switched off only once product is sufficient, the mirror image of lac's default-off catabolic logic, and can name TrpR's requirement for a bound corepressor as the reason the apo-repressor cannot function alone. Judges are especially alert to whether a student conflates trp's repressible logic with lac's inducible one.

questions.prompt: TrpR functions as an active repressor only after...

options.text: Binding tryptophan as a corepressor, which changes its shape to fit the operator
Losing a bound tryptophan molecule
Binding cAMP
Being phosphorylated by a sensor kinase

explanations.a: Correct — apo-TrpR cannot bind the operator; only tryptophan binding as corepressor produces the conformation that fits the operator.
explanations.b: Losing tryptophan reverses activation, returning TrpR to its inactive apo form.
explanations.c: cAMP is the effector for CAP in lac positive control, not for TrpR.
explanations.d: TrpR activity is controlled by direct small-molecule binding, not by phosphorylation.

questions.prompt: Why does the trp operon default to a transcriptionally ON state in the absence of added tryptophan, in contrast to lac's default-OFF state?

options.text: Because trp enzymes are cheaper to make than lac enzymes

Because tryptophan is a constantly needed biosynthetic product, so the cell should keep making it unless already sufficient, the opposite logic of a catabolic operon that should stay off until its substrate appears
Because TrpR cannot bind DNA under any conditions
Because RNA polymerase has no affinity for the trp promoter

explanations.a: Cost per enzyme molecule is not what determines the default state; the substrate-vs-product logic is.
explanations.b: Correct — anabolic pathways default on because the product is continuously needed, while catabolic pathways default off because the substrate is only intermittently available.
explanations.c: TrpR can and does bind DNA, but only once tryptophan is bound as corepressor.
explanations.d: RNA polymerase does bind the trp promoter; that is exactly why an unrepressed operon transcribes.

questions.prompt: Match each trp regulatory component to its role.

right.text: Cannot bind the operator; wrong conformation without corepressor
Binds the operator and blocks RNA polymerase
Tryptophan directly inhibits the first pathway enzyme within seconds
Slower feedback layer that reduces new enzyme synthesis over minutes

questions.explanation: TrpR only becomes operator-competent once tryptophan-bound, while the fast allosteric layer and slower transcriptional layer act on different timescales toward the same end: shutting down tryptophan overproduction.

questions.prompt: Order the feedback events that follow a sudden spike in intracellular tryptophan, fastest first.

items.text: Tryptophan allosterically inhibits TrpE, cutting flux through existing enzyme within seconds
Tryptophan binds TrpR, activating it to bind the operator
RNA polymerase is blocked from initiating new trp mRNA
Existing trp enzyme pools decline over minutes as protein is diluted by growth, with transcription held roughly 80-fold below the derepressed rate

questions.explanation: Allosteric inhibition of existing enzyme acts within seconds, while the transcriptional shutdown chain (TrpR activation, then blocked initiation, then declining protein pools) unfolds over the following minutes.

lessons.label: Attenuation: Control by Transcription-Translation Coupling

sections.heading: A leader peptide built to fail when tryptophan is scarce
sections.body: Upstream of the trp structural genes lies a leader region, trpL, transcribed before RNA polymerase ever reaches trpE. trpL encodes its own tiny leader peptide, only 14 amino acids long, but with a signature feature: two tryptophan codons sitting back-to-back near its middle. Tryptophan is among the rarest amino acids in the bacterial proteome, so a run of two consecutive Trp codons is a built-in bottleneck. A ribosome translating trpL can only clear those codons quickly if charged tryptophanyl-tRNA is abundant; if intracellular tryptophan is scarce, charged tRNA-Trp runs low and the ribosome stalls directly on top of the tandem codons, sitting there until the amino acid supply is sufficient to reload it.

sections.heading: Four segments, two competing hairpins
sections.body: The leader mRNA folds into four numbered segments capable of pairing as 1:2, 2:3, or 3:4 hairpins, and which pairing wins depends entirely on where the trailing ribosome sits. A stalled ribosome, parked on the tandem Trp codons within segment 1, physically covers segment 1 and prevents it from pairing with segment 2, freeing segment 2 to pair with segment 3 instead, forming the 2:3 antiterminator hairpin. That structure occludes segment 3, so segment 4 is left unpaired, RNA polymerase reads through, and the operon's structural genes get transcribed. Conversely, a ribosome that translates straight through the tandem codons (tryptophan abundant) advances and stalls at the leader peptide's own stop codon inside segment 2, covering segment 2 instead and leaving segments 3 and 4 free to pair. The 3:4 pairing is an intrinsic, Rho-independent terminator, a GC-rich hairpin followed by a run of U residues, and it collapses the elongation complex, ending transcription before the structural genes are ever reached.

sections.heading: Layered on repression, and why it needs coupling
sections.body: Attenuation is not a replacement for TrpR repression but an additional dial layered on top of it, tuning expression roughly another 10-fold beyond TrpR's roughly 80-fold repression, for a combined range on the order of several hundredfold across the full span of tryptophan availability. Attenuation can only exist in organisms where transcription and translation are physically coupled; a ribosome must be able to load onto and translate a transcript while RNA polymerase is still synthesizing it downstream, which is only possible in bacteria and archaea, where there is no nuclear envelope separating the two processes. In eukaryotes, transcription happens in the nucleus and translation in the cytoplasm on a finished, processed mRNA, so no ribosome is ever present to read a nascent transcript's leader region in real time.

lessons.workedExample: Predict trp transcription past the attenuator under two conditions, with TrpR repression set aside as already derepressed. Tryptophan starvation: charged tRNA-Trp is scarce, so the leader-peptide ribosome stalls on the tandem Trp codons in segment 1; segment 1 stays covered, segment 2 pairs with segment 3 (antiterminator), segment 4 stays single-stranded, and RNA polymerase reads through into trpE, giving a full-length transcript. Tryptophan abundance: charged tRNA-Trp is plentiful, the ribosome clears the tandem codons rapidly and stalls at the leader peptide's stop codon over segment 2; segments 3 and 4 pair into the terminator hairpin, RNA polymerase falls off the DNA before trpE, and roughly 90% of transcripts terminate early rather than reaching the structural genes.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about attenuation specifically to test whether a student can explain a mechanism with no eukaryotic equivalent, which forces real understanding rather than pattern-matching to 'operons have repressors.' A weak answer says tryptophan controls a hairpin without saying what positions the ribosome to choose one hairpin over the other. A strong answer walks through why the tandem Trp codons are diagnostic, a stalling site specific to the very amino acid being regulated, and explains that the mechanism is only mechanically possible because bacterial ribosomes translate a transcript while it is still being made, the coupling eukaryotes lack.

questions.prompt: Attenuation is only mechanistically possible in bacteria and archaea because...

options.text: Bacterial ribosomes are more efficient than eukaryotic ones
Transcription and translation are physically coupled; a ribosome can translate a transcript while RNA polymerase is still synthesizing it
Bacteria lack RNA polymerase pausing
Bacterial mRNA has no secondary structure

explanations.a: Ribosome efficiency is not the relevant difference; spatial and temporal coupling of transcription and translation is.
explanations.b: Correct — without a nuclear envelope separating transcription and translation, a bacterial ribosome can shape a nascent transcript's structure in real time.
explanations.c: RNA polymerase pausing occurs in bacteria and is part of the mechanism, not something bacteria lack.
explanations.d: The mechanism depends entirely on the leader RNA forming alternative secondary structures.

questions.prompt: When tryptophan is abundant, which hairpin forms in the trp leader RNA, and what is its effect?

options.text: 2:3 antiterminator; transcription continues
3:4 terminator; transcription ends before the structural genes
1:2 pause hairpin; transcription pauses indefinitely
3:4 antiterminator; transcription continues

explanations.a: The 2:3 antiterminator forms under tryptophan scarcity, when the ribosome stalls in segment 1, not abundance.
explanations.b: Correct — with tryptophan abundant, the ribosome covers segment 2, freeing segments 3 and 4 to form the intrinsic terminator, ending transcription early.
explanations.c: The 1:2 pairing is a transient pause structure formed early in transcription, not the outcome that determines readthrough versus termination.
explanations.d: The 3:4 structure is a terminator, not an antiterminator.

questions.prompt: Match each leader RNA segment to its role.

right.text: Contains the tandem Trp codons where ribosome stalling occurs
Contains the leader peptide's stop codon; covered when translation completes
Pairs with segment 2 to form the antiterminator, or with segment 4 to form the terminator
Together with segment 3, forms the GC-rich terminator hairpin followed by a run of U residues

questions.explanation: Ribosome position over segment 1 or segment 2 determines which of segment 3's two possible pairing partners wins, which in turn determines whether segment 4 forms the terminator.

questions.prompt: Order the events of attenuation under low tryptophan, from starvation to readthrough.

items.text: Charged tRNA-Trp is scarce
The leader-peptide ribosome stalls on the tandem Trp codons, covering segment 1
Segment 2 pairs with segment 3, forming the antiterminator instead of the terminator
RNA polymerase reads through the attenuator into trpE and the rest of the structural genes

questions.explanation: Scarcity of charged tRNA-Trp causes the stall, the stall determines which hairpin forms, and the antiterminator hairpin is what permits polymerase to continue past the attenuator.

lessons.label: Beyond Operons: Riboswitches, Sigma Factors, and Sensing

sections.heading: Redirecting RNA polymerase wholesale: alternative sigma factors
sections.body: Every prokaryotic promoter is read not by core RNA polymerase alone but by core polymerase bound to a sigma factor, and swapping which sigma factor is loaded redirects the polymerase to an entirely different set of promoters, regulating dozens or hundreds of genes at once instead of one operon at a time. E. coli's housekeeping sigma-70 recognizes ordinary promoters, but under heat stress the cell shifts to sigma-32 (RpoH), which redirects RNA polymerase to the heat-shock regulon encoding chaperones like DnaK and GroEL. Sigma-32 itself is normally kept scarce; it is degraded by the FtsH protease with a half-life around one minute at 37 degrees Celsius, but when heat denatures cellular proteins, the chaperones that would otherwise target sigma-32 for degradation get diverted to refolding the new backlog of unfolded protein, so sigma-32 escapes degradation and accumulates. Bacillus subtilis uses the same logic for sporulation, activating a cascade of dedicated sigma factors, sigma-F, sigma-E, sigma-G, and sigma-K, in strict sequence across the two compartments of a sporulating cell.

sections.heading: Riboswitches: the mRNA senses the metabolite itself
sections.body: Riboswitches remove the protein regulator from the circuit entirely: a metabolite-binding aptamer domain folded directly into the 5' untranslated region of an mRNA senses its target ligand and refolds an adjacent expression platform to block a ribosome-binding site or form a terminator hairpin, without any dedicated sensor protein. The thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) riboswitch, described independently by Breaker's and Mironov's groups in 2002, binds the active form of vitamin B1 directly and shuts down thiamine biosynthesis and transport genes once TPP is sufficient; it is the most phylogenetically widespread riboswitch class known, found across bacteria, archaea, fungi, and plants. The guanine riboswitch, characterized by Mandal and Breaker (2003) in the Bacillus subtilis xpt-pbuX operon, discriminates guanine from the chemically similar adenine using a single specific base-pairing contact in its aptamer, and represses purine biosynthesis genes once free guanine is abundant enough to satisfy demand.

sections.heading: Sensing without a single-molecule receptor: two-component systems and quorum sensing
