sections.body: Two-component systems generalize sensing into a reusable phosphorelay module: a membrane sensor histidine kinase autophosphorylates in response to a specific stimulus, then transfers that phosphate to a cognate cytoplasmic response regulator, which typically binds DNA as a transcription factor. The EnvZ-OmpR pair, which E. coli uses to sense osmolarity and adjust porin gene expression, is one of hundreds of such kinase-regulator pairs bacteria have evolved for signals ranging from nitrogen availability to antibiotic stress. Quorum sensing extends this logic to sensing population density rather than a chemical directly: in the bioluminescent marine bacterium Vibrio fischeri, described by Nealson, Platt, and Hastings (1970), the LuxI enzyme continuously synthesizes a diffusible acyl-homoserine lactone; as cell density rises, the autoinducer accumulates until it crosses a threshold concentration, binds LuxR, and switches on the luciferase operon, letting a population light up only once there are enough cells present for bioluminescence to be worth its cost.

lessons.workedExample: A microbiologist finds a Bacillus subtilis mutant that sporulates poorly and, on sequencing, finds a null mutation in sigF, encoding sigma-F. Because sigma-F is the first sporulation-specific sigma factor activated, exclusively in the forespore compartment, its loss prevents the entire downstream cascade: sigma-F normally helps trigger the signal that activates sigma-E in the mother cell, which in turn is required before sigma-G and sigma-K can ever be activated later in each compartment. A single sigma factor knockout therefore doesn't just remove one gene's expression; it collapses an entire multi-hundred-gene developmental program that depends on the ordered handoff between successive sigma factors, illustrating why sigma-factor cascades operate at a fundamentally different scale than a single operon's on/off switch.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges bring up sigma factors, riboswitches, or quorum sensing specifically to see whether a student can name a regulatory mechanism that operates above or below the scale of a single operon. A weak answer tries to force every example back into a repressor-operator story. A strong answer explains the actual scale mismatch: a sigma factor swap reprograms RNA polymerase's promoter preference across an entire regulon, a riboswitch senses its ligand without any protein intermediary at all, and quorum sensing regulates a whole population's collective behavior rather than one cell's single gene, three genuinely different logics, not variations on lac.

questions.prompt: What determines which set of promoters E. coli's RNA polymerase transcribes at a given moment?

options.text: DNA methylation state alone
Which sigma factor is currently bound to core RNA polymerase
The concentration of ribosomes in the cell
Chromosome supercoiling density alone

explanations.a: Methylation plays a role in some regulatory systems, but promoter recognition by RNA polymerase is set by its bound sigma factor.
explanations.b: Correct — different sigma factors direct core RNA polymerase to different promoter consensus sequences, redirecting it to an entirely different regulon.
explanations.c: Ribosome concentration affects translation, not which promoters RNA polymerase recognizes.
explanations.d: Supercoiling can modulate individual promoters but is not what globally redirects RNA polymerase between different sets of genes.

questions.prompt: How does a riboswitch differ fundamentally from a system like the trp operon's TrpR repressor?

options.text: A riboswitch's mRNA aptamer binds the regulatory metabolite directly, with no dedicated protein sensor required, unlike TrpR
A riboswitch always increases, never decreases, gene expression
A riboswitch works only in eukaryotic cells
A riboswitch requires a corepressor protein just like TrpR

explanations.a: Correct — the aptamer domain is part of the mRNA itself and binds its ligand directly, unlike TrpR, which is a separate protein that must bind tryptophan before it can bind DNA.
explanations.b: Riboswitches can either repress or activate expression depending on how the expression platform is wired, such as sequestering a ribosome-binding site.
explanations.c: Riboswitches are found across bacteria, archaea, fungi, and plants, not only eukaryotes, and are especially well characterized in bacteria.
explanations.d: Riboswitches bind their ligand directly and require no corepressor protein at all, unlike TrpR.

questions.prompt: Match each regulatory mechanism to its example system.

right.text: Sigma-32 (RpoH) redirecting RNA polymerase to the E. coli heat-shock regulon
A TPP aptamer in an mRNA 5' UTR gating thiamine genes without a protein sensor
The EnvZ-OmpR histidine kinase/response regulator pair sensing osmolarity
The LuxI/LuxR system in Vibrio fischeri sensing population density via an acyl-homoserine lactone

questions.explanation: Each mechanism operates at a different regulatory scale, from redirecting all of RNA polymerase's promoter choices to a single mRNA sensing its own ligand to a whole population sensing its own density.

questions.prompt: Order the sporulation sigma factors in the sequence they are activated across the two compartments of a sporulating Bacillus subtilis cell.

items.text: Sigma-F
Sigma-E
Sigma-G
Sigma-K

questions.explanation: Sigma-F activates first in the forespore, triggering sigma-E in the mother cell; sigma-E then enables sigma-G in the forespore, which finally enables sigma-K in the mother cell, each compartment-specific factor depending on the previous one's signal.

units.label: Eukaryotic Transcription Initiation: Promoters & the PIC

lessons.label: Three RNA polymerases and the Pol II CTD

sections.heading: One enzyme becomes three
sections.body: Bacteria transcribe every gene with a single RNA polymerase. Eukaryotes split the job three ways, a division Roeder and Rutter demonstrated in 1969 by running sea urchin and rat liver nuclear extracts over an ion-exchange column and finding three chromatographically distinct activities eluting off the same resin with differing salt and divalent-cation requirements; the follow-up work that showed those same three activities also have sharply different sensitivity to the toxin alpha-amanitin (Pol I resistant, Pol II acutely sensitive, Pol III sensitive only at high dose) came a year later, from Lindell, Weinberg, Morris, Roeder and Rutter in 1970. RNA Polymerase I sits in the nucleolus and transcribes the large pre-ribosomal RNA precursor that is processed into 28S, 18S, and 5.8S rRNA — the structural core of the ribosome. RNA Polymerase III, working in the nucleoplasm, makes the small, highly structured RNAs: tRNA and 5S rRNA, plus some snRNA and other short noncoding transcripts. RNA Polymerase II transcribes every protein-coding gene into pre-mRNA, along with most snRNA and microRNA precursors. Because Pol I and Pol III output is fixed and abundant per cell (a growing cell needs enormous numbers of ribosomes and tRNAs), while Pol II output must be gene-specific and inducible, the three enzymes evolved almost entirely separate promoter recognition machinery even though their catalytic cores are structurally homologous.

sections.heading: The CTD as a phospho-code
sections.body: What makes Pol II unique among the three is a tail bolted onto its largest subunit: the C-terminal domain, a tandem repeat of the heptapeptide Tyr-Ser-Pro-Thr-Ser-Pro-Ser (YSPTSPS) — 26 repeats in budding yeast, 52 in humans, with the repeats closest to the polymerase core most closely matching the consensus and those toward the C-terminus increasingly divergent. The CTD is unstructured and disordered in unphosphorylated Pol II, but as the enzyme transits from initiation into elongation, kinases install phosphate marks on specific serines that different factors read as a code. At initiation, TFIIH's CDK7 subunit phosphorylates Ser5 of the heptad; Ser5-P recruits the mRNA capping enzyme to the emerging 5' end and marks promoter-proximal Pol II. As the enzyme escapes the promoter and moves into productive elongation, P-TEFb's CDK9 subunit phosphorylates Ser2; Ser2-P accumulates toward the 3' end of genes and recruits splicing and 3'-cleavage factors. This Ser5-to-Ser2 phosphorylation gradient means the CTD is not a passive tail but a mobile platform that couples transcription in real time to mRNA processing.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher wants to know whether a stretch of chromatin is being actively transcribed by Pol II versus just poised there. A ChIP-seq antibody against total Pol II would light up both a paused promoter and an actively elongating gene body equally. Instead, using an antibody specific for Ser5-phosphorylated CTD picks out promoter-proximal, just-initiated polymerase, while an antibody specific for Ser2-phosphorylated CTD picks out polymerase deep in productive elongation toward the gene's 3' end. Comparing the two ChIP-seq profiles across a gene reveals a Ser5-P peak sitting right at the promoter and a Ser2-P signal ramping up across the gene body — a direct readout of where in the transcription cycle the enzyme sits, without ever measuring RNA itself.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who sees 'Pol II' or 'RNA polymerase' in a project asks which of the three eukaryotic polymerases is meant and why the CTD matters, because conflating them (or forgetting that only Pol II has a CTD) signals memorized vocabulary rather than mechanism. A weak answer says 'RNA polymerase makes mRNA.' A strong answer names which polymerase, states what it transcribes, and explains that the CTD's changing phosphorylation state is what times capping and splicing to transcription — showing the student understands transcription as a coupled, staged process rather than a single step.

questions.prompt: Match each RNA polymerase to its primary transcript.

right.text: Pre-ribosomal RNA (28S/18S/5.8S rRNA)
Pre-mRNA (protein-coding genes)
tRNA and 5S rRNA

questions.explanation: Pol I makes the large pre-rRNA precursor in the nucleolus, Pol II makes pre-mRNA (and most snRNA/miRNA precursors), and Pol III makes small structured RNAs like tRNA and 5S rRNA.

questions.prompt: Which kinase phosphorylates Ser5 of the Pol II CTD heptad repeat during initiation, and what does that mark recruit?

options.text: CDK9, which recruits splicing factors
CDK7 (via TFIIH), which recruits the mRNA capping enzyme
CDK8, which recruits the ribosome
CDK7, which recruits P-TEFb

explanations.a: CDK9 is the elongation kinase that phosphorylates Ser2, not Ser5, and its mark relates to 3' processing, not capping.
explanations.b: Correct — CDK7, a subunit of TFIIH, phosphorylates Ser5 at initiation, and Ser5-P is what recruits the capping machinery to the nascent 5' end.
explanations.c: CDK8 is a Mediator kinase-module subunit involved in regulating PIC assembly, not a direct CTD Ser5 kinase during core initiation.
explanations.d: CDK7 does phosphorylate Ser5, but that mark recruits the capping enzyme, not P-TEFb — P-TEFb acts later, independently, to release paused Pol II.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the CTD phosphorylation cycle from earliest to latest.

items.text: Pol II assembles into the PIC with an unphosphorylated CTD
TFIIH's CDK7 phosphorylates Ser5, recruiting the capping enzyme
P-TEFb's CDK9 phosphorylates Ser2 as Pol II enters productive elongation
Ser2-P accumulates toward the gene's 3' end, recruiting cleavage/polyadenylation factors

questions.explanation: The CTD starts unphosphorylated in the assembled PIC, gains Ser5-P at initiation (coupling to capping), then gains Ser2-P upon pause release into elongation, with Ser2-P building up toward the 3' end to recruit 3'-end processing factors.

questions.prompt: Roeder and Rutter's 1969 experiment distinguished the three eukaryotic RNA polymerases primarily by what property?

options.text: Their DNA sequence as revealed by early sequencing
Their differential elution from ion-exchange chromatography and differing salt/divalent-cation sensitivity
Direct visualization by electron microscopy of each enzyme bound to a gene
Antibody staining patterns in a fixed cell

explanations.a: DNA sequencing of protein-coding genes was not feasible in 1969; the polymerases were distinguished as biochemical activities, not by gene sequence.
explanations.b: Correct — Roeder and Rutter separated nuclear extracts by ion-exchange chromatography and found three activities with distinct elution positions and distinct sensitivity to salt and divalent cations. (Their differential sensitivity to the toxin alpha-amanitin was established the following year, in Lindell et al. 1970.)
explanations.c: Single-enzyme EM visualization on a specific gene was not the method used to originally distinguish the three activities.
explanations.d: Specific antibodies against each polymerase did not yet exist in 1969; the original distinction was purely biochemical/chromatographic.

lessons.label: Core promoter elements

sections.heading: The core promoter: a short DNA neighborhood
sections.body: The core promoter is the roughly 40-80 base pair stretch of DNA immediately surrounding the transcription start site (TSS) that is sufficient, on its own, to direct accurate initiation by RNA Polymerase II in a purified in vitro system — distinct from the wider promoter region, which extends further upstream and includes proximal regulatory sequences that boost but do not by themselves position initiation. The best-known core element is the TATA box, an AT-rich sequence (consensus TATAAA) typically centered 25-30 base pairs upstream of the TSS, first defined by comparative sequence analysis of animal promoters in the late 1970s and shown to be bound directly by the TATA-binding protein (TBP). But the TATA box is present in only a minority of human promoters — most human genes, especially broadly expressed housekeeping genes, instead sit in CpG islands: GC-rich, unmethylated stretches with no discernible TATA box, where initiation is instead specified by a looser Initiator (Inr) element straddling the TSS itself, first defined by Smale and Baltimore in 1989.

sections.heading: Downstream elements and the +1 nucleosome
sections.body: A second class of core element lies downstream of the TSS rather than upstream. The downstream promoter element (DPE), described by Burke and Kadonaga in 1996 working in Drosophila, sits about +28 to +34 relative to the TSS and is recognized by TFIID even in promoters that lack a TATA box, but only when spaced a very precise ~30 bp from a functional Inr — move the DPE a few base pairs and TFIID binding collapses. A related element, the BRE (TFIIB recognition element, described by Lagrange and coworkers in 1998), sits just upstream of the TATA box and is contacted directly by TFIIB, helping orient the polymerase in the correct direction. Layered on top of this DNA-sequence logic is chromatin structure: genome-wide nucleosome mapping studies (notably in yeast) showed that a well-positioned nucleosome, the +1 nucleosome, sits just downstream of the TSS in most genes, and its position and stability influence how easily Pol II can be recruited and how far it travels before pausing.

lessons.workedExample: A student is given two anonymized human promoter sequences and asked to predict, from sequence alone, whether each uses the TATA/Inr initiation mode or the CpG-island/Inr mode. Promoter A has no TATAAA-like sequence anywhere in the -40 to +40 region but is extremely GC-rich with numerous CG dinucleotides scattered through it; promoter B has a clear TATAAA around -28 and is not unusually GC-rich. The student correctly calls promoter A a CpG-island (TATA-less) promoter, likely for a broadly expressed housekeeping gene, and promoter B a classic TATA-box promoter, more typical of a tightly regulated, tissue-specific gene — and notes that only promoter B's TBP-TATA interaction would show up in an assay targeting TBP-DNA binding directly.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes core promoter architecture because it is where sequence meets mechanism: a student who can only say 'the promoter is where transcription starts' has not engaged with why most human genes lack a TATA box, or how TFIID can still find a TATA-less promoter. A strong answer distinguishes the core promoter from the broader promoter region, names at least two specific elements (TATA, Inr, DPE, BRE) with their approximate position relative to the TSS, and recognizes that different genes use different combinations — a weak answer treats 'the promoter' as one uniform, TATA-box-having sequence.

questions.prompt: Match each core promoter element to its approximate position relative to the transcription start site (+1).

right.text: Straddling the TSS itself

questions.explanation: The TATA box sits about 25-30 bp upstream of the TSS, the Inr straddles the TSS, and the DPE sits about 28-34 bp downstream, working together with the Inr at a fixed spacing.

questions.prompt: Why does the DPE only work when it sits at a very specific spacing from the Inr, unlike some other regulatory elements that tolerate being moved?

options.text: Because DPE and Inr are both bound as one composite surface by the same TFIID complex, so the spacing has to match the fixed geometry of that protein-DNA contact
Because the DPE is actually an enhancer and enhancers are always position-independent
Because RNA polymerase reads the DPE sequence directly as part of its catalytic active site
Because the spacing requirement is a historical artifact of the Drosophila genome and does not reflect a real mechanistic constraint

explanations.a: Correct — TFIID makes coordinated contacts with the Inr and the DPE as part of one binding event, so the two elements have to sit at the spacing that matches TFIID's fixed subunit geometry.
explanations.b: The DPE is a core promoter element read by the general transcription machinery, not an enhancer, and it is explicitly position-dependent, the opposite of typical enhancer behavior.
explanations.c: RNA Polymerase II does not directly read core promoter DNA sequence; sequence-specific recognition is done by TFIID (via TBP and TAFs), not the polymerase active site.
explanations.d: The spacing dependence has been confirmed functionally — shifting the DPE a few base pairs sharply reduces TFIID binding and transcription — so it reflects a real structural constraint, not an artifact.

questions.prompt: Most human promoters, especially housekeeping genes, lack a TATA box. What do they typically have instead?

options.text: No initiation elements at all — transcription starts stochastically
A CpG-island context with an Initiator (Inr) element specifying the start site
A second, redundant TATA box further upstream
An exclusively Pol III-style internal promoter

explanations.a: Initiation is not stochastic; TATA-less promoters still use defined elements like the Inr to fix the start site, just without a TATA box.
explanations.b: Correct — many human promoters, especially broadly expressed genes, sit in GC-rich, unmethylated CpG islands and rely on the Inr (often with a DPE) rather than a TATA box.
explanations.c: TATA-less promoters lack a TATA box altogether; they do not compensate with a second one elsewhere.
explanations.d: Pol III promoters use an entirely different, often internal, element set (like the A and B boxes for tRNA genes) and are irrelevant to Pol II TATA-less promoters.

lessons.label: Assembling the pre-initiation complex

sections.heading: TFIID lands first and bends the DNA
sections.body: In vitro reconstitution experiments through the 1980s and 1990s (much of it from the Roeder and Tjian labs) established that Pol II initiation requires an ordered handoff of general transcription factors, named TFIIA through TFIIH in the order they were biochemically fractionated, not the order they act. The first committed step is TFIID, a huge multi-subunit complex built around TATA-binding protein (TBP) plus roughly a dozen TBP-associated factors (TAFs). TBP itself is a saddle-shaped protein that clamps onto the minor groove of the TATA box; the 1993 crystal structure from the Sigler and Burley labs showed TBP inducing a severe, continuous bend of about 80 degrees in the DNA, kinking it toward the major groove. That bend is not incidental — it exposes the DNA on either side for the next factors to dock and helps commit the promoter to initiation. TFIIA arrives next, stabilizing the TBP-TATA interaction and displacing TAF1's auto-inhibitory contact with TBP's DNA-binding surface, and TFIIB binds next, contacting both TBP and the BRE element upstream of the TATA box and helping select the correct start site.

sections.heading: Pol II arrives already escorted, then TFIIE and TFIIH close the ring
sections.body: Unlike the earlier factors, RNA Polymerase II does not arrive alone — it is delivered as a pre-formed complex with TFIIF, which clamps onto the polymerase and suppresses its tendency to bind DNA nonspecifically, sharpening its ability to engage the TFIIB-marked start site. This TFIIB-Pol II-TFIIF assembly onto the TFIIA/TFIID-bound promoter forms what is called the closed complex — a stable protein-DNA assembly in which the double helix is still fully base-paired. Two more factors close out the core PIC: TFIIE, which binds near the polymerase's DNA-entry channel and helps recruit and regulate the final factor, and TFIIH, the largest and most complex GTF, a ten-subunit machine with its own DNA helicase and kinase activities. With TFIIH loaded, all six general transcription factors (TFIIA, B, D, E, F, H) plus Pol II are present on the core promoter — the complete pre-initiation complex, poised but not yet catalytically active, since the DNA strands have not yet been separated.

lessons.workedExample: A biochemist reconstitutes transcription in vitro from purified components and deliberately omits TFIIA from the reaction, keeping everything else (TFIID, TFIIB, Pol II-TFIIF, TFIIE, TFIIH) present. Transcription still occurs but at much lower efficiency and is far more sensitive to competing DNA or inhibitory TAF1 contacts, because TFIIA's normal job of stabilizing TBP on the TATA box and neutralizing TAF1's auto-inhibition is missing. This matches real biochemical data showing TFIIA is not strictly essential for minimal in vitro transcription the way TFIID, TFIIB, Pol II, or TFIIH are, but it substantially stabilizes the complex and boosts activated transcription — illustrating that 'required for the core reaction' and 'required for efficient, regulated initiation in a cell' are different bars.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about PIC assembly order to test whether a student understands transcription initiation as a structured, stepwise molecular assembly rather than a black box labeled 'transcription factors bind.' A weak answer lists the six general transcription factors with no order or role. A strong answer explains that TFIID nucleates the complex by bending the DNA at the TATA box, that Pol II arrives pre-bound to TFIIF rather than alone, and that TFIIH is the last factor in and the one that actually opens the DNA — showing the student can trace a mechanism, not just recite a factor alphabet.

questions.prompt: Order the general transcription factors/complexes by when they join the assembling PIC on the core promoter.

items.text: TFIID (TBP + TAFs) binds the core promoter and bends the DNA
TFIIA stabilizes TBP on the TATA box
TFIIB binds TBP and the BRE, helping select the start site
Pol II, pre-bound to TFIIF, joins the complex
TFIIE and then TFIIH complete the closed complex

questions.explanation: TFIID nucleates assembly by binding and bending the core promoter; TFIIA and TFIIB follow to stabilize TBP and help position the start site; Pol II arrives already complexed with TFIIF; TFIIE and TFIIH join last to complete the closed pre-initiation complex.

questions.prompt: The 1993 TBP-TATA crystal structure showed TBP inducing what kind of distortion in the DNA?

options.text: A single-stranded bubble, fully melting the DNA
A severe, continuous bend of about 80 degrees toward the major groove
No distortion at all — TBP binds B-form DNA without altering it
A right-handed supercoil spanning several kilobases

explanations.a: Melting (strand separation) is a later step performed by TFIIH's helicase activity, not something TBP itself does on binding.
explanations.b: Correct — TBP's saddle shape clamps the TATA box minor groove and induces a smooth, continuous ~80 degree bend toward the major groove, as shown in the Sigler-lab and Burley-lab 1993 structures.
explanations.c: TBP binding is famous precisely because it severely distorts the DNA rather than leaving it undisturbed — that bend is central to how it commits the promoter to initiation.
explanations.d: Supercoiling across kilobases is a topological, whole-domain phenomenon unrelated to the local, sequence-specific bend TBP induces at the TATA box itself.

questions.prompt: Why does Pol II arrive at the promoter already bound to TFIIF rather than binding DNA on its own first?

options.text: TFIIF suppresses Pol II's nonspecific DNA binding, sharpening its ability to engage the correct, TFIIB-marked start site
TFIIF is required to phosphorylate the CTD before Pol II can touch DNA
Pol II cannot fold correctly without TFIIF as a chaperone
TFIIF replaces the need for TFIID entirely at TATA-less promoters

explanations.a: Correct — TFIIF clamps the polymerase and dampens indiscriminate DNA binding, so Pol II is delivered in a state primed to recognize the specific start site set up by TFIIB rather than sticking anywhere on the DNA.
explanations.b: CTD Ser5 phosphorylation is performed later by TFIIH's CDK7 subunit, not by TFIIF.
explanations.c: TFIIF is not a general protein-folding chaperone for Pol II; its role is DNA-binding specificity within the PIC.
explanations.d: TFIID (via TBP/TAFs) is still required to nucleate the promoter even at TATA-less promoters (via Inr/DPE recognition by TAFs); TFIIF does not substitute for it.

lessons.label: Promoter melting, pausing, and escape

sections.heading: TFIIH opens the DNA and starts the CTD phospho-cycle
sections.body: The closed complex is transcriptionally inert until TFIIH acts. TFIIH is a ten-subunit machine with two enzymatic modules bolted onto a structural core: a helicase module built around the ATPase subunits XPB and XPD, and a kinase module (CDK7, cyclin H, MAT1) called the CDK-activating kinase (CAK) submodule. XPB uses ATP hydrolysis to translocate and torsionally unwind the DNA around the start site, converting the closed complex into an open complex with a single-stranded transcription bubble threaded into the Pol II active site. XPD's helicase activity is used less for promoter melting and more in TFIIH's separate role in nucleotide excision repair — mutations in either XPB or XPD cause the DNA-repair disease xeroderma pigmentosum, underscoring that TFIIH moonlights between transcription and repair. Once the bubble is open, CDK7 phosphorylates Ser5 of the Pol II CTD heptad repeats, and RNA synthesis begins.

sections.heading: Abortive cycling, clearance, and the pause checkpoint
sections.body: Newly initiated Pol II is unstable: it frequently synthesizes and releases short transcripts of only a few to a dozen nucleotides in a futile cycle called abortive initiation before it manages true promoter clearance — physically vacating the promoter-proximal DNA so a new PIC can assemble behind it. Even after clearance, most metazoan genes do not run straight into productive elongation. Instead, within about 20-60 nucleotides of the TSS, Pol II is captured by two factors: DSIF (identified by Wada and colleagues in 1998, a Spt4/Spt5 heterodimer) and NELF (identified by Yamaguchi and colleagues in 1999), which together clamp the elongation complex into a paused state — promoter-proximal pausing, now understood as a widespread regulatory checkpoint rather than a rare stall. Release from the pause requires P-TEFb, the CDK9/cyclin T kinase, which phosphorylates Ser2 of the CTD, phosphorylates DSIF (converting it into a positive elongation factor), and phosphorylates NELF, triggering NELF's dissociation from the complex — only then does Pol II accelerate into productive, processive elongation.

lessons.workedExample: A lab treats cultured cells with flavopiridol, a small-molecule inhibitor of CDK9 (P-TEFb's kinase subunit), and performs Pol II ChIP-seq before and after treatment. Before treatment, many genes show a sharp Pol II peak at the promoter (paused polymerase) plus a lower, roughly even signal across the gene body (elongating polymerase). After flavopiridol treatment, the promoter-proximal peak remains or grows while the gene-body signal collapses, because CDK9 can no longer phosphorylate Ser2 of the CTD or phosphorylate NELF to release it — polymerase gets loaded and paused but cannot be licensed into elongation. This is the classic experimental signature used to prove that P-TEFb activity, not PIC assembly, is the rate-limiting step for many genes.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing this concept wants to know whether the student understands that 'transcription starts' is not one event but a sequence of checkpoints, each independently regulatable. A weak answer says Pol II starts making RNA as soon as it binds the promoter. A strong answer distinguishes promoter melting (TFIIH-dependent), promoter clearance (abortive cycling ending), and pause release (P-TEFb-dependent) as three separable, druggable steps, and can name which factors enforce and which factors release the pause — showing they grasp that pausing is a real regulatory node genes use to poise for rapid induction, not a failure of the machinery.

questions.prompt: Match each factor or subunit to its role in melting, pausing, or releasing Pol II.

right.text: Unwinds promoter DNA to form the open complex
Clamp Pol II into a promoter-proximal paused state
Phosphorylates CTD Ser2 and NELF to release the pause

questions.explanation: XPB's ATPase/helicase activity opens the DNA around the start site; DSIF and NELF together enforce promoter-proximal pausing shortly after initiation; P-TEFb's CDK9 releases the pause by phosphorylating Ser2 and NELF, letting elongation proceed.

questions.prompt: Order these events from PIC formation through productive elongation.

items.text: Closed complex assembled (DNA still double-stranded)
TFIIH's XPB unwinds DNA, forming the open complex; CDK7 phosphorylates Ser5
Abortive initiation: short transcripts synthesized and released
Pol II clears the promoter but is captured by DSIF/NELF in a proximal pause
P-TEFb phosphorylates Ser2 and NELF, releasing Pol II into elongation

questions.explanation: The closed complex forms first, TFIIH opens the DNA and CDK7 marks Ser5, early abortive cycling occurs before true clearance, cleared Pol II is then captured in a DSIF/NELF-enforced pause, and P-TEFb finally releases it into productive elongation.

questions.prompt: Mutations in XPB or XPD, TFIIH's helicase subunits, cause xeroderma pigmentosum. What does this reveal about TFIIH?

options.text: TFIIH has no real connection to DNA repair; the disease link is coincidental
TFIIH moonlights between transcription initiation and nucleotide excision repair, using the same helicase subunits for both roles
XPB and XPD are only active in skin cells, which is why the disease is dermatological
TFIIH's helicase subunits are redundant and unrelated to transcription's melting step

explanations.a: The disease link is not coincidental — it reflects a real, well-established shared use of XPB/XPD in both pathways.
explanations.b: Correct — TFIIH's XPB and XPD helicase subunits function both in opening promoter DNA for transcription and in unwinding damaged DNA during nucleotide excision repair, so mutations disrupt both and produce the repair-deficiency disease xeroderma pigmentosum.
explanations.c: XPB and XPD function in essentially all nucleated cells (they are core transcription/repair machinery); the skin-predominant symptoms reflect UV damage exposure and repair failure, not tissue-restricted expression of the subunits.
explanations.d: XPB in particular is the subunit whose ATPase/translocase activity is used to unwind promoter DNA during transcription initiation — it is directly, not redundantly, involved in melting.

lessons.label: Mediator: the coactivator bridge

sections.heading: The missing link between activators and the PIC
sections.body: Sequence-specific activator proteins bound at enhancers, often tens of kilobases from a gene's promoter, somehow have to communicate with the general transcription machinery sitting at the core promoter. Through the 1980s biochemists could reconstitute basal transcription from purified GTFs and Pol II, but adding purified activator proteins to that minimal system produced little or no activation, and in some cases activators even squelched (inhibited) transcription by soaking up limiting GTFs without delivering any benefit — a sign that something was missing from the reconstitution. Kelleher, Flanagan, and Kornberg identified that missing factor in 1990, isolating a fraction from yeast nuclear extract that relieved squelching and enabled activator-dependent transcription; they named it Mediator. It was, historically, the last major component of the core Pol II initiation machinery to be discovered, and its finding (along with the broader reconstituted transcription system) was part of the body of work that earned Roger Kornberg the 2006 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

sections.heading: A modular complex with a detachable kinase
sections.body: Mediator is not a small factor — the human complex runs to roughly 30 subunits organized into four physically separable modules: a head module and a middle module that together dock directly onto Pol II and the core PIC, a tail module that reaches out to contact DNA-bound activators (and is structurally the most variable part, matching the diversity of activators it must bind), and a dissociable kinase module (built around CDK8, cyclin C, MED12, and MED13) that can reversibly join or leave the rest of the complex. Core Mediator (head + middle + tail) is generally activating: it stabilizes PIC assembly on the promoter, helps recruit and orient Pol II, and stimulates the CTD kinase activity of TFIIH, boosting Ser5 phosphorylation and productive initiation. The CDK8 kinase module, by contrast, is mostly associated with repressive or fine-tuning functions — its binding is structurally incompatible with core Mediator engaging Pol II at the same time, so a cell can toggle between an activating, Pol II-bound Mediator state and a CDK8-module-bound regulatory state.

lessons.workedExample: A gene has a strong enhancer 40 kb upstream bound by three activator proteins, but its core promoter alone (TATA box, Inr, TFIID binding site) is otherwise unremarkable. In a purified in vitro system containing only Pol II and the six GTFs, adding the activators produces almost no increase in transcription. Adding purified Mediator to the same reaction, however, produces a large activation, because Mediator's tail module physically bridges the DNA-bound activators to Mediator's head/middle modules, which are docked on Pol II — looping the distant enhancer DNA into contact with the promoter-bound PIC and stimulating TFIIH-dependent CTD phosphorylation. Remove any one activator and the fold-activation drops roughly in proportion, showing Mediator is integrating multiple activator inputs rather than just relaying a single strongest signal.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about Mediator because 'activators turn genes on' is often stated as if activators touch Pol II directly, which they generally do not for RNA Pol II in eukaryotes. A weak answer stops at 'activators bind enhancers and turn on transcription.' A strong answer explains that Mediator is the physical bridge — naming its modular structure and that the CDK8 kinase module can swap in for a repressive or regulatory function — and can explain why reconstituted systems without Mediator fail to show activator-dependent stimulation, which is direct evidence for the bridging model rather than an assumption.

questions.prompt: Match each Mediator module to its principal role.

right.text: Contacts DNA-bound activators at enhancers
Dock onto Pol II and stabilize PIC assembly
Dissociable module associated with repressive/regulatory functions, structurally incompatible with core Mediator binding Pol II

questions.explanation: The tail module is the activator-contacting end, the head and middle modules physically dock Mediator onto Pol II and the PIC, and the separable CDK8 kinase module cannot bind Mediator at the same time as Pol II and is generally linked to repression or fine-tuning.

questions.prompt: In early reconstituted transcription experiments, adding purified activator proteins to a minimal Pol II + GTF system often failed to activate transcription, and sometimes reduced it ('squelching'). What did this observation eventually reveal?

options.text: That activators do not actually matter for transcription in vivo
That a missing coactivator bridge (Mediator) was needed to translate activator binding into a boost in PIC function
That TFIID alone is sufficient to respond to activators without any other factor
That squelching proved activators work by directly displacing TFIIH

explanations.a: Activators clearly matter in vivo; the puzzle was why purified components alone did not reproduce activation, which pointed to a missing factor rather than activators being unimportant.
explanations.b: Correct — the failure of the minimal system to respond to activators, and the sequestration/squelching effect, indicated a missing bridging factor; Kelleher, Flanagan, and Kornberg identified this as Mediator in 1990.
explanations.c: TFIID alone did not resolve the squelching problem in these reconstitutions; the missing activity was Mediator, a separate multi-subunit complex.
explanations.d: Squelching reflects activators nonproductively sequestering limiting factors, not a demonstrated direct displacement of TFIIH.

questions.prompt: Why can the CDK8 kinase module and Pol II not both be bound to Mediator at the same time?

options.text: Because CDK8 phosphorylates and destroys Pol II on contact
Because the two are structurally/sterically incompatible — CDK8 module binding is mutually exclusive with the head/middle modules engaging Pol II
Because CDK8 only exists in yeast, not in the human Mediator complex
Because Pol II lacks a CTD when CDK8 is present

explanations.a: CDK8 module engagement does not degrade Pol II; the incompatibility is structural, about binding geometry, not enzymatic destruction.
explanations.b: Correct — the CDK8 kinase module occupies a position that structurally clashes with core Mediator's Pol II-binding surface, so a Mediator complex is either in a Pol II-engaged, generally activating state or a CDK8-module-bound, more regulatory state, not both.
explanations.c: The CDK8 kinase module (with cyclin C, MED12, MED13) is present and functionally important in the human Mediator complex as well as in yeast.
explanations.d: Pol II retains its CTD regardless of Mediator's CDK8-module occupancy; the CTD's phosphorylation state, not its presence, changes across the transcription cycle.

lessons.label: Reading a promoter map

sections.heading: The coordinate system: +1, upstream, downstream
sections.body: Every promoter diagram uses the same numbering convention, and misreading it is one of the fastest ways to misinterpret a regulatory figure. The transcription start site (TSS) — the first nucleotide actually incorporated into RNA — is designated +1; there is no position 0. Positions upstream of the TSS (in the direction the polymerase has not yet traveled, toward the 5' end of the coding strand) are numbered with negative integers counting outward, so the TATA box at '-28' sits 28 base pairs before the first transcribed nucleotide. Positions downstream, inside the transcribed region, count upward from +1, so the DPE at '+30' sits within the earliest stretch of the transcript itself. The template strand and the coding (sense) strand also require care: the coding/sense strand has the same sequence as the RNA transcript (with T for U), while the template (antisense) strand is what Pol II actually reads 3' to 5' to synthesize RNA 5' to 3' — a diagram usually shows the sense strand, so the polymerase is understood to be moving along the strand beneath it in the opposite direction.

sections.heading: cis, trans, and three tiers of promoter geography
sections.body: A second axis of promoter vocabulary separates DNA elements from the proteins that bind them. A cis-acting element is a DNA sequence — a TATA box, an Inr, an enhancer — that only affects genes physically linked to it on the same DNA molecule. A trans-acting factor is a diffusible protein, like an activator or a general transcription factor, that can act on any copy of its binding site anywhere in the genome or even on a separate plasmid, because it finds its target by diffusing through the nucleus rather than by physical linkage. Overlaid on that distinction is promoter geography at three tiers: the core promoter (roughly -40 to +40, sufficient for basal, unregulated initiation and containing TATA/Inr/BRE/DPE), the proximal promoter (typically within a few hundred base pairs upstream, containing additional cis-elements bound by more activators/repressors that modulate but do not by themselves position initiation), and distal enhancers, which can sit tens of thousands of base pairs away — upstream, downstream, or even within an intron — and reach the promoter only through DNA looping mediated by Mediator and activator proteins, not through linear proximity.

lessons.workedExample: A student is shown a gene diagram with a box labeled 'TATA' at position -27, a bent arrow at +1, a shaded region from +28 to +34 labeled 'DPE,' a cluster of transcription-factor binding sites around -150, and a separate shaded region far to the left labeled 'enhancer, -35 kb.' Asked to describe the figure in words, a correct reading is: the bent arrow marks the TSS (+1); the TATA box, 27 bp upstream, and the DPE, about 30 bp downstream, are both core promoter elements working together (via TFIID) to position that same TSS; the -150 cluster is proximal promoter, modulating but not positioning initiation; and the -35 kb enhancer is a distal cis-element that must physically loop, via Mediator and activators (trans-acting factors), to reach the core promoter rather than acting through linear DNA distance.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge hands a student an unlabeled or partially labeled promoter diagram specifically to see if 'upstream,' 'downstream,' 'cis,' and 'trans' are working vocabulary rather than memorized terms. A weak answer gets the direction of upstream/downstream backwards or calls a bound protein a cis-element. A strong answer correctly locates elements relative to +1 without hesitation, distinguishes cis-DNA from trans-protein, and can explain that a distal enhancer's regulatory reach comes from DNA looping (via Mediator) rather than genomic proximity — showing the student can navigate a novel diagram, not just recite one they memorized.

questions.prompt: A cis-acting element and a trans-acting factor differ in what fundamental way?

options.text: Cis elements are DNA sequences that only affect genes on the same DNA molecule; trans factors are diffusible proteins that can act on any matching site in the genome
Cis elements are always upstream and trans factors are always downstream
Cis elements are proteins and trans factors are DNA sequences
There is no real difference; the terms are interchangeable synonyms

explanations.a: Correct — cis-acting means physically linked-DNA-only in its effect (it only regulates genes on that same molecule), while trans-acting means diffusible and able to act wherever its target sequence occurs, linked or not.
explanations.b: Cis and trans describe the linkage/diffusibility distinction, not upstream/downstream position; both cis-elements and the sites trans-factors bind can be upstream, downstream, or distal.
explanations.c: This reverses the definitions — cis-acting elements are DNA sequences, and trans-acting factors are the diffusible proteins that bind them.
explanations.d: The terms describe a specific and non-interchangeable distinction (linked-only DNA vs. diffusible protein) that is central to classical genetics and molecular biology.

questions.prompt: Order these promoter regions from closest to farthest from the transcription start site.

items.text: Core promoter (~ -40 to +40)
Proximal promoter (within a few hundred bp upstream)
Distal enhancer (can be tens of kilobases away)

questions.explanation: The core promoter sits immediately around the TSS, the proximal promoter extends somewhat further upstream with additional modulatory elements, and distal enhancers can sit tens of thousands of base pairs away, reaching the promoter only via DNA looping.

questions.prompt: On a standard promoter diagram, a DPE element is labeled at position +30. What does the '+30' tell you?

options.text: It sits 30 base pairs upstream of the TSS, outside the transcribed region
It sits 30 base pairs downstream of the TSS, within the earliest part of the transcript
It is 30 base pairs long, with no defined position
It sits exactly at the TSS, overlapping position +1

explanations.a: Upstream positions are numbered negatively; +30 is unambiguously downstream, inside the transcribed region, not upstream.
explanations.b: Correct — positive numbers count downstream from the TSS (+1), so +30 places the DPE about 30 bp into the earliest part of the transcript, consistent with its known position at roughly +28 to +34.
explanations.c: The '+30' label denotes position, not element length; length would be given separately (the DPE is a short, roughly 7-nucleotide element).
explanations.d: Position +1 is the TSS itself; +30 is well downstream of it, not overlapping it.

questions.prompt: Why does an enhancer 35 kb from a promoter still regulate that gene, given that linear DNA distance is so large?

options.text: The enhancer's effect travels through the cytoplasm as a diffusible signal unrelated to DNA structure
DNA looping, mediated by activators and the Mediator complex, brings the enhancer into physical proximity with the promoter despite the linear distance
35 kb is actually within the core promoter's normal range
The enhancer works only because it is cis-acting, and cis-acting elements ignore distance entirely

explanations.a: Enhancer action is a DNA/chromatin-level, not cytoplasmic-diffusion, phenomenon; the enhancer's regulatory sequence itself does not travel — the DNA loops.
explanations.b: Correct — activators bound at the distal enhancer contact Mediator's tail module, and Mediator's head/middle modules dock on the promoter-bound PIC, physically looping the DNA so the enhancer and promoter meet despite tens of kilobases of linear separation.
explanations.c: The core promoter is defined as roughly -40 to +40; 35 kb is far outside that range and falls in distal-enhancer territory instead.
explanations.d: Being cis-acting means the enhancer only affects genes on the same DNA molecule, not that distance is irrelevant — looping is exactly the mechanism that overcomes the distance.

units.label: Transcriptional Activation: Enhancers, Activators & DNA-Binding Domains

lessons.label: Enhancers and Action at a Distance

sections.heading: A sequence that works from anywhere
sections.body: Banerji, Rusconi, and Schaffner (1981) fused a fragment of SV40 viral DNA to a rabbit beta-globin gene and found transcription jumped roughly 200-fold, even though the fragment was not a promoter. The result that defined the enhancer as its own regulatory class was what survived when they moved it: placed as far as 1,400 base pairs upstream of the gene's start site, or more than 3,300 base pairs downstream of it, and tested in both possible orientations at each position, the fragment still activated transcription to a similar degree every time. A promoter has to sit immediately upstream of the start site in a fixed orientation; an enhancer does not. That position- and orientation-independence, not activation strength itself, is the operational definition still used to call a sequence an enhancer today. Decades later, genome-wide chromatin profiling showed the same functional signature at thousands of endogenous mammalian loci: candidate enhancers are now routinely flagged by histone marks such as H3K27ac and H3K4me1 long before their target gene or exact distance is even known, which is only possible because position independence, not proximity, is what the definition actually demands.

sections.heading: Reaching the promoter by looping, not scanning
sections.body: If an enhancer can sit tens of kilobases from its target gene, how does it find the promoter? The accepted model is direct physical contact through DNA looping: the intervening DNA bulges out while activator proteins bound at the enhancer touch Mediator and the general transcription machinery bound at the promoter, with the loop often stabilized by cohesin. This is why enhancers are not simply diffusing signals — they require a specific loop to form, and a study locus can have several candidate enhancers of which only the one that loops to a given promoter drives it.

sections.heading: CTCF, cohesin, and insulators keep loops honest
sections.body: Unrestricted looping would let enhancers activate the wrong genes across a chromosome, so cells constrain which enhancer reaches which promoter. CTCF, identified by Lobanenkov and colleagues around 1990, binds thousands of genomic sites; cohesin extrudes DNA loops that stall at convergently-oriented CTCF sites, producing the topologically associating domain (TAD) boundaries described by Dixon and colleagues (2012). Enhancers and promoters loop efficiently within a TAD but are blocked from reaching across a boundary. Insulator elements make this concrete at single loci: the Drosophila gypsy insulator, bound by the Su(Hw) protein (Geyer and Corces, 1992), blocks an enhancer from activating a promoter only when placed between them, leaving both element's function intact elsewhere — proof that insulation is about position relative to the enhancer-promoter pair, not about disabling either element.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher studies a gene with an enhancer 40 kb upstream. In wild-type cells the two loop together and the gene is expressed. She inserts a CTCF-bound insulator sequence directly between the enhancer and the promoter, keeping both elements otherwise untouched, and expression drops close to baseline. Moving the same insulator to a position downstream of the gene, outside the enhancer-promoter interval, leaves expression normal. Deleting the CTCF sites from the insulator so it can no longer be bound restores looping and expression even when the sequence is still present between them. The pattern — blocked only when between, in a CTCF-dependent way — is what identifies insulator function experimentally, as opposed to simple silencing.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing an enhancer claim wants to know whether the student understands that distance and orientation are irrelevant to enhancer function but position relative to insulators is not. A weak answer says 'the enhancer turns the gene on from far away' without addressing how it reaches the promoter. A strong answer names the looping mechanism, explains why an insulator placed between the two elements blocks activation while placement elsewhere does not, and recognizes that CTCF/cohesin loop boundaries are what keep a given enhancer from mis-activating a neighboring gene's promoter.

questions.prompt: In the Banerji, Rusconi, and Schaffner (1981) experiment, what property of the SV40 fragment defined it as an enhancer rather than a promoter?

options.text: It only activated transcription when placed immediately upstream of the start site
It activated transcription even when moved to a new distance or flipped in orientation
It bound RNA polymerase directly and initiated transcription itself
It only worked in SV40-infected cells, not in the beta-globin construct

explanations.a: That behavior describes a promoter, which is exactly what the SV40 fragment was shown not to be.
explanations.b: Correct — surviving relocation and orientation flips, unlike a promoter, is the defining operational test for an enhancer.
explanations.c: Enhancers work through bound activator proteins contacting the machinery at the promoter, not by binding polymerase directly themselves.
explanations.d: The fragment worked in the beta-globin construct itself, which is the whole point of the experiment — it activated a heterologous gene.

questions.prompt: Why does a gypsy insulator only block gene expression when placed between the enhancer and the promoter, not when placed elsewhere?

options.text: Because Su(Hw) binding degrades the enhancer sequence itself
Because insulator function depends on interrupting the specific loop connecting that enhancer to that promoter
Because the insulator recruits HDACs that silence the whole chromosome
Because the promoter cannot initiate transcription once any insulator sequence exists nearby

explanations.a: The enhancer remains intact and functional elsewhere; the insulator does not chemically alter it.
explanations.b: Correct — insulators block enhancer-promoter communication positionally, by preventing the loop between that specific pair from forming or functioning.
explanations.c: Enhancer-blocking insulators act locally on a specific loop, not by broad chromatin silencing via HDACs.
explanations.d: Placement outside the enhancer-promoter interval leaves the promoter fully responsive, so nearby presence alone is not sufficient to block it.

questions.prompt: Order the events by which a distal enhancer activates its target gene.

items.text: Activator proteins bind the enhancer sequence
Cohesin-mediated loop extrusion brings the enhancer near the promoter, stalling at convergent CTCF sites
Enhancer-bound activators contact Mediator and the general transcription machinery at the promoter
Transcription is activated at the target gene

questions.explanation: Activators must first occupy the enhancer, then the loop bringing enhancer and promoter into proximity has to form (bounded by CTCF), before direct contact with the promoter-bound machinery can trigger transcription.

questions.prompt: Match each element or protein to its role in enhancer-promoter communication.

right.text: Marks TAD boundaries where loop extrusion stalls
Extrudes DNA to physically form enhancer-promoter loops
Blocks a specific enhancer from reaching a promoter when positioned between them

questions.explanation: CTCF sites define where loops are permitted to stall (TAD boundaries); cohesin is the motor that extrudes the loop itself; the gypsy insulator is a concrete single-locus example of position-dependent enhancer blocking.

lessons.label: Modular Activators: DNA-Binding Plus Activation Domains

sections.heading: Two jobs, two separable parts
sections.body: A transcriptional activator has to do two unrelated things: find its specific site in a genome of billions of base pairs, and then persuade the transcription machinery to act once it is there. Brent and Ptashne (1985) tested whether these jobs live in separable protein domains by fusing the DNA-binding domain of the bacterial repressor LexA to the activation domain of the yeast activator GAL4. The chimera bound LexA operator sites, as expected from its DNA-binding half, but it also activated transcription from a promoter carrying those sites — a function LexA alone never has. A related fusion pairing the GAL4 DNA-binding domain with the herpesvirus VP16 activation domain (the 'GAL4-VP16' fusion used constantly since as a research tool) showed the same modularity in the other direction. Swapping a domain between two proteins that share no evolutionary relationship and having both halves work exactly as their donors did is the clean evidence that DNA-binding and activation are independent modules, not a single folded surface.

sections.heading: Activation domains come in a few recurring flavors
sections.body: Once activation domains were known to be separable, their sequences turned out to cluster into a small number of types named for their amino acid bias rather than a shared fold. GAL4 and VP16 carry acidic activation domains, rich in aspartate and glutamate, and functionally interchangeable across species from yeast to human, which is why VP16 works when fused to a yeast DNA-binding domain at all (Triezenberg and colleagues, 1988). Sp1 carries glutamine-rich activation domains (Courey and Tjian, 1988). CTF/NF1 carries a proline-rich domain (Mermod and colleagues, 1989). None of these domains has a single defined structure on its own; most are intrinsically disordered until they contact a partner.

sections.heading: Recruitment, not allostery, is the mechanism
sections.body: Ptashne and Gann (1997) argued for what is now the standard model: an activator does not allosterically switch on an already-assembled transcription machine. It works by recruitment — the activation domain is simply a tethered interaction surface that raises the local concentration of Mediator, coactivators, and general transcription factors at the promoter, biasing an equilibrium binding reaction toward assembly. Evidence for recruitment over allostery comes from experiments in which an activation domain is replaced with an unrelated protein-interaction domain that binds a component of the machinery directly (bypassing normal signaling) and still activates transcription — the specific chemistry of the activation domain barely matters as long as it recruits the right target.

lessons.workedExample: A student wants to know whether a novel plant transcription factor's C-terminal 60 residues function as an activation domain, independent of its zinc-finger DNA-binding region. Following the Brent and Ptashne logic, she fuses just those 60 residues to the well-characterized GAL4 DNA-binding domain and places the construct in yeast alongside a reporter gene driven by GAL4-binding sites. If the reporter turns on, the 60 residues are activation-competent even divorced from their native DNA-binding context and species, which is exactly the modularity test the LexA-GAL4 and GAL4-VP16 fusions established as a standard assay decades earlier.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about modularity because it tests whether a student understands mechanism versus memorized vocabulary. A weak answer says an activator 'binds DNA and turns the gene on' as if that were one act. A strong answer explains that the two functions are separable because they live in different protein domains, cites the domain-swap logic (a DNA-binding domain from one protein fused to an activation domain from an unrelated one still works), and can explain recruitment — that the activation domain's job is to be a tether that raises local concentration of the machinery, not to flip an allosteric switch.

questions.prompt: What did the Brent and Ptashne (1985) LexA-GAL4 fusion experiment demonstrate?

options.text: That LexA and GAL4 evolved from a shared ancestral gene
That DNA-binding and activation functions reside in separable, independently swappable protein domains
That bacterial repressors cannot function in eukaryotic cells under any circumstances
That GAL4's activation domain only works when attached to its own native DNA-binding domain

explanations.a: LexA and GAL4 are unrelated proteins from different domains of life; the experiment's power comes from that lack of relatedness.
explanations.b: Correct — the fusion protein bound LexA operator sites and activated transcription, showing each half retained its donor's function independent of the other.
explanations.c: The fusion protein did function in the assay; the point was that LexA's DNA-binding domain, when paired with an activation domain, gained activation capability it lacked alone.
explanations.d: The opposite was shown: the GAL4 activation domain worked when fused to LexA's unrelated DNA-binding domain, proving it does not require its native partner.

questions.prompt: Under the recruitment model of Ptashne and Gann (1997), how does an activation domain increase transcription?

options.text: It allosterically changes the shape of an already-assembled polymerase complex
It tethers and raises the local concentration of Mediator and general transcription factors at the promoter
It directly catalyzes phosphodiester bond formation during RNA synthesis
It physically displaces the DNA-binding domain once bound

explanations.a: Recruitment was proposed as an alternative to allosteric activation of a pre-assembled complex; the machinery is not switched on by a shape change induced from a distance.
explanations.b: Correct — the activation domain acts as a tethered interaction surface, biasing assembly of the transcription machinery by local concentration, not by chemical catalysis or allostery.
explanations.c: Catalysis of the phosphodiester bond is RNA polymerase's job, unrelated to what an activation domain contributes.
explanations.d: The DNA-binding domain stays bound to DNA throughout; it is not displaced by the activation domain.

questions.prompt: Match each activation domain type to a transcription factor that carries it.

right.text: GAL4 / VP16
Sp1
CTF/NF1

questions.explanation: GAL4 and VP16 are the classic acidic-domain examples; Sp1's activation domain is glutamine-rich (Courey and Tjian, 1988); CTF/NF1 carries a proline-rich domain (Mermod and colleagues, 1989).

questions.prompt: Order the logical steps of the domain-swap test for modularity.

items.text: Identify two unrelated proteins, one with a known DNA-binding domain, one with a known activation domain
Fuse the DNA-binding domain of one to the activation domain of the other
Place the fusion protein's binding sites upstream of a reporter gene
Observe whether the reporter is activated, indicating both domains retained their function independent of their native partner

questions.explanation: The logic requires starting from unrelated donor proteins, constructing the chimera, placing it in a context that reports on DNA binding plus activation together, and then reading out whether the swap preserved function.

lessons.label: How Transcription Factors Read DNA

sections.heading: The major groove is where the message is
sections.body: DNA's major groove exposes a distinct pattern of hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors for each of the four base pairs, wide enough for an alpha helix to sit inside and read that pattern without unwinding the duplex. Most sequence-specific DNA-binding domains work by inserting a recognition helix into the major groove and making direct hydrogen bonds and van der Waals contacts to particular bases, plus indirect readout of the groove's local width and flexibility. The minor groove, by contrast, is narrow and gives comparatively little base-specific information, which is why almost every major DNA-binding-domain family converges on a major-groove recognition helix despite having no shared evolutionary origin.

sections.heading: Four families, four solutions
sections.body: The helix-turn-helix motif, characterized structurally in bacteriophage lambda repressor and conserved into the eukaryotic homeodomain (reviewed by Pabo and Sauer), uses a short helix-turn-helix unit in which the second, 'recognition' helix sits in the major groove while the first helix packs against it and the backbone. C2H2 zinc fingers, first identified in the RNA polymerase III factor TFIIIA (Miller, McLachlan, and Klug, 1985), use a zinc ion coordinated by two cysteines and two histidines to fold a small beta-beta-alpha unit whose alpha helix reads roughly three consecutive base pairs; the Pavletich and Pabo (1991) structure of Zif268 bound to DNA showed how tandem fingers can be strung together to read longer sequences finger by finger, which is why zinc-finger proteins are so easy to engineer for new targets. The basic leucine zipper (bZIP), named by Landschulz, Johnson, and McKnight (1988) for the C/EBP protein, pairs a coiled-coil dimerization helix (the 'zipper,' with leucines every seventh residue) with an adjacent stretch of basic residues that grips the major groove only once two monomers have zipped together, as the DNA-bound GCN4 structure of Ellenberger, Brandl, Struhl, and Harrison (1992) showed directly. The basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH) family, exemplified by the muscle regulator MyoD (Davis, Weintraub, and Lassar, 1987; family characterized by Murre, McCaw, and Baltimore, 1989), uses the same basic-region-plus-dimerization logic as bZIP but folds the dimerization interface as two short helices connected by a loop instead of a zipper.

sections.heading: Dimerization is a specificity switch, not just glue
sections.body: For bZIP and bHLH factors, the DNA-binding basic region only becomes ordered and DNA-competent after dimerization, so which partner a factor dimerizes with determines both the binding-site sequence read and whether the complex activates or represses at all. MyoD, for instance, must heterodimerize with the ubiquitous bHLH protein E12/E47 to bind DNA productively, and swapping which bHLH or bZIP partners pair together (as happens naturally between Fos and Jun, or Myc and Max) rewires binding-site preference without changing either partner's amino acid sequence.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher has two bZIP proteins, A and B, each of which forms a stable homodimer and a stable heterodimer (A-B) in vitro. Homodimer A-A binds the sequence TGACTCA, homodimer B-B binds a related but distinct sequence, and the heterodimer A-B binds a third, intermediate sequence not efficiently bound by either homodimer. This is expected under the leucine-zipper model: the basic region contributed by each monomer only folds into DNA-reading conformation once dimerized, so the composite binding surface facing the major groove differs depending on which two basic regions are brought together, giving the cell three genuinely different regulatory outputs from two gene products.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'how does this transcription factor recognize its target sequence' is testing whether the student can go past 'it binds DNA' to a structural mechanism. A weak answer stops at binding as a black box. A strong answer names the family (zinc finger, bZIP, bHLH, or homeodomain/HTH), explains that a helix reads bases in the major groove, and — for the dimerizing families — explains that specificity is only achieved after two monomers pair up, so partner choice itself is a regulatory variable.

questions.prompt: Why do most sequence-specific DNA-binding domains insert a recognition helix into the major groove rather than the minor groove?

options.text: The major groove is wide enough for a helix and exposes a base-specific hydrogen-bonding pattern; the minor groove gives little base-specific information
The minor groove is chemically identical for all four base pairs, so no protein has ever evolved to bind it
Helices cannot physically fit into the minor groove at any point along the helix
DNA polymerase blocks all minor-groove access during transcription

explanations.a: Correct — the major groove's width and distinct donor/acceptor pattern per base pair make it the information-rich groove for helix-based readout.
explanations.b: The minor groove is not chemically identical across base pairs, and some proteins do read it via indirect readout of shape, but it carries far less base-specific information than the major groove.
explanations.c: The minor groove is simply narrower and less informative, not physically inaccessible to any protein element.
explanations.d: DNA-binding-domain recognition is unrelated to polymerase activity and occurs independent of ongoing transcription.

questions.prompt: What did the Pavletich and Pabo (1991) Zif268-DNA structure show about C2H2 zinc fingers?

options.text: A single zinc finger reads an entire operator sequence of over ten base pairs alone
Tandem zinc fingers each read roughly three base pairs, so stringing fingers together reads longer sequences
Zinc fingers bind DNA without requiring a coordinated zinc ion
Zinc fingers only function as part of a leucine-zipper dimer

explanations.a: A single finger's alpha helix reads only a few base pairs, not an entire long operator on its own.
explanations.b: Correct — this modular, finger-by-finger readout of roughly three base pairs each is why zinc-finger arrays are readily engineered for new DNA targets.
explanations.c: The zinc ion, coordinated by two cysteines and two histidines, is required to fold the finger into its DNA-binding conformation.
explanations.d: Zinc fingers are a structurally distinct family from bZIP; they do not require leucine-zipper dimerization to bind DNA.

questions.prompt: Match each DNA-binding-domain family to a defining structural feature.

right.text: Recognition helix held by a second packing helix, no metal or dimerization required
Zinc ion coordinated by two cysteines and two histidines folds a small recognition unit
Coiled-coil dimerization helix adjacent to a basic DNA-reading region
Two short helices connected by a loop mediate dimerization next to a basic region

questions.explanation: Each family solves major-groove readout differently: HTH/homeodomain needs no metal or obligate dimer, zinc fingers use a structural zinc ion, bZIP uses a leucine-zipper coiled coil, and bHLH uses a helix-loop-helix dimerization interface.

questions.prompt: In the worked example, why does the A-B heterodimer bind a different sequence than either the A-A or B-B homodimer?

options.text: Because the basic DNA-reading region only folds productively once dimerization brings each monomer's basic region into a specific composite arrangement
Because heterodimers always bind DNA with lower affinity than homodimers
Because A and B have entirely different amino acid sequences in their heterodimer form
Because the leucine zipper region itself directly contacts the bases

explanations.a: Correct — bZIP basic regions are only DNA-competent after dimerization, so the identity of the dimer partner sets the composite binding surface and therefore the sequence preference.
explanations.b: The example does not establish an affinity ranking, only that the three dimers read different sequences; heterodimers are not inherently weaker binders.
explanations.c: Each protein's amino acid sequence is fixed regardless of dimer partner; only the pairing, not the sequence, changes.
explanations.d: The leucine zipper mediates dimerization; base contacts are made by the basic region, not the zipper helix itself.

lessons.label: Combinatorial Control and the Enhanceosome

sections.heading: A rigid assembly, not a loose crowd
sections.body: The human interferon-beta enhancer, roughly 55 base pairs of DNA activated within hours of viral infection, is the best-worked example of an enhanceosome: a higher-order nucleoprotein complex in which multiple transcription factors bind cooperatively in a fixed, precise arrangement to produce activation far greater than the sum of the factors acting alone. Thanos and Maniatis (1995) showed that the enhancer requires simultaneous binding of NF-kB (the p50/p65 dimer), interferon regulatory factors (the specific paralogs shown to occupy the enhancer in vivo, IRF-3 and IRF-7, were pinned down by follow-up work later in the 1990s), and the ATF-2/c-Jun heterodimer, together with the architectural protein HMGI(Y) (now called HMGA1), which bends the DNA to let the other factors dock against each other as well as against the DNA. That follow-up work culminated in Panne, Maniatis, and Harrison's 2007 crystal structure of the assembled interferon-beta enhanceosome, which visualized the cooperative, spacing-dependent geometry directly: the eight-protein complex wraps almost a full turn around the bent DNA, with NF-kB, the IRFs, and ATF-2/c-Jun packed edge-to-edge so that each factor's surface touches its neighbors' surfaces as well as the DNA backbone, leaving no gaps where an incorrectly spaced site could still support the same set of contacts.

sections.heading: Spacing is not decoration, it is the logic
sections.body: What makes the interferon-beta enhancer an enhanceosome rather than an ordinary cluster of binding sites is that the sites are essentially unchangeable in their spacing and helical phasing. Insertion or deletion of even a few base pairs between binding sites, which rotates the sites relative to each other around the double helix or shifts which face of the DNA each protein approaches from, collapses cooperative assembly and activation, even though every individual factor can still bind its own site in isolation. The complex only works as an integrated three-dimensional surface, with each protein contacting not just DNA but its neighbors — which is also why no single factor, including NF-kB alone, can substitute for the whole assembly; viral infection alone is not sufficient without all of the required signals converging.

sections.heading: Combinatorial control from a small factor set
sections.body: The deeper lesson generalizes past interferon-beta: a cell has on the order of one to two thousand transcription factors but needs to specify thousands of distinct expression programs across hundreds of cell types and countless combinations of inducing signals. Combinatorial control resolves that mismatch — a given enhancer requires a specific combination of factors present simultaneously (here, an antiviral signal through IRFs, an inflammatory signal through NF-kB, and a stress/growth-factor signal through ATF-2/Jun, all three at once), so genes are not switched by single master regulators one at a time but by the intersection of several independently regulated inputs. A cell type or condition is defined less by which transcription factors exist and more by which specific combinations are simultaneously active at each enhancer.

lessons.workedExample: A student is given four transcription factor binding sites cloned in their natural order and spacing upstream of a reporter gene, matching the interferon-beta enhancer layout, and observes strong, virus-inducible activation. She then makes two mutants: one that deletes five base pairs between two of the sites (altering spacing and helical phase without removing any binding site), and one that swaps the order of two sites while keeping the same overall spacing. Both mutants show sharply reduced induction even though every individual factor still binds its site by gel-shift assay — direct evidence that the enhanceosome's function depends on precise geometric arrangement, not merely the presence of the right binding sites somewhere in the region.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes enhanceosome assembly because it distinguishes students who understand cooperative, geometry-dependent transcription factor complexes from those who think of transcription factors as independent on/off switches. A weak answer says 'several transcription factors turn the gene on together.' A strong answer explains that the factors must bind in a fixed spatial arrangement enforced by exact spacing, names the interferon-beta enhanceosome and its factors (NF-kB, IRFs, ATF-2/Jun, HMGA1), and can predict that disrupting spacing (not just removing a site) would abolish cooperative activation even if every factor can still bind on its own.

questions.prompt: In the interferon-beta enhanceosome, why does inserting a few base pairs between two binding sites collapse activation even though both factors can still bind their individual sites?

options.text: Because the insertion mutates the binding sites themselves so the factors can no longer bind
Because it rotates the sites relative to each other on the helix, disrupting the precise protein-protein contacts the assembly requires
Because HMGI(Y) can no longer bind DNA at all once any base pair is added
Because the reporter gene's promoter is physically destroyed by the insertion

explanations.a: The premise states each factor can still bind its own site individually by assay, so the sites themselves remain intact.
explanations.b: Correct — the enhanceosome depends on fixed helical phasing so that factors bound at different sites present compatible surfaces to each other; shifting spacing breaks those protein-protein contacts even with intact DNA binding.
explanations.c: HMGI(Y)/HMGA1 bends DNA to assist assembly, but the described defect is spacing-dependent cooperativity, not a total loss of HMGI(Y) binding.
explanations.d: The insertion is between binding sites in the enhancer, not in the promoter, and the defect described is cooperative assembly, not promoter damage.

questions.prompt: What is the core idea of combinatorial control as illustrated by the interferon-beta enhancer needing NF-kB, IRFs, and ATF-2/Jun simultaneously?

options.text: A single master transcription factor is sufficient to activate any target gene given enough time
Specific gene expression outcomes arise from the simultaneous intersection of several independently regulated factors, not one factor acting alone
Every gene in the genome uses the identical set of transcription factors
Transcription factors act independently of each other and their effects simply add up linearly

explanations.a: The enhanceosome explicitly requires multiple factors together; no single one, including NF-kB, is sufficient alone.
explanations.b: Correct — combinatorial control lets a limited pool of transcription factors specify a huge number of distinct outcomes through which combinations co-occur at a given enhancer.
explanations.c: Different genes require different, often small, combinations of factors, which is exactly why combinatorial control gives specificity.
explanations.d: The whole enhanceosome finding is that these factors act cooperatively, producing more than an additive effect, not independently.

questions.prompt: Match each interferon-beta enhanceosome component to its contribution.

right.text: Bends the DNA to allow neighboring factors to contact each other
Carries the antiviral-signal-responsive binding activity
Carries the inflammatory-signal-responsive binding activity

questions.explanation: NF-kB responds to inflammatory/immune signaling, the IRFs respond to the antiviral signaling branch, and HMGI(Y)/HMGA1 is the architectural protein that bends DNA to enable the cooperative protein-protein surface.

questions.prompt: Order the requirements for the interferon-beta enhanceosome to activate transcription, from most basic to most specific.

items.text: Each individual transcription factor can bind its own site on naked DNA
All required factors (NF-kB, IRFs, ATF-2/Jun) are simultaneously present and active in the cell
The binding sites are arranged with exact natural spacing and helical phasing
Cooperative, higher-than-additive transcriptional activation occurs

questions.explanation: Individual site binding is a baseline capability; full activation additionally requires all signals to converge simultaneously and the correct geometric spacing, and only then does cooperative enhanceosome-level activation follow.

lessons.label: Signal-Responsive Transcription Factors

sections.heading: Nuclear receptors: the ligand is the switch
