sections.body: Steroid hormone receptors such as the glucocorticoid receptor and estrogen receptor, characterized in large part through work from Yamamoto's lab, sit latent in the cytoplasm bound to chaperones including hsp90, which masks their DNA-binding and nuclear-localization surfaces. Hormone binding to the receptor's ligand-binding domain triggers a conformational change that releases the chaperone, exposes a nuclear localization signal, and lets the receptor translocate to the nucleus, dimerize, and bind palindromic hormone-response elements (an HRE for glucocorticoid, an ERE for estrogen) to recruit coactivators. Because the ligand itself is small and membrane-permeant, this pathway couples an extracellular or circulating chemical signal to transcription with no cell-surface receptor or second messenger required at all.

sections.heading: NF-kB: held inactive by a dedicated inhibitor
sections.body: NF-kB, discovered by Sen and Baltimore (1986) as a B-cell nuclear factor binding an immunoglobulin enhancer, uses an entirely different latency mechanism: it is a preformed dimer (commonly p50/p65) sitting in the cytoplasm bound to the inhibitor IkB, which masks its nuclear localization signal (Baeuerle and Baltimore, 1988). Inflammatory or infection signals activate the IkB kinase (IKK) complex, which phosphorylates IkB, marking it for ubiquitination and rapid proteasomal degradation. Once IkB is destroyed, NF-kB is free to enter the nucleus within minutes — a much faster response than synthesizing a new transcription factor from scratch, because the protein was already made and simply waiting. That speed comes with a built-in shutoff: one of the genes NF-kB itself switches on is IkB-alpha, so newly made inhibitor accumulates, re-enters the nucleus, strips NF-kB back off its DNA sites, and exports it to the cytoplasm again. Hoffmann, Levchenko, Scott, and Baltimore (2002) showed this negative-feedback loop drives NF-kB activity into damped oscillations after a sustained stimulus rather than a single flat pulse, so the same nuclear-entry mechanism that makes the response fast is also what resolves it.

sections.heading: STAT and CREB/CBP: two more routes from signal to promoter
sections.body: The JAK-STAT pathway, worked out substantially by Darnell, Kerr, and Stark in the early 1990s, links cytokine receptors directly to transcription: cytokine binding activates receptor-associated Janus kinases (JAKs), which phosphorylate a tyrosine on a STAT protein; the phosphotyrosine is then recognized by the SH2 domain of a second STAT molecule, driving STAT dimerization, nuclear entry, and DNA binding, without a diffusible small-molecule second messenger at all. CREB works downstream of the diffusible second messenger cAMP: a rise in cAMP activates protein kinase A, which phosphorylates CREB at serine 133; that single phosphorylation creates a docking surface recognized by the coactivator CBP (Chrivia and colleagues, 1993; Kwok and colleagues, 1994 showed Ser133 phosphorylation is what CBP binding depends on), which then bridges CREB to the general transcription machinery.

lessons.workedExample: A cell is exposed to three stimuli in sequence: cortisol (a glucocorticoid), a bacterial lipopolysaccharide challenge, and a rise in cAMP from a Gs-coupled receptor. Tracing each to its transcription factor: cortisol diffuses into the cell, binds the glucocorticoid receptor in the cytoplasm, displaces hsp90, and the receptor dimer translocates to bind glucocorticoid-response elements. The bacterial challenge activates IKK, which phosphorylates and destroys IkB, freeing cytoplasmic NF-kB to enter the nucleus within minutes. The cAMP rise activates PKA, which phosphorylates CREB at Ser133, recruiting CBP. Three signals, three distinct latency-release mechanisms — ligand-triggered chaperone release, inhibitor destruction, and activating phosphorylation — converging on the same general strategy of getting a pre-existing or newly competent factor into the nucleus and onto DNA quickly.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking 'how does this factor get activated' wants the mechanistic link between an upstream signal and nuclear activity, not just the name of the pathway. A weak answer says 'the signal activates the transcription factor.' A strong answer names the specific latency-release event — chaperone release for nuclear receptors, IkB degradation for NF-kB, tyrosine phosphorylation and SH2-mediated dimerization for STAT, or Ser133 phosphorylation creating a CBP-docking site for CREB — and can explain why that mechanism gives a fast, reversible, and stimulus-specific response instead of requiring new protein synthesis.

questions.prompt: What keeps the glucocorticoid receptor inactive in the cytoplasm before hormone binding?

options.text: Binding to hsp90 and other chaperones, which masks its DNA-binding and nuclear-localization surfaces
Continuous phosphorylation by IKK
Sequestration by IkB
Its mRNA is not translated until hormone is present

explanations.a: Correct — chaperone binding, notably hsp90, masks the receptor's functional surfaces until hormone binding triggers their release.
explanations.b: IKK phosphorylation of IkB is the NF-kB activation mechanism, not the nuclear receptor mechanism.
explanations.c: IkB is the NF-kB inhibitor, a separate pathway from nuclear hormone receptors.
explanations.d: The receptor protein is already present and folded in the cytoplasm; it is chaperone-masked, not withheld at the translation step.

questions.prompt: Why does destroying IkB activate NF-kB faster than a pathway requiring new protein synthesis?

options.text: Because NF-kB itself is synthesized only after IkB is degraded
Because the NF-kB dimer is already made and simply waiting in the cytoplasm, so releasing it needs no transcription or translation
Because IkB degradation directly phosphorylates NF-kB, activating it chemically
Because proteasomal degradation of IkB takes hours, giving cells time to prepare NF-kB

explanations.a: NF-kB is preformed and cytoplasmic prior to signaling, not synthesized in response to IkB loss.
explanations.b: Correct — because the p50/p65 dimer already exists, simply removing its inhibitor is a fast, minutes-scale release rather than requiring gene expression.
explanations.c: IkB degradation removes the inhibitor; it does not itself chemically modify NF-kB.
explanations.d: IKK-triggered ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of IkB is rapid, which is precisely what makes this route fast, not slow.

questions.prompt: Match each signal-responsive transcription factor to the specific event that releases or activates it.

right.text: Hormone binding displaces chaperones, exposing nuclear localization signal
IKK-triggered phosphorylation and degradation of its inhibitor
JAK-mediated tyrosine phosphorylation drives SH2-domain dimerization
PKA phosphorylates Ser133, creating a CBP-docking site

questions.explanation: Each factor uses a distinct latency-release event: ligand-triggered chaperone release for nuclear receptors, inhibitor destruction for NF-kB, phosphorylation-driven dimerization for STAT, and a single activating phosphorylation creating a coactivator-docking site for CREB.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the JAK-STAT pathway from cytokine binding to transcription.

items.text: Cytokine binds its cell-surface receptor
Receptor-associated JAK phosphorylates a tyrosine on STAT
A second STAT's SH2 domain binds the phosphotyrosine, driving STAT dimerization
The STAT dimer enters the nucleus and binds DNA to activate transcription

questions.explanation: Cytokine binding activates the receptor-associated JAK, which phosphorylates STAT; that phosphotyrosine recruits a second STAT via its SH2 domain to form the dimer, which then translocates and binds DNA.

lessons.label: Repression Mechanisms

sections.heading: Passive repression: taking the activator's spot or its neighbor's function
sections.body: The simplest way to shut a gene off is competitive DNA binding: a repressor occupies the same or an overlapping site an activator would otherwise use, so the two can never bind simultaneously. The Myc-Max/Mad-Max system is a clean example — Myc heterodimerizes with Max to activate E-box-driven genes, while Mad proteins compete for the same Max partner and the same E-box sites, so which heterodimer wins access determines whether the gene turns on or off. A related but distinct passive mechanism is quenching, in which a repressor bound at its own nearby site does not touch the activator's DNA at all but instead directly contacts and neutralizes an activator bound a short distance away, blocking that activator's activation domain from reaching the machinery. Short-range quenching by the Drosophila repressors Knirps and Kruppel, studied extensively in the even-skipped stripe enhancers, works this way: the repressor's effect is confined to roughly 100 base pairs, so it silences only nearby activators, not ones further along the same enhancer.

sections.heading: Active repression: recruiting machinery that undoes activation
sections.body: Active repression instead recruits enzymatic machinery that changes chromatin state. The clearest example is nuclear hormone receptors in their unliganded state: the unliganded thyroid hormone receptor and retinoic acid receptor bind their response elements but, instead of recruiting coactivators, recruit the corepressors NCoR (Hörlein and colleagues, 1995) or the related SMRT (Chen and Evans, 1995). NCoR/SMRT in turn bring in histone deacetylase complexes (HDAC3 in particular), which strip acetyl groups from nearby histone tails, favoring a more condensed, less accessible chromatin state and directly opposing activation. Some repressors carry their own dedicated repression domains that recruit corepressors independent of any nuclear receptor — the homeodomain protein Engrailed, for instance, has a well-characterized repression domain distinct from any activation function.

sections.heading: Distinguishing the categories at a locus
sections.body: The practical distinction for an experimenter is what happens if you remove the repressor's binding site instead of the repressor's effector domain. Losing an insulator's CTCF site or a competitive repressor's overlapping binding site restores activation because it was blocking access, not adding a negative activity — a passive mechanism. Losing a corepressor-recruitment domain from a repressor that still binds DNA fine, by contrast, blocks its ability to actively silence even though it still occupies its site, because the repression came from actively recruited HDAC activity rather than merely obstructing an activator's access.

lessons.workedExample: A gene is silenced in undifferentiated cells and a repressor protein is found bound at its promoter. To test whether repression is active or passive, a researcher makes two mutants: one deletes the repressor's DNA-binding domain (it can no longer bind the promoter at all), and one deletes only a small C-terminal motif previously shown to recruit NCoR, leaving DNA binding intact. The DNA-binding mutant simply fails to occupy the site, so nothing can be concluded about mechanism from it alone. The NCoR-recruitment mutant, however, still binds the promoter (confirmed by chromatin immunoprecipitation) yet the gene is now expressed — direct evidence that repression required active corepressor recruitment, not merely occupancy of the site, which rules out simple competitive exclusion as the mechanism.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking 'how is this gene being repressed' wants a mechanism, not just the word 'repressor.' A weak answer treats all repression as interchangeable silencing. A strong answer distinguishes passive mechanisms (competitive binding, short-range quenching of a nearby activator) from active mechanisms (corepressor recruitment such as NCoR/SMRT bringing in HDACs, or a dedicated repression domain), and can describe the experimental test that tells them apart — does losing the repressor's binding site alone restore expression, or does the repressor need to be present but its effector function specifically disabled?

questions.prompt: What distinguishes quenching from simple competitive DNA binding as a repression mechanism?

options.text: Quenching involves the repressor binding its own nearby site and directly contacting a neighboring activator, rather than occupying the activator's own binding site
Quenching only occurs in bacteria, never in Drosophila or mammals
Competitive binding requires HDAC recruitment while quenching does not
Quenching and competitive binding are simply two names for the identical mechanism

explanations.a: Correct — in quenching the repressor binds its own site and reaches over to neutralize a nearby activator's activation domain, whereas competitive binding directly occupies the activator's site.
explanations.b: Quenching is specifically documented in Drosophila short-range repressors like Knirps and Kruppel at the even-skipped enhancers, among other systems.
explanations.c: Competitive DNA binding is a passive mechanism that does not require HDAC recruitment; that describes active corepressor-based repression instead.
explanations.d: They are mechanistically distinct: one blocks access to a shared site, the other neutralizes a nearby-bound activator directly.

questions.prompt: In the worked example, what does the NCoR-recruitment-domain deletion mutant (which still binds DNA) demonstrate when the gene becomes expressed?

options.text: That the repressor never actually bound the promoter in the first place
That repression depended on active corepressor recruitment, not merely on the repressor occupying its site
That the gene was never actually repressed to begin with
That HDAC activity is irrelevant to this gene's regulation

explanations.a: Chromatin immunoprecipitation confirmed the mutant still binds the promoter, ruling this out.
explanations.b: Correct — since binding was retained but repression was lost only when the corepressor-recruitment motif was removed, the effector function (not occupancy) was necessary, identifying active repression.
explanations.c: The premise states the gene is normally silenced by this repressor in undifferentiated cells; the mutant experiment is what reveals the mechanism.
explanations.d: Losing the NCoR-recruitment motif specifically relieved repression, which implicates the HDAC activity NCoR brings as functionally relevant.

questions.prompt: Match each repression mechanism to its category.

left.text: Mad-Max competing with Myc-Max for the same E-box
Unliganded thyroid hormone receptor recruiting NCoR/HDAC3
Knirps/Kruppel short-range quenching of a nearby activator

right.text: Active repression via corepressor and chromatin-modifying enzyme recruitment
Passive repression via competitive occupancy of a shared binding site
Passive repression via direct short-range neutralization of a nearby-bound activator

questions.explanation: Mad-Max blocks Myc-Max by competing for the same site and partner; NCoR/HDAC3 recruitment is an active, enzyme-recruiting mechanism; Knirps/Kruppel quenching neutralizes a nearby activator directly without occupying its site.

questions.prompt: Order the steps by which the unliganded thyroid hormone receptor actively represses a target gene.

items.text: Unliganded receptor binds its hormone-response element
The receptor recruits the corepressor NCoR or SMRT
NCoR/SMRT recruits HDAC3 to the locus
Histone tails are deacetylated, favoring a condensed, less accessible chromatin state

questions.explanation: DNA binding by the unliganded receptor comes first, followed by corepressor recruitment, which in turn brings in the HDAC enzymatic activity that produces the chromatin-level repressive outcome.

lessons.label: Nucleosomes and the chromatin fiber

sections.heading: The nucleosome core particle
sections.body: The basic repeating unit of chromatin is the nucleosome: roughly 147 base pairs of DNA wrapped in about 1.65 left-handed superhelical turns around a protein core called the histone octamer. Roger Kornberg proposed this repeating-particle model in 1974, reasoning from micrococcal-nuclease digestion patterns that produced a regular ladder of DNA fragments rather than a smooth smear. The octamer is built from two copies each of four core histones -- H2A, H2B, H3, and H4 -- arranged as a central (H3-H4)2 tetramer flanked by two H2A-H2B dimers. Each histone is a small, highly basic protein folded into a three-helix 'histone fold' that mediates histone-histone and histone-DNA contacts; the tight fit between the octamer's positively charged surface and DNA's negative phosphate backbone lets about 50 nm of DNA coil around a particle only 10 nm across. Karolin Luger and colleagues solved the nucleosome core particle crystal structure at 2.8-angstrom resolution in 1997, confirming this architecture and revealing flexible N-terminal histone tails protruding past the DNA gyres -- the tails later work showed are the target for chemical modification. A fifth histone, linker histone H1, sits at the DNA entry/exit point and clamps roughly 20 additional base pairs; octamer plus H1 plus its DNA is called a chromatosome.

sections.heading: From beads on a string to competing higher-order models
sections.body: Under the electron microscope, decondensed chromatin looks like beads on a string: nucleosomes as ~10 nm beads connected by short linker DNA, an image first captured by Ada and Donald Olins and by Christopher Woodcock around 1973-1974. At physiological salt this string is thought to fold further into a thicker fiber, and for decades the dominant model -- proposed by John Finch and Aaron Klug in 1976 from X-ray diffraction of purified chromatin -- was a 30-nm solenoid, with a rival zigzag two-start helix debated as an alternative geometry. What has shifted is whether a regular 30-nm fiber exists inside real, unperturbed nuclei at all: cryo-electron microscopy of intact cells, including work from Kazuhiro Maeshima's group around 2014, found no consistent 30-nm signal in vivo, instead showing chromatin behaving like an irregularly folded, liquid-like polymer of interconnected nucleosomes. So the 30-nm fiber is a well-supported in vitro structure whose physiological relevance is genuinely contested, not settled fact. Whatever the higher-order geometry, chromatin exists in two broad accessibility states first named by Emil Heitz in 1928: euchromatin, decondensed and transcriptionally accessible, and heterochromatin, densely packed and largely silent.

lessons.workedExample: A student examining a micrococcal nuclease (MNase) digestion gel of chromatin sees a ladder of bands at roughly 147 bp, 300 bp, 450 bp -- multiples of the nucleosome repeat -- rather than a smear. This is the classic experimental signature Kornberg's model explains: MNase cuts preferentially in exposed linker DNA between nucleosomes, leaving the DNA wrapped around each octamer protected. Digesting to completion yields a tight band near 147 bp (the core particle alone); partial digestion preserves multiples corresponding to 1, 2, 3... nucleosomes still joined by uncut linker DNA. A student who explains the ladder this way -- protection by the octamer, cutting in linker DNA -- demonstrates the physical basis of the model rather than just naming it.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about nucleosome structure because many students can say 'histone octamer' without knowing what physically solves chromatin's packaging problem: about two meters of DNA fit into a nucleus a few microns across. A weak answer stops at 'DNA wraps around histones.' A strong answer gives the numbers -- 147 bp, ~1.65 turns, two copies each of four histones -- and can explain why modified tails change accessibility without changing the wrap itself. Judges also probe whether students know the 30-nm fiber is a contested in vitro structure rather than settled fact, which separates a student who read a summary from one tracking current uncertainty in the field.

questions.prompt: The histone octamer at the core of a nucleosome is composed of which histones?

options.text: One H1 plus two H2A-H2B dimers
Two copies each of H2A, H2B, H3, and H4
Four copies of H3 and four of H4
Two copies each of H1, H2A, H3, and H4

explanations.a: H1 is the linker histone and is not part of the octamer core.
explanations.b: Correct -- two copies each of the four core histones assemble into the octamer that DNA wraps around.
explanations.c: This drops H2A and H2B entirely; the octamer needs all four core histones, not two.
explanations.d: H1 is not part of the octamer; only H2A, H2B, H3, and H4 are core histones.

questions.prompt: Why did MNase digestion of chromatin produce a ladder of DNA fragments at multiples of the nucleosome repeat instead of a smooth smear?

options.text: MNase only cuts at CpG sites, which happen to be evenly spaced
The histone octamer protects the ~147 bp of DNA it wraps, so MNase cuts preferentially in the exposed linker DNA between nucleosomes
Replication machinery pauses at fixed intervals, creating natural break points
Chromatin fibers shear into fixed 200 bp units mechanically, regardless of protein content

explanations.a: MNase is not CpG-specific; it is a relatively nonspecific nuclease that prefers accessible, protein-free DNA.
explanations.b: Correct -- protected core DNA survives digestion while exposed linker DNA is cut, producing multiples of the repeat length.
explanations.c: This is a digestion experiment on purified/permeabilized chromatin, not an in vivo replication process.
explanations.d: This describes mechanical shearing and ignores the protective role histones play, which is the actual mechanism.

questions.prompt: Order these structures from the smallest scale to the largest scale of chromatin packaging.

items.text: DNA double helix
Nucleosome core particle (~147 bp + octamer)
Chromatosome (core + H1 + linker DNA)
10 nm beads-on-a-string fiber
Proposed 30 nm fiber

questions.explanation: The double helix wraps around an octamer to form the core particle, which with H1 and its linker DNA forms a chromatosome; chromatosomes strung together form the 10 nm beads-on-a-string fiber, which some models propose folds further into a 30 nm fiber.

questions.prompt: Match each structure or state to its defining feature.

right.text: Two copies each of H2A, H2B, H3, and H4
Clamps ~20 bp of linker DNA at the nucleosome entry/exit point
Proposed solenoid packing, contested in intact nuclei by cryo-EM
Decondensed, transcriptionally accessible chromatin

questions.explanation: The octamer is the two-copies-of-four-histones core; H1 is the linker histone clamping extra DNA; the 30 nm fiber is a solenoid model whose in vivo existence cryo-EM has challenged; euchromatin is the decondensed, accessible state named by Heitz.

lessons.label: The histone modification marks

sections.heading: Four chemistries on flexible tails
sections.body: The N-terminal tails of the core histones protrude out past the DNA wrapped around the nucleosome, and it is mainly on these tails -- plus a few residues in the globular core -- that cells install a small alphabet of chemical marks. Acetylation adds an acetyl group to a lysine's positively charged amine, neutralizing that charge; because histone-DNA affinity depends partly on electrostatic attraction between basic tails and the acidic phosphate backbone, acetylation loosens the histone's grip on DNA and is generally permissive for transcription. Methylation instead adds one, two, or three methyl groups to a lysine (written me1, me2, me3) or one/two to an arginine, without removing the residue's charge; its effect comes not from altering DNA affinity but from creating a docking surface that specific reader proteins recognize, so the same chemical mark can mean 'active' or 'repressive' depending entirely on which residue carries it and how many methyls are attached. Phosphorylation adds a negatively charged phosphate to serine or threonine -- H3 serine-10 phosphorylation, for instance, rises sharply as chromosomes condense for mitosis. Ubiquitination attaches a much larger 8.5-kDa ubiquitin protein, most often to H2A lysine-119 (repressive, deposited by Polycomb) or H2B lysine-120 (associated with active transcription elongation).

sections.heading: Marks with well-established genomic addresses
sections.body: Genome-wide chromatin immunoprecipitation mapping, especially through the ENCODE consortium's chromatin-state work (Jason Ernst and Manolis Kellis's ChromHMM model, 2010), pinned specific marks to specific genomic contexts. H3K4me3 sits sharply at active and poised gene promoters, first tied to active transcription by Helena Santos-Rosa and colleagues in 2002. H3K27ac marks active enhancers and distinguishes them from merely primed ones, a distinction Menno Creyghton's group sharpened in 2010 by showing H3K27ac (not just H3K4me1) separates active from poised enhancer states. H3K36me3 is deposited co-transcriptionally across gene bodies, tracking RNA polymerase II elongation; Reini Luco and colleagues showed in 2010 that its density along a gene body can even influence alternative splicing decisions by recruiting splicing regulators to specific exons as polymerase passes. Two marks anchor repression: H3K9me3, bound by HP1 to nucleate constitutive heterochromatin at pericentromeric and telomeric regions, and H3K27me3, deposited by the Polycomb complex PRC2 to hold developmental genes in a facultatively silenced state. Because each mark's meaning depends on its exact residue and methylation number, researchers writing H3K4me3 versus H3K27me3 are naming chemically similar but functionally opposite marks on the same histone.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher ChIP-seqs a cell line for H3K4me3, H3K27ac, H3K36me3, and H3K27me3, then looks at one actively transcribed gene. The pattern that confirms it is genuinely active: a sharp H3K4me3 peak right at the transcription start site, H3K27ac decorating a nearby enhancer, H3K36me3 spread across the gene body correlating with polymerase progress, and an absence of H3K27me3 anywhere near the locus. If instead H3K27me3 blankets the promoter with no H3K4me3, that is the signature of Polycomb-mediated silencing rather than active expression -- the same assay, read against the canonical marks, distinguishes an on gene from an off one without ever measuring RNA directly.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe histone marks because it is easy to memorize 'H3K27ac equals active enhancer' as a flashcard fact without understanding that the modification's chemistry is doing the work. A strong answer explains mechanism: acetylation neutralizes charge and loosens DNA contacts, while methylation changes nothing about charge and instead creates a docking site for reader proteins, which is why the same lysine methylated to different degrees, or a different lysine on the same tail, can mean the opposite thing. A weak answer just recites mark-to-outcome pairs without being able to say why acetylation and methylation work through different physical mechanisms.

questions.prompt: Why does histone acetylation generally loosen histone-DNA contacts, while methylation does not?

options.text: Acetylation neutralizes the lysine's positive charge, weakening electrostatic attraction to DNA's backbone; methylation leaves the charge intact
Acetylation adds a large bulky group that physically pushes DNA away; methylation is chemically identical to acetylation
Methylation degrades the histone tail, while acetylation stabilizes it
Acetylation only occurs on arginine, which never contacts DNA

explanations.a: Correct -- acetylation removes the lysine's positive charge, reducing electrostatic attraction to the negatively charged DNA backbone.
explanations.b: Acetyl and methyl groups are both small; the effect is not primarily steric bulk, and they are chemically distinct modifications.
explanations.c: Neither modification degrades the histone tail; both are reversible chemical additions.
explanations.d: Acetylation occurs on lysine, not arginine, and lysines do contact DNA in the nucleosome.

questions.prompt: A ChIP-seq experiment shows H3K27me3 blanketing a gene's promoter with no H3K4me3 present. What does this pattern most likely indicate?

options.text: The gene is being actively transcribed at a high rate
The gene is Polycomb-repressed rather than active
The gene is undergoing DNA replication
The measurement failed and should be discarded

explanations.a: Active transcription is associated with H3K4me3 at the promoter and H3K36me3 across the body, not H3K27me3 alone.
explanations.b: Correct -- H3K27me3 without H3K4me3 is the canonical signature of Polycomb-mediated facultative silencing.
explanations.c: Histone marks reflect transcriptional/chromatin state, not replication timing directly.
explanations.d: This is a biologically meaningful and expected pattern for a repressed gene, not an assay failure.

questions.prompt: Match each histone mark to the genomic context it canonically marks.

right.text: Active promoters
Active enhancers
Transcribed gene bodies, tracking elongation
Polycomb-repressed, facultatively silenced genes

questions.explanation: H3K4me3 marks active promoters, H3K27ac marks active enhancers, H3K36me3 accumulates across gene bodies during elongation, and H3K27me3 marks Polycomb-silenced developmental genes.

questions.prompt: Order these histone modifications by the size of the chemical group added, from smallest to largest.

items.text: Methylation (methyl group)
Acetylation (acetyl group)
Phosphorylation (phosphate group)
Ubiquitination (8.5-kDa ubiquitin protein)

questions.explanation: Methyl groups are the smallest addition, acetyl groups slightly larger, phosphate groups larger still, and ubiquitin -- a full 8.5-kDa protein -- is far larger than any of the small chemical modifications.

lessons.label: Writers, erasers, and readers

sections.heading: Writers and erasers of acetylation and methylation
sections.body: Histone acetyltransferases (HATs) install acetyl marks; the first to be identified, in 1996 by James Brownell and colleagues, was a Tetrahymena protein homologous to yeast Gcn5, finally connecting a known transcriptional coactivator function to a direct enzymatic activity on histones. p300 and its close paralog CBP, shown to be histone acetyltransferases by Vasily Ogryzko and colleagues that same year, acetylate multiple lysines across all four core histones and are recruited by a huge range of sequence-specific transcription factors, making them general-purpose amplifiers of active chromatin. Histone deacetylases (HDACs) run the reaction in reverse, stripping acetyl groups and restoring the tail's positive charge; class I HDACs such as HDAC1 and HDAC2 work as catalytic subunits inside large corepressor complexes like Sin3 and NuRD. Histone methylation is written by SET-domain methyltransferases -- SUV39H1 deposits repressive H3K9 methylation, EZH2 (the catalytic core of Polycomb complex PRC2) deposits H3K27me3, and MLL/SET1-family complexes deposit active H3K4me3 -- and for a long time methylation was assumed irreversible. That changed when Yang Shi's group identified LSD1 in 2004 as the first histone demethylase, an amine oxidase that removes mono- and dimethyl marks but cannot touch trimethylated lysine; Yu-ichi Tsukada and colleagues then showed in 2006 that a separate JmjC-domain (Jumonji) family uses an iron- and alpha-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase mechanism that can strip even trimethyl marks.

sections.heading: Readers, the histone code hypothesis, and its critics
sections.body: Marks matter because dedicated reader domains recognize them and recruit downstream effectors. Bromodomains bind acetylated lysine -- the domain found in BRD4 and other BET-family proteins that recruit transcriptional machinery to acetylated promoters and enhancers. Chromodomains instead recognize methylated lysine; the chromodomain of HP1, shown by two groups in 2001 (Andrew Bannister's and Thomas Jenuwein's, working with Melanie Lachner) to bind H3K9me directly, is the mechanistic link between SUV39H1 writing that mark and heterochromatin actually compacting. Brian Strahl and C. David Allis synthesized these writer-reader relationships into the 'histone code' hypothesis in 2000, proposing that combinations of marks are read combinatorially by effector proteins to specify distinct downstream outcomes, much as a genetic code specifies amino acids. The hypothesis has been influential but is also contested: critics, including a pointed 2005 critique from Steven Henikoff, argue that most evidence for the code is correlational -- a mark's presence tracks with an outcome like active transcription without proof the mark causes that outcome -- and that many marks may instead be a downstream consequence of the transcription or repair machinery having passed through, rather than an instructive signal read beforehand. That correlation-versus-causation gap remains an open question for many specific marks even as the writer-eraser-reader framework itself is well established.

lessons.workedExample: A drug developer wants to reverse an aberrant H3K27me3-silenced tumor suppressor gene. Knowing the writer-eraser-reader logic, they target EZH2 (the PRC2 writer) with a small-molecule inhibitor rather than trying to directly block the reader proteins that interpret the mark, because blocking the writer prevents the mark from being deposited or re-deposited after each cell division, while blocking only a reader might leave the mark in place for other readers to interpret. EZH2 inhibitors following exactly this logic (such as tazemetostat) reached clinical use for cancers with PRC2 overactivity, illustrating that distinguishing 'writer' from 'reader' is not just a classification exercise -- it directly determines which node in the pathway is the most effective drug target.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges push on writer/eraser/reader vocabulary because it is easy to use the terms as labels without grasping that each category is a different kind of intervention point. A strong answer can say what happens mechanistically if you inhibit a writer (no new marks deposited, existing marks eventually diluted through replication) versus a reader (the mark stays but its downstream interpretation is blocked). A strong answer also knows the histone code hypothesis is a genuinely debated framework, not settled fact, and can state the correlation-versus-causation critique in one sentence. A weak answer treats 'histone code' as an established mechanism rather than a contested interpretive model.

questions.prompt: What key catalytic difference distinguishes LSD1 from the JmjC-domain (Jumonji) demethylases?

options.text: LSD1 uses an amine oxidase mechanism and cannot remove trimethyl marks; JmjC enzymes use an Fe(II)/alpha-ketoglutarate dioxygenase mechanism that can remove trimethyl marks
LSD1 only acts on DNA methylation, while JmjC enzymes act on histones
LSD1 adds methyl marks, while JmjC enzymes remove them
There is no mechanistic difference; both use identical chemistry

explanations.a: Correct -- LSD1's amine oxidase chemistry is limited to mono- and dimethyl marks, while the JmjC dioxygenase mechanism can also strip trimethylated lysine.
explanations.b: LSD1 acts on histone lysine methylation, not DNA methylation.
explanations.c: Both LSD1 and JmjC enzymes are demethylases (erasers), not methyltransferases (writers).
explanations.d: The two families use distinct enzymatic mechanisms, which is precisely why their substrate range differs.

questions.prompt: According to Steven Henikoff's critique of the histone code hypothesis, what is the main weakness in the evidence for the code?

options.text: Histone marks have never been detected reproducibly by any assay
Much of the evidence is correlational, and marks may often be a consequence of transcription or repair machinery passing through rather than an instructive prior signal
Writer enzymes like EZH2 and SUV39H1 do not actually exist
Reader domains such as bromodomains and chromodomains cannot bind their marks in vitro

explanations.a: Marks are robustly and reproducibly detected by ChIP and other assays; detectability is not the issue.
explanations.b: Correct -- the critique targets causal interpretation: correlation between a mark and an outcome does not prove the mark instructs that outcome.
explanations.c: These writer enzymes are well-established with known catalytic activity; their existence is not in dispute.
explanations.d: Reader domain binding to their cognate marks is well demonstrated biochemically; that is not what the critique targets.

questions.prompt: Match each protein or domain to its role in the histone modification system.

right.text: Writer: acetylates histone lysines, recruited by many transcription factors
Writer: deposits H3K27me3 as the catalytic core of PRC2
Reader: binds acetylated lysine
Reader: binds H3K9me, nucleating heterochromatin compaction

questions.explanation: p300/CBP write acetylation broadly; EZH2 writes H3K27me3 as part of PRC2; bromodomains read acetyl-lysine; the HP1 chromodomain reads H3K9me and helps compact heterochromatin.

questions.prompt: Order these historical findings in the writer/eraser/reader field chronologically, earliest first.

items.text: Brownell identifies Gcn5 homolog as the first histone acetyltransferase (1996)
Bannister and Lachner/Jenuwein show HP1 chromodomain binds H3K9me (2001)
Shi identifies LSD1 as the first histone demethylase (2004)
Tsukada shows JmjC-domain enzymes can remove trimethyl marks (2006)

questions.explanation: The first HAT was identified in 1996, the HP1 reader-mark connection in 2001, the first demethylase (LSD1) in 2004, and the trimethyl-capable JmjC demethylases in 2006.

lessons.label: DNA methylation

sections.heading: 5-methylcytosine, CpG islands, and two kinds of methyltransferase
sections.body: In vertebrate genomes, DNA methylation almost always means the addition of a methyl group to cytosine at position 5, forming 5-methylcytosine, and it occurs almost exclusively at cytosines followed by guanine -- CpG dinucleotides. CpG sites are globally underrepresented in the genome but cluster densely in short GC-rich stretches called CpG islands, which sit at roughly 70% of gene promoters and, unlike CpG elsewhere in the genome, stay largely unmethylated regardless of whether the downstream gene is active, a pattern described by Adrian Bird's group in the mid-1980s. Because a CpG's cytosine has a complementary CpG on the opposite strand, a fully methylated site has methyl groups on both strands, while a newly replicated site is briefly hemimethylated -- methylated only on the parental strand. DNMT1, the maintenance methyltransferase characterized by Timothy Bestor's work in the late 1980s and early 1990s, is recruited to replication forks and strongly prefers hemimethylated substrate, restoring full methylation on the new strand and thereby copying the existing pattern each cell division; the reader protein UHRF1 recognizes hemimethylated CpG and helps recruit DNMT1 there. DNMT3A and DNMT3B, identified as the de novo methyltransferases by Masaki Okano and colleagues in 1999, instead establish new methylation patterns during early development, working with their catalytically inactive cofactor DNMT3L.

sections.heading: Reading the mark, erasing it, and its consequence
sections.body: Methylated CpGs are interpreted by methyl-CpG-binding proteins, the best studied of which is MeCP2; loss-of-function mutations in the MECP2 gene were shown by Ruthie Amir and colleagues in 1999 to cause Rett syndrome, a severe neurodevelopmental disorder, directly demonstrating that misreading methylation marks has serious physiological consequences. For decades DNA methylation looked like a one-way, essentially permanent mark, but Mamta Tahiliani and colleagues showed in 2009 that the TET enzymes (TET1, TET2, TET3) oxidize 5-methylcytosine to 5-hydroxymethylcytosine, the first step of an active demethylation pathway that can eventually restore unmodified cytosine, giving cells a mechanism to erase methylation rather than only dilute it passively through replication in its absence. Functionally, promoter methylation is strongly associated with gene silencing: a densely methylated CpG island blocks binding of many transcription factors directly and recruits methyl-CpG readers that in turn recruit histone deacetylases and repressive chromatin machinery, compounding the silencing effect. This mechanism is exploited pathologically in cancer, where tumor-suppressor gene promoters are frequently hypermethylated and silenced -- an epigenetic route to loss of tumor-suppressor function that requires no mutation in the underlying DNA sequence at all.

lessons.workedExample: A lab compares methylation at a specific CpG island promoter across a parent cell and its two daughter cells immediately after DNA replication. Right after replication, each daughter's DNA at that CpG is hemimethylated: the old (parental) strand still carries 5-methylcytosine, but the newly synthesized strand is unmethylated. UHRF1 recognizes this hemimethylated state and recruits DNMT1, which methylates the new strand to match the old one -- restoring full, symmetric methylation before the next round of division. If DNMT1 is experimentally knocked out, this maintenance step fails, methylation is diluted by half with each replication cycle, and a gene that had been stably silenced by promoter methylation can become reactivated purely from loss of the maintenance enzyme, without any DNA sequence change.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe DNA methylation because 'methylation silences genes' is a one-line fact that can be repeated without understanding the maintenance-versus-de-novo distinction that makes methylation heritable through cell division at all. A strong answer explains why DNMT1 alone cannot establish a new pattern (it only copies an existing one from hemimethylated DNA) and why DNMT3A/3B are needed for that job, and can connect promoter hypermethylation in cancer to a concrete gene-silencing mechanism rather than a vague association. A weak answer conflates all DNMTs as interchangeable or cannot explain what 'hemimethylated' means and why it matters.

questions.prompt: Why does DNMT1 preferentially methylate hemimethylated DNA rather than acting equally on any CpG site?

options.text: DNMT1 is a maintenance enzyme that copies an existing methylation pattern onto the newly replicated strand, so it is recruited to sites that are already methylated on the parental strand
DNMT1 cannot recognize CpG dinucleotides at all and methylates DNA randomly
Hemimethylated DNA is the only DNA that exists in a cell
DNMT1 is a de novo methyltransferase that establishes entirely new patterns during development

explanations.a: Correct -- DNMT1's role is to maintain an inherited pattern by methylating the new strand to match the old one at hemimethylated sites, aided by UHRF1.
explanations.b: DNMT1 specifically recognizes hemimethylated CpG sites via UHRF1; it is not a random-acting enzyme.
explanations.c: Hemimethylated DNA is a transient state right after replication, not the only state DNA exists in.
explanations.d: That describes DNMT3A/DNMT3B, the de novo methyltransferases, not DNMT1.

questions.prompt: What did Tahiliani and colleagues' 2009 finding about TET enzymes establish?

options.text: That DNA methylation cannot be reversed under any circumstances
That TET enzymes oxidize 5-methylcytosine to 5-hydroxymethylcytosine, the first step of an active demethylation pathway
That TET enzymes are the primary de novo methyltransferases in development
That MeCP2 mutations cause Rett syndrome

explanations.a: This is the opposite of the finding -- TET enzymes showed methylation CAN be actively reversed.
explanations.b: Correct -- this 2009 finding identified the first enzymatic step of active DNA demethylation.
explanations.c: TET enzymes are oxidases that modify existing 5-methylcytosine; DNMT3A/3B are the de novo methyltransferases.
explanations.d: That finding is Amir and colleagues' 1999 result about MECP2 and Rett syndrome, a separate discovery.

questions.prompt: Match each protein to its role in DNA methylation biology.

right.text: Maintenance methyltransferase, acts on hemimethylated DNA after replication
De novo methyltransferases, establish new patterns in development
Methyl-CpG reader protein; mutations cause Rett syndrome
Oxidize 5-methylcytosine, initiating active demethylation

questions.explanation: DNMT1 maintains inherited patterns on hemimethylated DNA, DNMT3A/3B write new patterns de novo, MeCP2 reads the methyl mark and its loss causes Rett syndrome, and TET enzymes oxidize 5mC to begin active demethylation.

questions.prompt: Order these events for a CpG site during and after DNA replication.

items.text: Fully methylated CpG site before replication (both strands methylated)
DNA replication occurs, producing two daughter duplexes
Each daughter duplex is briefly hemimethylated (only parental strand methylated)
UHRF1 recognizes the hemimethylated site and recruits DNMT1
DNMT1 methylates the new strand, restoring full methylation

questions.explanation: A fully methylated site becomes hemimethylated immediately after replication, and the maintenance machinery -- UHRF1 recognizing the site and recruiting DNMT1 -- restores full methylation on the new strand before the pattern is inherited again.

lessons.label: Chromatin remodeling complexes

sections.heading: ATP-powered machines that move nucleosomes
sections.body: Histone marks change how DNA-bound proteins are read, but they do not physically move a nucleosome out of the way. That job belongs to a separate class of enzymes, the ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling complexes, which use energy from ATP hydrolysis to slide a nucleosome along DNA, eject it from the DNA entirely, or swap one of its histones for a variant. Four remodeler families dominate: SWI/SNF (called BAF in humans), first identified in yeast genetic screens in the late 1980s for genes required for mating-type switching and sucrose fermentation -- hence the name -- uses its ATPase subunit, BRG1 or BRM in humans, to slide and eject nucleosomes and open up promoter and enhancer regions. ISWI-family complexes tend to space nucleosomes evenly rather than eject them, important for assembling regularly spaced arrays after replication. CHD-family remodelers (named for their chromodomain-helicase-DNA-binding domains), including CHD1, also slide nucleosomes and contribute to spacing and transcription-coupled remodeling. INO80-family complexes combine remodeling with a specific ability to exchange histone variants into and out of nucleosomes and also participate in DNA double-strand break repair. All four families share a related ATPase motor domain but differ in the accessory subunits that determine which biological process recruits them.

sections.heading: The nucleosome-free region and histone variant deposition
sections.body: The combined action of these remodelers produces a striking, consistent feature of active promoters: a nucleosome-free region (NFR), typically several hundred base pairs wide, sitting just upstream of the transcription start site where general transcription factors and RNA polymerase II assemble. Flanking that NFR on either side, remodelers deposit histone variants in place of the canonical core histones. H2A.Z, deposited at nucleosomes immediately flanking the NFR by SWR1 in yeast and the related INO80-family/p400 machinery in mammals, destabilizes those flanking nucleosomes and helps keep the NFR open, marking promoters and enhancers. H3.3, a replication-independent variant of H3 that differs from canonical H3.1/H3.2 by only a handful of residues, is deposited by the HIRA complex at actively transcribed genes and regulatory regions throughout the cell cycle (not just during S-phase replication, when canonical histones are made), while a separate ATRX-DAXX complex deposits H3.3 at heterochromatic regions such as telomeres and pericentromeric repeats. Because variant deposition and canonical histone assembly use entirely different chaperone machinery, the presence of H2A.Z or H3.3 at a locus is itself a mark of that region's distinct regulatory or chromatin state, independent of any covalent histone modification.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher compares chromatin accessibility (via an ATAC-seq assay, which cuts preferentially in nucleosome-free DNA) at a promoter in a wild-type cell line versus one where the SWI/SNF ATPase BRG1 has been knocked out. In the wild-type cells, a clear nucleosome-free region appears just upstream of the transcription start site, flanked by well-positioned nucleosomes carrying H2A.Z. In the BRG1 knockout, that nucleosome-free region collapses -- a nucleosome moves back into the space where the transcription machinery needs to assemble -- and the gene's expression drops sharply, even though no histone modification enzyme was touched. This shows the NFR is not a passive consequence of low nucleosome density but an actively maintained state that requires an ATP-dependent remodeler working continuously against nucleosomes' intrinsic tendency to occupy any available DNA.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about remodeling complexes because students often conflate 'chromatin gets opened up' with histone acetylation alone, missing that acetylation changes affinity while remodelers do the physical work of sliding or ejecting nucleosomes using ATP. A strong answer distinguishes what a covalent mark does (change how tightly DNA is held or who binds it) from what a remodeler does (physically relocate or replace a nucleosome), and can name at least one remodeler family and its distinguishing behavior -- SWI/SNF ejecting, ISWI spacing, INO80 exchanging variants. A weak answer treats 'chromatin remodeling' and 'histone modification' as synonyms.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes an ATP-dependent chromatin remodeler from a histone-modifying enzyme like a HAT or HMT?

options.text: The remodeler physically moves, ejects, or exchanges nucleosomes using energy from ATP hydrolysis, rather than adding a covalent chemical mark to a histone
Remodelers only act on DNA methylation, not histones
Remodelers and histone-modifying enzymes are the same class of protein with different names
Remodelers exclusively repress transcription while modifying enzymes exclusively activate it

explanations.a: Correct -- remodelers are ATP-powered motors that reposition or replace nucleosomes rather than chemically modifying histone residues.
explanations.b: Remodelers act on nucleosome positioning, not DNA methylation directly.
explanations.c: These are mechanistically distinct enzyme classes: one adds/removes chemical marks, the other uses ATP hydrolysis to move nucleosomes.
explanations.d: Both classes contain members that activate and repress depending on context; neither is exclusively one or the other.

questions.prompt: In the BRG1 (SWI/SNF ATPase) knockout example, what happened to the nucleosome-free region at the promoter, and why?

options.text: It stayed open because histone acetylation alone maintains it
It collapsed, because SWI/SNF's ATP-dependent activity is required to actively keep that region clear of nucleosomes
It widened further, since BRG1 normally narrows the NFR
Nothing changed, since NFRs do not depend on remodelers

explanations.a: The example specifically shows acetylation enzymes were untouched, yet the NFR still collapsed -- so acetylation alone is not sufficient.
explanations.b: Correct -- losing the remodeler's ATP-dependent activity let a nucleosome move back into the NFR, showing the open state is actively maintained.
explanations.c: The knockout caused the NFR to collapse (narrow/disappear), not widen.
explanations.d: The example directly demonstrates NFR maintenance depends on remodeler activity.

questions.prompt: Match each remodeler family to its characteristic behavior.

right.text: Slides and ejects nucleosomes to open promoters/enhancers
Spaces nucleosomes evenly into regular arrays
Slides nucleosomes via chromodomain-helicase-DNA-binding domains
Exchanges histone variants and participates in DNA repair

questions.explanation: SWI/SNF ejects nucleosomes to open regulatory regions, ISWI spaces nucleosomes evenly, CHD slides nucleosomes via its namesake domains, and INO80 exchanges histone variants while also contributing to repair.

questions.prompt: Match each histone variant to where it is deposited and by which chaperone complex.

right.text: Deposited flanking the nucleosome-free region by SWR1/INO80-related machinery
Deposited replication-independently by the HIRA complex
Deposited by the ATRX-DAXX complex

questions.explanation: H2A.Z flanks the NFR via SWR1/INO80-related complexes, H3.3 is deposited at active genes by HIRA independent of replication, and a separate ATRX-DAXX complex deposits H3.3 at heterochromatic telomeric and pericentromeric regions.

lessons.label: Epigenetic inheritance and dosage compensation

sections.heading: X-inactivation: silencing a whole chromosome
sections.body: Female mammals carry two X chromosomes to a male's one, and without correction this would produce roughly double the dose of every X-linked gene product. Mary Lyon proposed the solution in 1961: early in female embryonic development, one X chromosome in each cell is randomly and permanently inactivated, so that adult females are mosaics of cells expressing either the maternal or paternal X. The inactivated X condenses into a compact structure visible under a light microscope, the Barr body, first described by Murray Barr and Ewart Bertram in 1949, decades before its cause was understood. The molecular trigger was identified in 1991 when Carolyn Brown and colleagues characterized Xist, a long noncoding RNA transcribed only from the future inactive X; Xist RNA spreads in cis, coating that chromosome along its length without diffusing to the active homolog, and recruits Polycomb repressive complex 2 to deposit H3K27me3 across the chromosome, triggering compaction, DNA methylation, and stable silencing that then persists through every subsequent cell division in that lineage.

sections.heading: Genomic imprinting, position-effect variegation, and mitotic memory
sections.body: A related but distinct phenomenon is genomic imprinting, in which a gene's expression depends on which parent it came from, independent of X-inactivation. The IGF2/H19 locus on human chromosome 11 is the textbook case: an imprinting control region (ICR) between the two genes is methylated only on the paternally inherited allele. On the unmethylated maternal allele, the insulator protein CTCF binds the ICR and blocks a downstream enhancer from reaching IGF2, so the enhancer instead activates H19 -- while on the paternal allele, ICR methylation blocks CTCF binding, freeing the enhancer to activate IGF2 instead of H19. Work from Adam Bell and Gary Felsenfeld, and separately Amy Hark and colleagues, worked this insulator mechanism out around 2000. A third classic phenomenon is position-effect variegation, discovered by Hermann Muller in 1930 when a chromosomal rearrangement relocated the Drosophila white gene next to heterochromatin, producing a mottled, cell-to-cell variable eye-color pattern that showed heterochromatin can spread into and silence a nearby gene unpredictably. All three phenomena depend on chromatin states surviving mitosis: DNA methylation is copied at each replication by DNMT1 acting on hemimethylated DNA, while histone marks propagate through reader-writer feedback loops -- HP1 reading H3K9me and recruiting SUV39H1 to write more of it on adjacent nucleosomes -- so a chromatin state, once established, becomes self-templating across cell generations without any change to the underlying DNA sequence.

lessons.workedExample: A calico cat's coat pattern is a visible readout of X-inactivation in action. The gene for orange versus black fur pigment sits on the X chromosome, and a female cat heterozygous for the two color alleles randomly inactivates one X per cell early in development; every patch of fur descends clonally from one of those early cells, so patches are either orange or black depending on which X stayed active in that clonal lineage, with the mosaic boundaries reflecting where cell lineages diverged. Male cats, having only one X, cannot be calico (barring rare XXY genotypes) -- which is why the calico pattern is a direct, visual demonstration of random, clonally inherited X-inactivation rather than a coincidence of coat genetics.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe epigenetic inheritance because it is the clearest case where 'epigenetic' has a precise, testable meaning -- a chromatin state that is heritable through cell division without a DNA sequence change -- rather than being used loosely as a synonym for 'gene regulation' in general. A strong answer can trace the mechanism end to end: Xist coats a chromosome, recruits PRC2, and the resulting H3K27me3 and DNA methylation propagate through subsequent divisions via reader-writer loops. A weak answer says 'X-inactivation silences a chromosome' without being able to explain what keeps it silenced across the millions of divisions between early embryo and an adult tissue sample.

questions.prompt: What is the direct molecular trigger that initiates X-chromosome inactivation on the future inactive X?

options.text: DNMT1 methylating the entire chromosome simultaneously
The Xist long noncoding RNA coating the chromosome in cis and recruiting PRC2 to deposit H3K27me3
CTCF binding across the whole chromosome to block all transcription
Random fragmentation of the chromosome during meiosis

explanations.a: DNA methylation is part of the eventual stable silencing but is not the initiating trigger; Xist coating comes first.
explanations.b: Correct -- Xist RNA coats the chromosome in cis and recruits PRC2, whose H3K27me3 deposition drives compaction and silencing.
explanations.c: CTCF's role in this unit is at the IGF2/H19 imprinting locus, not as the trigger for whole-chromosome X-inactivation.
explanations.d: X-inactivation is an epigenetic silencing process in somatic cells, not a meiotic fragmentation event.

questions.prompt: At the IGF2/H19 locus, why does methylation of the paternal ICR allele lead to IGF2 expression rather than H19 expression?

options.text: Methylation blocks CTCF from binding the paternal ICR, freeing the downstream enhancer to activate IGF2 instead of H19
Methylation directly recruits RNA polymerase to the IGF2 promoter
Methylation has no effect on CTCF binding at this locus
The maternal allele is always methylated instead of the paternal allele

explanations.a: Correct -- on the unmethylated maternal allele CTCF binds and blocks the enhancer from reaching IGF2, so the enhancer activates H19 instead; methylation on the paternal allele prevents CTCF binding, redirecting the enhancer to IGF2.
explanations.b: Methylation acts indirectly here, through blocking CTCF, not by directly recruiting polymerase to IGF2.
explanations.c: Methylation directly blocks CTCF binding at the ICR, which is the entire mechanism of this imprinting switch.
explanations.d: It is the paternal allele that carries ICR methylation in this locus, not the maternal allele.

questions.prompt: Match each phenomenon to the scientist(s) or year associated with its discovery or mechanism.

right.text: Mary Lyon, 1961
Barr and Bertram, 1949
Carolyn Brown and colleagues, 1991
Hermann Muller, 1930

questions.explanation: Lyon proposed random X-inactivation in 1961; Barr and Bertram described the Barr body in 1949, before its cause was known; Brown and colleagues identified Xist in 1991; Muller discovered position-effect variegation in Drosophila in 1930.

questions.prompt: Order the events of X-chromosome inactivation from earliest to latest in a developing female embryo cell.

items.text: One X is randomly selected to become inactive
Xist RNA is transcribed and coats that X chromosome in cis
PRC2 is recruited and deposits H3K27me3 across the chromosome
The chromosome condenses into a Barr body and stays stably silenced through later divisions

questions.explanation: Random selection of the future inactive X precedes Xist coating, which recruits PRC2 to deposit H3K27me3, which drives condensation into a stably silenced Barr body maintained across subsequent cell divisions.

lessons.label: Polycomb, Trithorax, and cellular memory

sections.heading: Two opposing systems discovered through Hox gene mistakes
sections.body: Polycomb and Trithorax group genes were both discovered in Drosophila through mutations that scrambled body-segment identity by misregulating Hox genes, the master regulators of anterior-posterior patterning. Edward Lewis's work through the 1970s, including his influential 1978 paper on the bithorax gene complex, established that losing Polycomb function let Hox genes turn on in segments where they should stay off, while Trithorax group mutations produced the opposite failure, Hox genes turning off where they should stay on -- revealing two antagonistic systems built specifically to remember, not decide, a gene's on/off state through development. Polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2) is the writer half of the repressive system: its catalytic core, EZH2 (or the related EZH1), works together with SUZ12 and EED to trimethylate histone H3 at lysine 27, producing the H3K27me3 mark. That mark is then read by Polycomb repressive complex 1 (PRC1), whose CBX subunit contains a chromodomain that recognizes H3K27me3; canonical PRC1 compacts the resulting chromatin and, through its RING1A/RING1B subunits, monoubiquitinates histone H2A at lysine 119, reinforcing repression through a second independent modification.

sections.heading: Bivalent domains and how chromatin remembers cell identity
sections.body: Trithorax group proteins maintain the opposing active state, chiefly through MLL/COMPASS-family complexes that deposit and maintain H3K4me3 at genes that need to stay poised or active, directly opposing the Polycomb system at the same class of developmental loci. The clearest demonstration that these two systems can coexist at a single gene came from embryonic stem cell studies: Bradley Bernstein's group and, separately, Amanda Fisher's group, including Veronique Azuara and Matthias Merkenschlager, both reported in 2006 that many developmental gene promoters in embryonic stem cells carry H3K4me3 and H3K27me3 simultaneously -- a bivalent domain. A bivalent promoter is transcriptionally quiet but poised: it can resolve quickly toward stable activation, losing H3K27me3 and keeping H3K4me3, or toward stable repression, losing H3K4me3 and keeping H3K27me3, depending on which developmental signal a cell receives. This bivalency lets stem cells hold lineage-choice genes in a primed, decision-ready state rather than either fully off or fully on. More broadly, the Polycomb/Trithorax system illustrates the core idea of cellular memory in chromatin: once a cell commits to silencing or activating a developmental gene, self-reinforcing writer-reader loops (PRC2 depositing H3K27me3 that PRC1 reads and compacts, or COMPASS maintaining H3K4me3) propagate that decision through every subsequent division, keeping a liver cell's descendants liver cells without re-reading any developmental signal each time.

lessons.workedExample: An embryonic stem cell line is profiled by ChIP-seq at a key lineage-determining gene, and its promoter shows both H3K4me3 and H3K27me3 simultaneously -- a bivalent domain -- while the gene itself is not being transcribed. When those stem cells are differentiated down one lineage, ChIP-seq on the resulting cells shows H3K27me3 has been lost from that promoter while H3K4me3 remains, and the gene is now actively transcribed; differentiating a parallel batch down a different lineage instead shows loss of H3K4me3 with H3K27me3 retained, and the gene stays silent. The same starting bivalent mark resolved in opposite directions depending on the differentiation signal, which is exactly the poised, decision-ready state bivalency is thought to provide.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe Polycomb/Trithorax because bivalent domains are a favorite topic for exposing whether a student actually understands 'poised' versus simply memorizing that stem cells have 'both marks.' A strong answer explains what resolving a bivalent domain means mechanistically -- losing one mark while retaining the other -- and can connect that to a concrete developmental decision. A strong answer also knows PRC1 and PRC2 are functionally coupled (PRC2 writes H3K27me3, PRC1 reads it and compacts chromatin plus adds H2AK119ub) rather than treating 'Polycomb' as a single undifferentiated complex. A weak answer says 'Polycomb silences genes' without any writer-reader mechanism.

questions.prompt: What is a bivalent chromatin domain, and what does it represent functionally?

options.text: A promoter carrying both H3K4me3 and H3K27me3 simultaneously, representing a poised state that can resolve toward activation or repression
A promoter bound by two different RNA polymerases at once
A gene with two separate transcription start sites
A chromosome region methylated on both DNA strands

explanations.a: Correct -- bivalency is the simultaneous presence of the active H3K4me3 mark and the repressive H3K27me3 mark, poising the gene for either outcome.
explanations.b: Bivalency refers to histone marks, not simultaneous polymerase binding.
explanations.c: This describes alternative transcription start sites, an unrelated concept.
explanations.d: Symmetric DNA methylation on both strands is a normal state at methylated CpGs, not what 'bivalent' refers to in this context.

questions.prompt: How does PRC1 reinforce the repression that PRC2 initiates?

options.text: PRC1's CBX chromodomain reads the H3K27me3 mark PRC2 deposited, then PRC1 compacts chromatin and adds H2AK119 monoubiquitination
PRC1 removes H3K27me3 to prevent over-repression
PRC1 and PRC2 act completely independently with no functional connection
PRC1 deposits H3K4me3 to balance the repressive signal

explanations.a: Correct -- PRC1 reads the mark PRC2 wrote and adds a second layer of repression through compaction and H2AK119ub.
explanations.b: Removing H3K27me3 would be a demethylase's job and would undo repression, not reinforce it.
explanations.c: PRC1 and PRC2 are functionally coupled -- PRC1's reader domain specifically recognizes PRC2's product.
explanations.d: H3K4me3 is deposited by Trithorax/COMPASS complexes to maintain the active state, not by PRC1.

questions.prompt: Match each complex or system to its role at developmental genes.

right.text: Writes H3K27me3 via EZH2/EZH1
Reads H3K27me3, compacts chromatin, adds H2AK119ub
Maintains H3K4me3 to keep genes active or poised
Carries both H3K4me3 and H3K27me3, poised to resolve either way

questions.explanation: PRC2 writes H3K27me3, PRC1 reads it and compacts chromatin while adding H2AK119ub, Trithorax/COMPASS maintains the opposing active H3K4me3 mark, and a bivalent domain carries both marks in a poised state.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the history of Polycomb/Trithorax discovery and characterization.

items.text: Edward Lewis's work on the bithorax complex shows Polycomb loss misregulates Hox genes (through 1978)
PRC2 is characterized as the H3K27 methyltransferase complex
Bernstein's and Azuara's groups report bivalent domains in embryonic stem cells (2006)

questions.explanation: Lewis's Drosophila genetics through the 1970s first revealed Polycomb's role in Hox regulation, PRC2's molecular characterization as an H3K27 methyltransferase followed, and the bivalent domain concept in embryonic stem cells was reported in 2006.

lessons.label: 5' Capping

sections.heading: A cap added while the transcript is still being made
sections.body: Almost as soon as RNA polymerase II emerges from the promoter, the growing transcript gets modified at its 5' end. Once the nascent RNA is about 20-25 nucleotides long, a three-enzyme relay converts its triphosphate end into a 7-methylguanosine (m7G) cap. RNA triphosphatase removes the terminal gamma phosphate, guanylyltransferase attaches a GMP in an unusual reversed 5'-5' triphosphate linkage, and guanine-N7-methyltransferase methylates that added guanine. A further 2'-O-methylation of the first transcribed nucleotide by CMTr1 produces the more common cap 1 structure. Aaron Shatkin and Yasuhiro Furuichi first described this cap on reovirus mRNA in 1975, and it turned out to be universal to eukaryotic Pol II transcripts. The reaction is not a post-transcriptional afterthought: the capping enzymes dock directly onto the Pol II C-terminal domain (CTD) once its heptad repeats (tandem YSPTSPS motifs) are phosphorylated on serine 5 by the TFIIH kinase CDK7 during early elongation. That phosphorylation mark recruits the capping enzyme complex and is later removed as Pol II moves into productive elongation, so capping is physically coupled to the act of transcribing.

sections.heading: What the cap buys the transcript
sections.body: The cap does four distinct jobs. First, it blocks the 5' end from the exonuclease XRN1, which otherwise chews RNA in the 5' to 3' direction; an uncapped transcript is degraded within minutes. Second, in the nucleus the cap is bound by the nuclear cap-binding complex (CBP80/CBP20), which helps license the mRNA for export through the nuclear pore. Third, once in the cytoplasm CBP20 is replaced by eIF4E, the cap-binding subunit of the eIF4F initiation complex (with eIF4G and eIF4A); eIF4E is the rate-limiting factor that lets ribosomes find the start codon by scanning, so cap recognition is the first committed step of cap-dependent translation. Fourth, the cap-binding complex promotes efficient removal of the first intron by helping recruit U1 snRNP to the nearby 5' splice site, linking capping mechanically to splicing rather than leaving the two processes independent. Fifth, the cap structure is a self-versus-nonself signal for innate immunity: CMTr1's 2'-O-methylation of the first transcribed nucleotide (producing cap 1) is what lets cytosolic sensors such as RIG-I and IFIT1 recognize a 5' end as host mRNA. An mRNA whose cap is only the unmethylated cap-0 form, as is typical of many viral transcripts when CMTr1-like activity is absent, is instead flagged as foreign, triggering a type-I interferon response; losing CMTr1 activity in a human cell has the same effect, mistakenly marking self mRNA as viral.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher in vitro-transcribes two versions of the same reporter mRNA: one capped with an m7G analog, one left with a 5' triphosphate. Both are injected into cultured cells at equal amounts. Within 30 minutes, the uncapped version is largely gone (degraded 5' to 3' by XRN1 once any residual triphosphate is converted), while the capped version persists and is translated efficiently, because it can recruit eIF4E and assemble the eIF4F complex at its 5' end. The experiment isolates the cap's stability and translation functions from any downstream 3' or coding-sequence effects.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing 5' capping wants to see that a student understands it as a co-transcriptional, CTD-coupled event, not a generic 'protective tag' added at some unspecified later step. A weak answer says 'the cap protects the mRNA.' A strong answer explains that capping enzymes dock on Ser5-phosphorylated CTD during early elongation, names the three catalytic steps, and can connect the cap to at least two distinct downstream consequences, such as XRN1 protection and eIF4E-dependent translation initiation, rather than treating 'stability' and 'translation' as the same fact stated twice.

questions.prompt: The 5' cap is added onto the nascent transcript while Pol II is still transcribing because the capping enzymes dock onto which modified feature?

options.text: Serine 5-phosphorylated repeats of the Pol II CTD
The poly(A) tail at the 3' end
Methylated histone H3 on nearby nucleosomes
The branch-point adenosine of the first intron

explanations.a: Correct — TFIIH's kinase CDK7 phosphorylates Ser5 of the CTD heptad repeats early in elongation, and that mark recruits the capping enzyme complex to the emerging 5' end.
explanations.b: The poly(A) tail is added at the opposite (3') end of the transcript, long after capping, by a separate machinery.
explanations.c: Histone modifications influence chromatin accessibility and transcription rate but are not the docking site for capping enzymes.
explanations.d: The branch point is an intronic splicing signal recognized by U2 snRNP, unrelated to how capping enzymes are recruited.

questions.prompt: Order the three catalytic steps that convert a nascent transcript's 5' triphosphate into an m7G cap.

items.text: RNA triphosphatase removes the terminal gamma phosphate
Guanylyltransferase adds GMP via a 5'-5' linkage
Guanine-N7-methyltransferase methylates the added guanine

questions.explanation: The diphosphate end created by triphosphatase is the substrate for guanylyltransferase, which creates the reversed 5'-5' bond; only after that guanine is attached can the methyltransferase methylate it to complete the m7G cap.

questions.prompt: Match each cap-binding factor to the process it supports.

right.text: Cap-dependent translation initiation in the cytoplasm
5' to 3' exonucleolytic decay, blocked by an intact cap
Nuclear export and first-intron splicing enhancement

questions.explanation: CBP80/CBP20 binds the cap in the nucleus and promotes export plus U1 recruitment to the first intron; eIF4E replaces it in the cytoplasm to nucleate the eIF4F translation initiation complex; XRN1 is the exonuclease the cap structure physically blocks.

questions.prompt: Furuichi and Aaron Shatkin's 1975 discovery that established the existence of the m7G cap structure was made using which system?

options.text: Reovirus mRNA
Yeast ribosomal RNA
Human genomic DNA
Bacterial operon transcripts

explanations.a: Correct — Furuichi and Aaron Shatkin characterized the 5' cap on reovirus mRNA in 1975, and the structure was subsequently found to be a general feature of eukaryotic Pol II transcripts.
explanations.b: Ribosomal RNA is processed differently and was not the system used to first characterize the cap structure.
explanations.c: Genomic DNA is not transcribed RNA and has no cap; the discovery required an mRNA population to analyze.
explanations.d: Bacterial mRNAs are not capped at all, since bacteria lack this eukaryotic modification.

lessons.label: The Spliceosome and Splicing Chemistry

sections.heading: The signals that mark an intron
sections.body: Introns are bounded by nearly invariant dinucleotides: they begin with GU at the 5' splice site and end with AG at the 3' splice site, the 'GT-AG rule' described by Richard Breathnach and Pierre Chambon and by Louise Chow's group in 1977-78 soon after introns themselves were discovered. Two more elements mark the 3' end of the intron: a branch-point adenosine, typically 18-40 nucleotides upstream of the 3' splice site within a loosely conserved sequence, and a polypyrimidine tract of C's and U's lying between the branch point and the terminal AG. None of these signals is very information-rich on its own, which is why splicing depends on a large machine to read them collectively.

sections.heading: Stepwise assembly of the spliceosome
sections.body: The spliceosome assembles fresh on every intron from five small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (snRNPs): U1, U2, U4, U5, and U6. U1 snRNP first base-pairs its snRNA with the 5' splice site (complex E), while the branch point is initially bound by the protein SF1 and the polypyrimidine tract and 3' AG by the U2AF65/U2AF35 heterodimer. In an ATP-dependent step, U2 snRNP displaces SF1 and base-pairs directly with the branch-point sequence, bulging out the branch adenosine (complex A). The preassembled U4/U6.U5 tri-snRNP then joins to form complex B. A major rearrangement follows: U1 and U4 are released, and U6 snRNA takes over the 5' splice site while also pairing with U2, generating the catalytically active site (Bact, then B*).

sections.heading: Two transesterifications, one ribozyme
sections.body: Catalysis proceeds through two sequential transesterification reactions, each simply swapping one phosphodiester bond for another with no net change in bond energy. In step one, the 2'-OH of the branch-point adenosine attacks the phosphate at the 5' splice site, cleaving the exon-intron junction and forming a lariat intermediate in which the intron's 5' end is joined to the branch adenosine through an unusual 2'-5' bond, freeing exon 1. In step two, the newly freed 3'-OH of exon 1 attacks the phosphate at the 3' splice site, joining exon 1 to exon 2 and releasing the intron as a lariat. Genetic work from Christine Guthrie's lab and later cryo-EM studies established that the catalytic core is formed by U6 and U2 snRNA, not protein, making the spliceosome fundamentally a ribozyme that is mechanistically related to self-splicing group II introns.

lessons.workedExample: Consider a 400-nucleotide intron whose branch point A sits 25 nucleotides upstream of the terminal AG, with a 15-nucleotide polypyrimidine tract in between. U2AF65 first binds that pyrimidine tract, SF1 sits on the branch A, and U1 snRNP pairs with the GU at the intron's start. After U2 snRNP swaps in for SF1 and the tri-snRNP joins, the branch A's 2'-OH attacks the 5' splice-site phosphate roughly 375 nucleotides away, looping the intron into a lariat and releasing exon 1's 3'-OH, which then attacks the 3' AG to ligate the exons and release the lariat intron for debranching and decay.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probing splicing chemistry are checking whether a student can distinguish the cis-acting sequence signals (5' GU, branch point, polypyrimidine tract, 3' AG) from the trans-acting machinery (the snRNPs) and can describe the two-step transesterification mechanism rather than just saying 'the spliceosome cuts out introns.' A weak answer treats splicing as a single cut. A strong answer names the lariat intermediate, explains why it is a 2'-5' bond rather than the usual 3'-5', and can state that catalysis is RNA-based, not protein-based — a detail that surprises most students and signals real understanding.

questions.prompt: What structure is formed as the intermediate in the first transesterification reaction of splicing?

options.text: A lariat, with the intron's 5' end joined to the branch-point A via a 2'-5' bond
A fully linear intron with both exons already ligated
A DNA-RNA hybrid at the branch point
A double-stranded RNA duplex spanning the whole intron

explanations.a: Correct — the branch-point adenosine's 2'-OH attacks the 5' splice site, forming the unusual 2'-5' phosphodiester bond that gives the lariat its loop, while exon 1 is released as a free fragment.
explanations.b: Exon ligation only happens in the second transesterification step, after the lariat intermediate has already formed.
explanations.c: Splicing chemistry operates entirely on RNA; no DNA is involved at any step.
explanations.d: The intron does not form an extended duplex with itself; the lariat is defined by a single branch-point linkage, not base-pairing along its length.

questions.prompt: Order the events of spliceosome assembly and catalysis from first to last.

items.text: U1 snRNP binds the 5' splice site; SF1 and U2AF bind the branch point and polypyrimidine tract/3' AG
U2 snRNP displaces SF1 and base-pairs with the branch-point sequence
