The U4/U6.U5 tri-snRNP joins, followed by release of U1 and U4 and formation of the catalytic core
Two transesterification reactions form the lariat and ligate the exons

questions.explanation: Assembly is strictly ordered: early recognition (complex E) precedes ATP-dependent U2 engagement (complex A), which precedes tri-snRNP joining and rearrangement into the catalytically active spliceosome, which precedes the two chemical steps of splicing itself.

questions.prompt: Match each intron sequence element to the factor that recognizes it during early spliceosome assembly.

right.text: U1 snRNP
SF1 (later replaced by U2 snRNP)
U2AF65/U2AF35

questions.explanation: In the earliest recognition complex, U1 snRNP base-pairs with the 5' GU, SF1 sits on the branch point before being displaced by U2 snRNP, and the U2AF heterodimer reads the polypyrimidine tract and terminal AG.

lessons.label: Alternative Splicing

sections.heading: Four ways to splice the same pre-mRNA differently
sections.body: A single gene can be spliced into multiple mature mRNAs by varying which exons are joined. Exon skipping, where a cassette exon is left out of some transcripts, is the most common pattern in vertebrates. Mutually exclusive exons occur when exactly one of a cluster of alternative exons is retained per transcript, never zero and never more than one. Alternative 5' or 3' splice site usage shifts the exact boundary where an exon is cut, changing its length by anywhere from a few to hundreds of nucleotides. Intron retention leaves a whole intron in the mature transcript, often introducing a premature stop codon or novel protein sequence. Large-scale RNA-seq surveys around 2008, including work from Christopher Burge's and Benjamin Blencowe's groups, estimated that roughly 95% of human multi-exon genes undergo some form of alternative splicing, making it a major source of proteome diversity beyond the roughly 20,000 protein-coding genes in the genome.

sections.heading: A combinatorial code of enhancers and silencers
sections.body: Which splice sites the spliceosome actually uses is controlled by short cis-regulatory elements scattered through exons and introns: exonic and intronic splicing enhancers (ESEs, ISEs) and silencers (ESSs, ISSs). SR proteins, a family of proteins rich in serine-arginine repeats, typically bind ESEs and promote exon inclusion by helping recruit U1 snRNP and U2AF to nearby splice sites. Heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoproteins (hnRNPs) more often bind exonic or intronic silencers and antagonize SR protein activity, promoting exon skipping. No single factor decides an exon's fate; splicing outcome is a combinatorial readout of which enhancers and silencers happen to be occupied in a given cell type, which is why the same gene can be spliced differently in neurons versus muscle.

sections.heading: Dscam: the extreme case
sections.body: The Drosophila gene Dscam (Down syndrome cell adhesion molecule) illustrates how far this can scale. It contains four clusters of mutually exclusive alternative exons — variable numbers of options at exon positions 4, 6, 9, and 17 — and Dror Schmucker and colleagues calculated in 2000 that these clusters could combine to produce 38,016 distinct ectodomain variants from one gene. Larry Zipursky's lab later showed each Drosophila neuron expresses a largely unique subset of these isoforms, which mediate self-avoidance: a neuron's own branches repel each other via homophilic Dscam binding but tolerate branches from other neurons, letting dendrites and axons tile space without collapsing onto themselves.

lessons.workedExample: A pre-mRNA has three exons, 1-2-3, where exon 2 carries a strong ESE bound by SR proteins in most cell types, causing inclusion (exon 1-2-3 spliced together). In a specific neuronal cell type, an hnRNP is expressed that binds an ISS just inside the flanking intron and blocks U2AF from engaging the exon 2 3' splice site, so exon 2 is skipped and only exon 1-3 is produced. The same gene, same DNA sequence, yields two different proteins purely because the ratio of SR protein to that particular hnRNP differs between cell types.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking about alternative splicing wants to know whether a student understands it as a regulated, sequence-driven choice rather than random noise or an error in transcription. A weak answer says 'genes can make different proteins.' A strong answer names a specific splicing pattern (exon skipping versus mutually exclusive exons, for instance), explains that SR proteins and hnRNPs compete at enhancer and silencer elements to set the outcome, and can cite a concrete case like Dscam's tens of thousands of isoforms to show the regulatory logic scales to an extreme.

questions.prompt: Match each alternative splicing pattern to its description.

right.text: A cassette exon is included in some transcripts and left out of others
Exactly one exon from a cluster is retained in every transcript, never more than one
An intron is left in the mature mRNA rather than being removed

questions.explanation: Exon skipping varies whether a single exon appears at all; mutually exclusive exons guarantee one-and-only-one choice from a cluster; intron retention keeps intronic sequence in the final transcript instead of splicing it out.

questions.prompt: SR proteins bound to exonic splicing enhancers generally have what effect on exon inclusion?

options.text: They promote inclusion by helping recruit U1 snRNP and U2AF to nearby splice sites
They promote exon skipping by blocking the branch point
They have no effect on splice site choice, only on 3' end cleavage
They degrade the pre-mRNA before splicing can occur

explanations.a: Correct — SR proteins bound to ESEs recruit spliceosome components to adjacent splice sites, favoring inclusion of that exon.
explanations.b: Promoting skipping via silencer elements is more characteristic of hnRNPs, which often antagonize SR protein activity.
explanations.c: SR proteins act specifically on splice site selection, not on 3' end cleavage and polyadenylation, which is a separate process.
explanations.d: SR proteins are splicing regulators, not decay factors; they do not degrade the transcript.

questions.prompt: The Drosophila Dscam gene's four clusters of mutually exclusive exons were calculated by Schmucker and colleagues in 2000 to yield how many potential ectodomain isoforms?

options.text: About 400
Over 1 million

explanations.a: Correct — the combinatorial product of the exon 4, 6, 9, and 17 clusters gives 38,016 potential isoforms, an often-cited figure exceeding the number of genes in the Drosophila genome.
explanations.b: 12 is roughly the number of variants at just one cluster (exon 4), not the combined total across all four clusters.
explanations.c: A few hundred undercounts the combinatorial scale of four independent exon clusters multiplying together.
explanations.d: Over a million overstates the actual calculated total; the combinatorics of the four clusters land at 38,016, not into the millions.

lessons.label: 3' End Formation and Polyadenylation

sections.heading: Cleavage at a sequence-defined site
sections.body: Unlike the 3' end of a bacterial transcript, which simply stops where RNA polymerase terminates, a eukaryotic mRNA's 3' end is created by endonucleolytic cleavage of a much longer precursor, followed by addition of a poly(A) tail. The key signal is the hexamer AAUAAA, identified by Nick Proudfoot and George Brownlee in 1976, located 10-30 nucleotides upstream of the actual cleavage site. It is recognized by the multi-subunit cleavage and polyadenylation specificity factor (CPSF). A second, more variable GU-rich or U-rich element downstream of the cleavage site is recognized by cleavage stimulation factor (CstF). CPSF and CstF binding on either side of the site, together with additional cleavage factors, positions an endonuclease to cut the RNA, generating a free 3'-OH end that becomes the substrate for polyadenylation.

sections.heading: Building and using the poly(A) tail
sections.body: Immediately after cleavage, poly(A) polymerase (PAP), still tethered through CPSF, adds adenosines to the new 3' end without a template — in mammalian cells this reaches roughly 200-250 adenosines, appreciably longer than the 60-80 nucleotide tails typical of yeast. As the tail grows, poly(A)-binding protein (PABP) coats it, which both protects the tail from premature shortening and, through an interaction with the translation factor eIF4G, helps circularize the mRNA into the 'closed loop' that stimulates translation initiation and links the 5' cap functionally to the 3' end.

sections.heading: Alternative polyadenylation changes which regulatory elements survive
sections.body: Most genes have more than one potential poly(A) site, and using a proximal site instead of a distal one shortens the 3' UTR, sometimes dramatically. Because microRNA target sites and AU-rich destabilizing elements are concentrated in the distal portion of many 3' UTRs, a shift to a proximal poly(A) site can delete those sites wholesale, leaving the mRNA immune to regulation it would otherwise be subject to. Mayr and David Bartel's 2009 comparison of proliferating cancer cell lines against normal fibroblasts found that proliferating cells systematically favor shorter 3' UTRs via proximal polyadenylation, which removes miRNA binding sites from transcripts including growth-promoting genes and stabilizes their expression — tying a 3' end processing choice directly to a proliferative phenotype. A developmentally programmed example predates the cancer work: during B-cell activation, the immunoglobulin heavy-chain (IgM) gene shifts from the distal poly(A) site, which produces the membrane-bound receptor form, to a proximal site that yields the secreted antibody form. Takagaki and Manley showed this switch tracks rising levels of the cleavage factor CstF-64, which binds the weaker proximal site more effectively as its concentration increases, showing that APA is not just a disease-associated accident but a normal developmental control mechanism.

lessons.workedExample: A gene has two poly(A) sites: a proximal one 200 nucleotides after the stop codon and a distal one 1,800 nucleotides after it, with three miRNA target sites and an AU-rich element sitting between those two positions. In a normal cell using the distal site, the long 3' UTR carries all three miRNA sites plus the ARE, so the mRNA is kept in check by both miRNA-mediated repression and rapid ARE-driven turnover. In a fast-dividing cell that shifts CPSF/CstF usage toward the proximal site, the resulting short-UTR transcript physically lacks those elements, so it escapes both regulatory mechanisms and accumulates to higher levels even though the coding sequence and protein are identical.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing 3' end formation wants to see the mechanism (AAUAAA plus CPSF/CstF cleavage, then untemplated poly(A) addition) distinguished from its downstream regulatory consequence (alternative polyadenylation changing which cis-elements a transcript retains). A weak answer says 'a poly(A) tail is added to protect mRNA.' A strong answer explains that shortening the 3' UTR via proximal-site usage can delete real regulatory sequence, not just add or remove a generic tail length, and can connect that to a specific outcome such as escaping miRNA repression.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of 3' end formation from signal recognition through completion of the poly(A) tail.

items.text: CPSF binds the AAUAAA hexamer and CstF binds the downstream GU/U-rich element
The pre-mRNA is endonucleolytically cleaved, generating a free 3'-OH
Poly(A) polymerase adds roughly 200-250 adenosines without a template
PABP coats the tail and helps circularize the mRNA via eIF4G

questions.explanation: CPSF/CstF must first bind their respective signals to position the cleavage machinery; only after the cut creates a free 3'-OH can PAP extend it; only after the tail exists can PABP coat it and bridge to the cap-binding translation machinery.

questions.prompt: What is the primary consequence of a shift from a distal to a proximal poly(A) site (alternative polyadenylation)?

options.text: The 3' UTR shortens and can lose miRNA target sites and AU-rich elements that lay downstream of the proximal site
The poly(A) tail becomes permanently untethered from PABP
The AAUAAA hexamer is mutated to a new sequence
The mRNA is exported to the cytoplasm without a cap

explanations.a: Correct — using a closer poly(A) site truncates the 3' UTR, physically removing any regulatory elements, such as miRNA sites or AREs, that were located between the proximal and distal sites.
explanations.b: PABP still binds whatever poly(A) tail is synthesized at the new site; the shift changes UTR length, not PABP binding per se.
explanations.c: Proximal versus distal site choice is about which of two (or more) AAUAAA-marked sites is used, not a mutation of the sequence itself.
explanations.d: Capping occurs independently at the 5' end during early transcription and is unaffected by which 3' cleavage site is chosen.

questions.prompt: The hexamer sequence recognized by CPSF during 3' end cleavage, identified by Proudfoot and Brownlee in 1976, is:

options.text: AAUAAA
GUAAGU
UACUAAC
AUG

explanations.a: Correct — AAUAAA is the canonical polyadenylation signal recognized by CPSF, positioned 10-30 nucleotides upstream of the cleavage site.
explanations.b: GUAAGU approximates a 5' splice site consensus, not the polyadenylation signal.
explanations.c: UACUAAC resembles a yeast branch-point consensus sequence used in splicing, not 3' end cleavage.
explanations.d: AUG is the translation start codon and has no role in defining the 3' cleavage site.

lessons.label: mRNA Stability and Decay

sections.heading: The general pathway: deadenylation opens the door
sections.body: Most eukaryotic mRNA decay begins the same way regardless of the transcript: gradual shortening of the poly(A) tail by deadenylase complexes, principally CCR4-NOT and PAN2-PAN3. Once the tail is short enough that PABP can no longer stabilize the 5' end through the closed-loop interaction, the mRNA becomes a substrate for decapping by the DCP1/DCP2 complex, which removes the m7G cap. From there, decay can proceed in either direction. The exonuclease XRN1 degrades the body of the transcript 5' to 3' starting from the now-exposed 5' end, which is the dominant route for most bulk mRNA turnover in the cytoplasm. Alternatively, the RNA can be degraded 3' to 5' by the exosome, a large multi-subunit complex that also handles most nuclear RNA surveillance and processing of stable RNA precursors.

sections.heading: AU-rich elements: built-in short half-life
sections.body: Some transcripts are built for rapid turnover by default. Many cytokine and proto-oncogene mRNAs, including GM-CSF, c-fos, and TNF-alpha, carry AU-rich elements (AREs) in their 3' UTRs, often clusters of the pentamer AUUUA. Proteins such as tristetraprolin (TTP) and AUF1 bind these AREs and recruit deadenylases and the decapping machinery directly to the transcript, bypassing the slow default kinetics of ordinary deadenylation. The functional payoff is a half-life of minutes rather than the many hours typical of a stable housekeeping mRNA, letting the cell shut off an inflammatory or growth signal quickly once it is no longer needed; TTP-knockout mice, for instance, overproduce TNF-alpha and develop chronic inflammatory disease.

sections.heading: Nonsense-mediated decay: a splicing-linked quality check
sections.body: A separate surveillance pathway, nonsense-mediated decay (NMD), targets transcripts with a premature termination codon (PTC). During splicing, the spliceosome deposits an exon junction complex (EJC) roughly 20-24 nucleotides upstream of every exon-exon junction, and normal translation displaces each EJC as the ribosome passes. If a stop codon occurs upstream of the last exon-exon junction — because of a nonsense mutation or a frameshifting splicing error — the terminating ribosome leaves at least one EJC downstream still bound. Factors including UPF1, UPF2, and UPF3, work first characterized in yeast and extensively developed by Lynne Maquat's lab in mammalian systems, recognize this abnormal arrangement and trigger rapid decay of the transcript, preventing translation of a truncated, potentially harmful protein. Two related surveillance pathways catch different failure modes. No-go decay targets mRNAs where the ribosome stalls on a strong secondary structure or a damaged base; Dom34/Hbs1-like factors recognize the stalled ribosome and recruit an endonuclease to cleave the transcript near the stall site. Non-stop decay handles mRNAs that lack a stop codon altogether, often because of premature polyadenylation within the coding sequence; the ribosome simply reads into and through the poly(A) tail, and this abnormal event triggers rapid degradation of the faulty transcript.

lessons.workedExample: A gene has 5 exons; a nonsense mutation creates a premature stop codon within exon 3. After splicing, EJCs are deposited at the exon 3-4 and exon 4-5 junctions. The ribosome translates through exon 3 and terminates at the premature stop, well upstream of both remaining EJCs. UPF1 bound to the terminating ribosome, together with UPF2 and UPF3 on the downstream EJCs, triggers NMD, and the transcript is degraded before it can produce a truncated protein. If the same mutation instead fell in the final exon, no EJC would remain downstream of the stop, translation would appear normal to the surveillance machinery, and the truncated protein would likely be made.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing mRNA decay is checking whether a student can name the actual triggers and machinery, not just say 'unstable mRNAs get degraded.' A weak answer treats decay as uniform and unregulated. A strong answer separates the default deadenylation-decapping-exonuclease pathway from at least one dedicated surveillance system, such as ARE-driven rapid turnover or EJC-based nonsense-mediated decay, and explains the underlying logic: NMD works because the exon-junction complex acts as a positional marker of 'where splicing said the last exon boundary should be' relative to where translation actually stopped.

questions.prompt: Order the events of the general (bulk) mRNA decay pathway.

items.text: CCR4-NOT/PAN2-PAN3 shorten the poly(A) tail
PABP can no longer stabilize the closed-loop 5' end
DCP1/DCP2 remove the m7G cap
XRN1 degrades the transcript 5' to 3' (or the exosome degrades it 3' to 5')

questions.explanation: Deadenylation must shorten the tail before PABP loses its grip; loss of the closed loop exposes the mRNA to decapping; only after the cap is removed can 5'-to-3' exonucleolytic decay by XRN1 proceed (or the exosome degrade from the 3' end).

questions.prompt: Why does a premature termination codon located in an internal exon trigger nonsense-mediated decay, while one in the final exon typically does not?

options.text: An internal PTC leaves at least one exon junction complex downstream of the terminating ribosome, which the final-exon case lacks
Internal exons are transcribed at a slower rate, giving UPF1 more time to bind
Only mutations in internal exons change the reading frame
The poly(A) tail is shorter when the mutation is internal

explanations.a: Correct — EJCs are deposited at exon-exon junctions during splicing; if the ribosome terminates upstream of the last junction, an unremoved EJC signals abnormal termination and triggers NMD, whereas a stop in the final exon leaves no EJC downstream to trigger it.
explanations.b: Transcription rate is not part of the mechanism NMD uses to distinguish premature from normal stop codons.
explanations.c: A premature stop codon can arise from a point mutation as well as a frameshift, and its exon location, not the type of mutation, is what matters for EJC positioning.
explanations.d: Poly(A) tail length is set independently at the 3' end and is not what signals premature termination to the NMD machinery.

questions.prompt: Match each decay factor or element to its role.

right.text: Marks exon-exon junctions from splicing; unremoved copies trigger NMD
Recruits deadenylase/decapping machinery for rapid turnover of specific transcripts
Exonuclease that degrades decapped mRNA 5' to 3'

questions.explanation: AREs recruit TTP/AUF1 to accelerate decay of specific unstable transcripts; EJCs deposited during splicing serve as positional markers that NMD uses; XRN1 is the exonuclease that carries out bulk 5'-to-3' degradation once a transcript is decapped.

lessons.label: miRNA Biogenesis and RNAi

sections.heading: From hairpin transcript to mature guide strand
sections.body: MicroRNAs are encoded in the genome and transcribed by Pol II as long primary transcripts (pri-miRNAs) that fold back on themselves into hairpin structures. In the nucleus, the Microprocessor complex, built around the RNase III enzyme Drosha and its partner DGCR8, crops the hairpin out of the pri-miRNA, leaving a roughly 70-nucleotide stem-loop called the pre-miRNA. Exportin-5, together with RanGTP, carries the pre-miRNA through the nuclear pore into the cytoplasm. There, a second RNase III enzyme, Dicer, cleaves off the loop to leave a roughly 22-nucleotide double-stranded RNA duplex. One strand, the guide strand, is loaded into an Argonaute protein (AGO2 in humans) to form the core of RISC (RNA-induced silencing complex), while the other strand, the passenger, is typically degraded. This pathway was built on the discovery of the first microRNA, lin-4, by Rosalind Lee, Rhonda Feinbaum, and Victor Ambros in 1993 in C. elegans, later joined by let-7, described by Reinhart and colleagues in 2000, which turned out to be conserved across animals. Not every pre-miRNA is made this way: mirtrons are an alternate class encoded entirely within short introns, where the spliceosome itself excises the hairpin as a byproduct of normal splicing and debranching, bypassing Drosha/DGCR8 processing entirely. A mirtron hairpin only rejoins the canonical pathway downstream, at the Exportin-5-mediated export and Dicer cleavage steps, showing that Microprocessor cropping is a common entry point into the pathway rather than an obligatory one.

sections.heading: The seed match: imperfect pairing, big consequences
sections.body: Once loaded into RISC, a miRNA finds its targets mainly through Watson-Crick pairing of just nucleotides 2 through 8 from its 5' end, the seed region, to complementary sites usually located in a target mRNA's 3' UTR. Because the seed match tolerates mismatches elsewhere along the miRNA, a single miRNA can regulate hundreds of different transcripts, and a single 3' UTR often carries sites for several different miRNAs. Seed pairing recruits GW182/TNRC6 proteins to AGO2, which in turn recruit the CCR4-NOT deadenylase complex, so the dominant outcome in animals is a combination of translational repression and accelerated deadenylation rather than direct cleavage of the target.

sections.heading: miRNA versus siRNA
sections.body: Small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) are processed by the same Dicer enzyme but differ in origin and outcome. siRNAs typically derive from long, perfectly double-stranded RNA — exogenous, viral, or experimentally introduced, as in Andrew Fire and Craig Mello's foundational 1998 RNAi paper in C. elegans, work that earned the 2006 Nobel Prize. Because an siRNA duplex pairs essentially perfectly with its target rather than through a short imperfect seed, AGO2 uses its slicer endonuclease activity to cleave the target mRNA directly, in contrast to the seed-based translational repression and deadenylation typical of endogenous miRNAs.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher wants to silence a specific gene. Option one: introduce a synthetic siRNA duplex fully complementary to the target mRNA's coding sequence — Dicer is not even needed since the duplex is already the right size, and loaded AGO2 directly slices the transcript in two, giving fast, potent, but transcript-specific knockdown. Option two: express a hairpin mimicking an endogenous pri-miRNA with a seed only partially complementary to several related transcripts sharing a UTR motif — this produces broader, gentler translational repression and deadenylation across a family of targets rather than clean cleavage of one, illustrating why the two strategies are chosen for different purposes.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing miRNA biogenesis wants a student to trace the pathway with the right enzymes in the right compartments (Drosha/DGCR8 in the nucleus, Dicer in the cytoplasm) rather than saying 'small RNAs regulate genes.' A weak answer conflates miRNA and siRNA as the same thing. A strong answer explains why seed-based imperfect pairing (nucleotides 2-8) produces translational repression and deadenylation for miRNAs, while the near-perfect pairing typical of siRNAs allows AGO2's slicer activity to cleave the target directly — a mechanistic distinction, not just a vocabulary one.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of miRNA biogenesis from transcription to RISC loading.

items.text: Pol II transcribes the pri-miRNA hairpin
Drosha/DGCR8 (Microprocessor) crop the pri-miRNA into the pre-miRNA
Exportin-5/RanGTP export the pre-miRNA to the cytoplasm
Dicer cleaves the loop, and the guide strand is loaded into AGO2/RISC

questions.explanation: The pri-miRNA must be transcribed before it can be cropped in the nucleus by Drosha/DGCR8; only the resulting pre-miRNA is a substrate for Exportin-5-mediated export; only in the cytoplasm does Dicer process it further and hand the guide strand to AGO2.

questions.prompt: Which nucleotides of a mature miRNA make up the seed region primarily responsible for target recognition?

options.text: Nucleotides 2 through 8 from the 5' end
The entire 22-nucleotide length, requiring perfect complementarity
Only the single nucleotide at the extreme 3' end
Nucleotides in the loop removed by Dicer

explanations.a: Correct — the seed region, nucleotides 2-8 from the 5' end, provides the core Watson-Crick pairing that identifies 3' UTR target sites, while the rest of the miRNA can tolerate mismatches.
explanations.b: Full-length perfect complementarity describes the siRNA mode of target recognition, not the typical animal miRNA seed-based mechanism.
explanations.c: A single 3' nucleotide is far too little sequence to confer any meaningful target specificity.
explanations.d: The loop is cleaved away by Dicer during processing and is not part of the mature miRNA that pairs with targets.

questions.prompt: Match each RNA silencing feature to whether it typically describes an endogenous miRNA or an experimental/viral siRNA.

left.text: Derives from a long, perfectly double-stranded precursor (exogenous or viral)
Pairs via a short imperfect seed match in the target 3' UTR
Directs AGO2 slicer-mediated cleavage of a near-perfectly complementary target

right.text: siRNA — perfect duplex origin
miRNA
siRNA — slicer-mediated cleavage

questions.explanation: siRNAs arise from long perfect duplexes and direct near-perfect-match cleavage via AGO2's slicer activity, while endogenous miRNAs rely on short seed matches that favor translational repression and deadenylation over direct cleavage.

lessons.label: Translational and Localized Control

sections.heading: Controlling translation before the main start codon
sections.body: Regulation of an mRNA does not stop once it reaches the cytoplasm; the 5' UTR itself can gate translation. Upstream open reading frames (uORFs) are short coding sequences positioned before the main start codon: a scanning ribosome often translates the uORF, terminates, and either dissociates or must re-acquire initiation factors before reaching the main ORF, generally repressing the downstream protein. The yeast gene GCN4 turns this into a regulatory switch, a model developed largely by Alan Hinnebusch's lab: under normal amino acid levels, ribosomes that terminate at GCN4's uORF1 efficiently reinitiate at further inhibitory uORFs and never reach the main ORF, but during amino acid starvation, reduced levels of active eIF2-GTP delay reinitiation just long enough that ribosomes skip the inhibitory uORFs and instead initiate at GCN4 itself, inducing it. Separately, some mRNAs recruit ribosomes through an internal ribosome entry site (IRES), first demonstrated by Nahum Sonenberg and Jerry Pelletier in 1988 in poliovirus RNA, allowing cap-independent initiation when normal cap-dependent translation is shut down, such as during viral infection or apoptosis.

sections.heading: The IRE/IRP switch: one signal, opposite outcomes
sections.body: Iron homeostasis provides an unusually clean example of post-transcriptional control because the same regulatory logic produces opposite effects depending on where a stem-loop called the iron-response element (IRE) sits. Ferritin mRNA, which encodes the iron-storage protein, carries a single IRE in its 5' UTR. When cellular iron is low, iron regulatory proteins (IRPs) bind that 5' IRE and physically block the scanning ribosome, repressing ferritin translation. Transferrin receptor (TfR) mRNA, which imports iron, instead carries several IREs in its 3' UTR. When iron is low, IRP binding at those 3' IREs protects the transcript from endonucleolytic cleavage, stabilizing it and increasing TfR protein to bring in more iron. The same low-iron signal and the same IRP protein thus repress one mRNA's translation while stabilizing another's, purely as a function of IRE location — work developed through the 1980s and 1990s by researchers including Richard Klausner, Tracey Rouault, and Matthias Hentze.

sections.heading: Sending mRNAs to a location, and parking them in granules
sections.body: Some transcripts are regulated by where they go rather than only when they are translated. Beta-actin mRNA carries a 'zipcode' sequence in its 3' UTR bound by zipcode-binding protein 1 (ZBP1), which Robert Singer's lab showed transports the mRNA to the leading edge of migrating fibroblasts and to growth cones, where local translation supports cytoskeletal remodeling exactly where it is needed. Repressed or decay-bound mRNAs can also be sequestered into cytoplasmic granules: P-bodies, enriched in decapping and 5'-to-3' decay factors such as DCP1/2 and XRN1, and stress granules, which form under conditions like heat or oxidative stress and hold stalled translation preinitiation complexes; the two granule types can exchange contents, functioning as linked hubs for mRNA storage, triage, and decay.

lessons.workedExample: A cell experiences an iron shortage. IRP binds the single 5' IRE on ferritin mRNA, blocking ribosome scanning and shutting off synthesis of an iron-storage protein the cell has no iron to fill anyway. Simultaneously, IRP binds the multiple 3' IREs on transferrin receptor mRNA, protecting it from cleavage; TfR protein consequently rises and pulls more iron in from outside. When iron becomes abundant again, IRP loses its RNA-binding conformation, ferritin translation resumes to store the new iron, and unprotected TfR mRNA is degraded, lowering further iron uptake — one small protein producing a coordinated, opposite-direction response from two different transcripts.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing this material wants to see that a student can explain a specific regulatory mechanism end to end rather than gesturing at 'translation can be controlled.' The IRE/IRP system is a favorite because it rewards precision: a strong answer states which UTR carries the IRE for each transcript and explains why identical IRP binding produces repression in one case and stabilization in the other. A weak answer says 'iron regulates gene expression' without connecting the 5' versus 3' location of the element to the opposite mechanistic outcomes it produces.

questions.prompt: Match each transcript to the effect of IRP binding to its IRE under low-iron conditions.

right.text: Translation is repressed by blocking ribosome scanning
The mRNA is stabilized against endonucleolytic cleavage, increasing protein levels

questions.explanation: IRP bound to the 5' IRE on ferritin mRNA sterically blocks scanning ribosomes, repressing translation, while IRP bound to the 3' IREs on transferrin receptor mRNA instead shields the transcript from decay, increasing its abundance and thus TfR protein.

questions.prompt: An internal ribosome entry site (IRES), first demonstrated in poliovirus RNA by Pelletier and Sonenberg in 1988, allows translation to proceed by what mechanism?

options.text: Cap-independent recruitment of the ribosome directly to an internal site in the mRNA
Enhanced binding of eIF4E to the 5' cap
Extension of the poly(A) tail to recruit more PABP
Removal of all upstream open reading frames from the transcript

explanations.a: Correct — an IRES lets the ribosome initiate internally without needing to recognize and scan from the 5' cap, which is especially useful when cap-dependent initiation is shut down.
explanations.b: IRES-mediated initiation is specifically defined by not depending on eIF4E/cap recognition, the opposite of this option.
explanations.c: Poly(A) tail extension is unrelated to IRES function, which concerns ribosome recruitment at the 5' end region, not tail length.
explanations.d: IRES elements are a distinct regulatory feature from uORFs; having an IRES does not require or imply the absence of uORFs elsewhere in the transcript.

questions.prompt: Beta-actin mRNA's 'zipcode' sequence, bound by ZBP1, functions to:

options.text: Localize the mRNA to the leading edge of migrating cells or growth cones for local translation
Mark the transcript for immediate decapping and decay
Recruit the exon junction complex during splicing
Extend the poly(A) tail beyond the normal 200-250 adenosine range

explanations.a: Correct — Singer's lab showed the 3' UTR zipcode bound by ZBP1 directs beta-actin mRNA transport to specific subcellular locations, enabling localized translation where cytoskeletal remodeling is needed.
explanations.b: The zipcode is a localization signal, not a decay signal; it does not recruit decapping or exonucleolytic machinery.
explanations.c: Exon junction complex deposition happens during splicing in the nucleus and is unrelated to the cytoplasmic zipcode/ZBP1 localization system.
explanations.d: Zipcode-mediated localization does not alter poly(A) tail length; tail length is set by the separate 3' end processing machinery.

questions.prompt: P-bodies and stress granules are best described as:

options.text: Cytoplasmic foci enriched in decay/repression machinery or stalled preinitiation complexes, which can exchange contents
Nuclear structures where splicing occurs
Membrane-bound organelles that import iron
Sites of poly(A) tail addition during 3' end processing

explanations.a: Correct — P-bodies concentrate decapping and 5'-to-3' decay factors while stress granules hold stalled translation preinitiation complexes under stress, and the two compartments can exchange mRNAs and proteins.
explanations.b: Both are cytoplasmic, membraneless compartments, not nuclear sites, and splicing occurs co-transcriptionally in the nucleus, not in these granules.
explanations.c: Neither structure is membrane-bound or involved in iron transport; that role belongs to different systems such as transferrin receptor-mediated uptake.
explanations.d: 3' end processing and polyadenylation occur in the nucleus during pre-mRNA maturation, not in these cytoplasmic granules.

units.label: Methods: Dissecting Regulation at a Single Locus

lessons.label: Reporter Assays and Cis-Element Mapping

sections.heading: Why fuse a promoter to a reporter
sections.body: You cannot easily watch a single gene's transcription happen in real time inside a cell, so molecular biologists substitute a surrogate: clone the candidate promoter or enhancer upstream of a reporter gene whose product is trivial to measure, then read the reporter as a proxy for transcriptional activity of that DNA element. Firefly luciferase (from Photinus pyralis) oxidizes luciferin and emits light with single-photon sensitivity and a huge linear dynamic range, which is why it displaced the older chloramphenicol acetyltransferase (CAT) assay, which required a radioactive substrate and thin-layer chromatography. Beta-galactosidase (lacZ) gives a cheap colorimetric or blue/white readout but is far less sensitive to small changes. GFP is unmatched for visualizing which individual live cells are transcribing, but its slow maturation and broad autofluorescence background make it a poor tool for quantifying subtle fold-changes.

sections.heading: Normalizing with dual-luciferase
sections.body: Firefly signal on its own is confounded by transfection efficiency, cell number, and lysis variability between wells. The dual-luciferase system cotransfects a second, constitutively expressed Renilla luciferase (from the sea pansy Renilla reniformis) as an internal control and reports the firefly:Renilla ratio, canceling out well-to-well noise that has nothing to do with the promoter being tested.

sections.heading: Localizing the element: deletion series and linker scanning
sections.body: A nested 5' promoter-deletion series truncates progressively more upstream sequence in each construct; a sharp drop in reporter activity between two adjacent deletion endpoints brackets a positive element, while a rise brackets a repressive one. Deletions can be misleading, though, because removing sequence also changes the spacing between remaining elements. McKnight and Kingsbury's 1982 work on the herpes simplex virus thymidine kinase promoter introduced linker-scanning mutagenesis to fix this: a series of short, fixed-length substitutions is walked across the region so total length and spacing never change, isolating the effect of disrupting one element at a time.

sections.heading: Confirming necessity with point mutation
sections.body: Once a footprint or a sequence match to a known consensus (an Sp1 GC box, a CREB CRE) nominates a specific binding site, mutating just the predicted contact bases and retesting in the reporter tests whether that exact sequence is necessary for activity. Loss of activity supports necessity, but remains correlative on its own until paired with a direct binding assay such as EMSA or ChIP. The luciferase reporter itself traces back to de Wet and colleagues, who in 1987 first cloned firefly luciferase as a quantitative promoter-activity readout, and the same necessity logic scales down cleanly to a single element: in classic dissections of viral early promoters, mutating just the core hexanucleotide of one Sp1 GC box can cut reporter activity by roughly 80-90%, showing that a handful of specific base pairs, not merely the surrounding region, account for most of the transcriptional output.

lessons.workedExample: A student clones 2 kb upstream of a heat-shock gene into a firefly-luciferase vector, cotransfects Renilla for normalization, and builds five nested 5' deletions (-2000, -500, -250, -150, -100). Normalized activity is flat from -2000 to -150 but collapses 10-fold at -100, bracketing a 50 bp window. Scanning that window turns up a heat-shock element (HSE) consensus (nGAAn repeats). Mutating the HSE core in the full-length -2000 construct abolishes heat-inducibility entirely, supporting that this specific site is necessary for the induced response.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing a reporter figure is really asking whether the student tested sufficiency and necessity of a specific piece of DNA, not just correlated an mRNA change with a treatment. A weak answer shows one bar of luciferase activity for the full-length promoter with no normalization control and no narrowing step. A strong answer walks through the deletion series that bracketed the element, explains why linker scanning (not just deletion) was used to rule out spacing artifacts, and shows that mutating the specific candidate site killed the response.

questions.prompt: Why cotransfect a constitutive Renilla luciferase alongside the firefly reporter driven by the candidate promoter?

options.text: Renilla luciferase directly measures the candidate promoter's activity more accurately than firefly
It normalizes for well-to-well differences in transfection efficiency and cell number, unrelated to the promoter itself
It replaces the need for a 5' deletion series
It converts the assay from qualitative to colorimetric

explanations.a: Renilla is driven by a constitutive promoter unrelated to the candidate element; it is a control, not a second readout of the promoter under study.
explanations.b: Correct — dividing firefly by Renilla signal cancels out variability in how efficiently each well was transfected and lysed, isolating the promoter-specific signal.
explanations.c: Normalization and element mapping are separate steps; Renilla says nothing about which sequence within the promoter matters.
explanations.d: Both luciferases are luminescent, not colorimetric; that trait belongs to lacZ.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of narrowing an enhancer down to a single necessary binding site.

items.text: Build a nested 5' deletion series of the candidate region in a luciferase reporter
Transfect each construct and measure normalized (firefly:Renilla) activity
Identify the deletion interval where activity sharply drops
Point-mutate the candidate binding site's core bases within that interval
Retest the mutant and confirm loss of activity

questions.explanation: Deletion mapping first brackets a coarse window, then targeted point mutation within that window tests necessity of the specific predicted site.

questions.prompt: Match each reporter to the property that distinguishes it.

right.text: Light output from luciferin oxidation; extremely sensitive, wide dynamic range
Requires a radioactive acetylation assay; largely superseded
Colorimetric blue/white readout; cheap but low sensitivity to small changes
Best for visualizing which live single cells are transcribing, not for subtle fold-changes

questions.explanation: Each reporter trades sensitivity, quantitative precision, and live-cell visualization differently; luciferase wins on sensitivity, CAT is the historical radioactive method, lacZ is cheap but coarse, and GFP is best for single-cell live imaging.

questions.prompt: Why is linker-scanning mutagenesis preferred over simple deletion when finer-resolution mapping is needed?

options.text: It is cheaper and faster to construct than a deletion series
It keeps total construct length and element spacing constant, avoiding artifacts from altered distances between elements
It does not require a luciferase reporter
It directly identifies the transcription factor that binds, unlike deletion

explanations.a: Linker scanning requires building many overlapping substitution constructs, generally more labor than a deletion series.
explanations.b: Correct — because each construct swaps in a fixed-length linker rather than removing sequence, spacing between surviving elements never changes, isolating the effect of disrupting one element at a time.
explanations.c: Linker-scanning constructs are still tested in the same reporter framework as deletions.
explanations.d: Neither method identifies the binding factor's identity; that requires EMSA or ChIP.

lessons.label: Detecting Protein-DNA Binding: EMSA and Footprinting

sections.heading: The gel-shift principle
sections.body: The electrophoretic mobility shift assay (EMSA), developed independently by Fried and Crothers and by Garner and Revzin in 1981, incubates a short labeled double-stranded DNA probe spanning a candidate site with nuclear extract or purified protein, then runs the mixture on a native polyacrylamide gel. Free probe runs fast; probe bound by protein carries extra mass and altered charge, so it migrates slower and appears as an upshifted band above the free-probe band. A shift alone shows something in the extract binds that sequence, nothing more.

sections.heading: Confirming identity and specificity
sections.body: Two controls turn a shift into a claim. An antibody supershift adds an antibody against the candidate factor to the binding reaction; if that factor sits in the shifted complex, the antibody either adds further mass, pushing the band even higher (a supershift), or sterically blocks binding and abolishes the shift, either result identifying the protein. A cold-competitor assay adds molar excess of unlabeled probe of the same sequence; if the shift disappears, binding is sequence-specific and saturable. A parallel unlabeled competitor carrying a mutated core site should fail to compete, ruling out the alternative explanation that the protein sticks to any DNA nonspecifically.

sections.heading: DNase I footprinting: base-pair resolution
sections.body: EMSA shows that something binds within a probe, not exactly where. Galas and Schmitz's 1978 footprinting method resolves that: one strand of a labeled fragment is partially digested with DNase I, which cuts at low, roughly random frequency so most molecules carry a single nick, then run on a sequencing gel alongside a Maxam-Gilbert or Sanger ladder. Bound protein physically blocks the nuclease over the contact region, leaving a gap of missing bands, a footprint, that maps the protected bases to single-nucleotide resolution.

sections.heading: The in vitro versus in vivo caveat
sections.body: Both assays use protein extracted or purified outside the cell and DNA stripped of its native chromatin context. A site can bind readily in a tube yet sit nucleosome-occluded and never actually be occupied in a living cell, or conversely require cofactors present in vivo that a simple extract lacks. In vitro binding data show capacity to bind, not proof of in vivo occupancy; that distinction is exactly why chromatin immunoprecipitation, covered next, is the necessary follow-up. One technique bridges the gap directly: in vivo (genomic) footprinting treats intact living cells with dimethyl sulfate (DMS), which methylates accessible guanines, then reads the resulting methylation pattern out by ligation-mediated PCR, the technique Mueller and Wold introduced in 1989 by adding PCR amplification to the genomic-sequencing/footprinting approach Church and Gilbert had pioneered in 1984. Because the DMS treatment happens before the cell is ever lysed, a footprint produced this way demonstrates actual in vivo occupancy rather than the mere binding capacity that EMSA and DNase I footprinting on naked, extracted DNA can only imply.

lessons.workedExample: A student suspects NF-kB binds a candidate kappaB site in a cytokine promoter. They label a 30 bp probe spanning the site, incubate it with extract from stimulated cells, and see a shifted band. Adding an anti-p65 antibody produces a supershift, identifying the p65 subunit of NF-kB in the complex. Adding 100-fold molar excess unlabeled wild-type probe abolishes the shift; the same excess of a probe with the kappaB core scrambled fails to compete, confirming the binding is specific to that sequence and not just sticky protein-DNA contact.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing an EMSA figure is testing whether the student can distinguish specific binding from any protein sticking to DNA. A weak answer shows a single shifted band and calls it proof. A strong answer walks through both controls: the antibody supershift that names the factor, and the wild-type-versus-mutant cold-competitor pair that shows the shift depends on that exact sequence, then explicitly flags that binding in a tube is not the same as occupancy in a living cell.

questions.prompt: In an EMSA, why does a protein-bound probe migrate more slowly through the gel than free probe?

options.text: The protein degrades part of the DNA, making the fragment shorter
The bound complex has greater mass and altered charge, retarding its migration through the native gel
The label detaches from bound probe, reducing signal but not position
Protein binding denatures the DNA into single strands, which run faster

explanations.a: EMSA uses a non-denaturing, non-nuclease binding reaction; the probe is not cleaved by the bound factor.
explanations.b: Correct — added protein mass and charge slow migration through the native polyacrylamide matrix, producing the characteristic upshifted band.
explanations.c: The label stays attached to the probe; it is the migration position, not signal intensity, that changes upon binding.
explanations.d: The assay is run under native conditions specifically to preserve the double-stranded, protein-bound complex; denaturation would defeat the method.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of an EMSA specificity experiment from setup to interpretation.

items.text: Incubate labeled probe with nuclear extract, run gel, observe a shifted band
Add excess unlabeled wild-type probe; shift disappears, confirming sequence-specific, saturable binding
Add excess unlabeled mutant-site probe; shift persists, ruling out nonspecific competition
Add antibody against the candidate factor; observe a supershift or loss of shift, identifying the protein

questions.explanation: The base shift is established first, then wild-type competition tests specificity, mutant competition confirms that specificity depends on the exact sequence, and the antibody step identifies which protein is responsible.

questions.prompt: Match each EMSA control to what it rules in or out.

left.text: The in vitro nature of the whole assay

right.text: Confirms binding is sequence-specific and saturable
Rules out that the protein binds any DNA nonspecifically
Identifies which factor is present in the shifted complex
Means binding capacity is shown, not proof of occupancy in living cells

questions.explanation: Wild-type competition tests specificity, mutant competition tests that specificity depends on sequence rather than generic stickiness, antibody supershift names the protein, and the in vitro format itself limits every EMSA conclusion to binding capacity rather than in vivo occupancy.

questions.prompt: What advantage does DNase I footprinting have over EMSA for mapping a binding site?

options.text: It works with unpurified whole-cell lysate only
It maps the protected region to single-nucleotide resolution rather than just showing that something within the probe binds
It does not require a labeled probe
It measures binding affinity quantitatively while EMSA cannot

explanations.a: Footprinting can use purified protein or extract; the lysate source is not what distinguishes it from EMSA.
explanations.b: Correct — comparing the DNase I cleavage ladder with and without protein, against a sequencing ladder, pinpoints exactly which bases are protected, far more precise than a shift showing only that binding occurred somewhere in the probe.
explanations.c: Footprinting still requires an end-labeled fragment to visualize the cleavage ladder.
explanations.d: Both assays can be made semi-quantitative with titration, but footprinting's real advantage is spatial resolution, not affinity measurement.

lessons.label: ChIP at a Single Locus

sections.heading: Crosslinking and shearing chromatin
sections.body: Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) answers the question EMSA and footprinting cannot: is this factor actually occupying this site inside a living cell? Living cells are treated with formaldehyde (typically about 1% for around 10 minutes), which covalently crosslinks proteins to DNA and to each other, freezing the in vivo binding state in place. Cells are lysed and the crosslinked chromatin is sheared, usually by sonication, down to roughly 200-500 bp fragments, fine enough to distinguish a proximal promoter from an enhancer only a few hundred base pairs away.

sections.heading: Immunoprecipitation and locus-specific readout
sections.body: An antibody against the transcription factor of interest, or against a histone modification such as H3K4me3 (marking active promoters), H3K27ac (marking active enhancers), or H3K27me3 (marking Polycomb-repressed chromatin), captures crosslinked fragments bound by or near that target via protein A/G beads. Crosslinks are then reversed with heat and proteinase K, and the purified DNA is quantified by locus-specific qPCR using primers spanning the candidate regulatory region. This ChIP-qPCR readout asks how much of one specific locus came down, a fundamentally different question from genome-wide ChIP-seq, which surveys every bound region across the genome and belongs to a genomics toolkit rather than this single-locus one.

sections.heading: The indispensable controls: IgG and input
sections.body: A nonspecific IgG immunoprecipitation, matched in species and isotype to the real antibody but with no true target, measures background pulldown; a real signal at the candidate locus must clear this floor. A fraction of the sonicated chromatin set aside before immunoprecipitation, the input, is purified and quantified directly, representing 100% of starting material, and is used to compute percent input (%IP divided by %input), the standard normalized enrichment metric that corrects for differences in locus accessibility, copy number, and primer efficiency between amplicons. A distal control amplicon at a locus the factor should not bind is a further specificity check.

sections.heading: Native ChIP for histone marks
sections.body: Native ChIP skips crosslinking entirely, relying on the inherently stable, non-covalent histone-DNA interaction, and fragments chromatin with micrococcal nuclease (MNase) down to mononucleosomes rather than by sonication. It is often preferred for histone-modification ChIP because formaldehyde crosslinking can mask or alter the epitopes some histone antibodies recognize, and MNase digestion yields cleaner, nucleosome-resolution fragments than sonication does. Concretely, a mononucleosome core wraps about 147 bp of DNA, so MNase digestion down to mononucleosomes typically yields fragments in the roughly 147-200 bp range, tighter and more uniform than the 200-500 bp fragments typical of sonicated, crosslinked ChIP, which is what gives native ChIP its sharper effective resolution for mapping a histone mark's boundary at a locus.

lessons.workedExample: Having seen a transcription factor bind a promoter site by EMSA, a student crosslinks cells with 1% formaldehyde for 10 minutes, sonicates chromatin to an average 300 bp, and splits the lysate three ways: input set aside, IP with the anti-factor antibody, and IP with matched IgG. After reversing crosslinks, qPCR with primers over the candidate site and a control amplicon 5 kb away gives percent input values of 5% at the candidate site with the specific antibody, versus 0.1% with IgG and 0.15% at the distal control, a real, specific in vivo occupancy signal.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges push hardest on the IgG and input controls because ChIP is notoriously prone to nonspecific pulldown and high background. A weak presenter shows a single 'enrichment' bar for their target locus with nothing to compare it against. A strong presenter reports percent input at the target locus versus IgG and versus a distal control locus, and can explain that crosslinking is what lets this assay capture in vivo occupancy, the exact limitation EMSA and footprinting cannot overcome on their own.

questions.prompt: Why is a nonspecific IgG immunoprecipitation a required control, rather than just comparing to an untreated sample?

options.text: IgG measures the fraction of chromatin lost during sonication
IgG establishes the background level of nonspecific pulldown that any real signal must exceed
IgG replaces the need for an input sample
IgG confirms the crosslinking reaction worked

explanations.a: Sonication efficiency is checked separately, typically by gel or bioanalyzer, not by an IgG pulldown.
explanations.b: Correct — beads and antibody isotype pull down some chromatin nonspecifically regardless of target; IgG measures that floor so a real signal can be judged against it.
explanations.c: Input and IgG serve different purposes: input is the normalization denominator, IgG is the specificity floor; neither substitutes for the other.
explanations.d: Crosslinking efficiency is not what an IgG control assesses; it assesses antibody specificity of the pulldown.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a single-locus ChIP-qPCR experiment.

items.text: Crosslink living cells with formaldehyde
Lyse cells and sonicate chromatin to ~200-500 bp fragments
Split sample into input, specific-antibody IP, and IgG IP
Reverse crosslinks and purify DNA
Run locus-specific qPCR and calculate percent input

questions.explanation: Crosslinking must happen in living cells before lysis and shearing; the split into input/IP/IgG happens on the sheared chromatin; crosslinks are reversed only after immunoprecipitation; qPCR and normalization are the final readout.

questions.prompt: Match each ChIP element to its role.

right.text: Measures nonspecific pulldown background
Serves as the normalization denominator (percent input)
Checks that enrichment is specific to the candidate locus
Marks active promoter chromatin

questions.explanation: IgG sets the background floor, input is the 100% denominator for percent-input normalization, a distal amplicon confirms locus specificity, and H3K4me3 is a well-established active-promoter histone mark.

questions.prompt: Why might native ChIP (MNase-based, no crosslinking) be preferred over crosslinked, sonicated ChIP for a histone modification?

options.text: Native ChIP works for transcription factors but not for histones
Formaldehyde crosslinking can mask the epitope some histone antibodies recognize, and MNase gives cleaner nucleosome-resolution fragments
Native ChIP does not require any antibody
Native ChIP eliminates the need for an input control

explanations.a: Native ChIP is used specifically for histone marks, relying on the stable histone-DNA interaction; it is generally unsuitable for transcription factors, which bind far less tightly without crosslinking.
explanations.b: Correct — skipping formaldehyde avoids epitope masking on the histone tail and MNase digestion to mononucleosomes gives more uniform, higher-resolution fragments than sonication.
explanations.c: Native ChIP still requires a specific antibody against the histone mark of interest; only the crosslinking step is skipped.
explanations.d: Input and specificity controls remain necessary in native ChIP exactly as in crosslinked ChIP.

lessons.label: Reading Chromatin and Methylation State at a Locus

sections.heading: Bisulfite conversion: methylation at base resolution
sections.body: Frommer and colleagues' 1992 bisulfite sequencing method remains the gold standard for reading 5-methylcytosine at single-base resolution. Sodium bisulfite deaminates unmethylated cytosine to uracil, which reads as thymine after PCR amplification, while 5-methylcytosine resists conversion and is read as cytosine. Sequencing PCR product amplified from bisulfite-treated genomic DNA at a locus, ideally after cloning many individual amplicons to see allele-to-allele variation, produces a base-resolution methylation map across every CpG in the region.

sections.heading: Methylation-specific PCR: a fast screen
sections.body: Herman and colleagues' 1996 methylation-specific PCR (MSP) offers a faster, cheaper alternative built on the same bisulfite chemistry. Two primer pairs are designed against the converted sequence, one matching the pattern expected if the region was methylated, one matching the pattern expected if unmethylated. Whichever pair amplifies, visualized simply as a band on a gel, indicates the predominant methylation state. MSP is qualitative to semi-quantitative and reports only what its specific primers cover, not the per-CpG resolution that full bisulfite sequencing provides.

sections.heading: Nucleosome accessibility: MNase, DNase, and FAIRE
sections.body: A silenced promoter is typically nucleosome-occluded; an active one is nucleosome-depleted, at least over its core. Micrococcal nuclease (MNase) digestion or DNase I treatment of chromatin maps this directly: cutting is enhanced where DNA is nucleosome-free (a DNase I hypersensitive site, mapped this way long before genome-wide DNase-seq existed) and suppressed where a nucleosome protects the DNA. FAIRE (formaldehyde-assisted isolation of regulatory elements), introduced by Giresi and colleagues in 2007, takes a simpler, antibody-free route: light formaldehyde crosslinking followed by phenol-chloroform extraction partitions nucleosome-depleted DNA into the aqueous phase while protein-crosslinked, nucleosome-bound DNA stays trapped at the organic interphase.

sections.heading: Interpreting an accessibility trace
sections.body: Plotting signal, cut frequency or FAIRE enrichment, across a regulatory region produces a recognizable shape: an active promoter shows a sharp accessibility peak, a nucleosome-depleted region (NDR), typically flanked by peaks of positioned nucleosomes just upstream and downstream. Silencing of that same promoter correlates with the peak flattening as a nucleosome moves in to occlude the site, a shift readable directly from the trace without any antibody at all. Concretely, a typical NDR spans roughly 150-200 bp, flanked by well-positioned -1 and +1 nucleosomes immediately upstream and downstream of the transcription start site, a pattern first mapped genome-wide by Yuan and colleagues in 2005 using high-resolution nucleosome positioning in yeast. That same width shows up locus by locus in single-region accessibility assays: an active promoter's MNase- or DNase-sensitive gap typically matches that 150-200 bp span almost exactly, which is why a trace that instead shows only a narrow dip or a diffuse, poorly bounded region is often a sign of incomplete nucleosome depletion rather than a fully active state.

lessons.workedExample: A student tests whether a tumor-suppressor promoter is silenced by DNA methylation in a cancer line versus a matched normal line. They bisulfite-treat genomic DNA from both, PCR-amplify the CpG island spanning the promoter, and clone and sequence 10 individual alleles per sample. Normal cells show roughly 5% of CpGs retaining cytosine (mostly converted to thymine, consistent with unmethylated DNA); the cancer line shows over 80% retained cytosine across the same CpGs. MSP with methylation-specific primers confirms a band only in the cancer sample, and this pattern correlates with the gene's expression loss measured separately by RT-qPCR.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probing this territory want to see whether a student can distinguish 'this region is transcriptionally silent' from a specific mechanistic claim about why, methylation versus nucleosome occlusion versus something else entirely. A weak answer treats any chromatin assay as interchangeable evidence for silencing. A strong answer names the specific technique, bisulfite sequencing or MSP for methylation, MNase/DNase or FAIRE for accessibility, that supports the particular mechanism being claimed, and does not treat a correlation between methylation and low expression as proof of causation, which requires the perturbation experiments covered later in this unit.

questions.prompt: In bisulfite sequencing, what happens to an unmethylated cytosine during treatment?

options.text: It is deaminated to uracil, which reads as thymine after PCR
It is oxidized and cleaved out of the DNA strand
It is converted to 5-methylcytosine
It remains unchanged, identical to a methylated cytosine

explanations.a: Correct — bisulfite deaminates unmethylated cytosine to uracil, amplified and read as thymine, while 5-methylcytosine resists this conversion and stays cytosine, creating the readable contrast.
explanations.b: Bisulfite treatment is a chemical deamination, not a strand-cleaving reaction.
explanations.c: Bisulfite treatment does not add methyl groups; it only distinguishes cytosines that already carry one from those that do not.
explanations.d: The entire method depends on unmethylated and methylated cytosines behaving differently under bisulfite; if they were unchanged, no methylation map could be read out.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a bisulfite sequencing workflow at a single locus.

items.text: Treat genomic DNA with sodium bisulfite
PCR-amplify the locus of interest from converted DNA
Clone individual amplicons
Sequence multiple clones and read cytosine (methylated) versus thymine (unmethylated) at each CpG

questions.explanation: Conversion must happen on genomic DNA before amplification, since bisulfite acts on cytosine chemistry; cloning separates individual alleles before sequencing reveals the per-CpG pattern.

questions.prompt: Match each method to what it directly measures.

right.text: Base-resolution methylation state across every CpG in a region
Fast qualitative screen for predominant methylation state via which primer pair amplifies
Antibody-free enrichment of nucleosome-depleted DNA via phase partitioning
Locations where nuclease cutting is enhanced because a nucleosome is absent

questions.explanation: Bisulfite sequencing gives per-CpG resolution, MSP gives a fast qualitative call, FAIRE exploits phase partitioning without an antibody, and DNase hypersensitivity mapping directly reads nuclease accessibility.

lessons.label: Quantifying RNA Output

sections.heading: RT-qPCR and the delta-delta-Ct method
sections.body: RNA is reverse-transcribed into cDNA, then amplified with locus-specific primers in qPCR. Relative quantification typically uses the delta-delta-Ct method described by Livak and Schmittgen in 2001: within each sample, the target gene's cycle threshold (Ct) is normalized against a stable reference gene's Ct (delta-Ct), and delta-Ct is then compared between treatment and control (delta-delta-Ct), with fold change computed as 2 raised to the negative delta-delta-Ct. The reference gene matters more than it looks: a default choice like GAPDH or ACTB can itself shift under certain treatments, so a validated stable reference, or an average of several, is required rather than assumed.

sections.heading: Northern blot: size and isoform
sections.body: The Northern blot, from the method Alwine, Kemp, and Stark described in 1977, runs total or poly(A)-selected RNA on a denaturing gel, transfers it to a membrane, and probes with a labeled complementary sequence. Unlike RT-qPCR, which cannot distinguish isoforms sharing the primer-binding exons, a Northern blot directly resolves transcripts by size, showing whether a locus produces one dominant mRNA or several splice or length variants, with band intensity giving a rough abundance estimate. That size resolution comes at a real sensitivity cost: a standard Northern blot typically needs several micrograms of total RNA per lane to produce a visible band, while RT-qPCR can detect a target from nanogram-to-picogram quantities of input RNA, which is the main reason RT-qPCR, not Northern blotting, is the default choice for routine quantification despite Northern's unique ability to resolve isoforms directly.

sections.heading: Nuclear run-on: rate versus steady state
sections.body: RT-qPCR and Northern blotting both measure steady-state RNA level, the net result of transcription rate minus decay rate; a change in steady-state level cannot say which side moved. A nuclear run-on assay isolates nuclei with RNA polymerase molecules still engaged mid-transcript, lets them resume elongation in vitro in the presence of a labeled nucleotide, and measures new labeled transcript specifically arising from a locus, a direct snapshot of transcription rate at the moment of isolation, uncoupled from whatever is happening to RNA stability.

sections.heading: Measuring mRNA half-life with actinomycin D
sections.body: To isolate the decay side of the equation, actinomycin D, a small molecule that intercalates DNA and halts RNA polymerase II elongation, is added to block new transcription entirely. RNA is then sampled at multiple timepoints afterward, and the target transcript's decline is measured by qPCR or Northern blot; fitting the decline to an exponential decay curve yields the mRNA's half-life. Paired with a nuclear run-on, this lets a change in steady-state RNA be attributed specifically to altered synthesis, altered stability, or both.

lessons.workedExample: A student observes an 8-fold rise in a heat-shock gene's mRNA by RT-qPCR after 42C heat shock, using delta-delta-Ct with GAPDH validated as stable under heat shock in a pilot experiment. To determine whether that rise reflects more transcription or slower decay, they run a nuclear run-on before and after heat shock and see 6-fold more labeled nascent RNA at that locus, closely tracking the steady-state increase. As a complement, an actinomycin D chase shows the transcript's half-life is roughly 2 hours in both conditions, ruling out a stability contribution and pinning the change on transcription.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probing this material want to know whether a claimed 'expression change' is a transcription effect or a stability effect, since RT-qPCR alone cannot distinguish the two. A weak answer treats a steady-state RNA increase as automatic proof of more transcription. A strong answer names the disambiguating experiment, nuclear run-on for rate, an actinomycin D chase for half-life, and explains what result from each would confirm or rule out a transcriptional mechanism.

questions.prompt: In the delta-delta-Ct method, what is the purpose of normalizing the target gene's Ct to a reference gene's Ct within each sample first?

options.text: It corrects for differences in RNA input amount and reverse-transcription efficiency between samples
It eliminates the need for a treatment-versus-control comparison
It converts Ct values directly into transcript copy number
It is only necessary when using a Northern blot, not qPCR

explanations.a: Correct — a stable reference gene's Ct reflects how much material and how efficiently it was converted to cDNA in that particular sample, so subtracting it removes those technical differences before comparing across conditions.
explanations.b: The treatment-versus-control comparison is the second step (delta-delta-Ct), which still requires the within-sample normalization step first.
explanations.c: Ct values are cycle numbers, not copy numbers; converting to copy number would require a standard curve, a separate step from delta-delta-Ct.
explanations.d: Reference-gene normalization is specific to qPCR-based quantification; Northern blotting uses a different normalization approach (e.g., total RNA loading).

questions.prompt: Order the steps of measuring mRNA half-life with an actinomycin D chase.

items.text: Add actinomycin D to block new transcription
Sample RNA at multiple timepoints after the block
Measure the target transcript's level at each timepoint by qPCR or Northern blot
Fit the decline to an exponential decay curve to calculate half-life

questions.explanation: Transcription must be blocked first so any subsequent loss of the transcript reflects decay alone; timepoint sampling and quantification generate the decay curve that half-life is calculated from.

questions.prompt: Match each method to what it measures.

right.text: Steady-state relative RNA level
Transcript size and isoform identity
Transcription rate at the moment of nuclei isolation
mRNA half-life (decay rate)

questions.explanation: RT-qPCR gives relative steady-state level, Northern resolves size/isoform, nuclear run-on isolates transcription rate, and an actinomycin D chase isolates decay rate.

lessons.label: Perturbation and Proving Causality

sections.heading: Loss- and gain-of-function tools
sections.body: RNA interference (RNAi), discovered by Fire and Mello in 1998 in C. elegans and later awarded the 2006 Nobel Prize, adapted to mammalian cells by Elbashir and colleagues in 2001, delivers a short interfering RNA (siRNA) or an expressed short hairpin RNA (shRNA) that guides the RNA-induced silencing complex to degrade a target mRNA, reducing but rarely eliminating that factor's level. This tests whether a factor is needed for a target's expression. Overexpression, transfecting extra copies of a factor's cDNA, tests the opposite question, sufficiency: does adding more of the factor turn the target up. A dominant-negative construct, a mutant that still binds DNA or a partner but cannot activate, blocks the endogenous factor's function without full knockdown, useful when redundant family members would blunt an RNAi approach.

sections.heading: CRISPRi and CRISPRa: regulation without editing
sections.body: A catalytically dead Cas9 (dCas9), with both nuclease domains inactivated so it binds DNA but cannot cut it, guided by an sgRNA to a promoter, was first used on its own to sterically block transcription, the original CRISPRi concept described by Qi and colleagues in 2013, though unfused dCas9 gives only modest repression and was demonstrated most effectively in bacteria. Fusing dCas9 to a repressor domain such as KRAB, introduced by Gilbert and colleagues in 2013, recruits repressive chromatin and gives far more robust silencing in human cells. The same dCas9 fused to an activator domain, VP64 or the more potent VPR and SAM systems, recruits activating machinery instead, CRISPRa, described in that same Gilbert and colleagues 2013 paper. Because dCas9 cannot cut, this perturbs expression reversibly, without altering the underlying DNA sequence, and can be aimed precisely at a single candidate element already narrowed down by reporter-deletion mapping.

sections.heading: Controls that separate correlation from cause
sections.body: A nontargeting or scrambled siRNA and sgRNA, and an empty-vector overexpression control, are non-negotiable, because the act of transfecting or transducing cells perturbs them nonspecifically regardless of what is being delivered. The strongest evidence of all is a rescue experiment: re-expressing an RNAi-resistant version of the knocked-down gene, or restoring wild-type function after a dominant-negative, and showing the phenotype reverses. A reversible phenotype tied to the specific factor, not merely correlated with a treatment, is what separates a causal claim from a coincidental one.

sections.heading: Defending a figure under judge Q&A
sections.body: A single EMSA shift, a ChIP-qPCR enrichment bar, or a reporter drop upon deletion is necessary evidence but not sufficient on its own: binding data show occupancy, not function; a reporter drop shows that a region matters, not which factor acts there. Only perturbing the specific candidate factor, with a nontargeting control and ideally a rescue, and showing the endogenous target's expression changes accordingly, closes the loop from correlation to mechanism.

lessons.workedExample: A student has shown by ChIP-qPCR that a candidate transcription factor sits at a target promoter with 5% input enrichment. To test necessity, they transfect siRNA against the factor alongside a scrambled control and see the target's mRNA, by RT-qPCR, drop 70% only with the specific siRNA, not the scrambled one. To test sufficiency at that exact element, independent of the factor's other roles elsewhere in the genome, they instead deliver dCas9-VP64 (CRISPRa) with an sgRNA targeted to the ChIP-enriched region and see the target gene rise 4-fold relative to a nontargeting sgRNA, directly implicating that regulatory element rather than the factor's broader effects.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges press hardest here on 'how do you know it's this factor, and not an off-target or global stress effect of your knockdown.' A strong defense points to the nontargeting control's result directly and, when available, a rescue that reverses the phenotype. A weak defense shows only the treated condition with no comparator at all, which is uninterpretable no matter how large the measured effect looks, since a nonspecific transfection stress could produce the same number.

questions.prompt: Why can dCas9-based CRISPRi repress a target gene without editing its DNA sequence?

options.text: dCas9 still cuts DNA but repairs it perfectly afterward
Both nuclease domains of dCas9 are inactivated, so it binds the sgRNA-targeted site without cutting, and any effect comes from steric blockage or a fused repressor domain
dCas9 only works on RNA, never on DNA
CRISPRi uses a different guide RNA chemistry that cannot reach genomic DNA

explanations.a: dCas9 does not cut at all; there is no cutting-then-repair cycle involved.
explanations.b: Correct — dCas9 retains sgRNA-guided DNA binding but has lost both nuclease activities, so a fused domain like KRAB (or simple steric occlusion of the promoter) is what drives the effect, leaving the sequence untouched.
explanations.c: dCas9 is guided to genomic DNA by the sgRNA and binds DNA directly, not RNA.
explanations.d: CRISPRi uses the same sgRNA targeting mechanism as cutting CRISPR/Cas9; only the Cas9 protein's catalytic activity differs.

questions.prompt: Order the logical sequence of experiments a student would run to move from a binding observation to a causal claim.

items.text: Observe factor occupancy at the candidate site by ChIP-qPCR
Knock down the factor with siRNA (plus a scrambled control) and test for loss of target expression
Activate the specific element with CRISPRa (plus a nontargeting sgRNA control) and test for gain of target expression
Rescue with an RNAi-resistant version of the factor and confirm the phenotype reverses

questions.explanation: Occupancy is established first, then necessity (knockdown) and sufficiency (CRISPRa at the specific element) are tested with matched controls, and a rescue is the strongest final step confirming the effect is due to that specific factor rather than an off-target artifact.

questions.prompt: Match each perturbation tool to what it tests or provides.

right.text: Loss of function via mRNA degradation
Transcriptional repression targeted to a specific site, without cutting DNA
Blocks a factor's function without needing full knockdown, useful against redundant paralogs
Confirms specificity by reversing the phenotype when the factor is restored

questions.explanation: Each tool addresses a different weakness: siRNA tests necessity via degradation, CRISPRi represses a specific site without editing, a dominant-negative sidesteps redundancy, and rescue is the strongest confirmation that an effect is due to the specific factor.

questions.prompt: A student knocks down a candidate factor with siRNA and sees the target gene drop, but includes no scrambled-siRNA control. Why does a judge treat this result as uninterpretable?

options.text: Because siRNA knockdown never reduces mRNA levels enough to matter
Because transfection or transduction itself can nonspecifically stress cells and alter expression, so without a nontargeting control there is no way to know the drop is due to the specific factor
Because RT-qPCR cannot detect changes smaller than 10-fold
Because siRNA always causes complete, not partial, loss of the target protein

explanations.a: siRNA knockdown can produce substantial, biologically meaningful reductions; that is not the issue here.
explanations.b: Correct — the delivery method itself, not just the specific sequence, can perturb cells, so a scrambled/nontargeting control is what isolates the effect of silencing that one factor from generic transfection stress.
explanations.c: RT-qPCR can detect much smaller fold-changes than 10-fold; sensitivity is not the limiting issue in this scenario.
