explanations.d: siRNA typically produces partial, not complete, knockdown, which is exactly why a specific comparator condition is needed to interpret a partial effect.

units.label: Landmark Discoveries & Open Debates in Gene Regulation

lessons.label: Jacob, Monod, and the Operon (1961)

sections.heading: PaJaMo: watching a gene switch off in real time
sections.body: In 1959, Arthur Pardee, Francois Jacob, and Jacques Monod ran what became known as the PaJaMo experiment: they mated an Hfr E. coli male carrying lac+ genes (including a functional regulator gene, lacI+) into a lacI- female that was making beta-galactosidase constitutively because it had no working repressor of its own. Beta-galactosidase synthesis began within minutes of the male DNA entering the female, before any repressor could act. Then came the decisive reciprocal result: as the incoming lacI+ gene began producing repressor protein inside the female, expression shut off over roughly an hour. Repressor made from the newly delivered gene diffused through the cytoplasm and bound the operators -- so the repressor had to be a trans-acting, diffusible substance, not something locked to the DNA that made it. The speed of the on-switch was the other key data point: a stable protein population could not appear that fast, so whatever carried the genetic message from DNA to the ribosome had to be short-lived. That inference became the messenger RNA hypothesis, published with Sydney Brenner and Matthew Meselson in 1961.

sections.heading: The operon model
sections.body: Jacob and Monod formalized the picture later in 1961 in 'Genetic Regulatory Mechanisms in the Synthesis of Proteins': structural genes (lacZ, lacY, lacA) are transcribed together as one unit under a shared operator, and a separate regulator gene (lacI) produces a repressor that binds the operator and blocks transcription until an inducer (allolactose, mimicked experimentally by IPTG) removes it. This was a genetic model built entirely from mutant phenotypes and mating experiments -- no one had yet seen a repressor molecule.

sections.heading: Proving it with a protein in hand
sections.body: Walter Gilbert and Benno Muller-Hill closed that gap in 1966, purifying the lac repressor itself and showing it bound specifically to lac operator DNA and was released by IPTG -- the operon model's central molecule, isolated. The following year, in 1967, Mark Ptashne isolated the bacteriophage lambda repressor and showed it too bound directly to specific operator DNA, proving the mechanism was not a lac-specific quirk but a general strategy for gene control. Arthur Riggs, H. Suzuki, and Suzanne Bourgeois followed up in 1970 with equilibrium-binding assays that put a number on the specificity Gilbert and Muller-Hill had only shown qualitatively: purified repressor bound the lac operator with an affinity roughly a million times greater than its affinity for bulk, non-operator DNA. That quantitative gap -- not just 'binds DNA' but 'binds this short operator a millionfold better than anywhere else in the genome' -- was what turned the repressor from a plausible candidate into a molecule whose behavior matched the operon model's genetic predictions number for number. Jacob, Monod, and Andre Lwoff shared the 1965 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the regulatory concepts; the 1966-1970 isolations and binding measurements supplied the physical proof those concepts demanded.

lessons.workedExample: A student wants to explain why bacteria don't waste energy making lactose-digesting enzymes when only glucose is around. Citing PaJaMo, they explain: the lacI gene constantly makes repressor protein, which sits on the lac operator and physically blocks RNA polymerase from transcribing lacZYA. When lactose appears, a metabolite of it (allolactose) binds the repressor, changes its shape, and knocks it off the DNA -- transcription starts within minutes, matching the fast on/off kinetics Pardee, Jacob, and Monod actually measured in their mating experiments, not just described abstractly.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'how do you know it's a repressor blocking DNA, and not something regulating the enzyme after it's made?' because the operon model specifically claims control happens at the level of transcription, and that claim rests on the PaJaMo mating-kinetics data plus the physical isolation of a DNA-binding protein. A weak answer says 'genes get turned on and off.' A strong answer names the operator, the repressor, and points to Gilbert and Muller-Hill's 1966 isolation as the moment the hypothesis became a measured, DNA-binding molecule rather than a genetic inference.

questions.prompt: What was the key observation in the 1959 PaJaMo experiment that pointed toward a short-lived messenger molecule?

options.text: Beta-galactosidase activity appeared or disappeared within minutes of DNA transfer, too fast for a stable protein to explain
The lac operon was found on a plasmid instead of the chromosome
Beta-galactosidase was shown to be made of RNA rather than protein
Repressor protein was directly visualized binding DNA under a microscope

explanations.a: Correct -- the on/off switching happened faster than a stable protein or ribosome population could plausibly turn over, implying an unstable intermediate carrying the message from gene to enzyme.
explanations.b: PaJaMo used Hfr-to-F- chromosomal conjugation, not plasmids, and location wasn't the point of the experiment.
explanations.c: Beta-galactosidase is an enzyme (protein); the experiment never questioned its composition.
explanations.d: No molecule was visualized in 1959 -- this was a genetic/kinetic inference, not microscopy; direct isolation came later, in 1966.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the discovery of the lac operon and repressor.

items.text: Pardee, Jacob, and Monod run the PaJaMo mating experiment
Jacob and Monod publish the operon model with the messenger RNA hypothesis
Jacob, Monod, and Lwoff share the Nobel Prize
Gilbert and Muller-Hill isolate the lac repressor protein and show it binds operator DNA

questions.explanation: The mating experiment (1959) preceded the formal operon/messenger model (1961), which was recognized with the 1965 Nobel Prize, and the repressor protein itself was not physically isolated until 1966.

questions.prompt: Why was Ptashne's 1967 isolation of the lambda repressor scientifically important beyond confirming lac?

options.text: It showed repressor-operator binding was a general regulatory strategy, not unique to the lac system
It disproved the operon model by finding a repressor that did not bind DNA
It showed lambda phage has no genes at all
It proved that RNA, not protein, does the repressing

explanations.a: Correct -- finding the same DNA-binding repressor mechanism in an unrelated system (a phage, not lac) generalized Jacob and Monod's model beyond one operon.
explanations.b: Ptashne's lambda repressor did bind DNA directly, which supported rather than disproved the model.
explanations.c: Lambda is a well-characterized phage with genes; this claim is unrelated to the finding.
explanations.d: Both the lac repressor (isolated 1966) and the lambda repressor (isolated 1967) were proteins that bound DNA directly.

questions.prompt: Match each lac operon component to its function.

right.text: Binds repressor and pulls it off the DNA
Structural genes transcribed as one unit
Repressor protein that binds the operator
DNA sequence the repressor binds to block transcription

questions.explanation: lacI encodes the repressor, which binds the operator DNA to block RNA polymerase; allolactose binds and removes the repressor; lacZYA are the co-transcribed structural genes the operon controls.

lessons.label: Split Genes and Catalytic RNA (1977-1982)

sections.heading: A gene in pieces: the adenovirus R-loop experiment
sections.body: In 1977, Phillip Sharp's group and Richard Roberts's group, working independently on adenovirus, ran a deceptively simple electron-microscopy experiment: hybridize mature viral mRNA to the single-stranded genomic DNA it came from and look at the resulting molecule. If the gene were continuous, the RNA-DNA hybrid would form one unbroken duplex. Instead, they saw the mRNA hybridize to DNA in several separate segments, with loops of unpaired, single-stranded DNA bulging out between them -- DNA that had been transcribed but was missing from the finished mRNA. That meant the gene itself was not one continuous coding stretch; it was split into coding segments (exons) separated by sequences (introns) that get transcribed and then physically removed, with the exons stitched together during RNA splicing. Roberts and Sharp shared the 1993 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the discovery.

sections.heading: RNA that cuts itself: Cech and the Tetrahymena intron
sections.body: The assumption at the time was that splicing, like every other biochemical reaction, must be carried out by a protein enzyme. Thomas Cech's lab tested this directly with the self-splicing intron of the Tetrahymena thermophila ribosomal RNA precursor and, in a 1982 paper, showed the intron excised itself with no protein present at all -- the RNA folded into a structure that performed its own catalysis. A year later, Sidney Altman's group showed that RNase P, the enzyme that trims precursor tRNAs, is a ribonucleoprotein whose RNA subunit (not its protein subunit) does the actual cutting. Cech and Altman shared the 1989 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for discovering that RNA can be a catalyst, not just a passive carrier of sequence information.

sections.heading: Why this reframed how regulation could evolve
sections.body: Before 1982, the central dogma implied a strict division of labor: DNA and RNA store and transmit information, proteins do the chemistry. Ribozymes broke that division and gave weight to the RNA-world hypothesis -- the idea, argued by Carl Woese, Francis Crick, and Leslie Orgel in the late 1960s and later named by Walter Gilbert in 1986, that early life may have used RNA alone to both encode genes and catalyze reactions, with proteins and DNA arriving later. For gene regulation specifically, it meant self-splicing and RNA catalysis were plausible ancestral mechanisms, not evolutionary afterthoughts -- a foothold for later discoveries that small and structured RNAs (ribozymes, and later microRNAs) could sit inside regulatory pathways rather than merely deliver messages between them.

lessons.workedExample: A student examining an R-loop electron micrograph from an adenovirus experiment sees the mRNA hybridized to genomic DNA in three separate duplex segments, with two single-stranded DNA loops bulging out between them and one extra tail of unhybridized DNA at one end. They correctly interpret this as three exons (the hybridized segments), two introns (the two loops, transcribed as pre-mRNA but spliced out before the mature mRNA was isolated), and flanking untranscribed genomic DNA (the tail) -- exactly the logic Roberts and Sharp used in 1977 to conclude the adenovirus gene was discontinuous.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing this concept asks 'how do you know an RNA is actually catalyzing that reaction, rather than a trace protein contaminant doing it?' because that was the exact skepticism Cech had to overcome in 1982. A weak answer just asserts 'RNA can be an enzyme.' A strong answer describes the control: the self-splicing reaction still occurred when protein was rigorously removed or when the intron RNA was synthesized entirely in vitro, isolating the RNA itself as the catalytic agent rather than an artifact of a real but undetected protein.

questions.prompt: In the 1977 adenovirus R-loop experiments, what did the single-stranded DNA loops between hybridized segments represent?

options.text: Introns: DNA transcribed into pre-mRNA but removed before the mature mRNA hybridized
Regions of the genome that were never transcribed at all
Errors introduced during the electron microscopy sample preparation
Duplicated copies of the exons

explanations.a: Correct -- the loops were DNA sequences with no complementary mRNA present because they had been spliced out of the transcript, revealing the gene was split into exons and introns.
explanations.b: Untranscribed flanking DNA would appear as a single-stranded tail at the ends, not as internal loops between hybridized exon segments.
explanations.c: The loop pattern was reproducible across molecules and consistent with a real biological mechanism, not an artifact.
explanations.d: Duplicated exons would still hybridize to the mRNA; the loops specifically failed to hybridize, meaning they had no mRNA counterpart.

questions.prompt: What did Cech's 1982 Tetrahymena experiment demonstrate that overturned a prior assumption?

options.text: That an RNA intron could splice itself out with no protein present, showing RNA can catalyze reactions
That introns exist in bacterial genomes as well as eukaryotic ones
That ribosomal RNA is translated into protein
That DNA polymerase requires an RNA primer to begin replication

explanations.a: Correct -- self-splicing with no protein present directly contradicted the assumption that only proteins could catalyze biochemical reactions.
explanations.b: The experiment concerned the Tetrahymena ribosomal RNA precursor, a eukaryotic ciliate system; it did not address bacterial introns.
explanations.c: Ribosomal RNA is a structural/catalytic component of ribosomes, not itself translated into protein.
explanations.d: RNA priming of DNA replication is a real phenomenon but unrelated to Cech's self-splicing result.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the discovery of split genes and catalytic RNA.

items.text: Roberts and Sharp find split genes via adenovirus R-loop electron microscopy
Cech shows the Tetrahymena intron splices itself with no protein present
Altman's group shows the RNA subunit of RNase P is the catalytic component
Cech and Altman share the Nobel Prize in Chemistry

questions.explanation: Split genes were identified in 1977; Cech's self-splicing result came in 1982, Altman's RNase P catalytic-RNA result followed in 1983, and the two were jointly recognized with the 1989 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

questions.prompt: Match each researcher or pair to their landmark contribution.

right.text: Discovered split genes via adenovirus mRNA-DNA hybridization
Showed a Tetrahymena intron self-splices without protein
Showed the RNA subunit of RNase P performs catalysis

questions.explanation: Roberts and Sharp discovered introns in adenovirus; Cech demonstrated self-splicing catalytic RNA in Tetrahymena; Altman showed RNase P's RNA subunit, not its protein subunit, cleaves tRNA precursors.

lessons.label: Enhancers and the Recruitment Model

sections.heading: A DNA element that works at a distance
sections.body: In 1981, Julian Banerji, Sandro Rusconi, and Walter Schaffner cloned a rabbit beta-globin gene into a plasmid and tested its expression in HeLa cells. Alone, the gene produced almost no detectable transcript. Adding a roughly 200 base-pair segment of SV40 viral DNA elsewhere on the same plasmid boosted beta-globin transcription about 200-fold, and the boost held even when that segment was moved to the far side of the gene, flipped in orientation, or placed thousands of base pairs away. That combination -- activity independent of position and orientation -- was the operational definition of an enhancer, distinguishing it from a promoter, which must sit immediately upstream and in a fixed orientation. The finding meant regulatory DNA did not need direct contact with the promoter to control it, forcing the field to explain how a distant sequence reaches genes at all -- an answer that later work located in DNA looping that brings enhancer-bound proteins into contact with the promoter.

sections.heading: How does a bound activator actually turn genes on?
sections.body: Mark Ptashne, building on his own lambda repressor work, argued for what became known as the recruitment model: an activator's only job is to physically recruit the general transcription machinery and RNA polymerase II to the promoter through protein-protein contacts, with no need to alter the polymerase's intrinsic chemistry. He and Stephen Gann laid this out explicitly in a 1997 Nature paper, 'Transcriptional activation by recruitment.' The competing idea, allostery, held that activators might instead induce a conformational change in the machinery that makes it catalytically more effective once assembled, not just present. The debate mattered because it set the rules for what an activator's DNA-binding domain and its separate activation surface each need to do -- purely bring partners together, or also reshape them.

sections.heading: Proving activation domains are modular
sections.body: The cleanest test of the recruitment idea came from a chimera. In 1988, Ptashne's lab (Sadowski, Ma, Triezenberg, and Ptashne) fused the DNA-binding domain of the yeast activator GAL4 to the acidic activation domain of VP16, a herpes simplex virus protein with no evolutionary relationship to GAL4. The hybrid protein activated transcription from a promoter carrying GAL4 binding sites, and did so more strongly than GAL4 itself. Because two unrelated domains could be swapped and still work, activation had to be modular: a separable DNA-targeting module and a separable machinery-recruiting module, exactly what the recruitment model predicts and what a rigid allosteric mechanism, tied to one activator's specific structure, would not easily explain.

lessons.workedExample: A student is asked to design a test for whether a candidate protein is a true enhancer element rather than a second promoter. Following Banerji, Rusconi, and Schaffner's logic, they clone the element downstream of a reporter gene instead of upstream, flip its orientation, and move it several kilobases away -- if reporter expression stays elevated in all three configurations, the element meets the operational definition of an enhancer (position- and orientation-independent); if activity collapses when it's flipped or moved, it behaves like a promoter instead.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'how does an activator bound far from the gene actually turn it on?' is testing whether a student can separate the enhancer's defining property (works at a distance, in either orientation) from the mechanistic question of what the bound protein does once there. A weak answer says 'it turns the gene on.' A strong answer names the GAL4-VP16 chimera experiment as evidence that activation works through a separable, swappable activation domain recruiting the transcription machinery, and can state that this recruitment view is itself still debated against models where activators also allosterically improve the machinery's efficiency.

questions.prompt: What two properties define an enhancer in the operational sense established by Banerji, Rusconi, and Schaffner's 1981 experiment?

options.text: It must sit immediately upstream of the promoter and cannot be inverted
It boosts transcription independent of its distance and orientation relative to the gene
It only functions when integrated into the host chromosome, never on a plasmid
It encodes a small RNA that base-pairs with the promoter

explanations.a: That description fits a promoter, which is position- and orientation-fixed -- the opposite of what Banerji and colleagues found for their SV40 element.
explanations.b: Correct -- the SV40 element boosted beta-globin transcription roughly 200-fold whether moved to the other side of the gene, flipped, or placed far away, which is the defining operational test for an enhancer.
explanations.c: The original experiment demonstrated the effect using transient transfection of a plasmid in HeLa cells, not chromosomal integration.
explanations.d: The 1981 experiment identified a DNA regulatory sequence acting through bound proteins, not an RNA base-pairing mechanism.

questions.prompt: What did the GAL4-VP16 chimera experiment demonstrate about transcriptional activators?

options.text: DNA-binding and activation functions are modular and can be swapped between unrelated proteins
GAL4 cannot activate transcription under any conditions
VP16 requires GAL4's DNA-binding domain to enter the nucleus
Activation domains must come from the same species as the DNA-binding domain to function

explanations.a: Correct -- fusing GAL4's DNA-binding domain to the unrelated viral VP16 activation domain still produced a working, even stronger, activator, showing the two functions are separable modules.
explanations.b: GAL4 is itself a functional yeast activator; the experiment used its DNA-binding domain specifically, not evidence of GAL4's inactivity.
explanations.c: The experiment tested transcriptional activation via GAL4 DNA-binding sites, not nuclear import requirements.
explanations.d: The entire point was that a human/herpesvirus-derived domain (VP16) worked when fused to a yeast domain (GAL4), across species lines.

questions.prompt: Match each finding to the researcher(s) responsible.

left.text: SV40 enhancer boosts distant beta-globin transcription ~200-fold
Formalized the recruitment model of activation
Built the GAL4-VP16 chimera showing modular activation domains

right.text: Banerji, Rusconi, and Schaffner
Ptashne and Gann
Sadowski, Ma, Triezenberg, and Ptashne

questions.explanation: Banerji, Rusconi, and Schaffner discovered the SV40 enhancer's distance/orientation-independent effect in 1981; Ptashne and Gann articulated the recruitment model in 1997; Sadowski, Ma, Triezenberg, and Ptashne built the GAL4-VP16 chimera in 1988.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the enhancer and recruitment-model story.

items.text: Banerji, Rusconi, and Schaffner identify the SV40 enhancer's distance-independent effect
Sadowski, Ma, Triezenberg, and Ptashne build the GAL4-VP16 chimera
Ptashne and Gann formally publish the recruitment model

questions.explanation: The enhancer's defining property was established in 1981, the modular GAL4-VP16 chimera evidence came in 1988, and the recruitment model was articulated as an explicit theoretical framework in 1997.

lessons.label: Histones, Acetylation, and the Histone-Code Debate

sections.heading: A correlation, decades before a mechanism
sections.body: In 1964, Vincent Allfrey, Rosemary Faulkner, and Alfred Mirsky reported something that had no explanation at the time: cells with actively transcribed chromatin carried more acetyl groups on their histones than transcriptionally quiet chromatin, and treating cells with agents that raised histone acetylation also raised RNA synthesis. The correlation was solid, but for over thirty years no one could identify an enzyme that placed those acetyl marks on histones in a way clearly tied to gene activity, so the finding sat as a suggestive but mechanistically empty observation. Histones are unusually rich in the basic amino acids lysine and arginine, whose side chains carry a positive charge at physiological pH; that positive charge is what lets the histone tails grip the negatively charged DNA backbone tightly in the first place, and it is exactly the property Allfrey's correlation would later turn out to hinge on.

sections.heading: Finding the enzyme: Gcn5 as a histone acetyltransferase
sections.body: The gap closed in 1996, when James Brownell and C. David Allis, working in Tetrahymena thermophila, purified a transcription-linked histone acetyltransferase (HAT) activity and found it was structurally homologous to a yeast protein already known as a transcriptional coactivator: Gcn5. Showing that recombinant Gcn5 itself carried HAT activity connected the two separate research threads at once -- a known activator of transcription turned out to be, physically, an enzyme that acetylates histones. This gave Allfrey's 1964 correlation a mechanism: acetylation transfers an acetyl group onto the epsilon-amino group of a histone tail lysine, neutralizing the positive charge that residue normally carries and so weakening the electrostatic grip of the tail on the negatively charged DNA phosphate backbone. That physical loosening of histone-DNA contacts also exposes docking surfaces for other regulatory proteins, and Gcn5-family HATs were the tool cells use to write that mark during activation.

sections.heading: The histone-code hypothesis and its critics
sections.body: With HATs, and soon methyltransferases and other 'writer' enzymes, in hand, Brian Strahl and Allis proposed in a 2000 Nature paper, 'The Language of Covalent Histone Modifications,' that combinations of histone marks form a 'histone code': specific patterns of acetylation, methylation, and phosphorylation across the tails of H3 and H4 are read by dedicated 'reader' proteins to specify a defined transcriptional outcome, analogous to how a genetic codon specifies an amino acid. The hypothesis organized a huge amount of subsequent chromatin biology, but it drew a persistent critique: unlike the genetic code, no fixed, universal lookup table linking mark-combinations to outcomes has ever been demonstrated. Many marks correlate with, rather than cause, transcriptional states -- H3K4me3 and active promoters track together, but H3K4me3 is often a consequence of transcription initiation rather than its cause. Critics argue 'histone context' or 'histone grammar' is a more honest description than 'code': marks matter, they're read by real reader domains, but they function combinatorially and context-dependently rather than through a deterministic cipher.

lessons.workedExample: A student finds that a gene's promoter gains H3K9 and H3K14 acetylation exactly when the gene turns on, and cites this as proof of a histone code operating at that locus. A judge would press: does acetylation cause activation, or does an activator recruit RNA polymerase and a HAT (like Gcn5) together, so acetylation and transcription rise in step without one strictly causing the other? The stronger framing, following the code's critics, treats the acetylation mark as a correlated and mechanistically supportive event (it loosens chromatin and recruits readers) rather than as a deterministic instruction that alone specifies the outcome.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'is that a cause or a correlation?' about a histone mark is probing exactly the weakness that has dogged the histone-code hypothesis since 2000. A weak answer treats any acetylation-transcription correlation as proof of a code. A strong answer cites Allfrey's original 1964 correlation, Brownell and Allis's 1996 enzyme (Gcn5) as the mechanistic bridge, and then explicitly flags that Strahl and Allis's 'code' framing remains debated because marks are frequently consequences of transcription as much as instructions for it.

questions.prompt: What did Allfrey, Faulkner, and Mirsky report in 1964, and what was missing from their finding?

options.text: A correlation between histone acetylation and active transcription, with no known enzyme responsible
The first histone acetyltransferase enzyme, Gcn5, purified from Tetrahymena
Direct proof that DNA methylation silences genes
The first crystal structure of a nucleosome

explanations.a: Correct -- they linked histone acetylation to active RNA synthesis by correlation, but no enzyme catalyzing the mark was identified until Brownell and Allis in 1996.
explanations.b: The Gcn5 histone acetyltransferase was identified by Brownell and Allis in 1996, over three decades after Allfrey's correlation.
explanations.c: Allfrey's 1964 work concerned histone acetylation, not DNA methylation.
explanations.d: No nucleosome structure was involved; this was a biochemical/metabolic-labeling correlation study.

questions.prompt: Why was Brownell and Allis's 1996 identification of Gcn5 as a histone acetyltransferase significant?

options.text: It linked a previously known transcriptional coactivator to a direct enzymatic activity that could explain Allfrey's 1964 correlation
It showed Gcn5 has no effect on histones at all
It disproved the existence of histone acetylation
It was the first evidence that any protein could bind DNA

explanations.a: Correct -- Gcn5 was already known as a coactivator of transcription; showing it directly acetylates histones supplied the missing mechanistic link to Allfrey's decades-old correlation.
explanations.b: The entire finding was that Gcn5 does acetylate histones, providing the mechanistic enzyme.
explanations.c: Allfrey had already established histone acetylation existed in 1964; Brownell and Allis identified its enzyme, not its existence.
explanations.d: DNA-protein binding was established decades earlier (e.g., Gilbert and Muller-Hill, 1966); this was unrelated to that question.

questions.prompt: What is the main critique of the Strahl-Allis 'histone code' hypothesis?

options.text: Many histone marks correlate with transcriptional states without a demonstrated fixed, universal rule linking mark combinations to outcomes
No enzyme has ever been shown to modify histones
Histones do not actually associate with DNA
The hypothesis has been fully validated with no remaining objections

explanations.a: Correct -- unlike the genetic code's fixed codon table, no deterministic lookup table from mark-combination to transcriptional outcome has been shown, and many marks appear to be consequences of transcription rather than instructive causes.
explanations.b: Multiple histone-modifying enzymes, including Gcn5, are well established; this is not the critique.
explanations.c: Histone-DNA association is foundational and uncontested chromatin biology.
explanations.d: The hypothesis remains actively debated, not settled; that is the premise of this lesson.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the histone-acetylation story.

items.text: Allfrey, Faulkner, and Mirsky correlate histone acetylation with active transcription
Brownell and Allis identify Gcn5 as a histone acetyltransferase
Strahl and Allis propose the histone-code hypothesis

questions.explanation: The correlation was reported in 1964, the causal enzyme (Gcn5) was identified in 1996, and the broader code hypothesis synthesizing these findings was proposed in 2000.

lessons.label: RNAi, MicroRNAs, and Epigenetic Silencing

sections.heading: Fire and Mello: double-stranded RNA silences genes
sections.body: Andrew Fire and Craig Mello injected Caenorhabditis elegans with single-stranded sense RNA, single-stranded antisense RNA, and double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) matching a target gene, and found that only the double-stranded form produced strong, specific silencing of that gene -- far more potent than either strand alone, and effective at surprisingly low doses, implying the effect was catalytic rather than a simple one-to-one binding reaction. Their 1998 Nature paper named the phenomenon RNA interference (RNAi) and showed the silencing could even spread between cells and persist across generations. Fire and Mello shared the 2006 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the discovery, just eight years after publication -- an unusually fast recognition that reflected how quickly RNAi became both a fundamental regulatory mechanism and a widely used laboratory tool for knocking down genes.

sections.heading: lin-4 and let-7: RNAi's regulatory cousin, the microRNA
sections.body: RNAi's silencing machinery turned out to overlap with a naturally occurring class of small regulatory RNAs. In 1993, Rosalind Lee, Rhonda Feinbaum, and Victor Ambros identified lin-4 in C. elegans, a small RNA that did not encode a protein but instead base-paired with the 3' untranslated region of the lin-14 mRNA to repress its translation and control developmental timing -- at the time treated as a nematode oddity. That changed in 2000, when Brenda Reinhart and colleagues in Gary Ruvkun's lab identified a second small regulatory RNA, let-7, and showed it was conserved across species from worms to humans, establishing that lin-4 was not a one-off but the founding member of a broad microRNA class embedded throughout animal gene regulation.

sections.heading: Silencing that outlasts the signal: X-inactivation and imprinting
sections.body: Small RNAs are one route to silencing; heritable chromatin states are another. In 1961, Mary Lyon proposed what became known as the Lyon hypothesis: in female mammals, one of the two X chromosomes in each cell is randomly and permanently inactivated early in development, and that inactivated state is then faithfully copied through every subsequent cell division, producing the patchy calico-cat coat pattern as a visible readout of clonal X-inactivation. The molecular basis -- DNA methylation and chromatin modification maintaining a silenced state across cell generations without any change to the underlying sequence -- is now the textbook example of epigenetic inheritance, shared with genomic imprinting, in which methylation marks silence one parental copy of a gene while leaving the other active.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher wants to silence a specific C. elegans gene and observes that injecting double-stranded RNA works far better than injecting either single strand alone, and that a small amount of dsRNA silences far more mRNA than a 1:1 stoichiometric reaction could explain. Following Fire and Mello's 1998 logic, they conclude the dsRNA is triggering a catalytic, amplifiable silencing pathway (RNAi) rather than simple antisense hybridization -- the same evidentiary signature (potency at low dose, dsRNA specifically required) that originally distinguished RNAi from earlier, weaker antisense-RNA silencing attempts.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'is your silencing mechanism sequence-specific and heritable, or a permanent change to the DNA sequence itself?' because that distinction is the core of epigenetic regulation. A weak answer conflates RNAi, microRNAs, and X-inactivation as 'the same kind of gene silencing.' A strong answer separates them by mechanism and durability: RNAi/microRNAs act post-transcriptionally on specific mRNAs (Fire and Mello 1998; Lee, Feinbaum, and Ambros 1993), while X-inactivation and imprinting are chromatin-level, heritable-but-reversible silencing states (Lyon 1961) that persist across cell divisions without altering the DNA sequence.

questions.prompt: In Fire and Mello's 1998 experiment, what distinguished double-stranded RNA from single-stranded sense or antisense RNA alone?

options.text: Double-stranded RNA produced far stronger, catalytic-seeming silencing at low doses
Only single-stranded antisense RNA produced any silencing at all
Double-stranded RNA had no effect on gene expression
Single-stranded sense RNA silenced genes more effectively than double-stranded RNA

explanations.a: Correct -- dsRNA triggered potent, specific silencing at doses too low to explain by simple stoichiometric hybridization, implying an amplifying, catalytic mechanism -- what they named RNA interference.
explanations.b: Single-stranded antisense alone produced much weaker silencing than the double-stranded form in their comparison.
explanations.c: dsRNA was the most effective silencer in the experiment, not an inactive control.
explanations.d: Sense RNA alone was among the weaker conditions; dsRNA outperformed both single-stranded forms.

questions.prompt: Match each discovery to the researcher(s) who made it.

left.text: let-7, showing microRNAs are conserved across species

right.text: Lee, Feinbaum, and Ambros
Reinhart and colleagues, in Ruvkun's lab
Fire and Mello
Lyon

questions.explanation: Lee, Feinbaum, and Ambros identified lin-4 in 1993; Reinhart and colleagues in Ruvkun's lab identified the conserved let-7 in 2000; Fire and Mello discovered RNAi in 1998; Lyon proposed X-inactivation in 1961.

questions.prompt: What made the 2000 discovery of let-7 significant beyond confirming lin-4's mechanism?

options.text: It showed the small-RNA regulatory mechanism was conserved across species, not a nematode-specific oddity
It disproved that lin-4 was a real regulatory RNA
It showed microRNAs directly edit the DNA sequence of their targets
It was the first RNA molecule ever discovered

explanations.a: Correct -- finding let-7 conserved from worms to humans generalized lin-4's mechanism into a broad, evolutionarily conserved gene-regulatory class: the microRNA.
explanations.b: let-7 built on and extended lin-4's significance; it did not disprove lin-4.
explanations.c: MicroRNAs act post-transcriptionally, typically repressing translation or promoting mRNA degradation, not editing DNA sequence.
explanations.d: RNA had been known since the early 20th century; let-7 was notable as a conserved microRNA, not as RNA's discovery.

questions.prompt: Order these events from earliest to most recent.

items.text: Lyon proposes the X-inactivation hypothesis
Lee, Feinbaum, and Ambros identify lin-4
Fire and Mello publish the RNAi discovery
Reinhart and colleagues identify the conserved let-7 microRNA

questions.explanation: Lyon's hypothesis dates to 1961, lin-4 was identified in 1993, Fire and Mello published RNAi in 1998, and let-7's conservation was reported in 2000.

lessons.label: Live Debates in Regulation Today

sections.heading: Instructive or merely permissive enhancers?
sections.body: Even with enhancers well established since 1981, their role at any given locus is still argued case by case. An enhancer is 'instructive' if its specific sequence and bound factors determine which gene turns on, when, and how strongly -- swap the enhancer and you change the outcome. It is 'permissive' if it mainly opens or maintains an accessible chromatin state that lets a gene respond to signals arriving through other routes, contributing little sequence-specific information of its own. The distinction is not settled in general; it is argued locus by locus, using enhancer-swap and deletion experiments in specific developmental contexts, because the same regulatory element can behave more instructively at one gene and more permissively at another depending on what else is bound nearby.

sections.heading: Condensates and super-enhancers: real physics or overreach?
sections.body: In 2017, Denes Hnisz, Richard Young, and colleagues proposed that super-enhancers -- large clusters of enhancers bound by dense concentrations of transcription factors and coactivators -- work partly through liquid-liquid phase separation, forming transient droplet-like condensates that concentrate the transcription machinery at active genes. The model elegantly explained several odd features of super-enhancers, including their outsized sensitivity to small perturbations. But the claim drew sharp pushback: a widely cited 2019 critique from David McSwiggen, Mahdi Mir, Xavier Darzacq, Robert Tjian, and colleagues argued that many phase-separation claims rest on overexpressed, fluorescently tagged proteins imaged under conditions that can themselves induce artificial droplet formation, and that live-cell evidence at endogenous expression levels is much harder to obtain than the fixed-cell and overexpression data the field leaned on. The dispute is still open: condensate formation is real biophysics in some systems, but whether it is the general mechanism explaining super-enhancer function -- or a secondary consequence of the real, sequence-specific binding events -- remains contested.

sections.heading: ENCODE's '80% functional' claim, fought locus by locus
sections.body: In 2012, the ENCODE Consortium reported that roughly 80% of the human genome shows some 'biochemical activity' -- transcription, transcription-factor binding, or a chromatin mark -- and framed this as evidence against the idea that most of the genome is inert junk DNA. Dan Graur and coauthors sharply disputed the conclusion in a 2013 paper, arguing that ENCODE's definition of 'function' (any measurable biochemical signature) was far looser than evolutionary definitions requiring the sequence to be under selection, and that population-genetic and mutation-rate arguments limit truly functional sequence to a much smaller fraction of the genome. That framing disagreement plays out locus by locus: a transcription-factor peak or a stretch of open chromatin found in an ENCODE assay does not by itself prove the sequence does anything selectable, and resolving any single case requires the kind of deletion, reporter, and evolutionary-conservation evidence used to establish real enhancers in the first place -- exactly why an individual locus can still be argued over even after genome-wide surveys.

lessons.workedExample: A student reports that a chromatin-accessibility assay found an open, transcription-factor-bound region near their gene of interest and concludes it is 'a functional regulatory element.' A rigorous version of this claim, following the ENCODE controversy, would instead treat the accessibility signal as a hypothesis: deleting the element and testing whether target-gene expression changes (an instructive-versus-permissive test) is the evidence that actually distinguishes a biochemically active but non-functional sequence from a true regulatory element, the same standard Graur's critique argued ENCODE's genome-wide survey did not meet on its own.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'is that mechanism established, or is it still argued?' specifically to see if a student can locate their claim on the map of live debate rather than presenting a contested model as settled fact. A weak answer states 'super-enhancers work via phase separation' as textbook fact. A strong answer names Hnisz and Young's 2017 model, flags the 2019 live-cell/overexpression critique, and states plainly that the field has not resolved whether condensates are causal or incidental -- the same discipline applies to calling a chromatin-accessible region 'functional' without locus-specific deletion evidence.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes an 'instructive' enhancer from a 'permissive' one?

options.text: An instructive enhancer's specific sequence determines the regulatory outcome; a permissive one mainly enables accessibility for signals arriving another way
An instructive enhancer is always closer to the promoter than a permissive one
Permissive enhancers are found only in bacteria
Instructive enhancers never contain transcription-factor binding sites

explanations.a: Correct -- instructive enhancers supply sequence-specific information that determines the outcome, while permissive enhancers mainly open or maintain chromatin accessibility for signals delivered through other routes.
explanations.b: Physical distance from the promoter is not the defining criterion; both types can act at a distance.
explanations.c: Enhancers, whether instructive or permissive, are a eukaryotic gene-regulatory feature; the terms don't apply to bacterial operons.
explanations.d: Instructive enhancers are specifically defined by their transcription-factor binding, not its absence.

questions.prompt: What was the core critique leveled against the Hnisz/Young phase-separation model of super-enhancers?

options.text: Much of the supporting evidence relied on overexpressed, tagged proteins under conditions that can artificially induce droplet formation, unlike endogenous-level live-cell data
No super-enhancer has ever been observed to be perturbation-sensitive
Phase separation had never been observed in any biological system before 2017
The model claimed super-enhancers do not involve transcription factors at all

explanations.a: Correct -- the 2019 critique argued that overexpression and fixed-cell imaging can generate condensate-like artifacts, and that rigorous endogenous, live-cell evidence for the model was comparatively thin.
explanations.b: Super-enhancer sensitivity to perturbation was one of the observations the phase-separation model was proposed to explain, not something the critique denied.
explanations.c: Phase separation was documented in other biological contexts (e.g., stress granules) before being applied to transcription; the critique concerned its application here, not its general existence.
explanations.d: The model specifically proposed that dense clusters of transcription factors and coactivators drive condensate formation; it did not exclude them.

questions.prompt: What was the central disagreement in the Graur et al. critique of ENCODE's 2012 '80% functional' claim?

options.text: ENCODE's definition of function (any biochemical signature) was much looser than an evolutionary definition requiring sequence under selection
ENCODE claimed 0% of the genome has any biochemical activity
Graur argued the entire human genome is functional
The dispute was purely about which sequencing technology ENCODE used

explanations.a: Correct -- Graur and coauthors argued that a strict evolutionary definition of function implies a much smaller functional fraction of the genome than ENCODE's broad biochemical-activity definition suggested.
explanations.b: ENCODE's claim was the opposite: about 80% of the genome showed some biochemical signature.
explanations.c: Graur's position was that far less than 80%, plausibly closer to 10-25%, is truly functional by evolutionary criteria -- not that the whole genome is functional.
explanations.d: The dispute was conceptual, over what 'function' should mean, not a disagreement about sequencing methods.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the recent debates covered in this lesson.

items.text: ENCODE Consortium reports ~80% of the genome shows biochemical activity
Graur and coauthors publish a critique of ENCODE's functional claim
Hnisz, Young, and colleagues propose the phase-separation model of super-enhancers
McSwiggen, Mir, Darzacq, Tjian, and colleagues publish a critique of phase-separation evidence

questions.explanation: ENCODE's claim was published in 2012, Graur's critique followed in 2013, the phase-separation model was proposed in 2017, and the live-cell/overexpression critique of that model followed in 2019.

lessons.label: Credit, Reproducibility, and Reasoning Under Dispute

sections.heading: Who actually discovered RNA silencing first?
sections.body: Fire and Mello's 1998 dsRNA paper won the 2006 Nobel Prize, but RNA-triggered gene silencing had already been observed and reported eight years earlier by plant biologists. Napoli, Lemieux, and Jorgensen, trying to deepen the purple color of petunias in 1990, overexpressed a chalcone synthase transgene and instead got white flowers: the extra transgene copy silenced both itself and the plant's own chalcone synthase gene, a phenomenon they named cosuppression. Nobody in 1990 could explain the mechanism, and it took Fire and Mello's controlled worm experiments to identify double-stranded RNA as the actual trigger and give the field a mechanistic, Nobel-worthy answer. This is a recurring pattern in credit disputes: an early group observes a real, reproducible phenomenon it cannot yet explain, and a later group that supplies the mechanism receives the lasting recognition -- worth naming explicitly rather than treating the Nobel year as the discovery year.

sections.heading: CRISPR's regulatory lineage and its own credit fight
sections.body: A similar pattern shaped CRISPR. Francisco Mojica had identified and characterized the repetitive CRISPR sequences in bacterial and archaeal genomes years before their function as an adaptive immune system, or their repurposing as a programmable DNA-targeting tool, was worked out. Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier's 2012 biochemical demonstration that Cas9 could be programmed with a single guide RNA to cut specific DNA sequences won them the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry -- but Feng Zhang's near-simultaneous 2013 demonstration of CRISPR-Cas9 editing in mammalian cells, essential to the tool's use in human and animal systems, was left off that prize, a genuinely contested allocation of credit that specialists still argue over. For gene regulation specifically, this lineage matters because catalytically dead Cas9 (dCas9) fused to activator or repressor domains became a general-purpose tool -- CRISPRi and CRISPRa -- for silencing or activating any chosen gene, extending the same DNA-targeting logic Jacob and Monod's operator-repressor model first established, into a programmable, sequence-guided form.

sections.heading: When the measuring tool itself is unreliable
sections.body: Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) is the standard method for mapping where a histone mark or transcription factor sits on the genome, and its conclusions are only as good as the antibody used to pull down the target. Egelhofer and colleagues tested over 200 commercial antibodies raised against histone modifications across three species in a 2011 study and found more than a quarter failed basic specificity tests outright, with a substantial further fraction failing once used in an actual ChIP experiment. That meant a nontrivial slice of the field's published genome-wide histone-mark maps rested on antibodies that were cross-reacting with the wrong mark or the wrong protein entirely -- a reproducibility problem invisible unless someone went back and validated the reagent, and a standing reminder that a mechanism supported by a single unvalidated ChIP dataset is weaker evidence than one confirmed by an orthogonal method.

lessons.workedExample: A student claims a transcription factor 'definitely' binds a candidate enhancer because a single ChIP-seq experiment shows a peak there. A judge familiar with the Egelhofer findings would ask what validates the antibody's specificity and whether an independent method (a second antibody, a tagged version of the factor, or a functional deletion test) supports the same conclusion -- treating one unvalidated ChIP peak the way the field learned, after 2011, to treat any single result from a reagent of unknown quality: suggestive, not established.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'is that mechanism established, or is it the newest claim in an active argument?' is testing the exact skill this lesson builds: separating a landmark result that has been replicated and mechanistically explained (Fire and Mello's dsRNA trigger) from a phenomenon that was real but unexplained for years (Jorgensen's cosuppression), and from a measurement whose reliability depends on an unglamorous but critical detail like antibody validation. A weak answer cites a Nobel Prize as proof a topic is settled. A strong answer can state who saw the phenomenon first, who supplied the accepted mechanism, and what would need to be true (reagent validation, an orthogonal method, independent replication) for a specific measured claim to be trusted.

questions.prompt: What is the significance of Napoli, Lemieux, and Jorgensen's 1990 petunia cosuppression experiment relative to Fire and Mello's 1998 RNAi discovery?

options.text: It was an earlier observation of RNA-triggered gene silencing that lacked a mechanistic explanation until Fire and Mello identified double-stranded RNA as the trigger
It was performed after Fire and Mello's work, confirming their result in a second species
It showed that RNA silencing does not occur in plants
It directly identified double-stranded RNA as the causal trigger, predating Fire and Mello

explanations.a: Correct -- the 1990 petunia result was a real, reproducible silencing phenomenon (cosuppression) observed eight years before Fire and Mello supplied the mechanistic explanation involving double-stranded RNA.
explanations.b: The petunia experiment was published in 1990, eight years before Fire and Mello's 1998 paper, not after it.
explanations.c: The experiment demonstrated the opposite: RNA-triggered silencing does occur in plants, seen as an unexplained transgene-silencing effect.
explanations.d: Napoli, Lemieux, and Jorgensen observed the silencing phenomenon but did not identify double-stranded RNA as the trigger; that mechanistic identification came from Fire and Mello.

questions.prompt: According to Egelhofer and colleagues' 2011 study, what was the main reproducibility problem they identified in chromatin biology?

options.text: A substantial fraction of commercial histone-modification antibodies failed specificity tests or failed in ChIP experiments
Chromatin immunoprecipitation cannot be performed in any species
Histone modifications do not actually exist
All published ChIP-seq datasets before 2011 used the exact same single antibody

explanations.a: Correct -- testing over 200 antibodies across three species, they found more than a quarter failed basic specificity tests, with additional failures specific to ChIP conditions, undermining confidence in genome-wide maps built on unvalidated reagents.
explanations.b: ChIP is a widely used and generally valid technique; the issue was reagent (antibody) quality, not the method's feasibility.
explanations.c: Histone modifications are well-established biochemical marks; the study concerned measurement reliability, not their existence.
explanations.d: The study tested many different antibodies from various sources, not a single shared reagent.

questions.prompt: Match each credit or reproducibility dispute to its core issue.

right.text: Doudna and Charpentier recognized for CRISPR-Cas9 biochemistry; Zhang's mammalian-cell demonstration was not included
Napoli, Lemieux, and Jorgensen observed cosuppression years before Fire and Mello explained the mechanism
Egelhofer and colleagues found many commercial antibodies fail specificity or ChIP validation

questions.explanation: The RNAi priority dispute concerns who first observed silencing versus who explained it; the 2020 Nobel Prize dispute concerns which contributors to CRISPR-Cas9 editing were recognized; the ChIP dispute concerns antibody-driven measurement unreliability.

questions.prompt: Order these events from earliest to most recent.

items.text: Napoli, Lemieux, and Jorgensen observe cosuppression in petunias
Fire and Mello identify double-stranded RNA as the RNAi trigger
Egelhofer and colleagues publish their histone-antibody quality assessment
Doudna and Charpentier receive the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for CRISPR-Cas9

questions.explanation: Cosuppression was reported in 1990, the RNAi mechanism was published in 1998, the antibody quality assessment appeared in 2011, and the CRISPR-Cas9 Nobel Prize was awarded in 2020.

lessons.label: The Logic of Cell Signaling

sections.heading: A relay, not a wire
sections.body: Cell signaling is a relay, not a direct wire: a ligand (hormone, neurotransmitter, growth factor, or local chemical) binds a receptor, which activates a transducer, which often generates a second messenger, which flips an effector, which finally changes the cell's behavior (a gene turned on, a channel opened, an enzyme activated). Earl Sutherland's 1958 work on how adrenaline raises blood glucose without entering the liver cell established this whole idea: he found that adrenaline triggers production of an intracellular 'second messenger,' cyclic AMP, inside the cell, and that cAMP alone could reproduce the hormone's effect. That discovery, which won Sutherland the 1971 Nobel Prize, is why every signaling pathway is described as a chain of steps rather than a single lock-and-key event.

sections.heading: Five modes, defined by distance and delivery
sections.body: The same relay logic runs in five distinct geometries. Autocrine signaling: a cell secretes a ligand that binds receptors on itself, as when some tumor cells drive their own growth by secreting and re-binding their own growth factors. Paracrine signaling: a ligand diffuses to and acts on nearby cells, as with local growth factors coordinating wound healing. Endocrine signaling: a ligand is released into the bloodstream and acts on distant target cells, as with insulin traveling from the pancreas to muscle and fat. Juxtacrine signaling: a membrane-bound ligand on one cell binds a receptor on a cell it is physically touching, with no diffusion step at all, as in Notch-Delta signaling during development. Synaptic signaling: a neuron releases neurotransmitter across a narrow synaptic cleft directly onto an adjacent target cell's receptors, as with acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction. Distance and delivery scale together across these modes: a synaptic cleft is only about 20 nanometers wide, so synaptic signals cross in fractions of a millisecond; paracrine signals diffuse over tens of micrometers to reach neighboring cells over seconds; and endocrine signals travel the length of the entire bloodstream, taking seconds to minutes to reach a distant target.

sections.heading: The receptor decides the meaning
sections.body: A ligand does not carry a fixed instruction; the receptor repertoire of the receiving cell decides what the signal means. Acetylcholine slows the heart when it binds cardiac muscarinic receptors but contracts skeletal muscle when it binds nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction, two opposite outcomes from the identical molecule. Epinephrine likewise dilates blood vessels in skeletal muscle by acting on beta-adrenergic receptors there while constricting vessels in skin by acting on alpha-adrenergic receptors. This is why a science-fair project cannot claim a chemical 'does X' in general; it does whatever the target cell's receptor set converts it into.

lessons.workedExample: A student is testing how caffeine affects heart rate in Daphnia. Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors, and adenosine normally acts through Gi-coupled receptors to slow the heart via paracrine-like local release near cardiac tissue. Blocking that receptor removes the brake, so heart rate rises — not because caffeine itself is a stimulant signal at the heart, but because it interferes with an inhibitory relay. A judge would expect the student to explain the effect as receptor-mediated antagonism of an existing signaling relay, not simply 'caffeine speeds up the heart.'
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes the logic of signaling because it is the single fastest way to tell whether a student understands mechanism or is reciting an outcome. A weak answer says 'the hormone causes the response.' A strong answer names the relay (ligand to receptor to transducer to second messenger to effector) and, critically, explains that the response depends on which receptor the target cell expresses — so the same molecule can produce opposite effects in two tissues. Students who can name the signaling mode (autocrine, paracrine, endocrine, juxtacrine, synaptic) their own experiment involves, and justify why, stand out immediately.

questions.prompt: Epinephrine constricts blood vessels in the skin but dilates blood vessels in skeletal muscle. What best explains this difference?

options.text: Epinephrine is chemically altered differently in each tissue before it acts
The two tissues express different receptor subtypes for the same ligand
Skin blood vessels are simply less sensitive to any hormone
Epinephrine only reaches skeletal muscle in a diluted form

explanations.a: Epinephrine is not modified tissue by tissue before receptor binding; it acts as the same molecule everywhere.
explanations.b: Correct — skin vasculature carries more alpha-adrenergic receptors while skeletal muscle vasculature carries more beta-adrenergic receptors, and each subtype triggers an opposite response.
explanations.c: Sensitivity differences don't explain a reversal in direction of effect, only a difference in magnitude.
explanations.d: Blood-borne epinephrine reaches all tissues at comparable concentrations via the circulation; dilution is not the mechanism.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a generic signal relay from the outside of the cell inward.

items.text: Ligand binds receptor
Transducer is activated
Second messenger is generated
Effector protein changes activity
Cellular response occurs

questions.explanation: The canonical relay runs ligand-receptor binding, then transducer activation, then second-messenger production, then effector activation, and only then the observable cellular response.

questions.prompt: Match each signaling mode to its defining example.

right.text: A cell secretes a growth factor that binds receptors on itself
A local factor diffuses to nearby cells during wound healing
A pancreatic hormone travels through the bloodstream to muscle
A membrane-bound ligand binds a receptor on a directly touching cell

questions.explanation: Autocrine signaling targets the secreting cell itself, paracrine acts locally on neighbors, endocrine travels through blood to distant targets, and juxtacrine requires direct membrane-to-membrane contact.

questions.prompt: What did Sutherland's 1958 work on adrenaline and liver cells establish?

options.text: That hormones must physically enter a cell to have any effect
That an intracellular second messenger, cAMP, could reproduce the hormone's effect without the hormone itself
That adrenaline works identically in every cell type in the body
That receptors are unnecessary for hormone signaling

explanations.a: Sutherland's finding was the opposite: adrenaline never entered the cell, yet still caused an internal change via a messenger it generated at the membrane.
explanations.b: Correct — this is the origin of the second-messenger concept: cAMP, generated inside the cell, could reproduce adrenaline's effect on its own.
explanations.c: The work showed a mechanism, not that the hormone's effect is uniform across all tissues.
explanations.d: Receptors are exactly what allowed adrenaline to trigger cAMP production at the membrane without entering the cell.

lessons.label: G-Protein-Coupled Receptors (GPCRs)

sections.heading: Seven passes through the membrane, one switch cycle
sections.body: A GPCR is a single protein that weaves back and forth across the plasma membrane seven times, with the ligand-binding pocket facing outside and a heterotrimeric G protein (Galpha, Gbeta, Ggamma) docked on its cytoplasmic face at rest, Galpha holding GDP. Ligand binding reshapes the receptor's cytoplasmic loops so that it acts as a guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF): it forces Galpha to release GDP and pick up GTP instead. GTP-bound Galpha then dissociates from Gbeta-gamma, and both pieces are now free to activate downstream effectors independently. The cycle resets when Galpha's own slow GTPase activity hydrolyzes GTP back to GDP — often accelerated by RGS ('regulator of G protein signaling') proteins — letting Galpha and Gbeta-gamma reassociate and return to standby. Alfred Gilman and Martin Rodbell shared the 1994 Nobel Prize for working out this GTP/GDP cycle; Robert Lefkowitz and Brian Kobilka shared the 2012 Nobel Prize for later solving GPCR structures, including the beta-2 adrenergic receptor, that showed how ligand binding physically drives the conformational change.

sections.heading: Three effector routes: Gs, Gi, Gq
sections.body: Which effector a GPCR reaches depends on which Galpha subtype it carries. Gs-coupled receptors, such as beta-adrenergic receptors bound by epinephrine, stimulate adenylyl cyclase, raising cAMP and activating protein kinase A. Gi-coupled receptors, such as cardiac M2 muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, do the opposite: they inhibit adenylyl cyclase, lowering cAMP. Gq-coupled receptors, such as alpha-1 adrenergic receptors, activate phospholipase C-beta, which cleaves PIP2 into IP3 (releasing Ca2+ from the ER) and diacylglycerol (activating protein kinase C). Rhodopsin, the light receptor in rod photoreceptors, is a specialized GPCR that uses a fourth G protein, transducin (Gt): light isomerizes rhodopsin's bound retinal, activating transducin, which stimulates a phosphodiesterase that destroys cGMP and closes cGMP-gated channels, hyperpolarizing the cell in milliseconds.

sections.heading: Amplification is the point
sections.body: Because one activated GPCR can catalyze GDP-to-GTP exchange on many G-protein copies before it is shut off, and each activated Galpha or enzyme it triggers can act catalytically on many substrate molecules downstream, a single bound ligand is converted into a large, cascading intracellular signal — often orders of magnitude more molecules than the one that started it. The rhodopsin/transducin system puts numbers on this: a single light-activated rhodopsin can catalyze activation of several hundred transducin molecules within about a second, and each activated transducin in turn activates a phosphodiesterase that hydrolyzes many cGMP molecules, so one absorbed photon closes hundreds of channels. This amplification is why hormones and neurotransmitters work at picomolar-to-nanomolar concentrations rather than requiring one receptor per response.

lessons.workedExample: Epinephrine binds a beta-1 adrenergic receptor on a cardiac muscle cell. The receptor's Gs protein exchanges GDP for GTP; Galpha-GTP activates adenylyl cyclase, which converts many ATP molecules into cAMP. cAMP activates protein kinase A, which phosphorylates calcium channels and contractile proteins, increasing both heart rate and contraction force. Within seconds, Galpha's GTPase activity hydrolyzes the bound GTP, the signal ends, and heart rate returns toward baseline once epinephrine clears — illustrating that the GTP hydrolysis step, not just receptor binding, sets how long the response lasts.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing GPCR mechanism is testing whether a student understands that the pathway is a timed molecular switch, not a static connection. A weak answer says 'the hormone binds the receptor and turns on a pathway.' A strong answer names the GDP/GTP exchange step, explains that GTP hydrolysis is what turns the signal back off, and can say which Galpha subtype (Gs, Gi, or Gq) is in play and why that determines the direction of the effect (cAMP up, cAMP down, or Ca2+/PKC activation).

questions.prompt: Order the events of the heterotrimeric G-protein activation cycle.

items.text: Ligand binds the GPCR
Receptor acts as a GEF, GDP is exchanged for GTP on Galpha
Galpha-GTP dissociates from Gbeta-gamma
Effector proteins are activated by Galpha-GTP and/or Gbeta-gamma
Galpha hydrolyzes GTP to GDP and the trimer reassembles

questions.explanation: Ligand binding triggers GEF activity on the receptor, causing GDP-to-GTP exchange; the activated Galpha dissociates from Gbeta-gamma, both signal to effectors, and the cycle resets only once GTP is hydrolyzed back to GDP.

questions.prompt: Match each G-protein subtype to its characteristic effect.

right.text: Stimulates adenylyl cyclase, raising cAMP
Inhibits adenylyl cyclase, lowering cAMP
Activates phospholipase C-beta, raising IP3/DAG and Ca2+

questions.explanation: Gs stimulates and Gi inhibits adenylyl cyclase, controlling cAMP in opposite directions, while Gq engages an entirely different effector, phospholipase C-beta.

questions.prompt: Why is the GTPase activity of Galpha essential to normal GPCR signaling, not just a side detail?

options.text: It is what allows the receptor to bind its ligand in the first place
It terminates the signal by returning Galpha to its inactive, GDP-bound state
It amplifies the signal by generating more cAMP molecules
It is required for the receptor to dimerize with a second receptor

explanations.a: Ligand binding depends on the extracellular pocket of the receptor, not on Galpha's GTPase activity.
explanations.b: Correct — GTP hydrolysis is the built-in timer that shuts the G protein off and lets the cycle reset; without it, signaling would run continuously.
explanations.c: GTPase activity ends the signal rather than generating cAMP; cAMP is produced by adenylyl cyclase while Galpha is GTP-bound.
explanations.d: GPCRs are not defined by this kind of dimerization step in the core activation cycle described here.

questions.prompt: In rod photoreceptors, what does light do to trigger the phototransduction cascade through rhodopsin?

options.text: It directly opens a cGMP-gated ion channel without any receptor involved
It isomerizes retinal bound to rhodopsin, activating the G protein transducin
It raises intracellular cAMP directly, bypassing any G protein
It causes rhodopsin to bind IP3 directly

explanations.a: The channel closes as a downstream consequence of the cascade; light does not act on it directly.
explanations.b: Correct — light isomerizes rhodopsin's bound retinal, activating transducin (Gt), which stimulates a phosphodiesterase that lowers cGMP and closes channels.
explanations.c: The cascade lowers cGMP via a phosphodiesterase, not cAMP, and it proceeds through a G protein rather than bypassing one.
explanations.d: Rhodopsin signals through transducin and cGMP phosphodiesterase, not through IP3.

lessons.label: Receptor Tyrosine Kinases (RTKs)

sections.heading: Dimerize, then phosphorylate the partner
sections.body: A receptor tyrosine kinase is a single-pass membrane protein with an extracellular ligand-binding region and an intracellular tyrosine kinase domain. Stanley Cohen's 1962 discovery of epidermal growth factor (EGF) and its receptor, work that shared the 1986 Nobel Prize with Rita Levi-Montalcini, established this receptor class, which has since grown to 58 receptor tyrosine kinases encoded in the human genome, grouped into 20 subfamilies (Lemmon & Schlessinger, 2010). Most RTKs, including EGFR, exist as inactive monomers at rest. When EGF binds, it drives two receptor monomers together into a dimer; because the two kinase domains are now held next to each other, each one phosphorylates tyrosine residues on its partner's cytoplasmic tail rather than on itself. This trans-autophosphorylation, not self-phosphorylation, is the defining activation step of the RTK family, and it converts the receptor's tail into a cluster of phosphotyrosine docking sites.

sections.heading: SH2 domains read the docking sites
sections.body: Phosphotyrosines are read by proteins carrying SH2 domains, which bind phosphotyrosine in a specific sequence context. The adaptor protein Grb2 uses its SH2 domain to dock onto an activated RTK's phosphotyrosine, then uses two SH3 domains to recruit SOS, a guanine nucleotide exchange factor. SOS then catalyzes GDP-to-GTP exchange on the small GTPase Ras, switching Ras on. Active Ras launches the Ras-Raf-MEK-ERK (MAPK) cascade, a kinase relay that ultimately phosphorylates transcription factors controlling cell division and differentiation. This Grb2-SOS-Ras hand-off is the single most common route from an activated RTK to a change in gene expression.

sections.heading: EGFR versus the insulin receptor: two dimerization strategies
sections.body: EGFR illustrates ligand-induced dimerization: it is monomeric until EGF binds. The insulin receptor illustrates a variant: it is already a covalently disulfide-linked dimer (an alpha2-beta2 tetramer) before insulin ever arrives, so insulin binding does not create the dimer but instead triggers a conformational shift that brings the two intracellular kinase domains into an active trans-phosphorylating arrangement. Downstream, the insulin receptor phosphorylates a distinct adaptor, IRS-1, which in turn recruits PI3-kinase to activate the Akt pathway controlling glucose uptake, alongside the same Ras-MAPK route EGFR uses. The shared logic — dimerization or its equivalent, trans-autophosphorylation, SH2-domain docking — underlies both, even though the two hormones control very different physiology.

lessons.workedExample: In a subset of lung cancers, the EGFR gene carries a point mutation (L858R) in the kinase domain that makes the receptor adopt its active, trans-phosphorylating conformation even without EGF bound, driving continuous Grb2-SOS-Ras-MAPK signaling and uncontrolled proliferation. Drugs like erlotinib work by occupying the ATP-binding pocket of the kinase domain, blocking the trans-autophosphorylation step itself rather than blocking ligand binding — a strategy that only makes sense once you know activation depends on kinase activity, not just receptor occupancy.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking about RTKs is testing whether a student can distinguish 'the receptor turned on' from the specific molecular step that turns it on. A weak answer says EGF activates EGFR, which activates cell growth. A strong answer names dimerization and trans-autophosphorylation as the switch, identifies Grb2-SOS as the adaptor-GEF pair that reaches Ras, and — if the project touches cancer biology — can explain why a kinase-domain mutation, not just receptor overexpression, is often the more dangerous lesion.

questions.prompt: Order the steps from EGF binding to Ras activation.

items.text: EGF binds an EGFR monomer
Two receptor monomers dimerize
Each kinase domain trans-autophosphorylates the partner's tail
Grb2 docks on a phosphotyrosine via its SH2 domain
SOS, recruited by Grb2, activates Ras by GDP/GTP exchange

questions.explanation: Ligand binding drives dimerization, dimerization enables trans-autophosphorylation, the resulting phosphotyrosines recruit Grb2, and Grb2-bound SOS then activates Ras.

questions.prompt: What does 'trans-autophosphorylation' mean in the context of RTK activation?

options.text: Each receptor monomer phosphorylates tyrosines on itself
Each receptor monomer in a dimer phosphorylates tyrosines on its partner monomer
A separate kinase enzyme phosphorylates the receptor from the cytoplasm
The ligand itself carries a phosphate group that is transferred to the receptor

explanations.a: That would be cis-autophosphorylation; RTK activation specifically works in trans, across the dimer interface.
explanations.b: Correct — dimerization positions the two kinase domains so each phosphorylates the other, which is why the term is trans-, not cis-, autophosphorylation.
explanations.c: The kinase activity comes from the receptor's own intracellular domain, not a separate free-floating enzyme.
explanations.d: The phosphate comes from ATP hydrolyzed by the receptor's own kinase domain, not from the ligand.

questions.prompt: Match each receptor to its dimerization behavior at rest.

right.text: Monomeric until ligand binding drives dimerization
Already a disulfide-linked dimer before ligand binds; ligand triggers a conformational shift instead

questions.explanation: EGFR is the classic ligand-induced dimerization example, while the insulin receptor is pre-assembled as an alpha2-beta2 dimer and instead undergoes a conformational activation upon insulin binding.

questions.prompt: Why does an EGFR kinase-domain mutation like L858R promote cancer even without EGF present?

options.text: It increases how much EGF the cell secretes
It locks the receptor into an active conformation, driving trans-autophosphorylation and downstream signaling without ligand
It prevents Grb2 from ever binding the receptor
It converts EGFR into a GPCR

explanations.a: The mutation is in the receptor's own kinase domain, not in a gene controlling EGF secretion.
explanations.b: Correct — the mutation biases the kinase domain toward its active conformation, so the receptor signals continuously even without EGF binding.
explanations.c: Grb2 binding is enhanced, not blocked, since the mutation increases phosphotyrosine docking sites through constitutive activation.
explanations.d: The receptor remains an RTK; it does not switch signaling families.

lessons.label: Nuclear & Intracellular Receptors

sections.heading: Ligands small and greasy enough to cross the membrane
sections.body: Steroid hormones (cortisol, estrogen, testosterone, aldosterone), thyroid hormone, and retinoids (vitamin A derivatives) share one physical property that sets this whole receptor class apart: they are small and lipophilic enough to diffuse directly across the phospholipid bilayer of the plasma membrane, so they need no membrane receptor at all to get inside a cell. Their receptors sit in the cytoplasm or nucleus rather than embedded in the membrane. Elwood Jensen's 1958 experiments tracking radioactively labeled estrogen showed it accumulating in specific target tissues bound to an intracellular protein, work that established the existence of the estrogen receptor and the general model that these hormones act by binding a dedicated intracellular receptor rather than a surface one. The estrogen and glucocorticoid receptors are just two of 48 nuclear receptors encoded in the human genome (Nuclear Receptors Nomenclature Committee, 1999), a family that also includes receptors for other sex steroids, retinoids, vitamin D, and dozens of orphan receptors whose ligands are still unknown, all sharing the same core DNA-binding and ligand-binding domain architecture.

sections.heading: The receptor is itself a transcription factor
sections.body: Once bound, these receptors act directly as ligand-activated transcription factors: they bind specific DNA sequences called hormone-response elements (HREs) near target genes and recruit coactivator or corepressor complexes that open or close chromatin, changing how much a gene is transcribed. Some receptors, like the glucocorticoid receptor, sit inactive in the cytoplasm bound to the chaperone HSP90 until hormone binding causes HSP90 to release, allowing the receptor to dimerize and translocate into the nucleus. Others, like the thyroid hormone receptor, are already resident in the nucleus and bound to DNA even without hormone, actively repressing target genes at baseline and switching to activation only once hormone binds — so 'no ligand' is not the same as 'no effect' for this subclass.

sections.heading: Hours, not milliseconds
sections.body: Because the response requires transcription and then translation of new protein, nuclear receptor signaling plays out over hours to days rather than the milliseconds-to-seconds timescale of a ligand-gated channel or the seconds-to-minutes timescale of a GPCR cascade. This is a direct, testable consequence of the mechanism: a synthetic glucocorticoid like prednisone, used to suppress inflammation, does not produce its full anti-inflammatory effect until new anti-inflammatory proteins have been transcribed and translated, typically over several hours, even though the drug binds its receptor within minutes.

lessons.workedExample: Cortisol is released into the blood and diffuses across the membrane of a target immune cell. In the cytoplasm it binds the glucocorticoid receptor, displacing the chaperone HSP90. The freed receptor dimerizes and moves into the nucleus, binds glucocorticoid-response elements near anti-inflammatory genes, and recruits coactivators to increase their transcription. The resulting proteins are not present in meaningful amounts until several hours after cortisol first bound the receptor — which is why clinicians dosing a patient with a glucocorticoid for inflammation expect a delayed onset of action rather than a fast one, unlike an inhaled bronchodilator acting through a membrane GPCR within minutes.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about nuclear receptors to see whether a student connects mechanism to timescale rather than treating 'hormone effect' as instantaneous by default. A weak answer says the hormone 'turns on a response.' A strong answer explains that because the receptor itself is a transcription factor, the response is gated by transcription and translation, so the effect is necessarily slow — and can name the physical property (lipophilicity, letting the hormone cross the membrane unassisted) that made a nuclear rather than a membrane receptor mechanistically possible in the first place.

questions.prompt: Why can steroid hormones bind an intracellular receptor instead of a receptor embedded in the plasma membrane?

options.text: They are lipophilic enough to diffuse directly across the phospholipid bilayer
They are actively pumped across the membrane by a dedicated transporter
