explanations.d: Neurofibromin is a GAP that turns Ras off (by promoting GTP hydrolysis), not a kinase that turns it on.

questions.prompt: Why does thapsigargin cause a slow, uncontrolled rise in cytosolic calcium?

options.text: It opens the IP3 receptor directly, flooding the cytosol with ER calcium
It irreversibly inhibits SERCA, preventing calcium from being pumped back into the ER
It activates PMCA, pulling extra calcium into the cell from outside
It blocks calmodulin, preventing calcium from being buffered in the cytosol

explanations.a: Thapsigargin's target is the reuptake pump, not the release channel; it does not act on the IP3 receptor.
explanations.b: Correct — by irreversibly blocking SERCA, thapsigargin removes the mechanism that normally re-sequesters cytosolic calcium into the ER, so calcium accumulates in the cytosol.
explanations.c: PMCA extrudes calcium out of the cell rather than pulling it in, and thapsigargin's known target is SERCA, not PMCA.
explanations.d: Thapsigargin acts on a calcium pump's transport activity, not on calmodulin's calcium-binding function.

questions.prompt: In terms of steady-state phosphorylation, what determines how much of a given PKA or ERK substrate is phosphorylated at any moment?

options.text: Only the kinase's activity; phosphatases play no meaningful role once a kinase has acted
The balance between ongoing kinase activity and opposing phosphatase activity
Only the phosphatase's activity; kinases only matter at the initial moment of stimulation
The concentration of ATP alone, independent of either enzyme's activity

explanations.a: Phosphatases like PP1 and PP2A continuously remove phosphates, meaning the phosphorylation level reflects ongoing opposition, not a one-time kinase event.
explanations.b: Correct — phosphorylation state at any instant reflects a continuous tug-of-war between kinase addition and phosphatase removal, not a permanent mark from either enzyme alone.
explanations.c: Kinase activity continues to add phosphate as long as the pathway is engaged; it is not limited to only the initial stimulus.
explanations.d: ATP is a required substrate for kinases but does not by itself determine the balance; the opposing phosphatase activity is equally necessary to explain steady-state levels.

questions.prompt: Order these events for a cAMP-PKA signal being switched on and then off.

items.text: Adenylyl cyclase synthesizes cAMP, activating PKA
PKA phosphorylates its downstream targets
Phosphodiesterase hydrolyzes cAMP to 5'-AMP
Phosphatases remove the phosphates PKA added, resetting the targets

questions.explanation: The messenger must be made and act on PKA before PKA can phosphorylate targets; only after the messenger is cleared by PDE and the added phosphates are removed by phosphatases is the system fully reset for the next signal.

lessons.label: Bioenergetics & Energy Currency

sections.heading: Why ATP hydrolysis releases usable energy
sections.body: ATP + H2O -> ADP + Pi has a standard free-energy change (delta-G-not-prime) of about -30.5 kJ/mol (-7.3 kcal/mol), but that textbook number is not what a real cell runs on. Inside a cell, ATP, ADP, and Pi are never at the 1 M standard-state concentrations the prime symbol assumes; ATP is kept far above equilibrium with ADP, typically at a 5:1 to 10:1 ratio. Plugging real cytosolic concentrations into the Gibbs equation pushes the actual delta-G of hydrolysis to roughly -50 to -65 kJ/mol -- the cell spends metabolic effort continuously regenerating ATP just to keep the ratio skewed, and that skew is the actual energy source, not some special bond. Fritz Lipmann's 1941 paper on 'high-energy phosphate bonds' first framed ATP as the cell's shared energy currency, a concept that still organizes how bioenergetics is taught. The 'high-energy bond' language is a historical misnomer, though: the bond itself does not store the energy. ATP's three phosphate groups sit adjacent to each other, all carrying negative charge, and forcing them into close proximity costs energy to maintain -- hydrolysis releases that strain by letting the phosphates separate, relieving electrostatic repulsion. The inorganic phosphate freed by hydrolysis is also more stable than it was attached to ADP, because it can now delocalize its negative charge across multiple equivalent oxygen atoms -- resonance stabilization that is unavailable while it is locked into the triphosphate chain. Together, relief of charge repulsion and resonance stabilization of the products are the actual chemistry behind why hydrolysis is favorable, not any special energy stored in the bond.

sections.heading: Coupling: making the unfavorable happen
sections.body: Cells drive energetically unfavorable reactions (positive delta-G) by coupling them to ATP hydrolysis through a shared covalent intermediate, so the free energies sum. Hexokinase does not simply hydrolyze ATP next to glucose; it transfers ATP's terminal phosphate directly onto glucose's 6-hydroxyl, producing glucose-6-phosphate and ADP in one step. The unfavorable phosphorylation of glucose (delta-G around +13.8 kJ/mol) is chemically fused to the favorable hydrolysis, and the combined reaction is strongly favorable overall. This is coupling: not two reactions running side by side, but one enzyme active site making one happen because the other happens.

sections.heading: Electron carriers and the two phosphorylation routes
sections.body: NAD+ and FAD are reusable electron shuttles. NAD+ accepts a hydride (2 electrons plus one proton) to become NADH; FAD accepts two electrons and two protons to become FADH2. Both then donate those electrons downstream to generate ATP, but by different means. Substrate-level phosphorylation is direct: an enzyme transfers a phosphate group from a high-energy substrate straight onto ADP, no membrane or electron transport involved -- it happens twice in glycolysis and once per turn of the citric acid cycle. Oxidative phosphorylation is indirect: NADH and FADH2 donate electrons to the electron transport chain, which pumps protons to build a gradient that ATP synthase then taps to make ATP. Oxidative phosphorylation is slower to start but yields far more ATP per glucose than substrate-level phosphorylation alone.

lessons.workedExample: A student's poster claims 'ATP releases 7.3 kcal/mol of energy when it breaks down in the cell.' A judge should catch that this restates the standard-state value, delta-G-not-prime, not the actual cellular delta-G. The stronger claim: because a resting cell holds the ATP:ADP ratio far from the 1:1 equilibrium implied by standard conditions -- closer to 5:1 or higher -- the real free energy released is more negative, often cited near -50 to -60 kJ/mol. The fix is not a bigger number for its own sake; it is recognizing that delta-G-not-prime is a fixed reference constant while actual delta-G depends on the concentrations the cell maintains, which is itself an active, ATP-consuming process.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'why is ATP considered high-energy' to test whether a student understands coupling versus reciting a number. A weak answer says ATP has a 'high-energy bond' that stores energy, treating the phosphoanhydride bond itself as a battery. A strong answer explains that hydrolysis is favorable because of electrostatic repulsion release and resonance stabilization of products, and -- crucially -- that ATP is useful because cells couple its hydrolysis to specific unfavorable reactions through shared intermediates, not because the molecule is magically charged. Naming the actual delta-G range and distinguishing substrate-level from oxidative phosphorylation signals real command of the topic.

questions.prompt: Why is the actual free energy released by ATP hydrolysis inside a living cell typically more negative than the textbook standard value of -30.5 kJ/mol?

options.text: ATP molecules in cells contain an extra phosphate bond not present under standard conditions.
Cells maintain ATP concentrations far above equilibrium relative to ADP and Pi, and this deviation from standard-state conditions makes the real delta-G more negative.
Body temperature increases the standard free energy value directly.
The textbook value already accounts for cellular conditions, so there is no difference.

explanations.a: ATP always has the same three phosphates; no extra bond forms inside cells.
explanations.b: Correct -- the standard value assumes 1 M concentrations at equilibrium-like conditions; real cells hold ATP well above ADP, and that non-equilibrium ratio drives actual delta-G more negative.
explanations.c: Temperature affects the reaction rate and enters the Gibbs equation, but it is not the primary reason cellular delta-G diverges so much from the standard value.
explanations.d: The prime notation specifically denotes standard biochemical conditions (pH 7, 1 M concentrations), which cells do not actually maintain.

questions.prompt: Hexokinase phosphorylates glucose using ATP in a single enzymatic step rather than releasing free phosphate that glucose then picks up separately. What does this illustrate?

options.text: Energy coupling through a shared covalent intermediate, which sums the favorable and unfavorable free energies.
Substrate-level phosphorylation occurring in the electron transport chain.
Oxidative phosphorylation driven by a proton gradient.
An example of fermentation regenerating NAD+.

explanations.a: Correct -- transferring the phosphate directly in one active site couples the unfavorable phosphorylation of glucose to the favorable hydrolysis of ATP so their free energies combine into one favorable reaction.
explanations.b: This step is substrate-level phosphorylation in the sense of direct enzymatic transfer, but it happens in glycolysis, not the electron transport chain, and the question is really testing the coupling concept.
explanations.c: Oxidative phosphorylation requires the electron transport chain and ATP synthase; hexokinase uses neither.
explanations.d: Fermentation is unrelated to this single phosphorylation step.

questions.prompt: Match each electron carrier or phosphorylation term to its correct description.

right.text: Formed when NAD+ accepts a hydride (2 electrons + 1 proton)
Formed when FAD accepts 2 electrons and 2 protons
Direct enzymatic transfer of a phosphate group to ADP, no membrane involved
ATP made via a proton gradient generated by the electron transport chain

questions.explanation: NADH carries a hydride, FADH2 carries two electrons plus two protons, substrate-level phosphorylation transfers phosphate directly onto ADP, and oxidative phosphorylation uses the proton-motive force built by the electron transport chain.

questions.prompt: Order the logical steps of energy coupling as hexokinase phosphorylates glucose, from least to most specific.

items.text: ATP hydrolysis alone is thermodynamically favorable (negative delta-G)
Glucose phosphorylation alone is unfavorable (positive delta-G)
Hexokinase's active site physically links phosphate transfer from ATP to glucose in one step
The combined reaction has a net negative delta-G and proceeds readily

questions.explanation: The two half-reactions have opposite signs on their own; the enzyme physically couples them by transferring the phosphate directly, and only then does the summed free energy become favorable overall.

lessons.label: Glycolysis

sections.heading: Ten steps, two phases
sections.body: Glycolysis -- the Embden-Meyerhof-Parnas pathway, worked out through the 1930s by Gustav Embden, Otto Meyerhof, and Jakub Parnas, with Carl and Gerty Cori's parallel work on glucose metabolism earning a 1947 Nobel Prize -- splits one 6-carbon glucose into two 3-carbon pyruvate molecules across ten enzymatic steps in the cytosol. The pathway has two phases. The energy-investment phase (steps 1-5) spends 2 ATP: hexokinase phosphorylates glucose to glucose-6-phosphate, phosphoglucose isomerase converts it to fructose-6-phosphate, phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1) phosphorylates it again to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate, and aldolase splits that 6-carbon sugar into two 3-carbon triose phosphates (dihydroxyacetone phosphate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate), which triose phosphate isomerase interconverts so both continue as glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (G3P).

sections.heading: The payoff phase and net yield
sections.body: Because one glucose became two G3P molecules, every remaining step runs twice per glucose. Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase oxidizes G3P and reduces NAD+ to NADH while attaching a phosphate, forming 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate. Phosphoglycerate kinase then transfers that phosphate directly to ADP -- substrate-level phosphorylation -- making the pathway's first ATP and 3-phosphoglycerate. Phosphoglycerate mutase repositions the remaining phosphate, enolase removes water to form phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP), and pyruvate kinase transfers PEP's phosphate to ADP in a second substrate-level phosphorylation, yielding pyruvate and a second ATP. Doubled for both trioses, the payoff phase produces 4 ATP and 2 NADH. Subtracting the 2 ATP invested up front, glycolysis nets 2 ATP, 2 NADH, and 2 pyruvate per glucose -- a small direct yield, but one that requires no oxygen and no mitochondria.

sections.heading: Three irreversible checkpoints
sections.body: Three of the ten reactions release enough free energy to be effectively irreversible in the cell and are the pathway's control points. Hexokinase (step 1) is inhibited by its own product, glucose-6-phosphate, preventing the cell from over-committing glucose. Liver cells use a distinct isozyme instead, glucokinase (hexokinase IV): it is not inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate and has a much higher Km for glucose, so rather than saturating early like hexokinase it keeps phosphorylating glucose as blood glucose climbs after a meal, letting the liver buffer blood sugar instead of throttling uptake. PFK-1 (step 3) is the master regulator: ATP and citrate inhibit it, while AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate activate it, tuning flux to the cell's real-time energy state. Pyruvate kinase (step 10) is activated by fructose-1,6-bisphosphate feed-forward signaling -- upstream buildup pushes the pathway to finish -- and is inhibited by ATP and alanine. These three steps are the ones a cell actually throttles; the other seven run near equilibrium and simply follow substrate availability.

lessons.workedExample: A student measures glucose consumption in yeast and reports '1 glucose yields 2 ATP from glycolysis, full stop.' A judge should push: does that 2 ATP account for the NADH produced? Glycolysis nets 2 ATP directly via substrate-level phosphorylation plus 2 NADH, and those 2 NADH are worth roughly 3-5 additional ATP once shuttled into the mitochondria and run through oxidative phosphorylation (the exact number depends on which shuttle moves the electrons across the mitochondrial membrane). A complete answer separates the pathway's direct, oxygen-independent yield (2 ATP, 2 NADH, 2 pyruvate) from what those NADH are worth downstream, and explains why yeast under anaerobic conditions cannot cash in the NADH the same way.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing glycolysis is checking whether a student can separate the two phases and explain why an 'energy-investment' phase exists at all -- spending 2 ATP to net a claimed profit sounds backwards to someone who has not traced the pathway. A weak answer recites '2 ATP net, 2 NADH' without being able to say where the ATP is spent versus made. A strong answer names hexokinase and PFK-1 as the investment steps, phosphoglycerate kinase and pyruvate kinase as the payoff steps, and can explain that splitting one 6-carbon sugar into two 3-carbon units is why the payoff phase runs twice for every investment phase that runs once.

questions.prompt: Order these five glycolysis enzymes by the step they act at, starting from glucose.

items.text: Hexokinase
Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1)
Aldolase
Phosphoglycerate kinase
Pyruvate kinase

questions.explanation: Hexokinase phosphorylates glucose first, PFK-1 commits fructose-6-phosphate with a second phosphorylation, aldolase splits the 6-carbon sugar into two trioses, phosphoglycerate kinase makes the pathway's first ATP in the payoff phase, and pyruvate kinase makes the second ATP at the final step.

questions.prompt: Why does glycolysis invest 2 ATP in the first five steps before it ever produces any?

options.text: The phosphorylations trap and destabilize the sugar, and the resulting fructose-1,6-bisphosphate is what aldolase can actually cleave into two usable trioses.
It is a vestigial step left over from an earlier, less efficient version of the pathway with no current function.
ATP is invested to directly reduce NAD+ to NADH.
The investment phase pumps protons across the plasma membrane to build a gradient.

explanations.a: Correct -- phosphorylating glucose twice (via hexokinase and PFK-1) adds negatively charged groups that trap the sugar in the cell and destabilize it enough for aldolase to split it into two three-carbon phosphorylated trioses, which the payoff phase then oxidizes.
explanations.b: The investment phase is functionally required, not vestigial; removing it would leave aldolase nothing suitable to cleave.
explanations.c: NADH is produced later, in the payoff phase, by glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, not by the investment-phase kinases.
explanations.d: Glycolysis occurs in the cytosol and involves no membrane proton pumping; that describes the electron transport chain instead.

questions.prompt: Which enzyme is generally considered the primary rate-limiting, most heavily regulated step of glycolysis?

options.text: Triose phosphate isomerase
Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1)
Enolase
Phosphoglycerate mutase

explanations.a: Triose phosphate isomerase runs near equilibrium and simply interconverts the two trioses; it is not a control point.
explanations.b: Correct -- PFK-1 is allosterically inhibited by ATP and citrate and activated by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, making it the pathway's master throttle.
explanations.c: Enolase dehydrates 2-phosphoglycerate to PEP and runs near equilibrium; it is not a major regulatory checkpoint.
explanations.d: Phosphoglycerate mutase simply relocates a phosphate group and is not a significant control point.

questions.prompt: Match each glycolysis enzyme to what it produces or consumes.

right.text: Spends 1 ATP phosphorylating glucose
Spends 1 ATP at the pathway's committed, most regulated step
Produces NADH while oxidizing the triose
Produces ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation from PEP

questions.explanation: Hexokinase and PFK-1 each spend one ATP in the investment phase (PFK-1 being the regulated, committed step), while glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase generates NADH and pyruvate kinase generates ATP in the payoff phase.

lessons.label: The Fate of Pyruvate

sections.heading: The committed step: pyruvate dehydrogenase
sections.body: When oxygen is available, pyruvate crosses into the mitochondrial matrix through the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier (MPC), a dedicated transporter embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane, and meets the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC), one of the largest enzyme assemblies in the cell -- three catalytic subunits (E1, E2, E3) built around five cofactors (thiamine pyrophosphate, lipoic acid, coenzyme A, FAD, and NAD+). PDC performs oxidative decarboxylation: pyruvate + CoA + NAD+ -> acetyl-CoA + CO2 + NADH. This reaction is irreversible in the cell and is the true committed step into aerobic respiration -- once pyruvate becomes acetyl-CoA, the carbon cannot be converted back to glucose (a key reason animals cannot turn fat back into net new glucose). Each glucose yields two pyruvate, so this step alone produces 2 NADH and 2 CO2 before the citric acid cycle even begins.

sections.heading: Fermentation: the low-oxygen alternative
sections.body: Without enough oxygen to keep the electron transport chain running, cells cannot use it to regenerate NAD+, so they fall back on fermentation. In muscle and many bacteria, lactate dehydrogenase directly reduces pyruvate using NADH, forming lactate and regenerating NAD+ in a single step. In yeast and some plant tissues, ethanol fermentation takes two steps: pyruvate decarboxylase strips a CO2 to form acetaldehyde, then alcohol dehydrogenase reduces acetaldehyde to ethanol using NADH, again regenerating NAD+. Neither pathway makes any additional ATP -- their entire purpose is recycling the electron carrier, not extracting more energy.

sections.heading: Why NAD+/NADH balance forces the choice
sections.body: The decisive constraint is upstream, in glycolysis itself. Step six, catalyzed by glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, requires NAD+ as a substrate to make NADH; the cytosolic NAD+ pool is small, only enough for a few seconds of glycolysis running unchecked. If nothing regenerates NAD+, glycolysis stalls within seconds and ATP production stops. Fermentation exists purely to solve this bottleneck: it trades away the ATP that oxidative phosphorylation could have made from that NADH in exchange for keeping glycolysis's substrate-level phosphorylation running. Carl and Gerty Cori described the resulting shuttle in 1929: muscle-produced lactate travels through the blood to the liver, where it is reoxidized to pyruvate and rebuilt into glucose via gluconeogenesis, the glucose returning to muscle -- the Cori cycle.

lessons.workedExample: A team runs sprinting mice for 30 seconds and finds blood lactate spikes, then argues 'the muscle ran out of oxygen so it switched fully to fermentation for energy.' A judge should press on the wording: fermentation itself makes zero net ATP beyond what glycolysis already made -- lactate dehydrogenase's entire job is regenerating NAD+ so glycolysis can keep running its substrate-level phosphorylation steps, not generating additional energy. The accurate claim is that oxygen delivery could not keep pace with ATP demand, so pyruvate dehydrogenase flux was limited, NADH backed up, and lactate dehydrogenase became the dominant route for regenerating NAD+ to sustain glycolytic ATP output.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'why does your organism make lactate (or ethanol) instead of just running the citric acid cycle' to test whether a student understands that fermentation is not an energy-yielding pathway in its own right but a redox-balancing fix. A weak answer says fermentation 'produces energy when there's no oxygen.' A strong answer identifies the specific bottleneck -- glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase's need for NAD+ -- and explains that fermentation's only job is regenerating that NAD+ so glycolysis's 2 net ATP can keep being made, at the cost of forgoing the much larger ATP yield PDC and the citric acid cycle would have unlocked from the same pyruvate.

questions.prompt: What is the direct product of the reaction catalyzed by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, and what does it use as an electron acceptor?

options.text: Lactate, using NADH as the electron donor.
Acetyl-CoA plus CO2, using NAD+ as the electron acceptor to form NADH.
Ethanol plus CO2, using NADH as the electron donor.
Oxaloacetate, using FAD as the electron acceptor.

explanations.a: Lactate is the fermentation product of lactate dehydrogenase, a different enzyme entirely.
explanations.b: Correct -- pyruvate dehydrogenase oxidatively decarboxylates pyruvate, transferring electrons to NAD+ to form NADH while producing acetyl-CoA and releasing CO2.
explanations.c: Ethanol production requires pyruvate decarboxylase and alcohol dehydrogenase in yeast, not the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex.
explanations.d: Oxaloacetate is a citric acid cycle intermediate made by malate dehydrogenase, not a PDC product; FAD is not PDC's electron acceptor.

questions.prompt: Why can't a cell simply let glycolysis run without regenerating NAD+ when oxygen is scarce?

options.text: Because ATP synthase requires NAD+ directly as a substrate.
Because the cytosolic NAD+ pool is small, and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase needs NAD+ to keep glycolysis's payoff phase running.
Because pyruvate kinase cannot function without NAD+ present.
Because hexokinase is allosterically inhibited by NADH.

explanations.a: ATP synthase uses the proton-motive force, not NAD+, as its direct driver.
explanations.b: Correct -- the small NAD+ pool would be exhausted within seconds without regeneration, since GAPDH consumes it every time it oxidizes glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate, halting the payoff phase and its ATP output.
explanations.c: Pyruvate kinase transfers a phosphate from PEP to ADP and does not require NAD+.
explanations.d: Hexokinase's regulation is via glucose-6-phosphate feedback, not NADH.

questions.prompt: Match each fermentation pathway to its regenerating enzyme and final product.

right.text: Lactate dehydrogenase reduces pyruvate directly to lactate
Pyruvate decarboxylase releases CO2, then alcohol dehydrogenase reduces the product to ethanol

questions.explanation: Lactic acid fermentation is a single-step reduction of pyruvate to lactate; ethanol fermentation requires an extra decarboxylation step to acetaldehyde before the final reduction to ethanol.

questions.prompt: Order the events in a muscle cell as oxygen delivery falls behind ATP demand during sprinting.

items.text: ATP demand outpaces oxygen delivery, limiting electron transport chain throughput
NADH accumulates and NAD+ becomes scarce in the cytosol
Lactate dehydrogenase reduces pyruvate to lactate, regenerating NAD+
Glycolysis continues running, sustaining substrate-level phosphorylation ATP output

questions.explanation: Oxygen limitation backs up the electron transport chain, which depletes cytosolic NAD+; lactate dehydrogenase regenerates that NAD+ so glycolysis's own ATP-producing steps can keep running.

lessons.label: The Citric Acid (Krebs) Cycle

sections.heading: Eight steps in the matrix
sections.body: Hans Krebs worked out the cycle in 1937 using minced pigeon breast muscle, tracking how citrate and other organic acids were consumed and regenerated, work that won him the 1953 Nobel Prize. In the mitochondrial matrix, citrate synthase condenses acetyl-CoA (2 carbons) with oxaloacetate (4 carbons) to form citrate (6 carbons). Aconitase isomerizes citrate to isocitrate. Isocitrate dehydrogenase oxidizes and decarboxylates isocitrate to alpha-ketoglutarate, releasing CO2 and generating NADH -- a regulated, rate-limiting step. Alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase does the same again, releasing a second CO2 and a second NADH to form succinyl-CoA. Succinyl-CoA synthetase then transfers succinyl-CoA's high-energy thioester bond directly to GDP (or ADP in some tissues), the cycle's one substrate-level phosphorylation, yielding succinate and GTP.

sections.heading: Finishing the turn and the per-turn tally
sections.body: Succinate dehydrogenase oxidizes succinate to fumarate, reducing FAD to FADH2 -- notably, this enzyme is embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane and doubles as Complex II of the electron transport chain, the only citric acid cycle enzyme not free in the matrix. Fumarase hydrates fumarate to malate, and malate dehydrogenase oxidizes malate back to oxaloacetate, generating a third NADH and regenerating the starting molecule to accept the next acetyl-CoA. One full turn processes one acetyl-CoA (2 carbons in) and releases 2 CO2, yielding 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, and 1 GTP. A common misconception is that the two released CO2 come from the acetyl-CoA carbons just added; they actually come from carbons that entered the oxaloacetate backbone in an earlier turn, since the added acetyl carbons take several turns to work their way to a decarboxylation step.

sections.heading: Amphibolic: catabolism and biosynthesis at once
sections.body: The cycle is amphibolic, running both catabolic (energy-extracting) and anabolic (biosynthetic) roles simultaneously, because its intermediates double as precursors. Citrate can be exported to the cytosol as a carbon source for fatty acid synthesis; alpha-ketoglutarate is transaminated into glutamate for amino acid synthesis; succinyl-CoA feeds heme synthesis; oxaloacetate can be transaminated to aspartate or drawn off for gluconeogenesis. Because intermediates are constantly siphoned off for biosynthesis, anaplerotic reactions (like pyruvate carboxylase making oxaloacetate) must replenish the pool, or cycle flux would stall. Flux itself is throttled at three points: citrate synthase (inhibited by ATP, NADH, succinyl-CoA, and citrate itself), isocitrate dehydrogenase (activated by ADP and Ca2+, inhibited by ATP and NADH), and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (inhibited by NADH, succinyl-CoA, and ATP) -- all three sense the same signal: the cell's NADH/ATP energy state.

lessons.workedExample: A student traces radioactively labeled acetyl-CoA (carbons tagged) through one turn of the cycle and finds the labeled carbons are still present in oxaloacetate at the end, not yet released as CO2, then concludes their tracing must be wrong because 'the cycle should release the carbons that came in.' A judge should recognize this is actually correct pathway behavior, not an error: the two CO2 released each turn come from carbons already resident in oxaloacetate from a prior turn, while the newly added acetyl-CoA carbons are retained and only get released in later turns after several more rounds of the cycle. Isotope-labeling experiments in the 1940s-50s (using 14C) were exactly how this ordering was worked out and confirmed Krebs's proposed cycle topology.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes the citric acid cycle to see whether a student understands it as a hub rather than a simple 'ATP factory' step. A weak answer lists the eight enzymes from memory and stops. A strong answer explains why the cycle is called amphibolic -- that citrate, alpha-ketoglutarate, succinyl-CoA, and oxaloacetate are also biosynthetic precursors -- and can name at least one regulated enzyme and what signal it responds to, showing they understand the cycle is tuned to the cell's energy charge (ATP/NADH levels) rather than running at a fixed rate.

questions.prompt: Order these citric acid cycle enzymes as they act in one turn, starting from the condensation with acetyl-CoA.

items.text: Citrate synthase
Aconitase
Isocitrate dehydrogenase
Alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase
Succinate dehydrogenase
Malate dehydrogenase

questions.explanation: Citrate synthase forms citrate, aconitase isomerizes it to isocitrate, isocitrate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase each decarboxylate and release NADH, succinate dehydrogenase reduces FAD to FADH2, and malate dehydrogenase regenerates oxaloacetate at the end (succinyl-CoA synthetase's GTP-producing step sits between alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and succinate dehydrogenase but is omitted here).

questions.prompt: Which citric acid cycle enzyme is also a physical component of the electron transport chain?

options.text: Citrate synthase, as part of Complex I
Succinate dehydrogenase, as Complex II
Aconitase, as part of Complex III
Malate dehydrogenase, as part of Complex IV

explanations.a: Citrate synthase is a soluble matrix enzyme with no connection to the electron transport chain complexes.
explanations.b: Correct -- succinate dehydrogenase is embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane and functions as both a citric acid cycle enzyme and Complex II of the electron transport chain.
explanations.c: Aconitase is a soluble matrix enzyme, not a membrane-embedded electron transport complex.
explanations.d: Malate dehydrogenase is a soluble matrix enzyme; it has no role in the electron transport chain.

questions.prompt: Match each citric acid cycle intermediate to the biosynthetic pathway it commonly feeds.

right.text: Fatty acid synthesis (exported to cytosol as an acetyl-CoA source)
Amino acid synthesis (transaminated to glutamate)
Heme synthesis
Gluconeogenesis or transamination to aspartate

questions.explanation: Citrate is exported for fatty acid synthesis, alpha-ketoglutarate becomes glutamate, succinyl-CoA feeds heme synthesis, and oxaloacetate feeds gluconeogenesis or aspartate synthesis -- the amphibolic role of the cycle.

questions.prompt: What is the correct per-turn yield of the citric acid cycle from one acetyl-CoA?

options.text: 2 NADH, 1 FADH2, 1 ATP, 1 CO2
3 NADH, 1 FADH2, 1 GTP, 2 CO2
3 NADH, 2 FADH2, 2 GTP, 2 CO2
1 NADH, 3 FADH2, 1 GTP, 2 CO2

explanations.a: This undercounts NADH (isocitrate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and malate dehydrogenase each make one) and CO2 (two decarboxylations occur per turn).
explanations.b: Correct -- three NADH-producing steps (isocitrate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, malate dehydrogenase), one FADH2-producing step (succinate dehydrogenase), one substrate-level phosphorylation to GTP (succinyl-CoA synthetase), and two CO2 releases (from the two dehydrogenase/decarboxylation steps).
explanations.c: The cycle produces only one FADH2 per turn, from succinate dehydrogenase, and only one GTP, from succinyl-CoA synthetase.
explanations.d: This swaps the correct NADH and FADH2 counts; only one FADH2 is made per turn, and three NADH.

lessons.label: The Electron Transport Chain

sections.heading: Four complexes, one downhill cascade
sections.body: The electron transport chain sits in the inner mitochondrial membrane, folded into cristae to maximize surface area, and consists of four large protein complexes plus two mobile carriers. Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) accepts electrons from NADH, oxidizing it back to NAD+, and passes the electrons onward while pumping roughly 4 protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space. Complex II is succinate dehydrogenase, the same enzyme from the citric acid cycle -- it accepts electrons from FADH2 and feeds them into the chain at the same point Complex I does, but pumps no protons at all, which is exactly why FADH2-derived electrons ultimately yield less ATP than NADH-derived ones. English biochemist David Keilin's work in the 1920s, describing the cytochrome absorption spectra that change with oxidation state, first revealed this stepwise electron relay.

sections.heading: Mobile carriers linking the complexes
sections.body: Complexes I and II both hand their electrons to ubiquinone (coenzyme Q), a small, lipid-soluble molecule that diffuses freely within the membrane and ferries electrons to Complex III (cytochrome bc1 complex). Complex III pumps roughly 4 more protons across the membrane via the Q cycle and passes electrons to cytochrome c, a small, water-soluble protein tethered to the outer face of the inner membrane that shuttles electrons the rest of the way to Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase). Complex IV pumps about 2 more protons and finally hands the electrons to O2, the chain's terminal acceptor, reducing it along with 4 protons to form 2 water molecules.

sections.heading: Why oxygen has to be the endpoint
sections.body: Oxygen is used as the terminal acceptor because it has an extremely high affinity for electrons (a strongly positive reduction potential), which is what makes the whole electron cascade thermodynamically downhill from NADH through all four complexes to O2 -- without a strong enough final acceptor, electrons would back up and the chain would stall. Passing through NADH (least electron-hungry, most reducing) to O2 (most electron-hungry, best oxidizing agent commonly available) releases free energy in graded steps, each captured as a proton-pumping event rather than dissipated as heat all at once. Per NADH oxidized, roughly 10 protons are pumped across the membrane (4+4+2 through Complexes I, III, and IV); per FADH2, only about 6, since Complex II contributes none. This proton gradient -- not the electrons themselves -- is what ultimately powers ATP synthesis.

lessons.workedExample: A student's diagram shows FADH2 feeding electrons into Complex I alongside NADH, with an arrow labeled 'both pump the same protons.' A judge should flag this immediately: FADH2's electrons enter at Complex II, not Complex I, and Complex II pumps zero protons across the membrane, unlike Complex I's roughly 4. The corrected diagram should show two separate entry points converging on the shared ubiquinone pool, with a clear asymmetry in proton output -- this single correction is also the mechanistic reason FADH2 yields fewer ATP per molecule than NADH does downstream.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'why does the cell need oxygen at all if ATP is made by a proton gradient, not by oxygen directly' to test whether a student understands oxygen's specific role as the terminal electron acceptor rather than a vague 'fuel.' A weak answer says cells need oxygen to 'burn' glucose. A strong answer explains that oxygen's high electron affinity is what keeps the whole chain thermodynamically favorable from Complex I onward -- without it, electrons have nowhere to go, Complex I through IV back up, and the proton pumping that builds the gradient for ATP synthase stops, which is also why cyanide (which blocks Complex IV) is lethal.

questions.prompt: Order the path an electron takes from NADH to its final destination.

items.text: Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase)
Ubiquinone
Complex III (cytochrome bc1)
Cytochrome c
Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase)
O2, reduced to water

questions.explanation: Electrons flow from Complex I to the mobile carrier ubiquinone, into Complex III, onto the mobile carrier cytochrome c, into Complex IV, and finally to O2, which is reduced to water.

questions.prompt: Why do electrons donated by FADH2 ultimately generate less ATP than electrons donated by NADH?

options.text: FADH2's electrons enter the chain at Complex II, which pumps no protons, skipping Complex I's contribution to the gradient.
FADH2 cannot bind to ubiquinone at all, so its electrons are lost.
FADH2's electrons are used to make CO2 instead of water.
FADH2 inhibits Complex IV directly.

explanations.a: Correct -- FADH2 donates electrons via Complex II directly to ubiquinone, bypassing Complex I's roughly 4 pumped protons, so its electrons contribute to a smaller proton gradient overall.
explanations.b: FADH2's electrons do reach ubiquinone via Complex II; they are not lost.
explanations.c: CO2 is released during the citric acid cycle's decarboxylation steps, unrelated to what the electron transport chain does with electrons; the chain's product from O2 reduction is water.
explanations.d: FADH2 has no inhibitory effect on Complex IV; the two are simply at different points in the chain.

questions.prompt: Match each electron transport chain component to its correct role.

right.text: Oxidizes NADH and pumps protons into the intermembrane space
Accepts electrons from FADH2 and pumps no protons
Mobile, lipid-soluble carrier linking Complexes I/II to Complex III
Reduces O2 to water and pumps protons

questions.explanation: Complex I oxidizes NADH and pumps protons, Complex II accepts FADH2's electrons without pumping protons, ubiquinone shuttles electrons within the membrane to Complex III, and Complex IV reduces O2 to water while pumping protons.

questions.prompt: Why must oxygen -- rather than some weaker electron acceptor -- serve as the chain's terminal electron acceptor for the chain to keep functioning efficiently?

options.text: Oxygen's strong pull for electrons keeps the entire NADH-to-O2 cascade thermodynamically downhill, so each complex can release energy in graded, capturable steps.
Oxygen is required as a direct substrate for ATP synthase.
Oxygen physically carries protons across the membrane.
Oxygen is needed to phosphorylate ADP directly.

explanations.a: Correct -- oxygen's high electron affinity is what keeps the free-energy drop favorable across all four complexes; a weaker acceptor would stall electron flow partway through the chain.
explanations.b: ATP synthase's substrates are ADP and Pi, driven by the proton gradient; oxygen plays no direct role at the enzyme itself.
explanations.c: Protons are pumped by the complexes themselves (I, III, IV); oxygen does not transport protons.
explanations.d: ADP phosphorylation is catalyzed by ATP synthase using the proton-motive force, not by oxygen directly.

lessons.label: Oxidative Phosphorylation & ATP Yield

sections.heading: Chemiosmosis: a gradient as the energy store
sections.body: Peter Mitchell proposed the chemiosmotic hypothesis in 1961: rather than a chemical intermediate directly carrying energy from the electron transport chain to ATP synthesis, the chain builds a proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane, and that gradient itself is the energy store. The proposal was met with skepticism for over a decade -- it broke from the assumption that a shared chemical intermediate had to link oxidation and phosphorylation -- until mounting biochemical evidence vindicated it, earning Mitchell the 1978 Nobel Prize. The gradient, called the proton-motive force, has two components: a chemical piece (a lower pH in the intermembrane space than the matrix) and an electrical piece (the intermembrane space is more positive), both pushing protons to want to flow back into the matrix.

sections.heading: ATP synthase as a molecular turbine
sections.body: ATP synthase has two connected parts. Fo is a proton channel embedded in the membrane whose ring of subunits spins as protons flow down their gradient through it, much like water turning a turbine. That spinning rotor is mechanically coupled to F1, the catalytic head that projects into the matrix and contains three active sites for making ATP from ADP and Pi. Paul Boyer's binding-change mechanism, which earned him a share of the 1997 Nobel Prize, showed that F1's three sites cycle through different conformations (loose, tight, open) as the rotor turns, and it is this conformational cycling -- not the chemistry of bond formation itself -- that is the energetically demanding step; the gradient's job is to force the rotation that drives it.

sections.heading: Recounting the ATP yield honestly
sections.body: Older textbooks claimed 36-38 ATP per glucose, based on assuming a clean 3 ATP per NADH and 2 ATP per FADH2. More careful measurement of the actual P/O ratio -- protons needed per ATP made, and how many protons each complex really pumps -- brought those numbers down. Peter Hinkle's review work in the mid-2000s helped settle the field on approximately 2.5 ATP per NADH and 1.5 ATP per FADH2, non-integer values reflecting real stoichiometry rather than convenient rounding. Factoring in the cost of shuttling cytosolic NADH's electrons into the matrix (the malate-aspartate shuttle delivers them at full NADH value; the glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle delivers them at FADH2 value, losing efficiency), plus the ATP/ADP antiporter's own energetic cost and unavoidable proton leak across the membrane, the realistic total lands around 30-32 ATP per glucose -- most commonly cited near 30 -- not the 36-38 many students still memorize.

lessons.workedExample: A student calculates glucose's total ATP yield as '2 (glycolysis) + 2 (citric acid cycle GTP) + 10 NADH x 3 + 2 FADH2 x 2 = 38 ATP' and presents this as the final number. A judge should note this uses the outdated integer P/O ratios and ignores shuttle costs. A revised calculation using 2.5 ATP/NADH and 1.5 ATP/FADH2 -- with 10 total NADH (2 glycolysis, 2 pyruvate dehydrogenase, 6 citric acid cycle) and 2 FADH2 -- gives roughly 2 + 2 + 25 + 3 = 32 ATP before shuttle losses, and closer to 30 once the glycolytic NADH is shuttled via the less efficient glycerol-3-phosphate route in some tissues. The point is not memorizing a single 'correct' number but being able to defend which P/O ratios and shuttle assumptions were used.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'how many ATP does one glucose really yield' is testing whether a student parrots '36-38' from an old textbook or understands why that number changed. A weak answer states a fixed number with no caveats. A strong answer explains that ATP yield is not a fixed integer because P/O ratios are empirically measured non-integer values (2.5 and 1.5), that shuttle mechanism affects the glycolytic NADH's value, and that proton leak and antiporter costs further reduce the theoretical maximum -- landing the honest estimate around 30-32, and being able to say why that is lower than the old figure signals real understanding of chemiosmotic coupling, not just memorization.

questions.prompt: According to Peter Mitchell's chemiosmotic hypothesis, what directly powers ATP synthase?

options.text: A shared high-energy chemical intermediate transferred directly from the electron transport chain to ATP synthase.
The proton-motive force -- the electrochemical gradient of protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane.
Direct electron transfer from cytochrome c into ATP synthase's active site.
Heat released by the electron transport chain.

explanations.a: This was the competing hypothesis Mitchell's chemiosmotic model replaced; no such shared chemical intermediate was ever found.
explanations.b: Correct -- the chemiosmotic hypothesis holds that the electron transport chain's proton pumping builds an electrochemical gradient, and it is this gradient's tendency to flow back into the matrix that drives ATP synthase.
explanations.c: Cytochrome c donates electrons to Complex IV, not to ATP synthase, which has no electron transport role.
explanations.d: Heat is a byproduct, not the coupling mechanism; the gradient itself, not thermal energy, drives the synthase.

questions.prompt: Match each ATP synthase component or concept to its correct description.

right.text: Membrane-embedded rotor that spins as protons flow through it
Catalytic head with three sites that cycle through conformations to make ATP
Paul Boyer's model explaining how rotation drives ATP formation

questions.explanation: Fo is the proton-driven rotor, F1 is the catalytic head where ATP is actually made, and the binding-change mechanism describes how F1's conformational cycling, driven by Fo's rotation, produces ATP.

questions.prompt: Why did the accepted ATP yield per glucose fall from the older 36-38 figure to a modern estimate of roughly 30-32?

options.text: Glycolysis was found to produce fewer NADH than previously thought.
Measured, non-integer P/O ratios (about 2.5 ATP/NADH and 1.5 ATP/FADH2) replaced the older assumed integer ratios, and shuttle costs plus proton leak were factored in.
The citric acid cycle was found to run only every other turn.
Oxygen was found to accept fewer electrons per molecule than previously believed.
ATP synthase was discovered to make ADP instead of ATP under normal conditions.

explanations.a: Glycolysis's NADH yield (2 per glucose) has not changed; the recount concerns how much ATP each NADH is worth downstream.
explanations.b: Correct -- P/O ratios were empirically remeasured to be non-integer (2.5 and 1.5), and accounting for shuttle mechanism costs and inescapable proton leak brought the realistic total down from the old idealized figure.
explanations.c: The citric acid cycle runs once per acetyl-CoA every turn; this was never in question.
explanations.d: Oxygen's role as terminal acceptor, accepting 4 electrons per O2 to form 2 water, is unchanged.
explanations.e: ATP synthase's normal function is making ATP; this option describes no real finding in the field.

lessons.label: Regulation of Central Metabolism

sections.heading: PFK-1: four signals converging on one enzyme
sections.body: Phosphofructokinase-1 is glycolysis's master valve because it integrates several signals at once. ATP allosterically inhibits it at a site distinct from its catalytic site, so a high-energy cell throttles glycolysis even while ATP is technically also PFK-1's substrate. AMP reverses that inhibition, so a cell that has burned through its ATP reserves and accumulated AMP re-opens the valve. Citrate, an early citric acid cycle intermediate that can back up into the cytosol when the cycle is already saturated with input, also inhibits PFK-1 -- a direct link telling glycolysis to slow down when downstream capacity is full. The strongest activator is fructose-2,6-bisphosphate (F2,6BP), a signaling molecule distinct from the pathway's own fructose-1,6-bisphosphate substrate, made by a bifunctional enzyme (PFK-2/FBPase-2) whose activity flips with hormonal state; its role was worked out in the early 1980s by biochemists Henri-Géry Hers and Emile Van Schaftingen.

sections.heading: Energy charge and AMPK as the fuel gauge
sections.body: In 1968, Daniel Atkinson formalized the idea of energy charge: EC = ([ATP] + 0.5[ADP]) / ([ATP] + [ADP] + [AMP]), a single number from 0 to 1 summarizing how 'charged' a cell's adenine nucleotide pool is. Healthy cells hold EC around 0.8-0.9; because ATP, ADP, and AMP are interconverted by adenylate kinase (2 ADP <-> ATP + AMP), even a modest ATP drop produces a disproportionately large AMP spike, making AMP a sensitive alarm signal. AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), characterized starting in the early 1990s, is the cell's direct sensor of that alarm: rising AMP (and ADP) relative to ATP activates AMPK both allosterically and via upstream kinases, and active AMPK phosphorylates targets that shut down ATP-consuming anabolic processes (like inhibiting acetyl-CoA carboxylase to halt fatty acid synthesis) while switching on ATP-generating catabolic ones, such as promoting glucose uptake.

sections.heading: The Pasteur effect: oxygen slows fermentation down
sections.body: Louis Pasteur observed in the late 1850s and early 1860s that yeast consumes glucose far more slowly, and produces far less ethanol, when oxygen is present than when it is absent -- glucose consumption and fermentation rate drop sharply as soon as air is introduced, a phenomenon now called the Pasteur effect. The mechanism is exactly the regulatory logic above: aerobic metabolism through the citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation yields roughly 15 times more ATP per glucose than fermentation alone, so ATP and citrate levels rise and directly inhibit PFK-1, throttling glycolytic flux. Less glucose needs to be broken down to meet the same ATP demand, so flux falls even though more energy, not less, is ultimately being extracted per molecule consumed.

lessons.workedExample: A student grows yeast under alternating aerobic and anaerobic conditions and observes glucose uptake rate drop by roughly two-thirds when air is reintroduced, then writes 'oxygen slows down the cell's metabolism.' A judge should push back: oxidative metabolism is not slower, it is far more efficient per glucose, so less glucose needs to be consumed to meet the same ATP demand. The precise mechanism is that oxidative phosphorylation's higher ATP output raises cellular ATP and citrate levels, both of which allosterically inhibit PFK-1, throttling glycolytic flux -- this is the Pasteur effect, and naming PFK-1 as the specific target the two inhibitory signals converge on is what separates a mechanistic explanation from a restatement of the observation.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'what actually senses that the cell is low on energy, and what does it do about it' to test whether a student can name a specific molecular sensor rather than saying vaguely that 'the cell knows when it needs more ATP.' A weak answer stops at 'ATP levels go down and the cell makes more.' A strong answer names AMPK specifically, explains why AMP (not ATP) is the more sensitive signal because of the adenylate kinase equilibrium, and can connect it back to PFK-1 regulation and the Pasteur effect as a coherent regulatory system rather than three unrelated facts.

questions.prompt: Match each PFK-1 regulator to its effect on the enzyme.

right.text: Inhibits (signals high energy charge)
Activates (signals low energy charge)
Inhibits (signals citric acid cycle saturation)
Strongly activates (hormonally controlled signaling molecule)

questions.explanation: ATP and citrate both inhibit PFK-1, signaling high energy or a saturated cycle respectively; AMP activates it as a low-energy alarm; fructose-2,6-bisphosphate is the strongest activator and is set by hormonal signaling rather than direct energy state.

questions.prompt: Why is AMP a more sensitive low-energy alarm signal than a modest drop in ATP itself?

options.text: Because AMP is chemically identical to ATP and simply easier to measure.
Because the adenylate kinase reaction (2 ADP <-> ATP + AMP) amplifies a small ATP decline into a disproportionately large AMP increase.
Because AMP directly inhibits ATP synthase.
Because AMP is produced only during fermentation, not aerobic respiration.

explanations.a: AMP and ATP are chemically distinct molecules differing in phosphate count, not measurement convenience.
explanations.b: Correct -- because adenylate kinase keeps ADP, ATP, and AMP near equilibrium, a small fractional drop in ATP produces a much larger fractional rise in AMP, making AMP a sharper, more sensitive signal for AMPK to detect.
explanations.c: AMP does not act on ATP synthase directly; its role is activating AMPK and allosterically affecting enzymes like PFK-1.
explanations.d: AMP is produced by adenylate kinase activity under any condition of ATP demand, not specifically during fermentation.

questions.prompt: What is the correct mechanistic explanation for the Pasteur effect (glucose consumption dropping when oxygen is introduced)?

options.text: Oxygen directly binds and inactivates hexokinase.
Oxidative phosphorylation's much higher ATP yield per glucose raises ATP and citrate levels, which allosterically inhibit PFK-1 and reduce glycolytic flux.
Oxygen inhibits glucose transporters at the cell membrane.
Fermentation enzymes are irreversibly destroyed by oxygen exposure.

explanations.a: Hexokinase is regulated by its product, glucose-6-phosphate, not by oxygen binding directly.
explanations.b: Correct -- because aerobic ATP yield per glucose is so much higher than fermentation's, less glucose is needed to meet demand, and the resulting rise in ATP and citrate throttles PFK-1, which is the direct mechanistic link Pasteur's observation traces to.
explanations.c: Glucose transport is not the regulated step Pasteur's observation is explained by; the effect is intracellular, at PFK-1.
explanations.d: Fermentation enzymes like lactate dehydrogenase are not destroyed by oxygen; they simply become less necessary because NAD+ is regenerated by the electron transport chain instead.

questions.prompt: Order the events of the Pasteur effect as oxygen is reintroduced to actively fermenting yeast.

items.text: Oxygen becomes available, allowing the electron transport chain to run and pyruvate dehydrogenase and the citric acid cycle to process pyruvate
ATP yield per glucose rises sharply compared to fermentation alone
ATP and citrate levels rise, allosterically inhibiting PFK-1
Glycolytic flux and glucose consumption drop

questions.explanation: Oxygen availability unlocks the far higher ATP yield of oxidative metabolism, which raises ATP and citrate, which inhibit PFK-1, which slows glycolysis and glucose consumption -- the Pasteur effect.

lessons.label: Detecting Protein Phosphorylation

sections.heading: Why phosphorylation needs its own antibody
sections.body: A kinase turning a pathway on does not usually change how much of a protein exists — it adds a phosphate group to a specific serine, threonine, or tyrosine, flipping the protein's conformation and activity within seconds. An ordinary antibody against total ERK or total Akt cannot see that switch; it binds the protein whether or not the phosphate is there. Detecting activation requires a phospho-specific antibody, raised against the exact phosphorylated epitope — phospho-ERK1/2 (Thr202/Tyr204) or phospho-Akt (Ser473, the mTORC2 site, and Thr308, the PDK1 site) are the standard reagents. These are run by Western blotting, a technique built on Edwin Southern's 1975 DNA-blotting method: Towbin and colleagues (1979) worked out electrophoretic transfer of proteins to membranes, and Burnette (1981) coined 'Western blot' as the pun on Southern's name.

sections.heading: The normalization requirement
sections.body: A phospho-ERK band by itself is uninterpretable, because lane-to-lane loading differences, cell number, and cell-cycle stage all change total protein amount independent of signaling. A stronger phospho signal could mean more activation, or it could mean the lane simply had more protein. The fix is to strip and reprobe the same membrane for total ERK (not a generic loading control like GAPDH, which says nothing about ERK abundance specifically) and report the phospho-to-total ratio. That ratio, not the raw phospho band, is the activation readout. Getting from a blot image to that ratio is a densitometry step: imaging software integrates the pixel intensity inside each band's outline into a single arbitrary-unit (AU) value, background-subtracted against the surrounding membrane. Dividing the phospho-ERK AU by the total-ERK AU in the same lane gives that lane's phospho-to-total ratio, and normalizing every lane's ratio to the untreated or time-zero lane converts the raw AU numbers into a fold-activation value that can be compared across blots and experiments.

sections.heading: Single-cell resolution: phospho-flow cytometry
sections.body: A Western blot lysate averages every cell in the well into one number. Krutzik and Nolan (2003) developed fixation and permeabilization conditions — formaldehyde fixation followed by methanol permeabilization, gentler methods disrupt phospho-epitopes — that let phospho-specific antibodies work inside intact, single fixed cells on a flow cytometer, so each cell yields its own phospho-signal. Irish and colleagues (2004, Cell), working with Garry Nolan's lab, applied this to acute myeloid leukemia patient samples and found that individual leukemic cells activated STAT5 and ERK to very different degrees after the same cytokine stimulus — a heterogeneous, clinically relevant signaling pattern that bulk lysate Western blotting, which reports only the population average, had completely masked.

lessons.workedExample: A student runs an EGF stimulation timecourse (0, 5, 10, 30, 60 min) on a cell line and blots for phospho-ERK1/2 (Thr202/Tyr204). The phospho band is brightest at 5 min, so they report 'ERK activation peaks at 5 minutes.' A reviewer asks whether total ERK was checked. It turns out the 5-minute lane also has a visibly darker total-ERK band after reprobing — that lane simply had slightly more protein loaded. Once the student divides phospho-ERK band intensity by total-ERK band intensity in each lane and normalizes every ratio to the 0-minute baseline, the corrected activation curve still peaks near 5-10 minutes but the raw magnitude drops substantially, and a GAPDH loading control confirms the lanes were otherwise equally loaded.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who knows Western blotting will ask some version of: 'how do you know that's more activated protein, and not just more protein?' It is the single most common flaw in a student phospho-signaling poster. A weak answer shows one phospho-ERK band getting brighter and calls it activation. A strong answer shows the paired total-protein blot, reports a phospho-to-total ratio rather than a raw band intensity, and explains why a generic loading control like actin does not substitute for the total-protein reprobe — actin says the lanes were loaded evenly, but it says nothing about how much ERK specifically was in each lane.

questions.prompt: Why is a phospho-specific antibody blot alone, without a total-protein reprobe, insufficient to conclude a pathway was activated?

options.text: Phospho-specific antibodies are not specific enough to trust on their own
The raw phospho signal is confounded by total protein abundance, which varies independent of activation
Western blotting cannot resolve proteins smaller than 100 kDa
Phosphate groups are chemically unstable during SDS-PAGE and fall off

explanations.a: Well-validated phospho-specific antibodies are highly selective for their exact phosphorylated epitope; specificity is not the issue here.
explanations.b: Correct — a brighter phospho band could reflect more activated protein or simply more total protein loaded in that lane, so the phospho signal must be divided by total protein to isolate the activation fraction.
explanations.c: Western blotting routinely resolves proteins across a wide range of molecular weights, including ERK (~42-44 kDa) and Akt (~60 kDa); size is not the limiting factor described here.
explanations.d: Phosphorylation is a stable covalent modification under standard SDS-PAGE conditions; it does not spontaneously reverse during the run.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a paired phospho/total Western blot for measuring pathway activation.

items.text: Lyse cells to extract protein
Run SDS-PAGE and transfer proteins to a membrane
Probe the membrane with the phospho-specific antibody
Strip and reprobe the same membrane with the total-protein antibody
Quantify band intensities and compute the phospho-to-total ratio

questions.explanation: Protein must be extracted and separated before any antibody probing can occur; the phospho-specific probe typically comes first since stripping can degrade epitopes, and the ratio can only be computed once both signals are measured on the same membrane.

questions.prompt: Match each element of phosphorylation detection to what it provides.

right.text: Binds only the phosphorylated form of the target residue
Supplies the denominator needed to normalize the phospho signal
Reports a phospho-signal distribution across individual cells rather than one lysate average

questions.explanation: The phospho-antibody is what makes the assay activation-specific, the total-protein reprobe is what makes the ratio interpretable, and phospho-flow trades the single averaged lysate number for a per-cell distribution.

questions.prompt: What did Irish and colleagues (2004) find by applying phospho-flow cytometry to acute myeloid leukemia patient samples?

options.text: All leukemic cells in a sample activated STAT5 and ERK to the same degree after cytokine stimulation
Individual leukemic cells showed heterogeneous, subpopulation-specific phospho-signaling responses that bulk lysate Western blotting had masked
Phospho-flow cytometry could not detect phosphorylated STAT5 in fixed cells
Bulk Western blotting revealed the same cell-to-cell heterogeneity as flow cytometry

explanations.a: The opposite was true — responses varied substantially from cell to cell within the same patient sample.
explanations.b: Correct — single-cell resolution uncovered signaling heterogeneity among leukemic subpopulations that a bulk lysate average could not distinguish.
explanations.c: Krutzik and Nolan's fixation/permeabilization protocol was specifically designed to preserve phospho-epitopes like phospho-STAT5 for flow detection, and it worked.
explanations.d: This is backwards: bulk Western blotting reports only a population average and is exactly the method that cannot resolve per-cell heterogeneity.

lessons.label: Pathway Reporter Assays

sections.heading: Transcriptional reporters: CRE and SRE luciferase
sections.body: A reporter assay borrows a pathway's own downstream transcription factor to drive a gene you can easily measure, usually firefly luciferase, whose light output is proportional to how much enzyme got made. A CRE-luciferase construct places several copies of the cAMP response element upstream of luciferase; CREB, activated by protein kinase A downstream of Gs-coupled receptors and adenylyl cyclase, binds CRE and drives transcription, so luminescence tracks Gs/cAMP/PKA pathway activity. An SRE-luciferase construct instead uses the serum response element, which is bound by a ternary complex of serum response factor (SRF) and Elk-1 once Elk-1 is phosphorylated by ERK — so it reports Ras-MAPK-ERK activity, the kind triggered by growth factor receptors or Gq-coupled GPCRs signaling through PKC. Both assays are indirect and slow: they require transcription and translation of new luciferase protein, so a 4-6 hour endpoint reading integrates everything that happened in that window into a single number, with no information about the shape of the response over time.

sections.heading: GloSensor: cAMP in real time
sections.body: Promega's GloSensor system swaps a transcriptional readout for a direct biosensor: a cAMP-binding domain is fused to a circularly permuted luciferase, engineered so its natural N- and C-termini are joined and new ends created elsewhere in the structure. Binding cAMP changes the fusion protein's conformation and its light output within seconds, in live, unlysed cells, so a researcher can watch cAMP rise and fall in real time after adding a ligand rather than waiting hours for a transcriptional endpoint.

sections.heading: Beta-arrestin recruitment: a G-protein-independent readout
sections.body: Every activated GPCR gets phosphorylated by a GRK and recruits beta-arrestin, regardless of which G-protein family it couples to — a fact exploited by recruitment assays that read out receptor activation without needing a second-messenger change at all. In DiscoverX's PathHunter assay, beta-arrestin is fused to one inactive fragment of beta-galactosidase and the receptor to the other; recruitment brings the fragments together into an active, chemiluminescent enzyme. Kroeze and colleagues (2015, Nature Structural & Molecular Biology), from Bryan Roth's lab, built PRESTO-Tango on a related principle: arrestin fused to a TEV protease is recruited to an activated receptor, cleaves a tethered transcription factor free from the receptor's tail, and that factor drives a luciferase reporter in the nucleus. The published library covered over 300 human GPCRs and was validated against more than 120 non-orphan receptors, making it useful for screening ligands against receptors — including Gi-coupled and orphan receptors — where cAMP- or calcium-based assays give a weak or ambiguous signal.

lessons.workedExample: A student wants to test whether a candidate compound activates a specific orphan GPCR. They first try a CRE-luciferase reporter, reasoning 'GPCR activation raises luciferase.' After 5 hours of compound treatment, luminescence barely changes, and they conclude the compound is inactive. The problem: they never confirmed the receptor's G-protein coupling. If the receptor is Gi-coupled, activation lowers cAMP rather than raising it, so a CRE reporter built to detect a rise would show nothing informative — a false negative, not evidence of inactivity. Switching to a beta-arrestin recruitment assay such as PathHunter or PRESTO-Tango, which reads receptor activation directly through arrestin recruitment rather than through a specific G-protein's second messenger, reveals clear, dose-dependent activation by the same compound.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who knows GPCR pharmacology will ask why a student picked one reporter over another, not just whether the assay worked. The failure mode this catches is treating 'luciferase reporter' as one generic tool instead of recognizing that CRE and SRE reporters only see specific downstream pathways (Gs/cAMP and Ras-MAPK, respectively) and can produce a false negative for a receptor that signals a different way. A strong answer names the receptor's expected coupling and explains why the chosen reporter can or cannot see it; a weak answer says only 'we measured luminescence.'

questions.prompt: A receptor is known to be Gi-coupled (it lowers cAMP upon activation). Which reporter assay would most reliably detect its activation regardless of coupling type?

options.text: CRE-luciferase reporter
SRE-luciferase reporter
Beta-arrestin recruitment assay (e.g., PathHunter or PRESTO-Tango)
GloSensor cAMP biosensor

explanations.a: CRE-luciferase is built to detect a cAMP rise; a Gi-coupled receptor lowers cAMP, so this reporter gives an ambiguous or absent signal even when the receptor is genuinely active.
explanations.b: SRE reports Ras-MAPK-ERK activity, which a Gi-coupled receptor may or may not engage; it is not a reliable general-purpose activation readout.
explanations.c: Correct — beta-arrestin is recruited to any activated GPCR after GRK phosphorylation, independent of which G-protein family the receptor couples to, so recruitment assays work regardless of coupling.
explanations.d: GloSensor directly measures cAMP, so a Gi-coupled receptor produces a decrease rather than a clear activating signal, which is harder to distinguish from noise or reduced cell viability.

questions.prompt: Match each reporter or biosensor to what it reads out.

right.text: Gs/cAMP/PKA/CREB transcriptional activity
Ras-MAPK-ERK/Elk-1-SRF transcriptional activity
Real-time cAMP concentration in live cells
Receptor activation independent of G-protein coupling type

questions.explanation: CRE and SRE are transcriptional reporters tied to specific pathways (cAMP/PKA/CREB and Ras-MAPK/Elk-1, respectively); GloSensor gives a direct real-time cAMP reading; arrestin recruitment reports receptor activation regardless of which G-protein the receptor uses.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a Tango-style beta-arrestin recruitment assay from ligand binding to the final measurement.

items.text: Ligand binds and activates the GPCR
A GRK phosphorylates the activated receptor
TEV protease-fused beta-arrestin is recruited to the receptor
The protease cleaves a transcription factor free from the receptor's C-terminal tail
The freed transcription factor enters the nucleus and drives luciferase transcription
Luminescence is measured as the assay readout

questions.explanation: Receptor phosphorylation by a GRK precedes arrestin recruitment, which is what brings the fused protease close enough to cleave the tethered transcription factor; only after that factor reaches the nucleus can it drive the reporter gene that is ultimately measured.

questions.prompt: Why can't a CRE- or SRE-luciferase reporter resolve second-to-second changes in pathway activity the way GloSensor can?

options.text: Luciferase itself reacts too slowly with its substrate to produce fast light changes
Transcriptional reporters require new reporter protein to be transcribed and translated, so a multi-hour endpoint reading integrates the whole exposure window rather than tracking it moment to moment
CRE and SRE elements physically degrade within seconds of ligand exposure
Transcriptional reporters can only be read in fixed, dead cells

explanations.a: The luciferase-luciferin reaction itself is fast; the delay comes from needing to make new luciferase protein via transcription and translation, not from the light-producing chemistry.
explanations.b: Correct — building a new luciferase transcript and protein takes hours, so the assay's single endpoint reading reflects accumulated signaling over that whole period rather than its real-time dynamics.
explanations.c: DNA response elements are stable; they do not degrade on a timescale relevant to the assay.
explanations.d: Standard luciferase reporter assays are typically read in live cells; the slowness comes from reporter synthesis time, not a requirement for fixation.

lessons.label: Live-Cell Imaging of Signaling

sections.heading: Two ways to see calcium: a dye and a genetically encoded switch
sections.body: Calcium is the fastest-moving second messenger, rising and falling in a cell within milliseconds, so measuring it in a bulk lysate is nearly meaningless — you need to watch a living cell in real time. Grynkiewicz, Poenie, and Tsien (1985) developed Fura-2, a small-molecule dye whose excitation spectrum shifts when it binds Ca2+, from roughly 380 nm (Ca2+-free) toward 340 nm (Ca2+-bound). Taking the ratio of emission at those two excitation wavelengths cancels out artifacts from uneven dye loading, cell thickness, or photobleaching, so the 340/380 ratio gives a quantitative calcium concentration rather than just a relative brightness. Genetically encoded calcium indicators (GECIs) like GCaMP replace the dye with a fusion protein: a circularly permuted GFP sandwiched between calmodulin and the M13 peptide from myosin light chain kinase. Calcium binding drives calmodulin to wrap around M13, distorting the GFP barrel and boosting its fluorescence. Nakai and colleagues (2001) built the first GCaMP; Chen and colleagues (2013) engineered GCaMP6, sensitive and fast enough to report single action potentials in neurons. Because GECIs are DNA, not a loaded dye, they can be targeted to a specific cell type by promoter choice and used in a living, behaving animal.

sections.heading: FRET biosensors: watching cAMP and kinase activity change shape
sections.body: Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) occurs when two fluorophores — typically CFP and YFP — sit close enough that excited CFP transfers energy to YFP instead of emitting its own light; the transfer efficiency depends steeply on the distance and orientation between them. A biosensor exploits this by sandwiching a signal-sensitive domain between the two fluorophores, so that a conformational change on ligand binding pulls CFP and YFP closer or farther apart and shifts the donor/acceptor emission ratio. Zaccolo and Pozzan (2002) used a FRET sensor built from fluorescently labeled PKA regulatory and catalytic subunits — cAMP binding drives the subunits apart, changing the FRET signal — imaged in live cardiac myocytes, and found that cAMP does not diffuse uniformly through the cytoplasm as assumed: it forms discrete, high-concentration microdomains close to the plasma membrane, invisible to any assay that lyses the cell and averages the signal. Epac-based cAMP FRET sensors (Epac1-camps, ICUE), which fold a single Epac cAMP-binding domain between CFP and YFP, arrived a couple of years later (Nikolaev and colleagues, 2004; DiPilato, Cawley, and Zhang, 2004) and are now the more common design. A related design, the A-kinase activity reporter (AKAR), built by Zhang and colleagues (2001), reports PKA activity directly: PKA phosphorylates a substrate sequence built into the sensor, which then folds onto a phosphoamino-acid-binding domain and changes the intramolecular FRET signal in real time.

sections.heading: The trade: resolution for throughput
sections.body: Every method in this lesson buys spatial and temporal detail — where in the cell a signal occurs and how its waveform evolves millisecond to millisecond — that a bulk, population-averaged assay structurally cannot provide, because bulk methods sum or lyse across thousands of cells. The cost is throughput and simplicity: live imaging needs a microscope, careful calibration, and analysis of individual cells or subcellular regions rather than one plate-reader number.

lessons.workedExample: A student hypothesizes that activating a GPCR raises cAMP uniformly throughout the cytoplasm. Using a bulk GloSensor plate-reader assay, they see total luminescence rise after agonist addition, but that number is summed across the whole well and says nothing about location within a cell. Switching to a FRET-based Epac cAMP sensor imaged by confocal microscopy in individual live cells, they see the donor/acceptor ratio change first and most strongly in a thin region just under the plasma membrane, with a smaller, delayed change in the deep cytoplasm — the same kind of microdomain pattern Zaccolo and Pozzan reported in cardiac myocytes. The bulk assay could never have shown this, because averaging across the cell (and across the well) is exactly what erases spatial structure.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing this topic wants to know whether a student picked live-cell imaging because the hypothesis actually required spatial or millisecond temporal resolution, or just because fluorescence microscopy looks impressive on a poster. A weak answer treats imaging as a fancier version of a plate assay. A strong answer names what the bulk method structurally cannot see — subcellular location, oscillation timing, cell-to-cell heterogeneity — and ties that directly to what the hypothesis needed, the way Zaccolo and Pozzan's microdomain finding was invisible to any assay that lysed the cell first.

questions.prompt: Why is Fura-2 described as a 'ratiometric' calcium indicator?

options.text: It is used at a fixed ratio relative to the cell's total protein content
Taking the ratio of emission at two excitation wavelengths cancels out artifacts like uneven dye loading or path length, giving a quantitative calcium reading
It only works when calcium and sodium are present in a fixed ratio
It reports the ratio of bound to unbound GFP molecules

explanations.a: Fura-2's ratio is between two excitation wavelengths for the same dye, not a comparison to protein content.
explanations.b: Correct — Fura-2's excitation spectrum shifts with Ca2+ binding, so the ratio of emission at ~340 nm versus ~380 nm excitation cancels out variables like dye concentration and cell thickness that would otherwise confound a single-wavelength reading.
explanations.c: Fura-2 is calcium-selective; sodium concentration is not part of its ratiometric mechanism.
explanations.d: Fura-2 is a small-molecule dye, not a GFP-based sensor; GFP is used in GCaMP, a different indicator.

questions.prompt: Match each live-cell indicator to what actually changes when it responds to a signal.

right.text: Calmodulin-M13 folding around Ca2+ distorts a circularly permuted GFP, changing its brightness
The dye's excitation spectrum shifts upon binding Ca2+
A cAMP-induced conformational change alters the distance between CFP and YFP
PKA phosphorylation of a built-in substrate sequence changes intramolecular FRET

questions.explanation: GCaMP and Fura-2 both report calcium but through different physical mechanisms (protein folding versus dye spectral shift); the Epac and AKAR sensors both use FRET but respond to different inputs, a small-molecule ligand versus a kinase's phosphorylation event.

questions.prompt: What did Zaccolo and Pozzan (2002) discover about cAMP in cardiac myocytes using a FRET-based sensor?

options.text: cAMP diffuses uniformly and instantly throughout the entire cytoplasm
cAMP forms discrete, high-concentration microdomains near the plasma membrane rather than spreading evenly
cAMP cannot be detected by FRET-based methods
cAMP levels are identical whether measured by bulk assay or single-cell imaging

explanations.a: This was the prior assumption their FRET imaging overturned, not what they found.
explanations.b: Correct — live single-cell FRET imaging revealed localized, high-concentration cAMP microdomains near the membrane, a spatial pattern no bulk lysate assay could detect.
explanations.c: Their FRET sensor is exactly what made cAMP detectable with spatial resolution in living cells.
explanations.d: The whole point of the finding is that bulk, averaged measurements erase the spatial structure that single-cell imaging revealed, so the two are not equivalent.

questions.prompt: Order the events from receptor stimulation to an observed FRET signal change in an Epac-based cAMP sensor.

items.text: Ligand binds a Gs-coupled receptor
Adenylyl cyclase generates cAMP
cAMP binds the sensor's Epac domain
The domain undergoes a conformational change
The distance/orientation between CFP and YFP shifts
The donor/acceptor emission ratio changes and is recorded by the microscope
