questions.explanation: Biased-agonist design starts from recognizing the receptor's two branches, mapping each branch to an effect, engineering a ligand that favors one branch, and then testing whether that selectivity translates into the desired clinical separation.

lessons.label: Targeting Metabolism

sections.heading: The Warburg Effect and Its Diagnostic Payoff
sections.body: In the 1920s, Otto Warburg observed that cancer cells ferment glucose to lactate even when oxygen is plentiful -- a wasteful-looking strategy called aerobic glycolysis, since fermentation yields far less ATP per glucose than oxidative phosphorylation. Cells compensate by dramatically upregulating glucose uptake, and this hunger for glucose has become one of oncology's most useful diagnostic tools rather than just a curiosity. FDG-PET imaging exploits it directly: patients receive 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose, a radiolabeled glucose analog that hypermetabolic tumor cells take up avidly through overexpressed GLUT transporters and phosphorylate but cannot further metabolize, trapping the tracer inside the cell where PET scanners detect its radioactive decay. The same dependency makes glycolytic enzymes attractive drug targets, since a tumor's disproportionate reliance on glycolysis is, in principle, a selective vulnerability.

sections.heading: AMPK and mTOR: Opposing Metabolic Switches
sections.body: Two master regulators sit on opposite sides of cellular energy state. AMPK (AMP-activated protein kinase) is the cell's fuel gauge: it activates when the AMP/ATP ratio rises, signaling energy scarcity, and responds by shutting down energy-expensive biosynthesis while switching on catabolic, ATP-generating pathways. Metformin, the first-line type 2 diabetes drug, activates AMPK partly by mildly inhibiting mitochondrial complex I, and this activation is also under study for anticancer and anti-aging effects because it opposes growth-promoting signaling. mTOR (mechanistic target of rapamycin) sits at the opposite pole, driving biosynthesis -- protein synthesis, lipid synthesis, ribosome production -- when nutrients and growth factors are abundant. Rapamycin, isolated from a Streptomyces bacterium found in soil from Rapa Nui (Easter Island), inhibits mTOR by first binding the protein FKBP12; the rapamycin-FKBP12 complex then binds and blocks mTOR complex 1. AMPK activation and mTOR inhibition converge functionally, since active AMPK directly suppresses mTOR.

sections.heading: Immunometabolism: T Cells Warburg Themselves
sections.body: The Warburg effect is not unique to cancer. When a naive T cell encounters its antigen alongside costimulation, it rapidly reprograms from oxidative phosphorylation to aerobic glycolysis, even though oxygen is available -- the same metabolic switch Warburg described in tumors, now understood as a general feature of rapidly proliferating, biosynthetically active cells rather than a cancer-specific defect. This shift, characterized in T-cell biology by researchers including Erika Pearce, supplies the glycolytic intermediates T cells need to build new membranes, nucleotides, and proteins fast enough to mount a clonal expansion, and glycolytic flux itself has been shown to support effector cytokine production.

lessons.workedExample: A student proposes imaging a tumor xenograft with FDG-PET before and after treating with a glycolysis-inhibiting compound, predicting reduced tracer uptake if the drug works. To interpret results correctly, they must account for confounds: inflammation and actively dividing immune cells are also glycolytic (per the immunometabolism mechanism) and will pick up FDG too, so a drop in signal could reflect reduced immune infiltration rather than a direct anti-tumor metabolic effect. A stronger design pairs the PET readout with a direct biochemical measure, such as extracellular lactate production or a Western blot for phosphorylated AMPK, to confirm the mechanism rather than trusting imaging alone.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe metabolism questions to see if a student treats 'the Warburg effect' as a slogan or as a specific, mechanistic, and even non-cancer-specific phenomenon. A weak answer says cancer cells 'use more sugar.' A strong answer explains why aerobic glycolysis makes sense for a proliferating cell -- trading ATP yield for the glycolytic intermediates needed for biosynthesis -- and can extend the same logic to activated T cells, showing it as a proliferation program rather than a tumor-only defect. Naming a concrete tool tied to the mechanism, like FDG-PET's dependence on trapped, non-metabolizable tracer, or that metformin and rapamycin act on opposing sides of the AMPK-mTOR axis, separates a memorized fact from real understanding.

questions.prompt: Why does FDG accumulate inside metabolically active tumor cells instead of being processed further?

options.text: FDG is not a glucose analog and cannot enter glycolysis
FDG is phosphorylated but cannot proceed further in glycolysis, trapping it in the cell
Tumor cells lack GLUT transporters, so FDG binds their surface instead
FDG binds directly to mTOR and is retained there

explanations.a: FDG is specifically a radiolabeled glucose analog, which is why hypermetabolic cells take it up avidly.
explanations.b: Correct -- hexokinase phosphorylates FDG like glucose, but the resulting FDG-6-phosphate cannot proceed through the rest of glycolysis, so it stays trapped inside the cell.
explanations.c: Tumor cells characteristically overexpress GLUT transporters, which is why they take up FDG so avidly.
explanations.d: FDG is a metabolic tracer with no described binding interaction with mTOR.

questions.prompt: Metformin activates AMPK primarily through which mechanism described in this lesson?

options.text: Directly binding FKBP12
Mild inhibition of mitochondrial complex I, raising the AMP/ATP ratio
Blocking GLUT transporters
Directly inhibiting mTOR complex 1

explanations.a: FKBP12 binding describes rapamycin's mechanism, not metformin's.
explanations.b: Correct -- metformin mildly inhibits complex I, which raises the AMP/ATP ratio and activates AMPK as the cell's energy sensor.
explanations.c: Blocking GLUT transporters is not the mechanism given for metformin in this lesson.
explanations.d: Metformin acts upstream, through AMPK, which then suppresses mTOR indirectly -- it does not bind mTOR directly.

questions.prompt: Match each compound or process to its mechanism.

right.text: Binds FKBP12, then the complex blocks mTORC1
Mildly inhibits complex I to activate AMPK
Traces glucose uptake via a trapped, non-metabolizable analog
Reprograms metabolism toward aerobic glycolysis upon antigen and costimulation

questions.explanation: Rapamycin works through FKBP12 to block mTORC1; metformin works through mild complex I inhibition to activate AMPK; FDG-PET exploits trapped tracer uptake; T-cell activation switches on aerobic glycolysis much like tumor cells do.

questions.prompt: Order the steps by which rapamycin inhibits mTOR-driven biosynthesis.

items.text: Rapamycin is isolated from a soil bacterium found on Rapa Nui
Rapamycin binds the protein FKBP12
The rapamycin-FKBP12 complex binds and blocks mTOR complex 1
mTORC1-driven biosynthesis (protein, lipid, and ribosome synthesis) is suppressed

questions.explanation: Rapamycin's discovery preceded understanding of its mechanism: it first binds FKBP12, and only the resulting complex is able to bind and inhibit mTORC1, which shuts down the biosynthetic programs mTORC1 normally drives.

lessons.label: Integrating Signaling & Metabolism

sections.heading: Akt as the Metabolic Executor of Growth Signaling
sections.body: Insulin binding its receptor activates PI3K, which generates PIP3 and recruits Akt to the plasma membrane for activation -- the identical PI3K-Akt axis that acts as an oncogenic driver when mutated, here operating as normal physiology. In muscle and fat cells, activated Akt phosphorylates substrates that trigger GLUT4-containing vesicles to translocate to the plasma membrane, inserting new glucose transporters and driving a rapid rise in glucose uptake -- the central mechanism by which insulin lowers blood glucose after a meal. Akt simultaneously activates mTOR complex 1 by inhibiting the TSC1/TSC2 complex, which otherwise restrains the small GTPase Rheb, linking the same signal that turns on glucose uptake to the biosynthetic program: protein synthesis, lipid synthesis, and ribosome production all ramp up together, since a cell should only build new mass when it has both a growth signal and confirmed nutrient access.

sections.heading: HIF-1alpha: Rewiring Metabolism for Low Oxygen (and Growth Signals)
sections.body: HIF-1alpha is a transcription factor continuously produced and normally degraded within minutes under normal oxygen: prolyl hydroxylase domain (PHD) enzymes hydroxylate HIF-1alpha in an oxygen-dependent reaction, creating a binding site recognized by the von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) tumor suppressor, which ubiquitinates HIF-1alpha and flags it for proteasomal destruction. When oxygen falls, PHD activity stops and that degradation halts, HIF-1alpha accumulates and enters the nucleus, and it transcriptionally upregulates glycolytic enzymes and the GLUT1 transporter, shifting the cell toward glycolysis for ATP production when oxidative phosphorylation is oxygen-starved. Critically, HIF-1alpha is not triggered by hypoxia alone: oncogenic PI3K-Akt-mTOR signaling and Ras activation can stabilize or activate HIF-1alpha even under normal oxygen, giving growth-signaling mutations a direct route to imposing a Warburg-like glycolytic program on a cell independent of its actual oxygen supply.

sections.heading: Designing a Node-and-Endpoint Experiment
sections.body: A rigorous science-fair project in this space perturbs exactly one node in a signaling-metabolism circuit and reads out one defined, mechanistically justified endpoint, rather than treating cells with a compound and reporting only more or less growth. A student might inhibit PI3K with a small molecule and measure GLUT4 translocation by surface biotinylation or a glucose-uptake assay, or knock down HIF-1alpha and measure lactate production by an enzymatic assay, or block mTORC1 with rapamycin and measure protein synthesis directly via a puromycin-incorporation assay. The design principle running through this unit -- pathway in, defined molecular readout out -- is what separates a testable hypothesis about a mechanism from an untestable claim about a phenotype.

lessons.workedExample: A student hypothesizes that a PI3K inhibitor will blunt insulin-stimulated glucose uptake in cultured muscle cells. They serum-starve the cells, then treat half with the PI3K inhibitor and half with vehicle before adding insulin, and measure glucose uptake using a fluorescent glucose analog read on a plate reader. The PI3K-inhibited group shows uptake near the unstimulated baseline, while vehicle-treated cells show a large insulin-stimulated increase, directly demonstrating that PI3K activity, not just insulin binding, is required for GLUT4-mediated glucose uptake. Pairing this with a Western blot for phosphorylated Akt confirms the inhibitor blocked the intended node rather than acting off-target.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask integration questions -- how does this signal actually change what the cell does metabolically -- to check whether a student can trace a pathway all the way to a physiological output, not just to a phosphorylation event. A weak answer stops at 'Akt gets activated.' A strong answer names the downstream metabolic consequence: Akt drives GLUT4 to the membrane for glucose uptake, or activates mTORC1 for biosynthesis, or that oncogenic signaling can stabilize HIF-1alpha independent of real oxygen levels. The strongest answers also defend their experimental design, naming the single node they perturbed and the single mechanistically connected readout they measured, showing they can build a hypothesis a judge could falsify.

questions.prompt: In muscle and fat cells, activated Akt increases glucose uptake primarily by...

options.text: Directly phosphorylating GLUT4 mRNA to increase its translation
Triggering translocation of GLUT4-containing vesicles to the plasma membrane
Stabilizing HIF-1alpha to upregulate GLUT1
Inhibiting mTORC1 to conserve energy

explanations.a: Akt's effect on glucose uptake is post-translational vesicle trafficking, not mRNA regulation.
explanations.b: Correct -- Akt phosphorylates substrates that drive GLUT4-containing vesicles to fuse with the plasma membrane, inserting new transporters.
explanations.c: HIF-1alpha-driven GLUT1 upregulation is a separate, transcriptional mechanism tied to hypoxia or oncogenic signaling, not the insulin-Akt-GLUT4 route.
explanations.d: Akt activates mTORC1 rather than inhibiting it, by suppressing the TSC1/TSC2 brake.

questions.prompt: Which statement about HIF-1alpha is correct as described in this lesson?

options.text: It is degraded only when oxygen is low
It can be stabilized by oncogenic PI3K-Akt-mTOR or Ras signaling even under normal oxygen
It directly binds GLUT4 vesicles to move them to the membrane
It opposes glycolytic gene transcription

explanations.a: This is reversed -- HIF-1alpha is degraded under normal oxygen and stabilized when oxygen is low.
explanations.b: Correct -- growth-signaling mutations can stabilize or activate HIF-1alpha independent of actual oxygen levels, imposing a glycolytic program regardless of true hypoxia.
explanations.c: HIF-1alpha is a transcription factor acting in the nucleus; it has no described role moving GLUT4 vesicles.
explanations.d: HIF-1alpha upregulates, rather than opposes, glycolytic enzyme and GLUT1 transcription.

questions.prompt: Match each perturbed node to the readout that would confirm the perturbation worked.

right.text: Reduced lactate production
Reduced glucose uptake via GLUT4
Reduced protein synthesis (puromycin incorporation)

questions.explanation: Blocking PI3K removes the signal driving GLUT4 translocation, so glucose uptake falls; knocking down HIF-1alpha reduces glycolytic gene expression, lowering lactate output; blocking mTORC1 directly suppresses the biosynthetic machinery measured by protein-synthesis assays.

questions.prompt: Order the insulin-Akt-GLUT4-mTORC1 cascade from receptor binding to biosynthesis.

items.text: Insulin binds its receptor
PI3K generates PIP3 and recruits Akt
Akt triggers GLUT4 vesicle translocation and inhibits TSC1/TSC2
mTORC1 is activated via Rheb, driving biosynthesis

questions.explanation: Insulin binding activates PI3K to recruit and activate Akt, which both drives GLUT4 to the membrane and relieves the TSC1/TSC2 brake on Rheb, allowing Rheb to activate mTORC1 and turn on biosynthesis.

units.label: Restriction Enzymes, Ligation & the Molecular Toolkit

lessons.label: Restriction Endonucleases: How Bacteria Cut DNA

sections.heading: A molecular scissors that only cuts one word
sections.body: Type II restriction endonucleases recognize short, specific DNA sequences, almost always 4-8 base pairs long, and cut both strands within or right next to that site. The sequences are palindromic in the DNA sense: read 5' to 3' on one strand, they read the same 5' to 3' on the other. EcoRI, isolated from E. coli, recognizes GAATTC and cuts between the G and the A on each strand, leaving 4-base single-stranded 5' overhangs (AATT) called sticky ends, because two such ends can base-pair and re-anneal. BamHI (from Bacillus amyloliquefaciens H) cuts GGATCC the same way, and HindIII (from Haemophilus influenzae) cuts AAGCTT. Not every enzyme leaves an overhang: SmaI cuts CCCGGG dead center, between the two C's and the two G's, producing a blunt end with no overhang at all. Hamilton Smith characterized the first sequence-specific restriction enzyme, HindII, from H. influenzae in 1970, work that shared the 1978 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Werner Arber and Daniel Nathans.

sections.heading: Restriction-modification: a bacterium's way of knowing 'self'
sections.body: A restriction enzyme that cut any GAATTC it found would destroy the bacterium's own chromosome, which is riddled with that sequence by chance. Bacteria solve this with a paired restriction-modification (R-M) system: alongside each restriction enzyme, the cell carries a cognate methyltransferase that adds a methyl group to an adenine or cytosine within that same recognition site on the host's own DNA. Methylated self-DNA is invisible to the restriction enzyme; unmethylated foreign DNA, such as an invading bacteriophage genome, gets cut. Arber proposed this host-controlled restriction and modification model in the 1960s to explain why phage grown in one bacterial strain infected a related strain poorly, a phenomenon that had puzzled phage geneticists for years. It is, functionally, a primitive innate immune system, and it is the reason a plasmid grown in a dam+/dcm+ E. coli strain can behave differently in a digest than the same plasmid grown in a dam-/dcm- strain.

sections.heading: When the scissors get sloppy: star activity
sections.body: Under nonstandard reaction conditions, a restriction enzyme can lose its strict fidelity and cut sequences that differ from its canonical site by one base, a behavior called star activity. Common triggers are glycerol above about 5% by volume (enzymes are shipped in 50% glycerol storage buffer, so adding too much enzyme relative to reaction volume raises glycerol concentration), low or absent ionic strength, an enzyme-to-DNA ratio far above what is needed, substituting Mn2+ for the enzyme's normal Mg2+ cofactor, or the presence of organic solvents like DMSO or ethanol. EcoRI is a classic offender, cutting degenerate AATT-like sites under star conditions. The practical fix is simple: keep glycerol carryover under 5% of the final reaction volume, use the manufacturer's matched buffer, and don't add more enzyme than the digest needs.

lessons.workedExample: A student digests plasmid pUC19 with EcoRI and runs it on a gel expecting one linearized band, but sees a faint extra band at the wrong size. Troubleshooting: EcoRI stock is stored in 50% glycerol, and the protocol calls for enzyme volume to stay at or below 10% of the total reaction volume to keep final glycerol under 5%. The student had added double the recommended enzyme units to 'make sure it cuts,' pushing enzyme volume to 25% of the reaction and glycerol well past the star-activity threshold. Repeating the digest with the correct unit amount in 1x EcoRI buffer eliminates the extra band, confirming it was star activity, not a second true EcoRI site.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'why does this enzyme cut here and nowhere else?' is testing whether a student understands specificity as a chemical property, not a memorized fact. A weak answer says 'it recognizes the sequence.' A strong answer names the recognition site, explains that recognition is palindromic so both strands are read identically, and can explain an anomaly: an unexpected extra band is evidence worth investigating, and 'star activity from too much glycerol or the wrong buffer' is exactly the kind of mechanistic troubleshooting that separates a student who ran a real digest from one reciting a textbook definition.

questions.prompt: EcoRI cuts GAATTC between the G and A on each strand. What kind of end does this produce?

options.text: A blunt end with no overhang
A 5' sticky overhang (AATT)
A 3' sticky overhang (AATT)
A double-stranded break with random overhang length

explanations.a: A blunt end results from cutting at the exact center of a palindrome, like SmaI on CCCGGG, not from EcoRI's off-center cut.
explanations.b: Correct — cutting between G and A on each strand leaves a 4-base single-stranded overhang, AATT, on the 5' end of each fragment.
explanations.c: The overhang is on the 5' end, since the cut leaves the AATT bases dangling ahead of the recessed 3' end on the opposite strand.
explanations.d: EcoRI's cut is sequence-specific and produces a defined, reproducible overhang, not a random one.

questions.prompt: Match each restriction enzyme to its recognition sequence.

right.text: GAATTC
GGATCC
AAGCTT

questions.explanation: EcoRI recognizes GAATTC, BamHI recognizes GGATCC, and HindIII recognizes AAGCTT — each a 6-bp palindromic site read identically 5' to 3' on both strands.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't a bacterium's own restriction enzyme destroy its own chromosome, which contains many copies of the recognition sequence?

options.text: The chromosome is single-stranded, so the enzyme cannot bind it
A cognate methyltransferase methylates the host's own recognition sites, making them invisible to the enzyme
Restriction enzymes only function outside the cell
The chromosome's recognition sites are deleted through evolution

explanations.a: Bacterial chromosomes are double-stranded DNA, and that has no bearing on restriction protection.
explanations.b: Correct — the paired restriction-modification system methylates the host's own copies of the site, so the enzyme cuts only unmethylated (typically foreign) DNA.
explanations.c: Restriction enzymes act inside the bacterial cytoplasm on incoming phage DNA; they are not extracellular.
explanations.d: Recognition sites occur throughout the genome by chance and are not selectively deleted; methylation, not deletion, is the protection mechanism.

questions.prompt: Order the events of a restriction-modification system defending a bacterium against an infecting phage.

items.text: Bacteriophage injects its unmethylated DNA into the host cell
The host's restriction enzyme scans for its recognition sequence
The enzyme finds an unmethylated site on the phage DNA and cuts it
The host's own chromosome survives intact because its recognition sites are methylated

questions.explanation: Infection begins with DNA entry, the restriction enzyme then surveys all DNA in the cell, cuts only the unmethylated (foreign) sites it finds, and the host genome is spared because its own sites were already methylated by the cognate methyltransferase.

lessons.label: Reading a Restriction Map & Planning a Digest

sections.heading: Fragment sizes are just arithmetic on cut positions
sections.body: A restriction map lists where each enzyme cuts along a plasmid, numbered from an arbitrary position 1. For a circular plasmid, a single-enzyme digest with one site linearizes it into one fragment equal to the whole plasmid length. A double digest with two enzymes at different positions splits it into two fragments, and because the plasmid is circular, you compute sizes by subtracting adjacent cut positions and wrapping around: if EcoRI cuts at position 200 and HindIII at position 1200 on a 5000 bp plasmid, the fragments are 1200-200 = 1000 bp and 5000-1000 = 4000 bp. The two fragment sizes must always sum to the total plasmid length; if a gel shows a size that doesn't fit, that's evidence of a partial digest (uncut sites still present, adding a larger band) or an extra, unmapped site.

sections.heading: Isoschizomers, neoschizomers, and swapping enzymes
sections.body: Isoschizomers are different enzymes, usually isolated from different bacteria, that recognize the identical sequence and cut at the identical position, so they are interchangeable. Neoschizomers recognize the same sequence but cut at a different position within it, which changes the end chemistry. SmaI and XmaI both recognize CCCGGG, but SmaI cuts dead center (CCC^GGG) for a blunt end, while XmaI cuts off-center (C^CCGGG) for a 5' sticky overhang. That distinction matters for cloning strategy: swapping in a neoschizomer changes whether your fragment ends are blunt or sticky, even though the recognition footprint on the map looks the same.

sections.heading: Compatible overhangs and a shared buffer
sections.body: Enzymes with different recognition sequences can still leave identical overhangs. BamHI (G^GATCC), BglII (A^GATCT), and BclI (T^GATCA) all leave a 5' GATC overhang and can ligate to one another, which is useful when a convenient site isn't in your vector's polylinker — though the hybrid junction usually destroys both original recognition sites. Planning a double digest also means checking that both enzymes tolerate a common buffer and temperature simultaneously (manufacturers publish compatibility charts for this); if not, digest sequentially and heat-inactivate or clean up between steps.

sections.heading: Stopping the vector from ligating to itself
sections.body: A cut vector still has a free 5'-phosphate at both ends, and DNA ligase only needs one phosphate to seal a nick — so an empty vector can recircularize on itself with no insert at all, producing background colonies with no insert. Treating the digested vector with calf intestinal alkaline phosphatase (CIP) or shrimp alkaline phosphatase (SAP) strips those 5' phosphates. A dephosphorylated vector can no longer self-ligate, but it can still ligate to a phosphorylated insert, because the insert supplies the needed phosphate at each junction; the resulting molecule has two single-strand nicks that the host cell's own ligase repairs after transformation.

lessons.workedExample: A 5000 bp plasmid map lists an EcoRI site at position 200 and a HindIII site at position 1200. A single EcoRI digest should give one 5000 bp linear band; a single HindIII digest should also give one 5000 bp band. A double digest with both enzymes should give two bands: 1000 bp (1200-200) and 4000 bp (5000-1000), summing back to 5000 bp. On the gel, the student instead sees three bands: 4000, 1000, and a faint 5000 bp band. The faint 5000 bp band is uncut, doubly-intact plasmid — a partial digest, not a third site — solved by adding more enzyme or extending incubation time.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking 'how do you know your construct is right before you sequence it?' is testing diagnostic-digest reasoning. A weak answer says 'we ran a gel and saw bands.' A strong answer predicts expected fragment sizes from the map before cutting, checks that observed sizes sum to the expected total, and can explain an anomalous band — an extra faint high band as a partial digest, or a smaller total as a missing insert — rather than treating the gel as a pass/fail black box.

questions.prompt: SmaI (CCC^GGG, blunt) and XmaI (C^CCGGG, sticky) both recognize CCCGGG. What is the correct term for their relationship?

options.text: Isoschizomers, because they recognize the same sequence and cut identically
Neoschizomers, because they recognize the same sequence but cut at different positions
Star-activity variants of the same enzyme
Unrelated enzymes that coincidentally share a recognition site

explanations.a: Isoschizomers cut at the identical position, producing the same end chemistry — that is not the case here.
explanations.b: Correct — same recognition sequence, different cut position, which changes blunt vs. sticky end chemistry.
explanations.c: Star activity is relaxed specificity under nonstandard conditions, not a relationship between two distinct enzymes.
explanations.d: They are not coincidental — 'neoschizomer' specifically names enzymes that share a recognition sequence.

questions.prompt: On a 5000 bp circular plasmid, EcoRI cuts at position 200 and HindIII cuts at position 1200. What fragment sizes should a double digest produce?

options.text: 200 bp and 4800 bp
1000 bp and 4000 bp
1200 bp and 3800 bp
5000 bp as a single fragment

explanations.a: 200 bp is the EcoRI position itself, not a fragment size derived from the gap between the two cuts.
explanations.b: Correct — the gap between cuts is 1200-200=1000 bp, and the rest of the circle is 5000-1000=4000 bp; the two sum to the total plasmid size.
explanations.c: 1200 bp is the HindIII position itself, not a computed fragment length.
explanations.d: A single fragment would only result from a one-cut digest; two different enzymes at two positions produce two fragments.

questions.prompt: Why treat a digested vector with CIP or SAP before setting up a ligation?

options.text: To add 5'-phosphates so the ligase reaction can proceed at all
To remove 5'-phosphates from the vector ends, preventing the vector from self-ligating without an insert
To blunt sticky ends so any insert can be used regardless of overhang
To destroy any remaining restriction enzyme so it doesn't re-cut the ligated product

explanations.a: That is the opposite function — kinase adds phosphates; phosphatase removes them.
explanations.b: Correct — stripping the vector's 5'-phosphates blocks vector-to-vector self-ligation while still permitting ligation to a phosphorylated insert.
explanations.c: Phosphatases modify phosphate groups, not the overhang sequence itself; they do not blunt ends.
explanations.d: Phosphatase has no nuclease activity against restriction enzymes; that concern is handled by heat inactivation or column cleanup, not CIP/SAP.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of preparing a vector backbone for ligation after a diagnostic digest confirms the map is correct.

items.text: Digest the vector with the chosen restriction enzyme(s)
Run and confirm fragment sizes on a gel against the predicted map
Treat the linearized vector with CIP or SAP to remove 5'-phosphates
Purify the dephosphorylated vector and set up the ligation with a phosphorylated insert

questions.explanation: Digestion comes first, confirming the map on a gel validates the cut before investing further steps, dephosphorylation follows only on a confirmed linear vector, and purification precedes the ligation itself.

lessons.label: DNA Ligation: Joining Fragments

sections.heading: Sealing the backbone: what ligase actually does
sections.body: DNA ligase catalyzes the formation of a phosphodiester bond between a free 3'-hydroxyl and an adjacent 5'-phosphate on the same strand, sealing a nick in the sugar-phosphate backbone. T4 DNA ligase, encoded by bacteriophage T4 and first purified from infected E. coli in the late 1960s, needs ATP as its energy source. The reaction runs in three steps: ligase first reacts with ATP to form a covalent ligase-AMP intermediate (releasing pyrophosphate), the AMP is then transferred onto the 5'-phosphate of the nicked DNA to form a DNA-adenylate intermediate, and finally the enzyme catalyzes attack by the 3'-OH on that activated phosphate, forming the phosphodiester bond and releasing AMP. This is distinct from bacterial E. coli DNA ligase, which uses NAD+ instead of ATP as its cofactor — a difference that matters because in vitro cloning reactions almost always use the phage enzyme, T4 ligase, precisely because it is ATP-dependent and works well in a simple buffer.

sections.heading: Sticky ends beat blunt ends because proximity beats chance
sections.body: Ligation efficiency depends heavily on how the two ends find each other. Complementary sticky-end overhangs (from the same or compatible restriction enzymes) base-pair transiently through hydrogen bonding before ligase ever acts, holding the two DNA ends in close, correctly-aligned proximity — effectively raising their local concentration relative to solution. Blunt ends have no such pairing to rely on; two blunt ends must collide randomly in the right orientation, which is far less likely. In practice, blunt-end ligations typically need substantially more ligase and longer incubation, and are often boosted with a molecular crowding agent like PEG-4000 to force ends together, yet they still succeed less efficiently than a comparable sticky-end reaction.

sections.heading: Setting up the reaction: molar ratios and the temperature tradeoff
sections.body: Cloning reactions are set up by mass but reasoned about by molarity, because a 3000 bp vector and a 500 bp insert of equal mass contain very different numbers of molecules. A common starting point is a 3:1 molar ratio of insert to vector, which biases the reaction toward insert incorporation and away from vector-only recircularization; ng of insert needed = molar ratio x ng of vector x (insert length / vector length). Temperature is a second tradeoff: T4 ligase is most catalytically active near 37 degrees C, but short 4-base sticky-end overhangs are so short that their hydrogen bonding is unstable at that temperature and can melt apart before ligase seals them. The standard compromise is to incubate at 16 degrees C, often overnight, which keeps overhangs annealed long enough for the slower-but-still-functional enzyme to act; a faster room-temperature protocol trades some efficiency for turnaround time.

lessons.workedExample: A student has 50 ng of a 3000 bp vector and wants a 3:1 molar ratio of a 500 bp insert. Using ng of insert = molar ratio x ng of vector x (insert length / vector length): 3 x 50 ng x (500/3000) = 3 x 50 x 0.1667 = 25 ng of insert. They set up the ligation with 50 ng vector, 25 ng insert, T4 DNA ligase, and 1x ligase buffer (which supplies the ATP), and incubate at 16 degrees C overnight rather than at ligase's 37 degrees C optimum, because the insert and vector share a 4-base sticky overhang that needs the cooler temperature to stay annealed.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking 'why did you choose that insert-to-vector ratio, and why incubate overnight at 16 degrees instead of 37?' is testing whether the ligation step was designed or copied. A weak answer says 'that's what the protocol said.' A strong answer walks through the molar-ratio calculation from fragment sizes and masses, and explains the 16-degree compromise as balancing ligase's temperature optimum against the thermal instability of a short sticky-end overhang — showing the student understands both halves of the tradeoff, not just the number on a datasheet.

questions.prompt: What cofactor does T4 DNA ligase require to catalyze phosphodiester bond formation?

options.text: NAD+
ATP
GTP
No cofactor is required

explanations.a: NAD+ is the cofactor used by bacterial E. coli DNA ligase, not the phage T4 enzyme used in cloning reactions.
explanations.b: Correct — T4 DNA ligase forms a covalent ligase-AMP intermediate from ATP as the first step of the reaction.
explanations.c: GTP is not used by either major class of DNA ligase; it is not the relevant cofactor here.
explanations.d: Ligation is energetically unfavorable without an activating cofactor; ATP supplies that energy via the ligase-AMP intermediate.

questions.prompt: Why is sticky-end ligation generally more efficient than blunt-end ligation?

options.text: Sticky ends do not require ATP, while blunt ends do
Complementary overhangs base-pair transiently, holding ends in proximity before ligase seals them
Blunt-end fragments are always larger and diffuse more slowly
T4 ligase cannot chemically bond blunt ends at all

explanations.a: Both sticky-end and blunt-end ligation use the same ATP-dependent ligase mechanism; the cofactor requirement doesn't differ.
explanations.b: Correct — transient base-pairing between complementary overhangs raises local concentration and correct alignment, something blunt ends lack entirely.
explanations.c: Fragment size is unrelated to whether the ends are sticky or blunt; both can occur at any fragment length.
explanations.d: T4 ligase can join blunt ends, just less efficiently, typically needing more enzyme and longer incubation.

questions.prompt: For a 3:1 molar ratio of insert to vector, given 50 ng of a 3000 bp vector and a 500 bp insert, how much insert (in ng) should be added?

options.text: 8.3 ng
25 ng
50 ng
150 ng

explanations.a: 8.3 ng would result from using a 1:1 molar ratio, not the 3:1 ratio specified.
explanations.b: Correct — 3 x 50 ng x (500/3000) = 25 ng, the mass of insert that gives a 3:1 molar excess over the vector.
explanations.c: 50 ng equals the vector mass, but at different fragment lengths, equal mass does not mean equal molarity.
explanations.d: 150 ng would result from omitting the length-ratio correction (500/3000) and just multiplying vector mass by 3.

questions.prompt: Order the catalytic steps T4 DNA ligase performs to seal a nick.

items.text: Ligase reacts with ATP to form a covalent ligase-AMP intermediate
AMP is transferred to the 5'-phosphate of the nicked DNA, forming a DNA-adenylate intermediate
The 3'-OH attacks the activated phosphate, forming the phosphodiester bond and releasing AMP

questions.explanation: Ligase first activates itself with ATP, transfers that activation onto the DNA's 5'-phosphate, and only then does the 3'-OH complete the bond, releasing AMP as the final byproduct.

lessons.label: Modifying DNA Ends: Phosphatases, Kinases & Polymerases

sections.heading: Phosphatase and kinase: opposite ends of the same switch
sections.body: Ligase needs a 5'-phosphate to seal a junction, which makes phosphate groups a control knob for cloning. Alkaline phosphatase (calf intestinal, CIP, or shrimp, SAP) strips 5'-phosphates from DNA ends, most commonly used on a digested vector to block it from self-ligating without an insert. T4 polynucleotide kinase (T4 PNK) does the opposite: using ATP, it adds a 5'-phosphate to a DNA end that lacks one. This matters because chemically synthesized DNA — annealed synthetic oligonucleotides, and standard PCR primers ordered from a vendor — comes off the synthesizer without a 5'-phosphate by default. A PCR product amplified with two unphosphorylated primers is itself unphosphorylated at both 5' ends; if that fragment is meant for blunt-end ligation, it will not ligate at all until T4 PNK adds the missing phosphates, a step easy to forget because restriction-cut DNA already carries a phosphate courtesy of the enzyme's own cut mechanism.

sections.heading: Making ends blunt: fill in, or chew back
sections.body: Two different overhang geometries need two different fixes to reach blunt. A 5' overhang, like the AATT left by EcoRI, has a recessed 3' end; the Klenow fragment (the large fragment of E. coli DNA polymerase I, which retains 5' to 3' polymerase activity and 3' to 5' proofreading exonuclease activity but lacks the whole enzyme's 5' to 3' exonuclease) extends that recessed 3' end using the overhang as template, filling it in to blunt. A 3' overhang has the opposite problem — protruding single-stranded DNA past a recessed 5' end — and needs the overhang trimmed off rather than filled in; T4 DNA polymerase has a stronger 3' to 5' exonuclease than Klenow and is the enzyme of choice for cleanly chewing back a 3' overhang to blunt. Both enzymes can do either job in principle, but T4 DNA polymerase's more aggressive exonuclease makes it the standard pick specifically for 3'-overhang removal.

sections.heading: Taq's sloppy 3' end and TA cloning
sections.body: Taq polymerase, isolated from the thermophile Thermus aquaticus and the workhorse of standard PCR, lacks 3' to 5' proofreading exonuclease activity. As a side effect, its terminal transferase-like activity adds a single non-template-directed adenine to the 3' end of most PCR products it makes. TA cloning exploits this quirk directly: a linearized vector is supplied pre-cut with single 3'-T overhangs on both ends, so a Taq-generated PCR product's A overhangs anneal straight into the vector's T overhangs and ligate without any restriction digestion or blunting step at all — a fast, cheap route for cloning a fresh PCR product, though it only works with polymerases like Taq that lack proofreading; a high-fidelity, proofreading polymerase such as Pfu generates blunt ends instead and needs a different cloning strategy.

lessons.workedExample: A student PCR-amplifies an insert with ordinary (unphosphorylated) primers, then blunts one EcoRI-cut sticky end with Klenow fill-in so it matches a blunt-cut vector site. The ligation reaction fails to produce colonies. Troubleshooting reveals the missing step: because the PCR primers were synthesized without a 5'-phosphate modification, both ends of the insert are unphosphorylated, and blunt-end ligation needs at least one 5'-phosphate at each junction. Treating the insert with T4 polynucleotide kinase and ATP before the ligation step supplies the missing phosphates, and the repeat ligation succeeds.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'why did you use Klenow there instead of T4 DNA polymerase, and did you kinase the insert first?' is checking whether end-modification choices were reasoned from the actual overhang geometry or copied from a protocol. A weak answer conflates all 'end-fixing enzymes' as interchangeable. A strong answer distinguishes filling in a 5' overhang from chewing back a 3' overhang, and can explain, unprompted, why a PCR product made with standard unphosphorylated primers needs kinase treatment before it can be blunt-ligated at all.

questions.prompt: Match each enzyme to the function it performs in end modification for cloning.

right.text: Removes 5'-phosphates to block self-ligation
Adds 5'-phosphates using ATP
Fills in a recessed 3' end on a 5' overhang to make it blunt
Adds a single non-template-directed 3'-A overhang to PCR products

questions.explanation: CIP/SAP strips phosphates, T4 PNK adds them, Klenow fills in 5' overhangs by extending the recessed 3' strand, and Taq's lack of proofreading leaves it adding a stray 3'-A to most products it makes.

questions.prompt: A PCR product made with standard, unphosphorylated primers is blunted and needs to be blunt-ligated into a vector. What extra step does it need first, and why?

options.text: Treatment with alkaline phosphatase, because the ends have too much phosphate
Treatment with T4 polynucleotide kinase, because chemically synthesized primers lack a 5'-phosphate
Treatment with Klenow, because the ends are not yet blunt
No extra step, because Taq adds a 5'-phosphate automatically

explanations.a: The problem is a missing phosphate, not an excess one; phosphatase would make the situation worse, not better.
explanations.b: Correct — standard synthetic primers carry no 5'-phosphate, so the PCR product needs T4 PNK before ligase can seal a blunt junction.
explanations.c: The problem statement specifies the ends are already blunted; Klenow's fill-in role does not apply here.
explanations.d: Taq's terminal transferase activity adds a 3'-A base, not a 5'-phosphate; it does nothing to solve the missing-phosphate problem.

questions.prompt: Why does TA cloning work specifically with Taq-generated PCR products but not with a high-fidelity, proofreading polymerase like Pfu?

options.text: Taq lacks 3' to 5' proofreading exonuclease activity, so it non-specifically adds a 3'-A overhang, while a proofreading enzyme removes such mismatched additions and leaves blunt ends
Pfu cannot amplify DNA at all, so there is no product to clone
Taq products carry a 5'-phosphate that Pfu products lack
TA cloning vectors are only chemically compatible with Taq's reaction buffer

explanations.a: Correct — the absence of proofreading is exactly what lets Taq's non-template-directed terminal addition survive, generating the 3'-A that TA cloning depends on.
explanations.b: Pfu amplifies DNA readily; the issue is end chemistry, not amplification capability.
explanations.c: 5'-phosphate status is determined by the primers used, not by which polymerase performed the extension.
explanations.d: TA cloning's compatibility is about the 3'-A/3'-T overhang match, not buffer chemistry.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to take an EcoRI-cut fragment (5' sticky overhang) from digestion to a successful blunt ligation into a SmaI-cut vector, when the fragment came from unphosphorylated PCR primers.

items.text: Digest the fragment with EcoRI, leaving a 5' AATT overhang
Treat with Klenow fragment to fill in the recessed 3' end, creating a blunt end
Treat with T4 polynucleotide kinase and ATP to add the missing 5'-phosphates
Ligate the blunted, phosphorylated fragment into the blunt-cut vector

questions.explanation: The overhang must exist before it can be filled in, filling in must happen before the ends can be called blunt, phosphorylation must be added before ligase can act on those ends, and ligation is necessarily the last step.

lessons.label: Sizing & Purifying DNA for Cloning

sections.heading: Choosing gel percentage for the fragments you actually expect
sections.body: A cloning digest is only useful if the gel can resolve the fragments the restriction map predicts. Standard agarose gels around 0.7-1% cleanly resolve the 500 bp-10 kb range that most plasmid digests fall into, which is why it is the default for confirming a cloning digest. Fragments below roughly 500 bp, or two fragments that differ by only a small percentage of their length, need higher-percentage agarose, commonly 2-3%, to separate cleanly — small fragments move fast through a low-percentage gel and blur together near the dye front. Very large fragments, above about 10 kb, need the opposite adjustment: a lower percentage gel, closer to 0.5%, run longer, since high-percentage agarose barely lets large DNA migrate at all. Picking the gel percentage is therefore a direct consequence of the fragment-size math done when the map was planned, not a fixed default.

sections.heading: The ladder is the ruler that confirms the whole digest
sections.body: A DNA ladder of known fragment sizes run in an adjacent lane turns a gel from a picture into a measurement. Because migration distance is roughly inversely proportional to the logarithm of fragment size, comparing an unknown band's position against the ladder's known bands gives an estimated size. The real power for a cloning workflow is comparing that observed pattern against the pattern predicted from the restriction map: if a double digest was predicted to give 1000 bp and 4000 bp bands and the gel shows exactly that, both the digest and the identity of the starting plasmid are confirmed in one step — catching a wrong clone, a contaminated prep, or a failed digest before it gets carried into a ligation and wastes the transformation that follows.

sections.heading: Extracting the band you need without damaging it
sections.body: Once the correct band is identified against the ladder, it must be physically separated from the other digestion products, uncut plasmid, and leftover enzyme. The band is excised from the gel with a clean blade, the gel slice is dissolved in a chaotropic salt buffer that also disrupts agarose's structure, the released DNA is bound to a silica membrane in a spin column, washed to remove salts and agarose residue, and eluted in a low-salt buffer or water. Visualizing the band during excision matters as much as the chemistry: standard ethidium bromide requires strong UV (around 302 nm) to fluoresce, and that UV energy causes thymine dimers and strand nicks in the DNA being visualized, directly lowering the ligation and transformation efficiency of DNA that sat under the lamp too long. SYBR Safe stain is excited by blue light rather than UV and binds DNA less aggressively, so it is both far less mutagenic to handle and far gentler on the DNA being extracted — which is why it, not ethidium bromide, is the standard choice when the extracted band is headed into a ligation reaction rather than just being photographed for a record.

lessons.workedExample: A student's double digest is predicted to give a 4000 bp vector backbone and a 1000 bp insert on a 0.8% agarose gel. They run the digest next to a 1 kb-interval DNA ladder, confirm both bands land at the predicted sizes, and excise the 1000 bp insert band under a blue-light transilluminator with SYBR Safe stain in under 30 seconds of exposure. On an earlier attempt, they had used ethidium bromide and a standard 302 nm UV box, leaving the gel under the lamp for several minutes while photographing it before cutting the band — the resulting ligation had noticeably fewer colonies, consistent with UV-induced nicking of the extracted fragment.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'how did you know the band you cut out was the right one, and why blue light instead of UV?' is testing whether gel work was treated as measurement or as a picture-taking formality. A weak answer says 'we saw a band about the right size.' A strong answer cites the predicted fragment sizes from the restriction map, points to the ladder comparison that confirmed them, and explains — unprompted — that minimizing UV exposure (or using SYBR Safe with blue light) during excision protects the DNA's ability to ligate and transform afterward.

questions.prompt: A digest is predicted to produce two fragments only 80 bp apart in size, both under 300 bp. What gel percentage is the best choice to resolve them?

options.text: 0.5% agarose
0.8% agarose
2-3% agarose
Gel percentage does not affect resolution of small fragments

explanations.a: 0.5% is suited to very large fragments (>10 kb); small, closely-sized fragments would run together near the dye front and be unresolvable.
explanations.b: 0.8% is the standard choice for the 500 bp-10 kb range, but fragments under 300 bp and only 80 bp apart need finer resolution than that.
explanations.c: Correct — small fragments and small size differences need higher-percentage agarose, typically 2-3%, to separate cleanly.
explanations.d: Gel percentage directly controls the pore size DNA migrates through, and is the primary lever for resolving small size differences.

questions.prompt: Why is SYBR Safe with blue-light excitation preferred over ethidium bromide with UV excitation when the extracted band will be used in a ligation reaction?

options.text: SYBR Safe makes bands migrate faster through the gel
UV exposure used to visualize ethidium bromide causes DNA damage (nicks, thymine dimers) that lowers downstream ligation efficiency
Ethidium bromide cannot bind to double-stranded DNA fragments
SYBR Safe increases the total yield of DNA extracted from the gel slice

explanations.a: Neither stain changes a fragment's electrophoretic migration; migration is governed by size and gel percentage.
explanations.b: Correct — the UV needed to excite ethidium bromide damages the DNA being visualized, and that damage carries forward into a lower-efficiency ligation.
explanations.c: Ethidium bromide binds double-stranded DNA well; that is exactly why it fluoresces under UV in the first place.
explanations.d: Extraction yield is governed by the column chemistry and gel-dissolving step, not by which stain was used to see the band.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of extracting and purifying a specific band from an agarose gel.

items.text: Compare the digest pattern to the DNA ladder to identify the correct band
Excise the band from the gel under blue-light (not prolonged UV) illumination
Dissolve the gel slice in a chaotropic binding buffer and load onto a silica spin column
Wash the column and elute the purified DNA in a low-salt buffer or water

questions.explanation: Identification against the ladder must happen before excision, excision must happen before the gel slice can be dissolved and bound, and washing/elution is necessarily the final purification step.

questions.prompt: A student's double digest is predicted to give 1000 bp and 4000 bp bands. The gel instead shows a 1000 bp band and a faint 5000 bp band, with no 4000 bp band visible. What does the ladder comparison reveal?

options.text: The digest and plasmid identity are confirmed as correct
The digest is incomplete or the plasmid map does not match this sample, since the predicted 4000 bp band is missing
The gel percentage was too high to resolve any fragments
The ladder itself must be degraded

explanations.a: A confirmed digest would show both predicted bands (1000 and 4000 bp) summing to the total plasmid size; a missing predicted band is a mismatch, not a confirmation.
explanations.b: Correct — the ladder comparison is exactly what exposes this mismatch: the expected 4000 bp band is absent and an unpredicted 5000 bp band appears instead, pointing to an incomplete digest or a plasmid that does not match the map.
explanations.c: Both the observed bands (1000 and 5000 bp) are well within the resolving range of a standard gel; percentage is not the issue here.
explanations.d: The ladder's own bands would all appear off if it were degraded; a specific missing sample band points to the sample, not the ladder.

lessons.label: Quantifying & Quality-Checking Nucleic Acids

sections.heading: A260 gives you a concentration, by convention
sections.body: Nucleic acids absorb UV light maximally around 260 nm, because the purine and pyrimidine bases are aromatic rings that absorb strongly at that wavelength. A spectrophotometer reading, such as a NanoDrop, converts that absorbance into a concentration using a standard conversion factor derived from the Beer-Lambert relationship between absorbance and concentration: by convention, one absorbance unit (an A260 of 1.0) corresponds to about 50 ng/uL of double-stranded DNA, 40 ng/uL of RNA, or 33 ng/uL of single-stranded DNA, over a 1 cm pathlength. This means an A260 reading of 0.44 implies roughly 22 ng/uL of dsDNA. That number is only an estimate, though — it assumes everything absorbing at 260 nm in the sample is DNA, which is not always true.

sections.heading: Two ratios that flag two different contaminants
sections.body: Proteins absorb UV maximally around 280 nm, mostly from aromatic amino acids like tryptophan. The A260/A280 ratio compares nucleic acid signal to protein signal: pure double-stranded DNA sits around 1.8, and a lower ratio signals residual protein contamination, often from an incomplete deproteinization step during extraction. A second, separate contamination source shows up near 230 nm, where residual phenol, guanidine salts carried over from silica-column extraction kits, and other chaotropic reagents absorb strongly. The A260/A230 ratio for clean DNA typically falls around 2.0-2.2; a lower ratio points specifically to that organic-solvent or salt carryover, a common real-world problem with rushed column washes, and is a distinct failure mode from the protein contamination that A260/A280 flags.

sections.heading: When absorbance lies: switching to a fluorometric method
sections.body: A260 absorbance is indiscriminate: it sums the UV signal from intact double-stranded DNA, degraded DNA fragments, free nucleotides, contaminating RNA, and even some buffer components, all of which absorb near 260 nm. A degraded or contaminated prep can therefore read a higher concentration on a spectrophotometer than the amount of actually usable, full-length dsDNA it contains, because the instrument cannot distinguish the source of the signal. Fluorometric quantification, such as a Qubit assay, uses a dye that only fluoresces once it has physically intercalated into double-stranded DNA, so it reports signal specifically from intact dsDNA and ignores degraded fragments, free nucleotides, and RNA. That distinction is not academic for cloning: the insert-to-vector molar ratio math depends on an accurate mass input, and an inflated A260-based concentration means adding less real DNA than the calculation assumes, undermining a ligation that looked correctly designed on paper.

lessons.workedExample: A miniprep reads A260 = 0.44 on a NanoDrop, giving an estimated 22 ng/uL of dsDNA (0.44 x 50). The A260/A280 ratio is 1.65 (slightly low, hinting at residual protein) and the A260/A230 ratio is 1.2 (notably low, hinting at leftover guanidine salt from the column wash). Because both ratios flag contamination, the student re-runs the wash steps of the prep and re-measures. To confirm the true usable DNA amount before setting up a precise 3:1 insert:vector ligation, they also run the sample on a Qubit dsDNA assay, which reads 15 ng/uL — noticeably lower than the NanoDrop's 22 ng/uL, confirming the spectrophotometer had overestimated concentration due to contaminant absorbance, and the student recalculates their ligation masses using the Qubit number.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking 'how do you know your DNA concentration was accurate enough to trust your ligation math' is testing whether a student treats a spectrophotometer reading as ground truth or as an estimate with known failure modes. A weak answer quotes a single NanoDrop number with no context. A strong answer reports both quality ratios alongside the concentration, explains what a low A260/A280 or A260/A230 specifically indicates, and knows that when the ratios look poor or the concentration must be precise, a fluorometric method like Qubit is the more trustworthy input for downstream molar-ratio calculations.

questions.prompt: Match each measurement or ratio to what it indicates about a nucleic acid sample.

right.text: Total UV-absorbing signal near 260 nm, not specific to intact dsDNA
Residual protein contamination
Residual organic solvent or chaotropic salt carryover
Concentration specific to intact double-stranded DNA only

questions.explanation: A260 alone sums signal from anything absorbing near 260 nm; a low 260/280 flags protein; a low 260/230 flags organic solvent or salt; Qubit's dye only fluoresces when bound to dsDNA, so it reports intact dsDNA specifically.

questions.prompt: A NanoDrop reads A260 = 0.6 for a double-stranded DNA sample. Using the standard conversion (1 A260 unit = 50 ng/uL dsDNA), what is the estimated concentration?

options.text: 6 ng/uL
12 ng/uL
30 ng/uL
50 ng/uL

explanations.a: 6 ng/uL would result from using a factor of 10, not the standard 50 ng/uL-per-unit conversion for dsDNA.
explanations.b: 12 ng/uL does not follow from multiplying 0.6 by the standard 50 ng/uL factor.
explanations.c: Correct — 0.6 x 50 ng/uL = 30 ng/uL, the standard estimate for double-stranded DNA at that A260 reading.
explanations.d: 50 ng/uL is the conversion factor itself (the concentration at A260 = 1.0), not the result for a reading of 0.6.

questions.prompt: Why can a degraded or contaminated DNA prep read a higher concentration on a UV spectrophotometer than the amount of usable, intact dsDNA it actually contains?

options.text: UV spectrophotometers systematically underestimate all samples, regardless of purity
A260 absorbance sums signal from anything absorbing near 260 nm — degraded fragments, free nucleotides, RNA — not just intact dsDNA specifically
Degraded DNA absorbs at a completely different wavelength than intact DNA
Spectrophotometers cannot detect DNA at all, only protein
The 50 ng/uL conversion factor only applies to RNA, not DNA

explanations.a: Spectrophotometers do not systematically underestimate; the failure mode described here is overestimation from indiscriminate signal.
explanations.b: Correct — A260 cannot distinguish the source of the absorbing signal, so degraded fragments, free nucleotides, and contaminating RNA all inflate the apparent concentration.
explanations.c: Degraded DNA still absorbs near 260 nm, the same region as intact DNA, which is exactly why it inflates the reading rather than being ignored.
explanations.d: Spectrophotometers detect nucleic acids readily via the A260 peak; that is the basis of this entire quantification method.
explanations.e: 50 ng/uL is specifically the dsDNA conversion factor; RNA uses a different factor (about 40 ng/uL).

questions.prompt: Order the steps of assessing whether a DNA prep is trustworthy enough to use in a precise, molar-ratio-based ligation setup.

items.text: Measure A260 on a spectrophotometer and calculate the estimated concentration
Check the A260/A280 and A260/A230 ratios for signs of protein or solvent/salt contamination
If ratios are poor, re-purify the sample (e.g., repeat wash steps)
Confirm the final concentration with a fluorometric assay (e.g., Qubit) before calculating ligation masses

questions.explanation: An initial spectrophotometer reading comes first, its purity ratios are checked next, poor ratios trigger re-purification, and only a fluorometric measurement gives the trustworthy final concentration to feed into precise ligation math.

lessons.label: Anatomy of a Plasmid Vector

sections.heading: Three non-negotiable parts
sections.body: Every plasmid vector, no matter how specialized, needs three things to function as a cloning tool. First, an origin of replication (ori): a specific DNA sequence the host's replication machinery recognizes to start copying the plasmid independently of the chromosome; the ori also sets copy number, how many plasmid molecules end up per cell. Second, a selectable marker, almost always an antibiotic-resistance gene: bla, encoding beta-lactamase, which hydrolyzes ampicillin before it can kill the cell, or a kanamycin-resistance gene encoding an aminoglycoside phosphotransferase that inactivates the drug. Without it, there is no way to distinguish the rare cell that took up your ligated plasmid from the vast majority that didn't; you plate on antibiotic, and only resistant colonies grow. Third, a multiple cloning site (MCS or polylinker): a short stretch packed with restriction sites, each ideally cutting the plasmid exactly once, giving you places to open the circle and insert foreign DNA without wrecking anything else on the backbone.

sections.heading: Reading a real map: pUC19, pGEM, pET
sections.body: pUC19, sequenced by Yanisch-Perron, Vieira, and Messing in 1985 as part of the pUC series Vieira and Messing built in 1982, packs its MCS inside the lacZ-alpha coding sequence, itself under a lac promoter; insert DNA there disrupts alpha-complementation, the basis of blue-white screening on X-gal/IPTG plates. Its marker is ampR, its ori a high-copy pMB1 derivative. Promega's pGEM vectors keep a similar pUC-style backbone but flank the MCS with two different phage promoters, T7 on one side and SP6 on the other, facing opposite directions, so either strand of an insert can be transcribed in vitro depending on which polymerase you add. pET vectors, built on the T7 expression system Studier and Moffatt described in 1986, are read differently again: a T7 promoter, an overlapping lac operator for IPTG-inducible control, a ribosome binding site, then the MCS, often fused to an N- or C-terminal His-tag coding sequence, and a T7 terminator. A pET plasmid does nothing in an ordinary strain; it requires a host like BL21(DE3), carrying T7 RNA polymerase under the lacUV5 promoter in its chromosome. All three backbones trace back to pBR322, built by Bolivar, Rodriguez, and colleagues in 1977 as one of the first purpose-built cloning vectors, carrying the pMB1 ori and both ampR and tetR markers; pUC19 and the pET series each kept the ori lineage but stripped the backbone down, and the size difference matters practically, not just historically — pUC19 runs about 2.7 kb against roughly 5.4 kb for a typical pET28a, and the smaller circle transforms into competent cells markedly more efficiently, one more reason pUC-style backbones dominate routine subcloning while larger expression backbones are reserved for the step where expression is actually needed.

lessons.workedExample: A student wants an antisense RNA probe from a cDNA cloned into pGEM-3Z. Reading the map, they find the MCS flanked by a T7 promoter on one side and SP6 on the other, with their insert ligated in one fixed orientation. To make RNA complementary to the mRNA, they need the promoter that reads through the insert in the reverse direction relative to the coding strand. Checking which sites the insert used and where they sit relative to each promoter arrow on the map, they determine SP6, not T7, gives the antisense strand, then linearize the plasmid just downstream of the insert before in vitro transcription so the probe doesn't run into vector sequence.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks a student to walk through their own plasmid map is testing whether the vector was understood or just ordered. A weak answer stalls at 'it's the plasmid Addgene sent us.' A strong answer names the ori and what copy number it implies, explains why the marker has to match the antibiotic in the selection plates, and, for a pET construct, knows without hesitation why the host has to be BL21(DE3) and not an ordinary cloning strain like DH5-alpha.

questions.prompt: A colony grows on an LB+ampicillin plate after a transformation. What does this alone confirm?

options.text: The plasmid carries the correct insert
The cell took up a plasmid carrying a functional resistance marker
The insert is in the correct reading frame
The plasmid is present at high copy number

explanations.a: Growth on antibiotic only shows a functional marker was present; it says nothing about whether an insert is there at all.
explanations.b: Correct — the marker gene product (e.g. beta-lactamase) degraded the ampicillin, which is exactly what antibiotic selection tests; nothing else about the plasmid is confirmed yet.
explanations.c: Reading frame is irrelevant to antibiotic survival unless the marker gene itself was disrupted, which growth argues against.
explanations.d: Copy number is set by the ori and is invisible from colony growth alone.

questions.prompt: Match each vector element to its function.

right.text: Initiates and controls plasmid replication, setting copy number
Confers antibiotic resistance so transformed cells can be selected
Cluster of unique restriction sites for inserting foreign DNA
Drives transcription of the insert or a reporter gene

questions.explanation: Each part plays one distinct role: the ori governs replication and copy number, the marker enables selection, the MCS provides insertion points, and the promoter drives transcription of whatever sits downstream of it.

questions.prompt: In pUC19, why does successful insertion of foreign DNA into the MCS turn colonies white on X-gal/IPTG plates?

options.text: The insert disrupts the lacZ-alpha coding sequence, blocking alpha-complementation so no functional beta-galactosidase forms
The insert introduces a new promoter that represses lacZ
The ampR gene is inactivated by the insertion
The insert raises the plasmid's copy number

explanations.a: Correct — the MCS sits inside lacZ-alpha; an insert there breaks the reading frame needed for alpha-complementation with the host's omega-fragment, so X-gal isn't cleaved and the colony stays white.
explanations.b: Nothing about the insert adds a new promoter; the effect is disruption of a coding sequence, not repression.
explanations.c: ampR sits elsewhere on the backbone and is unaffected by MCS insertions; if it were disrupted, no colony would grow at all.
explanations.d: Copy number is a property of the ori, not of what's cloned into the MCS.

questions.prompt: Order these elements as encountered along a pET transcript, from promoter to the cloned insert.

items.text: T7 promoter
lac operator
Ribosome binding site
Multiple cloning site / insert

questions.explanation: T7 RNA polymerase initiates at the T7 promoter; the overlapping lac operator gates that initiation until IPTG is added; the ribosome binding site downstream positions the ribosome; the MCS, where the insert sits, comes last so the insert is what actually gets translated.

lessons.label: Types of Vectors & Matching One to the Goal

sections.heading: Cloning, expression, and shuttle vectors
sections.body: Not every plasmid is built to do the same job. A cloning vector, like pUC19 or pBluescript, is stripped down to the essentials — ori, marker, MCS — meant mainly to store, amplify, and subclone DNA; it has no strong promoter positioned to drive high-level production of whatever is in the MCS. An expression vector, like pET, adds a strong inducible promoter deliberately positioned upstream of the insert so the host cranks out protein from it. A shuttle vector solves a different problem: it replicates in two different organisms, carrying two origins (and often two markers), one recognized in E. coli for cheap bacterial amplification and one recognized in the target organism. pYES2 shuttles between E. coli and yeast; many mammalian expression and viral packaging plasmids carry a bacterial ori/ampR alongside a eukaryotic promoter, so the same physical plasmid can be prepped in bacteria and then used directly in mammalian cells.

sections.heading: Gateway cloning: recombination instead of digestion
sections.body: Invitrogen's Gateway system, built on lambda phage's site-specific recombination machinery worked out by Landy's group, sidesteps restriction enzymes entirely. A PCR product flanked by attB sites is BP-reacted with a donor vector carrying attP sites, generating an entry clone flanked by attL sites. That single entry clone can then be LR-reacted into any number of destination vectors carrying attR sites — bacterial expression, yeast two-hybrid, mammalian expression, tagged variants — regenerating attB sites each time, without redesigning restriction sites or rechecking internal cut sites for every new backbone. It earns its cost when one ORF needs to land in many different vectors.

sections.heading: When the insert won't fit: cosmids and BACs
sections.body: A standard high-copy plasmid tops out around 10-15 kb of insert before large fragments become unstable and prone to deletion. Cosmid vectors combine a plasmid ori and marker with lambda cos sites, then get packaged in vitro into phage particles, which require roughly 37-52 kb between cos sites for efficient packaging — pushing usable inserts up to about 35-45 kb. For genomic-scale fragments, bacterial artificial chromosomes (BACs) use the F-factor's own single-copy replication and partition system; Shizuya and colleagues showed in 1992 that this let E. coli stably maintain human DNA fragments of 300 kb, and BAC libraries became the backbone of large-scale genomic mapping and sequencing projects, precisely because single copy number curbs the recombination that shreds repetitive DNA on multi-copy plasmids.

lessons.workedExample: A lab needs one ORF expressed as a GST fusion in E. coli, tested in a yeast two-hybrid screen, and eventually packaged into a lentiviral construct. Instead of subcloning with restriction sites three separate times, they PCR the ORF once with attB-flanked primers, BP-react it into a pDONR221 entry vector, then LR-react that single entry clone into three different Gateway destination vectors — bacterial GST-fusion, yeast two-hybrid bait, and lentiviral expression — producing all three constructs without redesigning a single restriction site for each new backbone.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking 'why this vector?' is checking whether the choice reflects a real tradeoff or just came bundled with a kit. A weak answer says 'it's the one in the protocol.' A strong answer names the axis explicitly — storage versus driving expression versus carrying DNA into a second organism — and, for a large construct, states the roughly 10-15 kb ceiling of ordinary plasmids and explains in one sentence why a cosmid or BAC solves it instead.

questions.prompt: Match each vector type to its defining purpose.

right.text: Stores, amplifies, and subclones DNA without a strong promoter driving it
Carries a strong inducible promoter positioned to drive high protein yield
Replicates in two different host organisms
Maintains very large (100+ kb) inserts stably at single copy

questions.explanation: Each type is defined by what it's built to do: cloning vectors store DNA, expression vectors drive protein production, shuttle vectors bridge two organisms, and BACs trade copy number for capacity.

questions.prompt: The Gateway cloning system replaces restriction digestion and ligation with what mechanism?

options.text: Site-specific recombination between att sites
Heat-shock transformation
Blue-white colony screening
Chloramphenicol amplification

explanations.a: Correct — BP and LR reactions use lambda-derived site-specific recombination between att sites, so no restriction enzymes or ligase are involved in moving the insert between vectors.
explanations.b: Heat-shock transformation is how the resulting plasmid gets into cells, not how the insert moves between vectors.
explanations.c: Blue-white screening is a separate technique for distinguishing recombinants in lacZ-alpha vectors; Gateway doesn't rely on it.
explanations.d: Chloramphenicol amplification is a plasmid-prep trick unrelated to how the insert is transferred between vectors.

questions.prompt: Why can't a standard high-copy plasmid stably carry a 150 kb insert?

options.text: Restriction enzymes cannot cut fragments that large
Large inserts destabilize and delete under multi-copy replication, so single-copy F-factor-based vectors are used instead
E. coli cannot take up any plasmid larger than a few kilobases
Plasmid backbones lack enough promoters for a 150 kb insert

explanations.a: Restriction enzymes cut fine regardless of the fragment's downstream size; that's not the limiting factor.
explanations.b: Correct — replicating a huge insert many times per cell drives instability and deletion, which is exactly why BACs trade high copy number for the F-factor's single-copy, low-recombination replication.
explanations.c: E. coli can take up plasmids well beyond a few kilobases; uptake size isn't the bottleneck here.
explanations.d: Promoter count has nothing to do with an insert's physical stability during replication.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of moving a PCR product into a Gateway destination vector.

items.text: PCR the ORF with attB-site primers
BP react with a donor vector to generate an entry clone
LR react the entry clone with a destination vector
Transform the resulting expression clone into cells

questions.explanation: The attB-flanked PCR product is first BP-reacted into an attL-flanked entry clone, which is then LR-reacted into any attR-flanked destination vector, and only that final construct is transformed for use.

lessons.label: Origins, Copy Number & Plasmid Compatibility

sections.heading: How a ColE1-family origin counts its own copies
sections.body: pBR322 and its many descendants replicate from a pMB1/ColE1-type origin whose copy number is set by an RNA circuit, not a protein sensor. A transcript called RNA II is made across the origin and, if left uncut, is processed by RNase H into the primer that starts replication. A second, shorter transcript, RNA I, is made from the opposite strand in the convergent direction; if RNA I anneals to RNA II first, RNase H can't act, and that round of initiation is blocked. In pBR322, the Rop (Rom) protein, a small dimer encoded near the origin, stabilizes the RNA I-RNA II pairing and tightens this throttle, holding copy number to roughly 15-20 per cell. pUC-series vectors deleted rop and carry a point mutation in RNA II that weakens RNA I binding; the result is a temperature-sensitive origin running around 500-700 copies per cell at 37 degrees C and rising higher still at 42 degrees C, since the mutant RNA II structure destabilizes further as temperature climbs.

sections.heading: Relaxed versus stringent control
sections.body: ColE1-family origins are called relaxed-control: replication needs the host's own machinery and the RNA I/RNA II circuit, but no plasmid-encoded protein synthesis. That's why adding chloramphenicol late in a culture, which halts host chromosome replication and most new protein synthesis, still lets these plasmids keep copying — the classic amplification trick behind large-scale plasmid preps. The F-factor sits at the opposite extreme: stringent control, requiring its own initiator protein and partition machinery, holding copy number at one or two per cell and refusing to amplify under chloramphenicol at all.

sections.heading: Incompatibility and the toxicity tradeoff
sections.body: Two plasmids that share the same replication-control circuitry belong to the same incompatibility (Inc) group and cannot be maintained stably together: the cell's copy-number-counting machinery can't tell them apart, so at each division they segregate as one shared pool, and one type is stochastically lost over generations even without any selection against it. Keeping two plasmids stably in the same cell means pairing origins from different Inc groups — a ColE1-derived plasmid alongside a p15A-derived one, as in the pACYC-based vectors, is the standard combination. Copy number also isn't a free win: a gene product that's mildly toxic in excess, common for membrane proteins and some transcription factors, can select against a high-copy plasmid, producing colonies riddled with deletions or point mutations that knock the protein out; moving that gene to a low-copy vector is often the fix.

lessons.workedExample: A student clones a membrane transporter into a pUC-derived high-copy plasmid and gets almost no colonies, and the few that grow sequence back with frameshift mutations in the insert. Subcloning the identical insert into a pACYC184-derivative, whose p15A origin holds copy number to roughly 10-12 per cell, gives healthy colonies with an intact, correct sequence — the lower dose of transporter protein per cell no longer overwhelms the membrane, and there's far less selective pressure favoring cells that knocked the gene out.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking 'why this origin, why this copy number' is separating students who understand plasmid biology from those who picked a vector out of habit. A weak answer says high copy is simply better because it gives more DNA. A strong answer can sketch the RNA I/RNA II throttle in a sentence, and can name a concrete case where low copy is the right call — a toxic gene product, or the need to keep a second, compatible plasmid running in the same cell.

questions.prompt: What directly blocks replication initiation at a ColE1-type origin?

options.text: RNA I binding RNA II and preventing it from being processed into a primer
Methylation of the origin DNA
The antibiotic-resistance protein binding the origin
Direct binding of RNA polymerase to the origin sequence

explanations.a: Correct — when RNA I anneals to RNA II before RNase H can cleave it, RNA II can't become a primer, and that initiation attempt fails.
explanations.b: DNA methylation of the origin is not part of the ColE1 copy-number circuit; the regulation runs through RNA-RNA pairing.
explanations.c: The resistance marker has no role in replication control; it's a separate gene entirely.
explanations.d: RNA polymerase makes RNA II and RNA I, but the block itself comes from RNA I pairing with RNA II, not from polymerase binding directly.

questions.prompt: pUC19 reaches much higher copy number than its parent pBR322 mainly because it:

options.text: Carries a stronger promoter driving its resistance marker
Lacks Rop/Rom and carries a point mutation in RNA II that weakens RNA I binding
Uses a completely unrelated, high-copy-by-design origin
Has a larger multiple cloning site

explanations.a: Marker promoter strength affects antibiotic resistance levels, not plasmid copy number.
explanations.b: Correct — deleting rop and destabilizing the RNA I-RNA II pairing both loosen the throttle on initiation, pushing copy number from roughly 15-20 to 500-700 or more per cell.
explanations.c: pUC19's origin is a pMB1/ColE1 derivative, the same family as pBR322's, not an unrelated design.
explanations.d: MCS size has no bearing on how often the origin fires.

questions.prompt: Why does adding chloramphenicol late in a culture amplify ColE1-type plasmids for a maxiprep?

options.text: ColE1-type plasmids are relaxed-control, so they keep replicating using host machinery while chromosome replication and most new protein synthesis stop
Chloramphenicol directly activates the origin sequence
Chloramphenicol selectively kills only the host chromosome, leaving the cell intact
It permanently converts a low-copy origin into a high-copy one

explanations.a: Correct — relaxed control means the plasmid doesn't need new plasmid-encoded protein to keep initiating, so it keeps copying after chloramphenicol halts most host synthesis.
