sections.body: A pluripotent stem cell left alone in culture is not useful for most experiments; the value comes from directed differentiation, exposing the cells to a timed sequence of growth factors and small molecules that nudge them down a specific developmental path, toward neurons, cardiac muscle, or pancreatic beta cells, for example, by mimicking the signals an embryo would normally provide. Maintaining pluripotent cells in an undifferentiated state before that step traditionally required a feeder layer: a bed of mitotically inactivated mouse embryonic fibroblasts, treated with radiation or a drug like mitomycin C so they can no longer divide but still secrete supportive growth factors and lay down matrix for the stem cells to attach to. Feeder-free, chemically defined culture systems now exist for many applications, but feeder layers remain a standard, well-understood specialized setup, and both approaches sit on top of the same basic media, incubator, and aseptic principles covered earlier in this unit.

sections.heading: Proving pluripotency: markers, teratomas, and embryoid bodies
sections.body: Deriving an iPSC line is not the same as proving it is actually pluripotent, so labs run a standard battery of tests before trusting a line for downstream work. The fastest check is immunostaining for a marker panel associated with the pluripotent state, commonly Oct4, Nanog, and the surface marker SSEA-4, which should be present broadly across the colony. The strongest functional proof is the teratoma assay: injecting the candidate cells into an immunodeficient mouse and confirming that the resulting tumor contains differentiated tissue from all three embryonic germ layers, ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm, which only a genuinely pluripotent cell population can produce. A gentler in-vitro version of the same idea is embryoid body formation: growing the pluripotent cells as free-floating 3D aggregates in suspension rather than attached to a dish. Deprived of a flat surface and directed signals, the aggregate spontaneously differentiates into a disorganized mix of cell types from multiple lineages, and that spontaneous multi-lineage output is itself used as evidence that the starting cells were pluripotent.

lessons.workedExample: A lab wants iPSC-derived cardiac cells for a drug-screening project. They reprogram a small skin biopsy sample by introducing the four Yamanaka factors, confirm pluripotency, then apply a staged protocol of growth factors that first pushes the cells toward mesoderm and then specifically toward a cardiac fate, monitoring for spontaneously beating clusters as visual confirmation that differentiation succeeded. Each stage depends on the one before it: skipping straight from reprogrammed cell to expecting mature heart cells without the intermediate signals would simply fail, since directed differentiation works by replaying developmental steps in order, not by skipping to the destination.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges bring up stem cell methods to check that a student understands these as a specialized, higher-overhead culture system rather than a magic upgrade over ordinary cell lines. A weak answer says 'we used stem cells' without naming what kind or how they were maintained. A strong answer distinguishes ESCs from iPSCs, states why iPSCs sidestep the embryo-use debate, and can explain that differentiation into a specific cell type is a deliberate, staged process, not something that happens automatically.

questions.prompt: What made Yamanaka and Takahashi's 2006 discovery significant relative to embryonic stem cells?

options.text: It showed that ordinary adult cells could be reprogrammed to pluripotency using four introduced genes, without using an embryo
It proved that embryonic stem cells cannot be pluripotent
It replaced the need for growth media in stem cell culture
It was the first successful isolation of a blastocyst's inner cell mass

explanations.a: Correct — introducing Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, and c-Myc into an adult mouse cell reprogrammed it to a pluripotent state, giving a route to pluripotent cells that did not require an embryo.
explanations.b: The discovery did not challenge that ESCs are pluripotent; it offered an alternative source of pluripotent cells.
explanations.c: iPSC culture still requires standard growth media, incubation, and aseptic technique like any other cell culture.
explanations.d: That describes the earlier derivation of embryonic stem cells (Thomson, 1998), a separate achievement from reprogramming adult cells.

questions.prompt: What is the primary purpose of a mitotically inactivated mouse embryonic fibroblast feeder layer in stem cell culture?

options.text: To directly divide alongside the stem cells and increase their number
To provide supportive growth factors and matrix while the stem cells are maintained in an undifferentiated state
To trigger differentiation into neurons
To sterilize the culture dish

explanations.a: The feeder cells are deliberately treated so they can no longer divide; their role is supportive, not proliferative.
explanations.b: Correct — inactivated feeder cells secrete growth factors and matrix that help keep pluripotent cells attached and undifferentiated, without dividing themselves.
explanations.c: Feeder layers support the undifferentiated state; directed differentiation instead uses a separate, staged sequence of growth-factor signals.
explanations.d: Sterility is maintained through aseptic technique and the biosafety cabinet, not through the feeder layer.

questions.prompt: Order the steps in producing a specific differentiated cell type from a skin biopsy using reprogramming.

items.text: Collect adult somatic cells (e.g., skin biopsy)
Introduce the four Yamanaka factors to reprogram cells to pluripotency
Maintain the resulting iPSCs in an undifferentiated state
Apply a staged directed-differentiation protocol toward the target cell type

questions.explanation: Reprogramming must happen before differentiation can be directed, and the resulting pluripotent cells must first be stably maintained before a specific developmental path is imposed on them.

lessons.label: Setting Up an Experiment: Seeding & Design

sections.heading: Seeding density and plate format
sections.body: Seeding density, the number of cells placed per unit area at the start of an experiment, sets the pace of everything downstream: too sparse and cells take days longer to reach a usable confluency or may not signal to each other normally; too dense and they hit confluency and contact inhibition before the assay's endpoint, confounding a growth measurement with a density ceiling. Multiwell plates scale this decision by surface area: a standard 6-well plate gives roughly 9.6 square centimeters of growth surface per well, a 24-well plate about 1.9 square centimeters, and a 96-well plate about 0.32 square centimeters, a roughly 30-fold range across three common formats. A protocol's seeding density, given as cells per square centimeter, has to be recalculated for whichever plate format is actually being used, not copied directly as a cell count from a different plate size.

sections.heading: The edge effect
sections.body: Wells at the perimeter of a multiwell plate, especially a 96-well plate with its high surface-area-to-volume ratio, sit closer to the drier, more temperature-variable air near the incubator's edges and inside the plate's own outer rim. Medium in those outer wells evaporates measurably faster than medium in interior wells over the same incubation period, concentrating salts and nutrients and shifting local osmolality, which by itself can alter cell growth and skew a readout independent of any treatment being tested. This is the edge effect, and it is well documented enough that a common fix is to leave the outermost ring of wells filled with sterile PBS or plain medium and unused for actual samples, sacrificing plate capacity in exchange for not silently confounding the outer data points.

sections.heading: Technical versus biological replicates
sections.body: A technical replicate is the same biological sample, split and measured or plated more than once, for example pipetting one cell suspension into three separate wells; it captures pipetting and measurement noise but says nothing about whether the result would hold in a different dish, passage, or animal. A biological replicate is an independent sample, for example three separate dishes grown from separate passages or three different donor cultures, and it is what actually lets a result generalize beyond the one dish it was measured in. A plate with three technical replicates of a single culture, however carefully pipetted, still represents an experiment of n=1 for statistical purposes. Planning backward from the final readout, deciding how many biological replicates the statistics will need and how many wells each one requires before a single cell is ever seeded, is what turns a plate layout from a guess into a design.

lessons.workedExample: A student plans a 96-well drug-response assay comparing five drug doses against a control, and initially plates each condition once per row, filling every well on the plate including the outer rim, with all six replicate wells per condition drawn from a single flask of cells. The outer-well readings run consistently higher than interior wells for every condition, a signature of the edge effect rather than a drug interaction, and because every well traces back to one flask, the whole plate is one biological replicate no matter how many wells were used. The redesign leaves the outer ring filled with plain medium only, moves each condition's six wells fully into the interior, and repeats the entire plate on three separate days using cells from three independent passages, giving a true n=3 at the biological level.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about plate layout because it is where a well-run cell culture project and a naive one diverge most visibly, and because the technical-versus-biological replicate distinction is the single most common statistical error in student projects. A weak answer calls six wells from one flask 'six replicates' without qualification. A strong answer states the biological replicate count plainly, explains how the layout avoided the edge effect, and shows the plate was planned around the final statistical comparison rather than filled in ad hoc.

questions.prompt: A team pipettes the same cell suspension into six wells of a 96-well plate and treats this as six independent data points for statistics. What is the flaw?

options.text: There is no flaw; six wells is always six replicates
All six wells are technical replicates of one biological sample, so this represents n=1 biologically, not n=6
96-well plates cannot be used for drug-response assays
The wells should have been seeded at a lower density

explanations.a: Splitting one sample across wells captures measurement noise, not independent biological variability, so it cannot be treated as six true replicates.
explanations.b: Correct — since every well traces back to the same original flask, this is one biological replicate measured six times technically; generalizable statistics need independent biological replicates, not more wells from the same source.
explanations.c: 96-well plates are routinely used for exactly this kind of assay; the plate format is not the problem here.
explanations.d: Seeding density affects confluency and growth rate, but it does not resolve the technical-versus-biological replicate issue described.

questions.prompt: Why do outer wells on a 96-well plate often give systematically different readings than interior wells, independent of any treatment?

options.text: Outer wells receive more light exposure
Outer wells evaporate faster, concentrating salts and shifting osmolality — the edge effect
Outer wells are seeded with more cells by default
Outer wells are farther from the incubator's CO2 source

explanations.a: Standard incubators are kept dark or the plate is not the source of a light-exposure difference between well positions.
explanations.b: Correct — outer wells lose medium volume to evaporation faster than interior wells, concentrating the remaining solutes and altering the local environment enough to skew growth or assay readouts.
explanations.c: Seeding density is set by the researcher and does not vary by well position unless a pipetting error occurs.
explanations.d: CO2 diffuses through the incubator atmosphere at a scale much larger than well position on a single plate; that is not the mechanism behind the edge effect.

questions.prompt: Match each plate format to its approximate growth surface area per well.

right.text: ~9.6 cm² per well
~1.9 cm² per well
~0.32 cm² per well

questions.explanation: Growth surface area scales down substantially as well count goes up on a plate of similar overall footprint, from roughly 9.6 cm² in a 6-well down to roughly 0.32 cm² in a 96-well, a factor that must be used to convert a seeding density into an actual cell count per well.

questions.prompt: Order these steps in planning a plate layout backward from the final readout.

items.text: Decide the statistical comparison the final readout must support
Determine how many independent biological replicates that comparison requires
Calculate seeding density and wells needed per replicate, avoiding outer edge wells
Seed the plate and begin the experiment

questions.explanation: Designing backward from the readout means the statistical need drives the replicate count, which in turn drives how the plate is physically laid out, before any cells are actually seeded.

lessons.label: Passaging & Subculture

sections.heading: Reading confluency before it reads you
sections.body: Confluency is the visual estimate of how much of a flask's growth surface is covered by cells, judged by eye under a light microscope as a rough percentage. Most adherent lines are split somewhere in the 70-90% confluency window, not at 100%: past that point, cells run out of surface area and nutrients at the same time, normal (non-transformed) lines slow division under contact inhibition, and the culture's local pH drops as crowded cells dump acidic metabolic byproducts into a shrinking volume of medium. A flask left too long doesn't just stall, it changes — morphology shifts, some lines round up and detach spontaneously, and the population that eventually gets passaged is whichever cells tolerated the stress best, not a representative sample of the original culture.

sections.heading: Detaching the cells without killing them
sections.body: Adherent cells are stuck down by calcium- and magnesium-dependent adhesion proteins (cadherins and integrins binding the flask surface and each other), so lifting them requires breaking both. Spent medium is removed and the flask is rinsed with PBS to wash away serum, whose protease inhibitors would otherwise block the next step; trypsin-EDTA is then added, where trypsin is a serine protease that cleaves the extracellular adhesion proteins and EDTA chelates the Ca2+/Mg2+ those proteins need to function. After a short 37C incubation (typically 3-5 minutes), detachment is confirmed by gently tapping the flask, and the reaction is stopped by adding serum-containing medium, whose serum proteins inhibit the trypsin before it can start damaging membrane proteins on the now-detached, more vulnerable cells.

sections.heading: Split ratio and passage number as a tracked variable
sections.body: The split ratio (e.g., 1:3 or 1:10) is the fraction of the detached cell suspension reseeded into each new vessel, and it sets how many doublings pass before the next split is needed. Passage number counts how many times a line has been subcultured since it was established or thawed, and serious labs log it deliberately, because continuous passaging is not neutral: over months of splitting, fast-growing subclones are unintentionally selected for, chromosomal abnormalities accumulate, and differentiation markers or receptor expression can drift from the line's original phenotype. Finite (non-immortalized) normal cell lines additionally hit the Hayflick limit — Leonard Hayflick and Paul Moorhead's 1961 finding that normal human fibroblasts stop dividing after roughly 40-60 population doublings — after which the culture senesces outright rather than merely drifting.

lessons.workedExample: A team's HEK293 cells at passage 45 are growing more slowly and look visibly flatter and larger than a reference photo of the same line at passage 15. Rather than troubleshoot the medium or incubator, the correct diagnosis is passage-driven drift: continuous subculturing has likely selected for a phenotypically different subpopulation. The fix isn't a better protocol tweak on the current flask, it's discarding it and thawing a lower-passage vial from frozen stock, then capping future use at a defined passage ceiling (commonly passage 20-30 post-thaw) before repeating the same drift.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about passage number because it separates teams who treat culture maintenance as routine feeding from teams who treat it as a tracked experimental variable. A weak answer describes passaging as just splitting cells when the flask gets full. A strong answer states the current passage number for their line without hesitation, explains that they capped it below a defined ceiling, and names the actual risk — genetic or phenotypic drift, or the Hayflick limit for a finite line — rather than a vague 'contamination' worry.

questions.prompt: Why is EDTA included together with trypsin during passaging, rather than using trypsin alone?

options.text: EDTA kills any bacteria present in the flask before splitting
EDTA chelates the Ca2+/Mg2+ that adhesion proteins need to function, helping release cells trypsin alone leaves attached
EDTA neutralizes the trypsin so it stops working once cells detach
EDTA lowers the pH of the trypsin solution to activate the enzyme

explanations.a: EDTA has no antimicrobial function; it is a metal-ion chelator, not a disinfectant.
explanations.b: Correct — cadherins and integrins require divalent cations to hold cells to the surface and to each other; EDTA strips those ions away, working alongside trypsin's protein-cleaving action.
explanations.c: Neutralizing trypsin is the job of the serum-containing medium added afterward, not EDTA.
explanations.d: Trypsin's activity is not driven by EDTA-mediated pH change; the two act on different targets entirely.

questions.prompt: A team keeps a single flask of a normal (non-transformed) line growing for weeks without splitting, well past 100% confluency. What is the most direct consequence?

options.text: The cells will simply keep dividing at the same rate indefinitely
Contact inhibition slows division, and the surviving, harvested population is skewed toward whichever cells tolerated the crowded, acidic conditions best
The passage number resets automatically since no split occurred
Confluency has no effect on cell behavior, only on visual appearance

explanations.a: Normal cells are contact-inhibited; unchecked exponential growth past confluency does not occur.
explanations.b: Correct — overcrowding combines nutrient depletion, acidified medium, and contact inhibition, and the population that survives to be passaged is a stress-selected subset, not the original culture.
explanations.c: Passage number only increments on an actual subculture event; leaving a flask alone does not change it.
explanations.d: Confluency changes real cell physiology (division rate, morphology, metabolite output), not just appearance.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a standard adherent-cell passage.

items.text: Aspirate the spent growth medium
Rinse the flask with PBS to remove residual serum
Add trypsin-EDTA and incubate at 37C until cells detach
Add serum-containing medium to neutralize the trypsin
Count the suspension and dilute to the target split ratio
Reseed the diluted suspension into new vessels

questions.explanation: Medium is removed first, then serum residue is washed away so it cannot block the enzyme, then trypsin-EDTA detaches the cells, then serum-containing medium stops the enzyme, then the suspension is counted and diluted, and finally reseeded.

questions.prompt: Match each passaging concept to its correct description.

right.text: Estimated percent of the growth surface covered by cells
Fraction of a detached cell suspension reseeded into each new vessel
Count of how many times a line has been subcultured since establishment or thaw
Finite division ceiling (roughly 40-60 doublings) for normal, non-immortalized fibroblasts

questions.explanation: Confluency is a surface-coverage estimate that triggers passaging; split ratio sets the dilution at each passage; passage number tracks cumulative subculture events and drift risk; the Hayflick limit is the separate, hard division ceiling that finite normal lines eventually hit.

lessons.label: Counting Cells & Growth Kinetics

sections.heading: Hemocytometer counting and its automated cousins
sections.body: A hemocytometer is a thick glass slide with a precision-etched grid and a chamber of known depth (0.1 mm on an Improved Neubauer design), so a known volume of cell suspension sits over each counting square. A technician counts cells in the four large corner squares (1 mm2 each), averages them, and multiplies by the chamber's dilution factor (10^4 per mL, from the 0.1 mm depth) and any suspension dilution to get cells/mL. Counting error follows Poisson statistics — the relative counting error shrinks as the number of cells counted grows — so the standard practice is to dilute the suspension until each square holds roughly 100-200 cells rather than counting a handful or a swarm. Automated cell counters (image-based instruments like the Countess or Vi-CELL) apply the same size-and-density logic through image analysis, trading a few minutes of manual counting for speed and operator-independent consistency, at the cost of an instrument each lab must calibrate and trust.

sections.heading: Trypan blue and the viable-count problem
sections.body: A raw hemocytometer count includes dead cells unless the culture is treated with trypan blue, a dye first described by Paul Ehrlich in 1904 and adopted into cell-viability testing because it is excluded by an intact plasma membrane but freely enters cells whose membrane integrity has already failed, staining dead cells blue while live cells stay clear (refractile) under the microscope. Viability percent is calculated as live cells divided by total (live plus dead) cells counted, times 100; a healthy, actively growing culture typically reads above 90-95% viable, and a culture that drops toward 70% or below is generally considered too compromised to trust for a critical experiment, even if the total cell number looks adequate.

sections.heading: Growth phases and seeding math
sections.body: A culture's growth curve after seeding or thawing has three phases: lag phase, where cells attach and recover with little net division; log (exponential) phase, where division proceeds at a roughly constant doubling time and the culture is at its most uniform and experimentally useful; and plateau (stationary) phase, where density-dependent inhibition and nutrient depletion slow growth back down. Doubling time is calculated from two counts, td = t * ln(2) / ln(Nt/N0), where N0 and Nt are the starting and ending counts over elapsed time t. Knowing a line's doubling time lets a team work backward from a target: to land at a desired density on a specific assay day, seed at N0 = Ntarget / 2^(days/td), rather than guessing a seeding number and hoping the timing lines up.

lessons.workedExample: A team seeds 2 x 10^5 cells in a T25 flask and counts 8 x 10^5 cells three days later, giving td = 3 * ln(2)/ln(4) = 1.5 days. Planning an assay for day 4 that needs 1 x 10^6 cells, they solve N0 = 1x10^6 / 2^(4/1.5) = 1x10^6 / 2^2.67 ~ 1.6 x 10^5, and seed that density instead of reusing the original 2 x 10^5, landing the culture at the intended density on the intended day rather than over- or under-shooting it.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges push on seeding density and doubling time because it is one of the fastest ways to tell a team that ran real growth kinetics from one that eyeballed a flask and called it 'confluent enough.' A weak answer cannot say what density they seeded at or how they picked it. A strong answer states the measured doubling time for their specific line and passage, shows the seeding calculation that targeted their assay day, and can explain why they used trypan blue viable counts rather than raw hemocytometer totals to do it.

questions.prompt: On a standard Improved Neubauer hemocytometer, why is the suspension diluted until each large square holds roughly 100-200 cells before counting?

options.text: Because the chamber depth changes if too many cells are loaded
Because Poisson counting error shrinks as the number of cells counted per square increases
Because trypan blue only stains dead cells correctly below that density
Because the automated counter cannot process denser suspensions

explanations.a: Chamber depth is fixed by the glass etching; loading density does not change it.
explanations.b: Correct — counting statistics improve with more counted events, so a moderate, consistent count per square (rather than a handful or an overcrowded field) minimizes relative counting error.
explanations.c: Trypan blue's exclusion mechanism (intact vs. compromised membranes) does not depend on how many cells are in the field.
explanations.d: This question concerns manual hemocytometer counting, not an automated instrument's throughput limits.

questions.prompt: Why does trypan blue selectively stain dead cells rather than all cells in a suspension?

options.text: It binds specifically to DNA that is only exposed in dividing cells
It is excluded by an intact plasma membrane but enters cells whose membrane integrity has failed
It reacts chemically with trypsin residue left over from detachment
Live cells actively pump the dye back out through ion channels

explanations.a: Trypan blue is a membrane-exclusion dye, not a DNA-binding stain, and is unrelated to division state.
explanations.b: Correct — this is the exclusion principle: intact membranes keep the dye out, so only cells with compromised membranes take it up and appear blue.
explanations.c: There is no chemical reaction between trypan blue and trypsin; the mechanism is membrane permeability, not residual enzyme.
explanations.d: There is no active pump involved; exclusion is passive, based purely on membrane integrity.

questions.prompt: Order the phases of a standard post-seeding growth curve.

items.text: Lag phase
Log (exponential) phase
Plateau (stationary) phase

questions.explanation: Cells first attach and recover with little division (lag), then divide at a roughly constant doubling time (log), then slow as density and nutrient limits set in (plateau).

questions.prompt: Match each term to its correct role in cell counting and growth kinetics.

right.text: Fixed at 0.1 mm, giving the 10^4/mL dilution factor in the count formula
Distinguishes live from dead cells via membrane exclusion
Derived from two counts over elapsed time using td = t*ln2/ln(Nt/N0)
Works backward from a target density and day using the measured doubling time

questions.explanation: The fixed chamber depth defines the count-to-concentration conversion; trypan blue supplies the viable fraction; doubling time is calculated from paired counts; and seeding density is planned by inverting the doubling-time formula for a target day.

lessons.label: Contamination I: Bacteria, Fungi & Yeast

sections.heading: Reading the flask: turbidity, color, and colonies
sections.body: Gross contamination announces itself through signs visible without special equipment. Bacterial contamination clouds the medium (turbidity, from a dense bacterial suspension scattering light) and drives a fast, unmistakable color shift in phenol-red-buffered medium: bacteria metabolize glucose so rapidly that the medium turns from red toward yellow within hours to a day, far faster than the slow, gradual yellowing a healthy, growing culture produces over several days as it consumes nutrients normally. Yeast contamination often shows the same rapid acidification alongside a fine, granular haze under the microscope, sometimes with visible budding cells. Fungal contamination is typically slower to appear and looks different entirely: filamentous hyphae growing as visible threads or a fuzzy patch on the medium surface, sometimes with spore-like structures, often days after the inciting breach in technique.

sections.heading: Where contamination actually comes from
sections.body: The overwhelming majority of contamination events trace back to lapses in aseptic technique rather than to the incubator itself: talking or breathing over an open flask, working outside a laminar-flow hood's protected air zone, reusing a pipette tip between reagents, or touching a sterile cap to a non-sterile surface. Reagents and media are a second common source if a bottle is opened and closed carelessly or stored past its useful sterility. Incubators themselves can become a slow-building reservoir — the humidity water pan at the bottom, if not cleaned and refreshed regularly, can harbor bacteria and fungi that aerosolize into the chamber over weeks — but this is a maintenance failure layered on top of, not a substitute for, technique discipline at the bench.

sections.heading: Why penicillin-streptomycin is a crutch, not a fix
sections.body: Penicillin-streptomycin (pen-strep) added to routine culture medium suppresses many common susceptible bacteria at the working concentration, which is exactly why it is tempting to leave it in permanently as insurance. The problem is that this suppression can mask low-level or resistant contamination rather than eliminate it: a culture can look clean to the eye while quietly harboring bacteria kept just below the threshold of visible turbidity, and chronic antibiotic exposure additionally selects for resistant organisms over time, so when contamination does break through, it is more likely to be resistant to the very drug meant to control it. Pen-strep also does nothing for fungal or mycoplasma contamination. For these reasons, many core facilities recommend keeping stock and experimental cultures antibiotic-free by default, reserving antibiotics for specific, short, justified situations, precisely so that any real contamination reveals itself immediately rather than being chemically hidden.

lessons.workedExample: A team checks their T25 flask in the morning and finds the medium cloudy and distinctly more yellow than the identical flask fed the day before. Under the microscope they see motile rod-shaped organisms moving independently of the adherent cells. The correct response is immediate disposal of the flask (autoclave or appropriate biohazard protocol) and a review of the last technique steps used, not adding pen-strep to the medium and continuing, since surviving organisms already resistant to the antibiotic would simply persist unseen.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about contamination signs and pen-strep specifically because it tests whether a team understands aseptic technique as the actual safeguard, versus treating an antibiotic as a substitute for it. A weak answer says they 'just add pen-strep to be safe.' A strong answer names the specific visual tells (fast phenol-red shift and turbidity for bacteria, slower fuzzy growth for fungi), explains why chronic antibiotic use can mask low-grade or resistant contamination instead of preventing it, and describes what technique step they tightened after a contamination event rather than what drug they added.

questions.prompt: A flask of medium turns from red to yellow within hours and looks visibly cloudy. What does this timing and appearance most strongly suggest?

options.text: Normal healthy growth, since all growing cultures gradually turn the medium yellow
Bacterial or yeast contamination, whose rapid metabolism drives fast acidification and turbidity
Fungal contamination, which is defined by an overnight color change
A sign the medium was simply made incorrectly and needs no further action

explanations.a: Healthy cultures do yellow the medium, but gradually over days, not within hours, and without turbidity.
explanations.b: Correct — bacteria and yeast metabolize glucose fast enough to acidify phenol-red medium within hours, and dense microbial growth causes visible cloudiness that host cells alone do not.
explanations.c: Fungal contamination is typically slower to become visible and shows filamentous or fuzzy growth rather than this fast, generalized clouding.
explanations.d: A media preparation error would not typically cause this specific fast-onset, turbidity-plus-color-shift pattern; it points to active microbial growth.

questions.prompt: Why do many core facilities recommend keeping routine cultures antibiotic-free rather than always including penicillin-streptomycin?

options.text: Because pen-strep is more expensive than most culture media components
Because chronic exposure can mask low-level or resistant contamination and select for resistant organisms, while doing nothing for fungi or mycoplasma
Because pen-strep prevents cells from attaching to the flask surface
Because regulatory agencies ban antibiotic use in all research cell culture

explanations.a: Cost is a minor factor at most; it is not the reason facilities discourage routine use.
explanations.b: Correct — antibiotics can chemically hide contamination that would otherwise be visible, select for resistance with prolonged use, and leave fungal and mycoplasma contamination completely unaddressed.
explanations.c: Pen-strep does not interfere with normal cell adhesion at standard working concentrations.
explanations.d: There is no blanket regulatory ban; the recommendation is a best-practice norm, not a legal requirement.

questions.prompt: Match each contamination sign to the organism type it most strongly indicates.

left.text: Rapid turbidity plus fast phenol-red shift within hours
Visible filamentous threads or fuzzy patches appearing over several days
Fine granular haze with visible budding cells under the microscope

right.text: Bacterial contamination
Fungal contamination
Yeast contamination

questions.explanation: Bacteria act fastest, driving rapid acidification and turbidity; fungi grow more slowly into visible filamentous structures; yeast shows a distinct granular, budding appearance often with its own fast acidification.

lessons.label: Contamination II: The Mycoplasma Problem

sections.heading: A contaminant that looks like nothing at all
sections.body: Mycoplasma are among the smallest self-replicating bacteria, roughly 0.1-0.3 micrometers across, and they lack a cell wall entirely. Both properties matter for how dangerous they are in culture: their small size lets them pass straight through the 0.2-micrometer filters used to sterilize media and reagents, and because they never reach bacterial or fungal densities that cloud the medium, an infected flask stays clear, keeps a normal pH, and looks completely healthy to the naked eye and under a standard light microscope. Underneath that clean appearance, mycoplasma compete with host cells for glucose and amino acids, alter proliferation rate, and have been shown to shift gene expression, cytokine signaling, and cell morphology in the cells they infect — changing the actual biology a researcher believes they are studying while leaving no visible trace. Surveys have repeatedly found this is not a rare edge case: FDA testing of more than 20,000 cell cultures in the early 1990s found about 15% mycoplasma-positive, and broader literature surveys have put the range at roughly 15-35% of continuous cell lines contaminated at some point, making mycoplasma one of the most common invalidating problems in published cell-culture research.

sections.heading: Detecting what you cannot see
sections.body: Because mycoplasma gives no visual warning, detection requires a dedicated test. PCR-based assays amplify conserved regions of the mycoplasma 16S ribosomal RNA gene, returning a sensitive, same-day result, and are now the standard method at most core facilities. DAPI or Hoechst staining, dyes that bind DNA and fluoresce under UV light, reveal mycoplasma indirectly: because host-cell DNA is confined to the large nucleus, a heavily infected culture shows extra small, punctate DNA signals scattered in the cytoplasm outside the nucleus, which is mycoplasma DNA rather than host DNA, visible on any fluorescence microscope without specialized reagents. Luminescence-based kits take a third approach, detecting mycoplasma-specific enzyme activity released into the conditioned medium and converting it into a light signal read on a plate reader, giving a fast, microscope-free result well suited to screening many flasks at once. Because contamination can be introduced at any point, testing on a monthly cadence, and always before or after long-term storage or sharing reagents between labs, is the standard recommendation.

sections.heading: Why an infection this invisible still invalidates data
sections.body: Mycoplasma's damage lands directly on the variables cell-culture experiments most often measure: proliferation rate, apoptosis, signaling pathway activity, and cytokine output. Because the infected culture looks and grows normally to routine inspection, this confound is silent — a team can run, analyze, and publish an entire experiment without ever suspecting the result reflects mycoplasma metabolism rather than their intended biology. This is why major journals and funders now commonly require documented mycoplasma-testing before publication or grant renewal, treating a clear PCR or DAPI result as a baseline precondition for trusting any cell-culture-based finding, in the same way STR authentication is required to confirm identity.

lessons.workedExample: A team's proliferation assay shows unusually slow and inconsistent doubling times across replicate flasks, despite the medium staying clear and pH-normal the entire time. Suspecting an invisible cause rather than pipetting error, they run a PCR mycoplasma test, which comes back positive. Because established mycoplasma infections are difficult to eliminate reliably with antibiotics without risking incomplete clearance, they discard the infected line entirely and restart from a low-passage frozen stock that tests negative, rather than attempting to treat and reuse the contaminated flask.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe mycoplasma specifically because it is the contamination story that most rewards actually knowing the mechanism rather than pattern-matching 'contamination = cloudy flask.' A weak answer assumes a clear, normal-looking flask is automatically clean. A strong answer explains why mycoplasma evades visual detection (no cell wall, sub-filter size), names an actual detection method with how it works (PCR targeting 16S rRNA, or DAPI staining showing extranuclear DNA puncta), and states that a positive result invalidates prior data rather than being a minor housekeeping issue to fix quietly.

questions.prompt: Why can mycoplasma pass through the 0.2-micrometer filters used to sterilize cell culture media?

options.text: Because mycoplasma are resistant to the mechanical stress of filtration
Because mycoplasma lack a cell wall and are smaller than typical bacteria, roughly 0.1-0.3 micrometers across
Because filters are only rated to stop fungi, not bacteria of any kind
Because mycoplasma actively digest the filter membrane

explanations.a: The issue is size and cell-wall absence, not physical resistance to pressure or stress.
explanations.b: Correct — their small size and lack of a rigid cell wall let mycoplasma slip through pores that stop most other bacteria.
explanations.c: Standard 0.2-micrometer filters are rated to stop typical bacteria; mycoplasma is the well-known exception because of its size.
explanations.d: There is no enzymatic digestion of the filter membrane involved.

questions.prompt: In DAPI or Hoechst staining for mycoplasma, what visual pattern indicates infection?

options.text: The host nucleus disappears entirely, leaving no DNA signal
Small, punctate DNA signals appear in the cytoplasm outside the nucleus
The dye turns the entire medium a visibly different color
Host chromosomes become visibly fragmented inside the nucleus

explanations.a: The host nucleus remains intact and stained; mycoplasma infection does not eliminate it.
explanations.b: Correct — mycoplasma DNA sits outside the host nucleus, so the DNA-binding dye lights up small extranuclear puncta distinct from the large nuclear signal.
explanations.c: DAPI/Hoechst staining is read by fluorescence microscopy on the cells themselves, not as a bulk medium color change.
explanations.d: This staining detects DNA location, not chromosome fragmentation, and mycoplasma infection does not by itself fragment host chromosomes.

questions.prompt: Historical surveys, including FDA testing of over 20,000 cultures in the early 1990s, put continuous cell-line mycoplasma contamination rates in roughly what range?

options.text: Less than 1%
About 15-35%
Nearly 100%, essentially all cell lines
Exactly 50%, per a single fixed FDA figure

explanations.a: This badly understates the documented prevalence; contamination was far more common than a rare edge case.
explanations.b: Correct — the FDA's early-1990s survey found about 15% positive, and broader literature surveys reported up to roughly 35%, giving the commonly cited 15-35% range.
explanations.c: This overstates the finding; contamination was common but far from universal.
explanations.d: No single figure of exactly 50% was reported; the documented range spans roughly 15-35% depending on the survey.

questions.prompt: Match each mycoplasma detection method to how it actually works.

right.text: Amplifies conserved 16S ribosomal RNA gene sequences for a sensitive, same-day result
Fluorescent DNA dye reveals extranuclear DNA puncta outside the host nucleus
Detects mycoplasma-specific enzyme activity in conditioned medium as a light signal

questions.explanation: PCR targets a conserved mycoplasma gene sequence directly; DAPI/Hoechst staining exploits the fact that mycoplasma DNA sits outside the host nucleus; luminescence kits detect a mycoplasma enzymatic signature released into the medium.

lessons.label: Cryopreservation & Cell Banking

sections.heading: Freezing medium and the cryoprotectant it needs
sections.body: Standard freezing medium is complete growth medium (often with extra serum) plus roughly 10% DMSO (dimethyl sulfoxide) as a cryoprotectant. DMSO's protective effect against freezing injury was first reported by Lovelock and Bishop in a 1959 Nature paper: the small, highly membrane-permeant molecule enters the cell and modifies how intracellular water freezes, reducing the lethal concentration of solutes that would otherwise build up around the cell as ice forms outside it. An older cryoprotectant, glycerol, had been discovered by accident in 1949 by Polge, Smith, and Parkes while preserving fowl sperm, but DMSO's superior membrane permeability made it the practical standard for mammalian cell lines once its protective mechanism was understood a decade later.

sections.heading: Controlled-rate cooling and the two-factor problem
sections.body: Freezing damages cells through two competing mechanisms, formalized by Peter Mazur in a 1970 Science paper on cooling velocity: cool too fast and water inside the cell has no time to leave before it freezes, forming lethal intracellular ice; cool too slowly and the cell sits too long in an increasingly concentrated extracellular solute environment as surrounding water freezes into ice first, causing damaging osmotic dehydration. Mazur's two-factor hypothesis identified an intermediate cooling rate, near -1 degree C per minute for many mammalian cell types, that balances both risks. In practice this is achieved either with an isopropanol-jacketed passive freezing container placed in a -80C freezer, which approximates the target rate through the alcohol's controlled heat loss, or with a programmable rate-controlled freezer for more demanding applications, after which vials move to long-term storage in liquid or vapor-phase nitrogen (roughly -196C or -150C) where essentially all enzymatic and metabolic activity stops.

sections.heading: Rapid thaw and the master/working bank scheme
sections.body: Thawing reverses the timing logic: vials are moved from nitrogen storage directly into a 37C water bath for a fast, roughly 1-2 minute thaw, minimizing time spent at intermediate temperatures where damaging ice recrystallization can occur, then promptly diluted into fresh medium to dilute out the DMSO before it becomes cytotoxic at room temperature. Labs organize their frozen stock into two tiers: a master cell bank (MCB), a large batch frozen at the lowest practical, verified passage number immediately after a line is established or received, and a working cell bank (WCB), expanded from a single thawed master vial for day-to-day experimental use. When a working stock's passage number climbs high enough to raise drift concerns, the lab discards it and thaws a fresh vial from the master bank rather than continuing to passage indefinitely, resetting the passage count and containing the genetic and phenotypic drift that accumulates with continuous subculture.

lessons.workedExample: A lab receiving a new cell line immediately expands it just enough to freeze 50 vials at passage 5, sealing these away untouched as the master cell bank. All day-to-day experiments are run from a working cell bank expanded from one thawed master vial at a time; once that working stock reaches passage 20, the lab discards it rather than pushing it to passage 40, and thaws a fresh vial from the still-low-passage master bank instead, keeping every experiment within a bounded passage window rather than drifting further with each year of continuous use.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about banking strategy because it reveals whether a team understands cryopreservation as a planned system rather than a single freezer event. A weak answer says they 'froze some cells as backup.' A strong answer distinguishes a master bank from a working bank, states the DMSO concentration and approximate cooling rate they used and why (the two-factor damage tradeoff), and explains that returning to a low-passage frozen vial, not endless passaging, is the actual long-term defense against drift.

questions.prompt: What is the primary mechanism by which DMSO protects cells during freezing?

options.text: It coats the outside of the cell to physically block ice crystals from forming nearby
It permeates the cell membrane and modifies intracellular water freezing to reduce lethal solute concentration
It lowers the melting point of the growth medium so it never freezes at all
It kills any contaminating bacteria present in the frozen vial

explanations.a: DMSO's protection is intracellular and permeative, not an external physical coating.
explanations.b: Correct — as a small, membrane-permeant molecule, DMSO enters the cell and changes how intracellular water freezes, reducing the damaging solute concentration effect described by Lovelock and Bishop in 1959.
explanations.c: The freezing medium still freezes; DMSO changes how ice forms and how solutes concentrate, not whether freezing occurs.
explanations.d: DMSO is a cryoprotectant, not an antimicrobial agent.

questions.prompt: According to Mazur's two-factor hypothesis, what happens if a cell suspension is cooled much faster than the optimal rate?

options.text: Cells are damaged by osmotic dehydration from prolonged exposure to concentrated extracellular solutes
Intracellular water has no time to leave the cell before freezing, forming lethal intracellular ice
The cells simply enter a dormant state with no damage
DMSO becomes chemically inert below a certain cooling rate

explanations.a: Osmotic dehydration from prolonged solute exposure is the risk of cooling too slowly, not too fast.
explanations.b: Correct — Mazur's 1970 work showed that overly fast cooling traps water inside the cell before it can exit, and that water then freezes into damaging intracellular ice.
explanations.c: Fast cooling is actively damaging, not neutral or protective.
explanations.d: DMSO's protective chemistry is not switched off by cooling rate; the damage mechanism is physical ice formation, not DMSO inactivation.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of freezing and later using a banked cell line.

items.text: Harvest and count cells, then resuspend in freezing medium with ~10% DMSO
Cool at a controlled rate near -1C/min toward -80C
Transfer vials to long-term liquid or vapor-phase nitrogen storage
Thaw rapidly in a 37C water bath and dilute promptly into fresh medium

questions.explanation: Cells are first suspended in DMSO-containing freezing medium, then cooled at a controlled intermediate rate, then moved to nitrogen for stable long-term storage, and later thawed quickly and diluted to remove the cytotoxic DMSO before use.

questions.prompt: Match each cell-banking term to its correct role.

right.text: Large batch frozen at the lowest practical, verified passage number soon after a line is established
Stock expanded from one master vial and used for routine day-to-day experiments
Long-term storage temperature (~-196C or -150C) where enzymatic activity is effectively arrested

questions.explanation: The master bank preserves the lowest-passage reference stock; the working bank absorbs the wear of routine use and gets discarded and replenished from the master when passage number climbs too high; nitrogen storage is what keeps both banks biologically frozen in time between uses.

lessons.label: Cell Line Authentication

sections.heading: A problem that never fully went away
sections.body: Cell lines circulating between laboratories are not always what their label claims, ranging from outright mislabeling to one fast-growing line silently overtaking and replacing another in shared labware — the cross-contamination problem HeLa itself caused, documented by Walter Nelson-Rees through the 1970s and covered in this track's landmark unit. Systematic text-mining shows the problem never disappeared: a 2019 eLife study by Babic and colleagues scanned roughly two million PubMed Central papers, identifying over 300,000 cell-line name mentions, and found about 8.6% of those named cell lines were on the known-problematic list of misidentified or contaminated lines. The same study found papers that cited a formal Research Resource Identifier (RRID) for their cell line had a notably lower problematic rate, about 3.3%, suggesting that consistently documenting identity is itself part of the fix. The consequence is direct and silent: a misidentified line still grows, divides, and responds to reagents like some real cell type, so every downstream conclusion built on it inherits the error without any obvious warning sign.

sections.heading: STR profiling as the standard fix
sections.body: Short tandem repeat (STR) profiling authenticates a cell line by amplifying a defined panel of short, highly variable repeat-length markers scattered across the genome — the same underlying technology used in human forensic identity testing — and comparing the resulting pattern of allele lengths against a reference database of authenticated lines, such as those held by ATCC or DSMZ. Because STR repeat-length patterns are inherited and distinctive to an individual source (and, for many established cancer lines, retain a stable, characteristic signature despite ongoing chromosomal instability), a strong match confirms the culture is genuinely what it is labeled as, while a mismatch flags contamination or mislabeling directly. The practice was formalized into a technical standard in 2011 as ANSI/ATCC ASN-0002-2011, and documented STR authentication of human cell lines is now commonly required by journals and expected by funders, including as part of NIH grant review, before results are trusted or published.

sections.heading: Reading a match report
sections.body: An STR authentication report lists allele values, the repeat-unit counts at each of typically 8 to 20 marker loci, for the tested sample side by side with the same loci from the claimed reference line. Authentication software (or a manual comparison against a reference profile) computes a percent concordance across those loci, and the field's accepted convention treats roughly 80% or greater allele match as confirming identity, while a substantially lower score indicates the culture is a different line entirely, often a known, frequently mislabeled contaminant such as HeLa given its historical dominance among misidentified stocks, rather than the cell type it was assumed to be.

lessons.workedExample: A team submits their 'MCF-7' stock for STR testing before their science-fair project. The report comes back showing only about 40% allele concordance against the reference MCF-7 profile, well below the roughly 80% confirmation threshold, but a near-complete match against a different, unrelated registered line in the database. Rather than trust the freezer label, they treat the mismatch as conclusive evidence of upstream cross-contamination, discard the stock, and order freshly authenticated cells from a verified cell bank before continuing.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges raise cell-line authentication because it distinguishes a team that assumes the freezer label is ground truth from one that treats identity as something to be verified. A weak answer has never heard of STR profiling and assumes any line grown from a reputable source must be correct. A strong answer explains what STR profiling actually compares (repeat-length markers against a reference database), can state the roughly 80% concordance convention used to call a match, and connects the requirement to the real, ongoing rate of misidentified lines still found in the literature — not just to the historical HeLa story.

questions.prompt: What does STR profiling actually compare to authenticate a cell line's identity?

options.text: The line's growth rate against a published reference growth curve
The pattern of short tandem repeat allele lengths at a defined panel of genomic loci, compared to a reference database
Whether the cells stain positive for a single tissue-specific surface marker
The passage number recorded in the lab's freezer log

explanations.a: Growth rate is affected by many culture conditions and is not a reliable, specific identity marker.
explanations.b: Correct — STR profiling compares repeat-length markers across a defined set of loci against a known reference, the same underlying technology used in forensic identity testing.
explanations.c: A single marker is not sufficient for authentication; STR profiling uses a multi-locus panel precisely because one marker is not distinctive enough.
explanations.d: Passage number is a separate tracked variable about culture history, unrelated to confirming genetic identity.

questions.prompt: In the 2019 Babic and colleagues eLife text-mining study of PubMed Central papers, what pattern did citing a Research Resource Identifier (RRID) correlate with?

options.text: A higher rate of problematic cell-line citations, about 8.6% versus a lower baseline
A lower rate of problematic cell-line citations, about 3.3% versus 8.6% overall
No measurable difference in problematic cell-line rates
A complete elimination of all misidentified cell-line citations

explanations.a: This reverses the finding; RRID-citing papers had a lower problematic rate, not a higher one.
explanations.b: Correct — the study found about 8.6% of cell-line mentions overall were on the problematic list, versus about 3.3% among papers that cited an RRID, suggesting consistent identity documentation helps.
explanations.c: The study reported a clear difference between the two rates, not a null result.
explanations.d: RRID citation correlated with a lower rate, not a complete elimination, of problematic citations.

questions.prompt: Order these milestones in the history of cell-line authentication.

items.text: Nelson-Rees documents widespread HeLa cross-contamination of other cell lines through the 1970s
ANSI/ATCC ASN-0002-2011 formalizes STR profiling as a standard for human cell-line authentication
Babic and colleagues' eLife text-mining study finds ~8.6% of cited cell lines are problematic

questions.explanation: Nelson-Rees's 1970s documentation first exposed the scale of cross-contamination; the ANSI/ATCC standard formalized STR profiling as the fix in 2011; the 2019 text-mining study then quantified how much of the problem persisted in the published literature even after the standard existed.

questions.prompt: Match each authentication concept to its correct description.

right.text: The set of short tandem repeat loci amplified and compared for identity testing
The 2011 technical standard formalizing STR profiling for human cell-line authentication
The field's accepted cutoff for calling an STR match confirmed rather than a mismatch
Documentation practice associated with a lower rate of problematic cell-line reporting in Babic's 2019 study

questions.explanation: The STR panel is the actual genetic marker set tested; the ANSI/ATCC standard is the formal rule requiring the test; the ~80% threshold is the decision rule for reading the result; RRID citation is the documentation habit shown to correlate with fewer problematic citations.

lessons.label: What "Viability" Means & How We Measure It

sections.heading: There is no viability sensor
sections.body: No instrument measures "aliveness" directly. Every viability assay is a proxy: it reads one downstream consequence of being alive and infers the rest. That gap matters because a cell can lose one property of life while briefly keeping another — a cell with a punctured membrane can still hold ATP for minutes, and a cell committed to apoptosis can still exclude dye for hours before it visibly dies. Choosing an endpoint means choosing which consequence of death you are willing to trust as a stand-in for the whole.

sections.heading: Four proxies, four failure modes
sections.body: Practically, cell biologists reach for one of four measurable proxies. Membrane integrity — does the plasma membrane still exclude a dye or retain an enzyme — is fast and cheap but blind to cells that are metabolically dying with an intact membrane, the hallmark of early apoptosis. Metabolic activity — can the cell's enzymes still reduce a redox indicator or generate ATP — is sensitive and easy to automate, but reports enzyme activity per cell, not cell number, so anything that slows metabolism without killing (serum starvation, a drug's off-target enzyme inhibition, contact inhibition at confluency) produces a false-positive cytotoxicity signal. Proliferation — is the population still dividing, read by counting over days or by dye-dilution tracking — captures growth arrest that metabolic snapshots miss, but takes longer and cannot distinguish arrest from death. Programmed death markers — phosphatidylserine flipping, caspase cleavage, DNA fragmentation — tell you not just whether cells died but how, at the cost of assay complexity.

sections.heading: Matching the assay to the question
sections.body: A 2013 review by Riss and colleagues, documented in the NIH-hosted Assay Guidance Manual, argues that most published cytotoxicity screens default to a single tetrazolium or luminescent endpoint without asking whether growth arrest, delayed death, or acute lysis is the actual mechanism under study — and that mismatch is a commonly cited source of irreproducible IC50 values across labs testing the same compound. A drug that arrests the cell cycle without killing will look identical to a mild toxin on a same-day metabolic assay; only a proliferation or death-marker follow-up separates them. The practical rule that follows through the rest of this unit: pick the endpoint that answers your specific mechanistic question, and confirm with a second, orthogonal endpoint before trusting a strong result.

lessons.workedExample: A student treats cancer cells with a plant extract and, 24 hours later, runs an MTT assay showing 60% signal loss versus untreated wells — they conclude the extract is cytotoxic. A judge asks whether the cells were merely arrested. The student reruns the plate, adding a parallel trypan blue count at the same timepoint: cell number is unchanged, membranes are intact, but MTT signal is still down 60%. The extract slows mitochondrial reductase activity without killing anything — a metabolic-inhibition artifact, not cytotoxicity. The fix is a second, independent endpoint before the causal claim.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this because it is the fastest way to tell a student who ran one convenient kit from one who understands what the kit's number actually means. A weak answer treats "percent viability" as a single ground-truth output. A strong answer names which proxy was measured (membrane integrity, metabolism, proliferation, or death marker), states its specific blind spot, and explains why that blind spot could or could not explain the result — ideally backed by a second, orthogonal assay run to close the gap.

questions.prompt: Why is it misleading to say a viability assay measures whether cells are "alive"?

options.text: Because all viability assays require radioactive isotopes
Because every assay measures one downstream proxy of life, not aliveness itself, and each proxy has blind spots
Because viability assays only work on bacterial cells
Because viability cannot be quantified numerically

explanations.a: Most modern viability assays (colorimetric, fluorescent, luminescent) use no radioactivity at all.
explanations.b: Correct — membrane integrity, metabolic activity, proliferation, and death markers are each indirect readouts, and a cell can pass one test while failing another.
explanations.c: These assays are used across mammalian, bacterial, and other cell types.
explanations.d: Viability is routinely reported as a percentage relative to untreated controls; the issue is what that percentage actually reflects.

questions.prompt: Match each viability proxy to its main blind spot.

right.text: Misses cells dying by apoptosis with a still-intact membrane
Reports enzyme activity per cell, so slowed metabolism without death looks like toxicity
Takes days and cannot distinguish growth arrest from death without a second endpoint

questions.explanation: Membrane assays only catch lysed cells; metabolic assays conflate slowed enzyme activity with cell death; proliferation assays are slow and ambiguous between arrest and death.

questions.prompt: According to the Assay Guidance Manual review by Riss and colleagues, what is a common cause of irreproducible IC50 values across labs testing the same compound?

options.text: Labs use incompatible units for concentration
Defaulting to a single metabolic or luminescent endpoint without checking whether the real mechanism is arrest, delayed death, or acute lysis
IC50 values are inherently random and cannot be reproduced
Different labs use different cell lines from different species

explanations.a: Unit mismatches are a trivial, easily-caught error, not the systematic cause the review identifies.
explanations.b: Correct — a single default endpoint can mask whether the compound arrests, slowly kills, or rapidly lyses cells, producing endpoint-dependent IC50s that don't reproduce across assay choices.
explanations.c: IC50 values are reproducible when the mechanism and endpoint are matched; the irreproducibility has an identifiable cause.
explanations.d: Species/line differences matter but are a separate, well-controlled-for variable, not the endpoint-mismatch problem described.

questions.prompt: Order these events in a cell undergoing early apoptosis, from earliest to latest.

items.text: Cell commits to the death pathway
Metabolic/mitochondrial activity begins declining
Plasma membrane integrity is finally lost

questions.explanation: Apoptotic commitment precedes the metabolic decline that follows mitochondrial involvement, and membrane rupture is a late event — which is exactly why a membrane-integrity assay can miss cells that are already dying.

lessons.label: Dye-Exclusion & Membrane-Integrity Assays

sections.heading: Trypan blue: the century-old default
sections.body: Trypan blue is a large, negatively charged azo dye — synthesized by Paul Ehrlich in 1904 — that cannot cross an intact plasma membrane but floods in once the membrane is breached, staining the dead cell's cytoplasm a visible blue under a standard light microscope. Mixed with a cell suspension and loaded onto a hemocytometer, it lets a researcher count live (clear) versus dead (blue) cells by eye in minutes, at essentially zero reagent cost. Its weakness is exactly its simplicity: it is subjective (manual counting drifts between observers), low-throughput, insensitive to early apoptosis (membrane still intact), and gives no information about how or why the dead fraction died. Automated cell counters using the same dye and image-analysis software reduce the observer-bias problem but not the biological blind spot.

sections.heading: LDH release: turning lysis into a plate reader signal
sections.body: Lactate dehydrogenase is a stable cytosolic enzyme present in essentially every cell; it stays inside an intact cell and spills into the surrounding medium only when the plasma membrane ruptures. Korzeniewski and Callewaert described an enzyme-release assay exploiting this in 1983: a coupled reaction converts released LDH activity into a colorimetric or fluorescent signal read on a plate reader, so an entire 96-well plate of lysis events can be quantified in one read instead of counted cell-by-cell. Because it measures a population-level release event rather than individual live/dead calls, it scales far better than manual dye exclusion, but it inherits the same conceptual limit: LDH release reports necrotic-type membrane rupture, not the slower loss of function that precedes it, and serum-containing media or cells that naturally leak some LDH can add background noise that must be subtracted with a no-cell blank.

sections.heading: Calcein-AM/ethidium homodimer: two-color live-dead in one well
sections.body: A two-dye combination — calcein-AM together with ethidium homodimer-1, sold in kits since the 1990s — separates live and dead cells by two independent membrane-dependent mechanisms simultaneously. Calcein-AM is nonfluorescent and membrane-permeant; only cells with active intracellular esterases and an intact membrane to retain the product cleave it into free, green-fluorescent calcein, so it reports both membrane integrity and metabolic competence at once. Ethidium homodimer-1 is membrane-impermeant and weakly fluorescent until it binds nucleic acid; it only reaches DNA in cells whose membrane has failed, where it fluoresces bright red. Overlaying both channels under a fluorescence microscope gives a direct visual live(green)/dead(red) map of a whole field, useful for imaging-based screens, but it still cannot flag a cell that is metabolically failing before its membrane and esterase activity finally give out.

lessons.workedExample: A team wants to know if their disinfectant kills bacteria on a surface swab within 60 seconds. Trypan blue works poorly here (bacterial membranes and small size make manual counts unreliable), so they switch to an LDH-release-style readout on cultured mammalian skin cells exposed to disinfectant residue: absorbance at the coupled-reaction wavelength rises sharply above the no-treatment control, confirming membrane rupture. To rule out background leakage from a stressed-but-alive population, they include a no-cell (medium-only) blank and a 100%-lysis positive control (Triton X-100) to anchor the scale from 0% to 100% release.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks "what does your live/dead percentage actually detect?" because trypan blue and LDH release both report only membrane rupture — the last step of death, not the whole process. A weak answer treats a clean trypan-blue count as proof nothing subtler happened. A strong answer states explicitly that these assays cannot see apoptosis before membrane failure, and either accepts that limitation deliberately (the question was really "did the compound lyse cells") or pairs the assay with a metabolic or death-marker readout to cover the blind spot.

questions.prompt: Why does trypan blue stain dead cells but not live ones?

options.text: Dead cells actively pump the dye in through a transporter
The dye cannot cross an intact plasma membrane, but floods in once membrane integrity is lost
Live cells destroy the dye enzymatically before it can bind
Trypan blue only binds to DNA, which is exposed only in dead cells

explanations.a: There is no active transport involved; uptake is passive and depends only on membrane integrity.
explanations.b: Correct — trypan blue is excluded by an intact membrane and enters passively once that barrier is breached, the defining mechanism of a dye-exclusion assay.
explanations.c: No enzymatic destruction of the dye is involved in live-cell exclusion.
explanations.d: That describes ethidium homodimer's DNA-binding mechanism, not trypan blue's exclusion principle.

questions.prompt: What specifically does an LDH-release assay measure?

options.text: The rate of new protein synthesis in surviving cells
The activity of a stable cytosolic enzyme released into the medium when the plasma membrane ruptures
The amount of DNA fragmentation inside dying cells
The concentration of ATP remaining inside live cells

explanations.a: LDH release has nothing to do with protein synthesis rates.
explanations.b: Correct — LDH is normally retained inside cells and only appears in the medium once the membrane is compromised, described by Korzeniewski and Callewaert in 1983.
explanations.c: DNA fragmentation is assessed by other assays (e.g., TUNEL), not LDH release.
explanations.d: That describes ATP-luminescence assays, not LDH release.

questions.prompt: Match each dye in the calcein-AM/ethidium homodimer kit to what it reports.

right.text: Green fluorescence in cells with active esterases and an intact membrane to retain the product (live)
Red fluorescence only after binding nucleic acid in cells with a ruptured membrane (dead)

questions.explanation: Calcein-AM requires both an active esterase and an intact membrane to accumulate its fluorescent product, marking live cells; ethidium homodimer-1 is membrane-impermeant and only lights up once it reaches DNA in a membrane-compromised cell.

questions.prompt: Order these steps in running an LDH-release cytotoxicity assay on a treated plate.

items.text: Treat cells with the test compound alongside untreated and Triton X-100 (100%-lysis) controls
Collect a sample of the culture medium (supernatant)
Mix supernatant with the coupled LDH-detection reagent
Read absorbance or fluorescence on a plate reader and compare to the lysis control

questions.explanation: Cells must be treated and controls set up first, then the released enzyme is sampled from the medium, converted into a detectable signal by the coupled reaction, and finally quantified against the fully-lysed positive control.

lessons.label: Metabolic (Tetrazolium) Assays: MTT/MTS/XTT

sections.heading: Mosmann's colorimetric shortcut
sections.body: Tim Mosmann introduced the MTT assay in a 1983 paper in the Journal of Immunological Methods, describing a fast, quantitative alternative to radioactive thymidine incorporation for measuring cell growth and survival. The principle: NAD(P)H-dependent cellular oxidoreductase enzymes, concentrated in metabolically active mitochondria, reduce the yellow, water-soluble tetrazolium salt MTT into purple formazan crystals. Because only cells with active reducing enzymes perform this conversion, the amount of formazan produced correlates with the number of metabolically active cells in a well. A plate reader measures absorbance around 570 nm, and treated wells are compared to untreated controls as percent viability. Reduction is not purely mitochondrial, though: cytosolic and endoplasmic-reticulum-resident NAD(P)H-dependent reductases also contribute substantially to formazan formation (Berridge & Tan, 1993), which is part of why the signal tracks general reductase activity rather than mitochondrial health specifically. Plates are typically incubated with MTT reagent for 1-4 hours before solubilization, depending on cell type and density.

sections.heading: MTT's inconvenient insolubility, and MTS/XTT's fix
sections.body: MTT's formazan product is a problem in practice: it is insoluble in aqueous media and forms needle-like crystals inside and around cells, so every well needs a separate solubilization step — historically DMSO or an acidified detergent — before the plate can be read, adding time and a source of well-to-well variability. Newer tetrazolium salts developed later, MTS and XTT (the latter described by Scudiero and colleagues in 1988), were engineered to produce formazan that stays soluble directly in culture medium, letting the assay run in one step without a solubilization pause — useful for higher-throughput screens where minutes per plate compound across hundreds of plates. MTS is typically paired with an electron-coupling reagent (PMS) to boost signal, while XTT was designed to be reduced efficiently at the cell surface as well as intracellularly.

sections.heading: The core pitfall: signal without cell death
sections.body: All three assays share MTT's fundamental limitation: they report reductase enzyme activity, not cell number, and the two can diverge. A compound that inhibits mitochondrial respiration directly, glucose deprivation, hypoxia, or simple confluency-driven growth arrest can all suppress formazan production without killing a single cell, producing a false cytotoxicity signal exactly as described in Lesson 1's worked example. Conversely, a compound that transiently boosts metabolic rate can mask real toxicity by keeping absorbance high even as cell number falls. Because of this, tetrazolium assays are best treated as a screening-tier readout — fast and cheap for ranking many compounds — that gets confirmed with an orthogonal, cell-number-based method before any mechanistic claim is made.

lessons.workedExample: A screening team tests 40 candidate compounds against a cancer cell line using MTS in a one-step 96-well format, ranking them by percent-viability drop at a single 10 µM dose after 48 hours. Compound 17 shows the largest drop (78% signal loss) and moves forward as the lead hit. Before committing further resources, the team confirms with a parallel cell count: actual cell number is down only 15%, meaning most of the MTS signal loss reflects a strong mitochondrial-reductase inhibitor rather than a potent killer. The compound is reclassified as a metabolic modulator, not a top cytotoxicity hit, avoiding a wasted follow-up campaign.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe tetrazolium assays because they are the most commonly misused viability tool in student science-fair projects — cheap, available as a kit, and easy to run without understanding what the color change means. A weak answer reports "percent viability by MTT" as if it were a direct cell count. A strong answer explains that the absorbance reflects reductase enzyme activity, names a plausible reason activity could change without cell death (confluency, hypoxia, a metabolic off-target effect), and describes what orthogonal check would rule that reason out.

questions.prompt: What does the purple formazan produced in an MTT assay directly indicate?

options.text: The exact number of live cells in the well
Reduction of the tetrazolium salt by active cellular oxidoreductase enzymes
The concentration of DNA released from dead cells
The amount of ATP consumed by the well

explanations.a: Formazan production correlates with enzyme activity, which usually but not always tracks cell number — that gap is the assay's core pitfall.
explanations.b: Correct — Mosmann's 1983 assay reports the reduction of MTT to formazan by active NAD(P)H-dependent oxidoreductases, concentrated in metabolically active mitochondria.
explanations.c: MTT is unrelated to DNA release; that is closer to a necrosis-related readout.
explanations.d: MTT measures reductase-driven dye conversion, not ATP consumption directly (that is the ATP-luminescence assay in the next lesson).

questions.prompt: Why were MTS and XTT developed as alternatives to MTT?

options.text: Their formazan products stay soluble in medium, avoiding MTT's separate solubilization step
They no longer rely on any enzymatic reduction step
They measure ATP directly rather than reductase activity
They require radioactive labeling for detection

explanations.a: Correct — MTS and XTT (the latter described by Scudiero and colleagues in 1988) produce soluble formazan, enabling a one-step assay without MTT's crystal-dissolving step.
explanations.b: MTS and XTT are still reduced by the same class of cellular reductase enzymes as MTT; the chemistry principle is unchanged.
explanations.c: They still measure tetrazolium reduction, not ATP; ATP-based luminescence is a separate assay family.
explanations.d: None of the tetrazolium assays require radioactivity; that was precisely what Mosmann's 1983 method was designed to avoid.

questions.prompt: A compound causes a 70% drop in MTT absorbance after 24 hours, but a same-plate cell count shows almost no change in cell number. What does this combination most likely indicate?

options.text: The compound is a potent, fast-acting cytotoxic agent
The compound suppresses mitochondrial reductase activity without killing the cells
The MTT assay was run incorrectly and should be discarded
The cell count method is unreliable and should be ignored

explanations.a: A truly cytotoxic, fast-killing agent would also reduce the cell count, which stayed flat here.
explanations.b: Correct — this is the classic MTT pitfall: reductase activity per cell falls (e.g., from mitochondrial inhibition or metabolic stress) while cell number is unaffected, producing a false cytotoxicity signal.
explanations.c: The assay may have run correctly; the mismatch reflects a real biological limitation of the readout, not necessarily an error.
explanations.d: Cell counts are the orthogonal check specifically meant to catch this discrepancy; dismissing them defeats the purpose of running both.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a standard MTT cytotoxicity assay.

items.text: Expose cells to test compound and controls in a 96-well plate
Add MTT reagent and incubate to allow formazan formation
Add solubilization solution to dissolve the insoluble purple crystals
Read absorbance at approximately 570 nm on a plate reader

questions.explanation: Cells are treated first, then MTT is added and reduced to insoluble formazan, which must be solubilized before the plate can be read at 570 nm — the extra solubilization step is exactly what MTS and XTT were designed to skip.

lessons.label: Resazurin & ATP Assays

sections.heading: Resazurin: a one-step fluorescent alternative to tetrazolium
