This is exactly the measurement problem Sies's eustress and distress framework and the DCFH-DA critique both point to: a rising fluorescent signal alone cannot distinguish a productive signaling event from genuine oxidative damage.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks how a student knows their DCFH-DA result reflects real oxidative stress and not an assay artifact is testing whether they read past the protocol sheet. A weak answer treats rising DCF fluorescence as self-evidently proof of oxidative damage. A strong answer can name the specific artifact sources, such as autoxidation, cytochrome c involvement, and light sensitivity, cite that DCFH-DA is not H2O2-specific, and describe pairing it with a damage-specific downstream marker like protein carbonyls or 8-oxo-dG, or a genetically encoded probe like HyPer, to confirm the signal reflects a real redox event rather than probe chemistry alone.

questions.prompt: What specific chemical change occurs when H2O2 acts as a second messenger on a target protein like PTP1B?

options.text: The entire protein is degraded by the proteasome
A reactive cysteine is oxidized to a sulfenic acid, reversibly altering function
The protein's DNA-binding domain is nitrated
H2O2 permanently denatures the protein

explanations.a: Signaling-level oxidation does not trigger degradation; the protein remains intact and is later re-reduced.
explanations.b: Correct - this reversible cysteine oxidation is the chemical basis of H2O2 acting as a transient signaling event rather than causing lasting damage.
explanations.c: Protein tyrosine nitration is associated with peroxynitrite chemistry, a different pathway from H2O2-based cysteine signaling.
explanations.d: Permanent denaturation would make the effect irreversible, which contradicts the transient, reversible nature of this signaling mechanism.

questions.prompt: According to Sies's eustress and distress framework, what determines whether ROS activity counts as eustress or distress?

options.text: Only whether the ROS species involved is H2O2 rather than superoxide
The intensity, duration, and whether antioxidant capacity is overwhelmed
Whether the ROS was produced by mitochondria rather than NADPH oxidase
Whether the ROS reacts with DNA specifically

explanations.a: The framework is not defined by which ROS species is involved; the same species can be eustress or distress.
explanations.b: Correct - the same molecule can be productive signaling or damaging stress depending on how much is produced, for how long, and whether defenses keep pace.
explanations.c: The source enzyme does not by itself determine eustress versus distress; the same source can produce either depending on output level.
explanations.d: DNA reactivity is one possible downstream consequence of distress, not the defining criterion of the framework.

questions.prompt: Match each ROS measurement tool to its defining property.

right.text: Widely used but prone to artifacts from autoxidation, light exposure, and lack of H2O2 specificity
Genetically encoded; ratiometrically reports the glutathione redox potential
Genetically encoded from a bacterial H2O2-sensing domain; specific to H2O2

questions.explanation: DCFH-DA is the cheap but artifact-prone chemical dye, while roGFP and HyPer are genetically encoded probes offering greater specificity, respectively for glutathione redox potential and H2O2.

questions.prompt: Order the events of the PTP1B redox-signaling example.

items.text: A growth factor stimulates the cell
NADPH oxidase activity generates a transient burst of H2O2
H2O2 oxidizes PTP1B's catalytic cysteine to a sulfenic acid, inactivating the phosphatase
Tyrosine kinase signaling proceeds unopposed until PTP1B is re-reduced

questions.explanation: Growth factor stimulation triggers the H2O2 burst, which inactivates PTP1B, temporarily removing its brake on kinase signaling until the phosphatase is restored.

units.label: DNA Damage, Repair & the DNA-Damage Response

lessons.label: Types of DNA Damage

sections.heading: DNA is under constant chemical attack
sections.body: Genomic DNA is not inert; it decays. In his 1993 Nature review, Tomas Lindahl estimated that spontaneous depurination alone — the hydrolysis of the N-glycosidic bond linking a purine base to deoxyribose — generates roughly 2,000 to 10,000 abasic (AP) sites per human cell per day, simply from thermal wobble at 37°C. Cytosine deamination, which converts cytosine to uracil (or 5-methylcytosine to thymine at CpG sites), adds hundreds more spontaneous mutagenic lesions daily. Oxidative attack from reactive oxygen species (ROS) generated during normal mitochondrial respiration adds an estimated 10,000 or more oxidative base lesions per cell per day, including roughly 1,000 to 2,000 copies of 8-oxo-7,8-dihydroguanine (8-oxo-dG) alone — pushing the total endogenous lesion load per cell per day into the tens of thousands even before any external exposure. DNA repair is not an emergency system, it is a constant maintenance operation.

sections.heading: Damage classes, by mechanism
sections.body: Oxidative damage from reactive oxygen species (ROS) produces 8-oxo-7,8-dihydroguanine (8-oxo-dG), the most common oxidized base, which mispairs with adenine and drives G to T transversions if unrepaired. Alkylation adds a methyl or ethyl group to a base; O6-methylguanine is especially dangerous because it pairs with thymine, directly causing G to A transitions — it is the signature lesion of alkylating chemotherapy and tobacco-derived nitrosamines. Bulky adducts distort the double helix: ultraviolet light fuses adjacent pyrimidines into cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers (CPDs) or 6-4 photoproducts, while polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) from combustion, such as benzo[a]pyrene, form bulky covalent adducts on guanine. Strand breaks range from single-strand breaks (SSBs), common and usually tolerated, to double-strand breaks (DSBs), rarer but far more dangerous since both strands lose the template needed for accurate repair. Interstrand crosslinks (ICLs), covalently welding the two strands together, block both replication and transcription outright and are the lesion targeted by platinum chemotherapy drugs like cisplatin.

sections.heading: Endogenous versus environmental origin
sections.body: Damage sources split into two categories that matter for both biology and courtroom-style causal reasoning at a science fair. Endogenous damage arises from the cell's own chemistry: hydrolysis, ROS byproducts of mitochondrial respiration, and replication errors occur in every cell, every day, independent of any outside exposure. Environmental or xenobiotic damage comes from an external agent — UV radiation, tobacco smoke, industrial PAHs, ionizing radiation, or chemotherapy — and its dose is, in principle, measurable and attributable. Distinguishing the two matters because a mutational signature or a lesion type can often point back to its cause.

lessons.workedExample: A tumor sample shows an unusually high rate of G-to-T transversions at guanines flanked by two other purines. A student proposes this came from cigarette-smoke PAH adducts. To test the claim they would look for benzo[a]pyrene-diol-epoxide adducts specifically at guanine N2 positions and check whether the mutation pattern matches known PAH-adduct signatures rather than the C-to-T pattern typical of spontaneous cytosine deamination or the UV-specific CC-to-TT signature — the base-change spectrum itself is evidence about which damage class produced it.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing 'what kind of damage is this?' is testing whether a student can name the actual chemistry rather than saying 'DNA damage' as an undifferentiated blob. A weak answer says a chemical 'damaged the DNA.' A strong answer names the lesion class — an 8-oxo-dG oxidative lesion, an O6-methylguanine alkylation adduct, a CPD, an interstrand crosslink — and explains why that specific chemistry produces a specific downstream consequence, such as a particular base mispairing or a specific repair pathway being required.

questions.prompt: Lindahl's 1993 estimate for spontaneous depurination events per human cell per day was approximately:

options.text: 1 million
Zero — depurination requires an external mutagen

explanations.a: Far too low; depurination is one of the most common spontaneous lesions, not a rare event.
explanations.b: Correct — Lindahl's review put spontaneous depurination at roughly 2,000 to 10,000 abasic sites per cell per day from thermal hydrolysis alone.
explanations.c: This overstates depurination specifically, though the total endogenous lesion burden across all damage types can approach large daily numbers.
explanations.d: Depurination is spontaneous hydrolysis driven by ordinary thermal energy at body temperature — no external mutagen is required.

questions.prompt: Why is O6-methylguanine considered a particularly dangerous alkylation lesion?

options.text: It physically breaks both DNA strands
It mispairs with thymine, directly causing G to A transitions if unrepaired
It only forms in mitochondrial DNA
It cannot be recognized by any repair enzyme

explanations.a: Alkylation adds a chemical group to a base; it does not itself break the phosphodiester backbone.
explanations.b: Correct — the methylated O6 position of guanine mispairs with thymine during replication, fixing a G to A transition unless the lesion is reversed first.
explanations.c: O6-methylguanine forms wherever alkylating agents reach DNA, in both nuclear and mitochondrial genomes.
explanations.d: It is specifically recognized and reversed by the MGMT enzyme, covered in a later lesson.

questions.prompt: Match each DNA lesion to its typical cause.

right.text: Ultraviolet light
Reactive oxygen species from respiration
Platinum chemotherapy (e.g., cisplatin)
Combustion products (e.g., tobacco smoke)

questions.explanation: UV fuses adjacent pyrimidines into CPDs; mitochondrial ROS oxidizes guanine to 8-oxo-dG; platinum drugs covalently crosslink the two DNA strands; combustion-derived PAHs form bulky adducts on guanine.

questions.prompt: Order these lesions from least structurally disruptive to the double helix to most disruptive.

items.text: 8-oxo-dG (single oxidized base)
CPD (helix-distorting bulky lesion)
Double-strand break (both strands severed)
Interstrand crosslink (strands covalently fused)

questions.explanation: A single oxidized base barely perturbs helix geometry; a CPD distorts the helix enough to block replication and transcription; a DSB severs the physical continuity of the chromosome; an interstrand crosslink welds both strands together, blocking strand separation entirely.

lessons.label: Base & Nucleotide Excision Repair

sections.heading: Base excision repair: fixing small, non-distorting lesions
sections.body: Base excision repair (BER) handles small chemical modifications to a single base that barely perturb the helix — oxidized, alkylated, or deaminated bases. The pathway starts with a DNA glycosylase, a lesion-specific enzyme that flips the damaged base out of the helix and cleaves the N-glycosidic bond, leaving an abasic site. OGG1 is the human glycosylase specific for 8-oxo-dG, scanning the genome and excising the oxidized guanine before it can mispair with adenine at replication. AP endonuclease 1 (APE1) then incises the phosphodiester backbone 5' to the abasic site, DNA polymerase beta fills the single-nucleotide gap, and DNA ligase III (working with XRCC1) seals the nick. Because BER replaces just one or a few nucleotides, it is fast and does not require unwinding a large stretch of duplex — appropriate for a lesion that does not distort the double helix's overall shape.

sections.heading: Nucleotide excision repair: fixing bulky, helix-distorting lesions
sections.body: Nucleotide excision repair (NER) handles lesions large enough to physically warp the helix — UV-induced CPDs and 6-4 photoproducts, and bulky chemical adducts like those from PAHs. Rather than one glycosylase, NER uses a coordinated multi-protein incision complex, named for the human disease xeroderma pigmentosum (XP) complementation groups that defined its components: XPC (with RAD23B) recognizes the distortion, TFIIH (containing the XPB and XPD helicases) unwinds roughly 25-30 nucleotides around the lesion, XPA verifies the damage and helps position the complex, replication protein A (RPA) coats the exposed single strand, and the structure-specific endonucleases XPF-ERCC1 and XPG make dual incisions flanking the lesion on either side, excising it as a single oligonucleotide. A DNA polymerase and ligase then fill and seal the resulting gap.

sections.heading: Two sub-pathways, one disease that proves the point
sections.body: NER runs in two modes that differ only in how the lesion is first found. Global-genome NER (GG-NER) scans the entire genome via XPC-RAD23B, searching for helix distortion wherever it occurs. Transcription-coupled NER (TC-NER) is triggered instead when RNA polymerase II stalls at a lesion in an actively transcribed gene, recruiting the Cockayne syndrome proteins CSA and CSB to redirect repair to that stalled site preferentially — prioritizing the genes the cell is actually using. Xeroderma pigmentosum, first clinically described in the 1870s and shown by James Cleaver in 1968 to reflect a defect in UV-induced DNA repair, is the human disease of NER failure: patients across complementation groups XPA through XPG show extreme photosensitivity, severe freckling in sun-exposed skin during infancy, and roughly a 1,000-fold elevated risk of skin cancer, demonstrating in a single syndrome how essential NER is for surviving everyday UV exposure.

lessons.workedExample: A cultured skin fibroblast line is irradiated with UVB and its rate of CPD removal is tracked over 24 hours by antibody staining. A wild-type line clears most CPDs within hours. A line from an XP-C patient clears almost none, because XPC is the damage-recognition step of global-genome NER — without it, the rest of the incision complex is never recruited to bulk-genome lesions. A student explaining this result correctly names XPC's specific role (recognition, not incision) rather than saying vaguely that 'NER is broken.'
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'why does this lesion need excision repair rather than a simpler fix?' to test whether a student understands that repair pathway choice is dictated by lesion geometry, not by lesion identity alone. A weak answer treats BER and NER as interchangeable 'DNA repair.' A strong answer explains that a small non-distorting base modification is handled by a lesion-specific glycosylase (BER), while a bulky helix-distorting lesion requires a multi-protein incision complex that excises a whole damaged oligonucleotide (NER) — and can name XPC or XPA-type failures as the clinical proof that NER's specific machinery, not just 'repair in general,' is what protects against UV.

questions.prompt: Which enzyme initiates base excision repair of 8-oxo-dG by flipping the base out of the helix and cleaving it free?

options.text: OGG1, a DNA glycosylase
XPC, a damage-recognition factor
DNA ligase III
RNA polymerase II

explanations.a: Correct — OGG1 is the glycosylase specific for 8-oxo-dG, the first step of BER.
explanations.b: XPC recognizes helix-distorting lesions and initiates global-genome NER, not BER.
explanations.c: Ligase III seals the final nick in BER but does not initiate the pathway.
explanations.d: RNA polymerase II's stalling triggers transcription-coupled NER, not BER initiation.

questions.prompt: Why does NER excise the damaged lesion as part of a longer oligonucleotide rather than a single nucleotide the way BER does?

options.text: Because NER lesions are helix-distorting bulky adducts requiring a multi-protein incision complex (XPF-ERCC1 and XPG) that cuts on both sides of the lesion
Because NER is slower and less accurate than BER
Because NER only operates during S phase
Because NER lesions are always double-strand breaks

explanations.a: Correct — bulky lesions need the region around them unwound and dual-incised, so the excised patch is a whole oligonucleotide rather than one base.
explanations.b: NER is not inherently less accurate; it is matched to a different, bulkier lesion class than BER.
explanations.c: NER operates throughout the cell cycle, unlike replication-restricted pathways.
explanations.d: NER-repaired lesions like CPDs and bulky adducts are helix-distorting single-strand-level lesions, not double-strand breaks.

questions.prompt: Match each NER component to its function.

right.text: Recognizes helix distortion (global-genome pathway)
Unwinds DNA around the lesion
Makes the dual incisions flanking the lesion
Redirects repair to a stalled RNA polymerase (transcription-coupled pathway)

questions.explanation: XPC-RAD23B finds distortion genome-wide, TFIIH's helicases open the duplex, XPF-ERCC1/XPG cut on either side of the lesion, and CSB recruits repair to RNA-polymerase-II-stalling lesions in transcribed genes.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of nucleotide excision repair.

items.text: XPC recognizes helix distortion
TFIIH unwinds DNA around the lesion
XPF-ERCC1 and XPG make dual incisions
Polymerase fills the gap and ligase seals it

questions.explanation: Recognition must precede unwinding, unwinding exposes the site for dual incision, and only after the damaged oligonucleotide is excised can the gap be filled and sealed.

lessons.label: Mismatch Repair & Direct Reversal

sections.heading: Mismatch repair proofreads what replication got wrong
sections.body: DNA polymerases are accurate but not perfect, and their own proofreading exonuclease activity still lets a mis-incorporated base or a small insertion-deletion loop through roughly once per 10^7 bases replicated. Mismatch repair (MMR) is the cell's second proofreading pass, scanning newly replicated DNA for these errors after the polymerase has already moved on. Recognition is handled by MutS homolog complexes: MSH2 paired with MSH6 (forming MutS-alpha) recognizes single base-base mismatches and small loops, while MSH2 paired with MSH3 (MutS-beta) recognizes larger insertion-deletion loops, the kind generated when a polymerase slips on a repetitive microsatellite sequence. Once a mismatch is bound, MLH1 paired with PMS2 (forming MutL-alpha) is recruited to coordinate excision of the error-containing strand and resynthesis by the replicative polymerase — repair that must correctly identify the newly synthesized strand as the one to correct, since fixing the wrong strand would fix the error permanently into the genome.

sections.heading: MMR loss: microsatellite instability and Lynch syndrome
sections.body: Because MMR is what specifically catches slippage at repetitive microsatellite sequences, losing it produces a distinctive signature: microsatellite instability (MSI), in which the lengths of microsatellite repeats vary wildly from cell to cell because slippage errors accumulate uncorrected. Germline mutations in MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, or PMS2 cause Lynch syndrome (also called hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer, HNPCC), an inherited cancer predisposition responsible for roughly 3% of colorectal cancers and a substantially elevated lifetime risk of colorectal and endometrial cancer. Tumor MSI testing is now a standard clinical assay, both to flag Lynch syndrome in a patient's family and because MSI-high tumors respond unusually well to immune checkpoint inhibitors, since their high mutation burden makes them more visible to the immune system.

sections.heading: Direct reversal: undoing the damage in one step, no excision needed
sections.body: Excision repair removes and replaces a damaged base; direct reversal instead chemically undoes the damage in a single enzymatic step, without ever cutting the DNA backbone. The clearest example is O6-methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase (MGMT), which transfers the offending methyl group from O6-methylguanine directly onto one of its own cysteine residues. This is a 'suicide' reaction: the transfer irreversibly inactivates that MGMT molecule, so each repair event consumes one enzyme with no catalytic turnover. MGMT activity matters clinically because the chemotherapy drug temozolomide (used against glioblastoma) works by generating O6-methylguanine lesions to kill tumor cells; tumors with a silenced MGMT promoter (via methylation) cannot repair this damage and respond far better to the drug, making MGMT promoter methylation a clinically used predictive biomarker. Photolyases perform an analogous direct reversal of UV photoproducts using energy absorbed from blue/near-UV light, but humans and other placental mammals lack a functional photolyase, leaving NER as our only route to repairing CPDs.

lessons.workedExample: A glioblastoma patient's tumor is tested before starting temozolomide. The lab reports the MGMT promoter as methylated (silenced). A student explains why this predicts a better response: MGMT normally reverses the O6-methylguanine lesions temozolomide creates, restoring the tumor's DNA before the damage can trigger cell death; a tumor without active MGMT cannot repair that lesion, so temozolomide's damage sticks and the chemotherapy is more effective — the opposite of what intuition about 'more repair is always better' would suggest for a therapy that only works by causing unrepaired damage.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about MMR or MGMT to see whether a student can connect a specific molecular mechanism to a specific clinical consequence, not just recite gene names. A weak answer says 'MMR fixes DNA errors' with no mechanism. A strong answer explains why MMR loss specifically destabilizes microsatellites (because that is the sequence context where replication slippage happens), links that to Lynch syndrome, and — for MGMT — can explain the counterintuitive direction of the temozolomide relationship: repair capacity here predicts resistance, not protection.

questions.prompt: Why does loss of mismatch repair specifically cause instability at microsatellite sequences?

options.text: Microsatellites are the sequence context where replicative polymerase slippage creates insertion-deletion loops that MMR normally corrects
Microsatellites are only found in mitochondrial DNA, which lacks MMR entirely
MMR only functions during meiosis, when microsatellites replicate
Microsatellites are bulky adducts that only NER can remove

explanations.a: Correct — repetitive runs favor polymerase slippage, and MSH2/MSH3 (MutS-beta) is the complex that specifically recognizes the resulting loops.
explanations.b: Microsatellites are common in nuclear DNA, and nuclear MMR is what maintains their stability.
explanations.c: MMR corrects replication errors during normal mitotic S phase, not specifically meiosis.
explanations.d: Microsatellite slippage loops are a mismatch repair substrate, not a bulky NER substrate.

questions.prompt: Why is MGMT's repair mechanism described as a 'suicide' reaction?

options.text: It triggers apoptosis in the repaired cell
It transfers the methyl group onto its own cysteine residue and is irreversibly inactivated, with no catalytic turnover
It cuts both DNA strands, destroying the chromosome
It only functions in cells already committed to death

explanations.a: MGMT repairs the lesion; it does not trigger apoptosis as part of its mechanism.
explanations.b: Correct — MGMT is consumed in the act of repair, unlike a true catalytic enzyme that turns over many substrate molecules.
explanations.c: MGMT is a direct-reversal enzyme that never cuts the DNA backbone at all.
explanations.d: MGMT functions in normal, healthy cells as ongoing protection against alkylation damage.

questions.prompt: Match each MMR complex to what it recognizes.

right.text: Single base-base mismatches and small loops
Larger insertion-deletion loops from microsatellite slippage
Coordinates excision and resynthesis after a mismatch is bound

questions.explanation: MutS-alpha (MSH2/MSH6) catches point mismatches, MutS-beta (MSH2/MSH3) catches larger slippage loops, and MutL-alpha (MLH1/PMS2) is the downstream coordinator that acts once either MutS complex has bound.

questions.prompt: Order these events from a normal DNA replication error to a diagnosed Lynch syndrome tumor.

items.text: Polymerase slips at a microsatellite repeat
An inherited MLH1/MSH2/MSH6/PMS2 mutation means MMR cannot correct it
Uncorrected slippage accumulates as microsatellite instability across many loci
Clinical MSI testing flags the tumor and prompts a Lynch syndrome diagnosis

questions.explanation: The slippage event happens first; a pre-existing germline MMR defect means it isn't caught; instability accumulates over many replication cycles and loci; and MSI testing detects that accumulated pattern clinically.

lessons.label: Double-Strand Break Repair: HR vs NHEJ

sections.heading: A double-strand break has no intact template
sections.body: A double-strand break (DSB) severs both strands at once, so unlike every excision pathway covered so far, there is no intact complementary strand left to copy from at that exact location. The cell has two structurally different ways to close this gap, and which one it uses is largely dictated by the cell cycle. Homologous recombination (HR) is accurate because it copies the missing sequence from an intact homologous template — but that template must be a sister chromatid, which only exists after S phase, restricting HR to S and G2. Non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) instead ligates the two broken ends back together with little or no reference to a template, works in any cell-cycle phase including G1, and is fast — but exactly because it does not verify sequence against a template, it is inherently error-prone, often producing small insertions or deletions at the junction.

sections.heading: Homologous recombination, step by step
sections.body: HR begins when the MRN complex (MRE11-RAD50-NBS1) detects the break and initiates end resection, chewing back the 5' strand at each end to expose a 3' single-stranded overhang. Replication protein A (RPA) immediately coats this exposed ssDNA. RAD51 then displaces RPA to form a helical nucleoprotein filament — the active search-and-invade machine of HR — and this handoff is orchestrated by BRCA2, which loads RAD51 onto the RPA-coated DNA. BRCA1 acts earlier, promoting the resection step and coordinating the choice toward HR in the first place. The RAD51 filament then searches the genome for a homologous sequence, typically the sister chromatid, invades the duplex to form a displacement loop, and uses the intact strand as a template to accurately resynthesize the missing sequence.

sections.heading: NHEJ, and the PARP-inhibitor synthetic-lethality principle
sections.body: NHEJ starts when the Ku70/Ku80 heterodimer rapidly clamps onto each broken DNA end, protecting them and recruiting the kinase DNA-PKcs to hold the two ends in proximity; after any necessary end processing, DNA ligase IV (with its cofactor XRCC4) seals the break. This speed makes NHEJ the dominant DSB pathway in G1, at the cost of precision. The clinical consequence of the HR/NHEJ split is the PARP-inhibitor synthetic-lethality strategy: BRCA1- or BRCA2-mutant tumor cells are HR-deficient, so they rely on backup pathways to survive the ordinary single-strand breaks that PARP enzymes normally repair. Blocking PARP with a drug like olaparib lets those single-strand breaks collapse into double-strand breaks during replication that an HR-competent cell would fix cleanly — but an HR-deficient BRCA-mutant cell cannot, so it dies, while the patient's normal HR-competent cells tolerate the drug. Foundational work by Bryant and colleagues and by Farmer and colleagues, both published in Nature in 2005, established this synthetic-lethal relationship, and olaparib became the first PARP inhibitor approved for BRCA-mutant ovarian cancer in 2014.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher is deciding which DSB repair pathway dominates in a population of skin cells sampled immediately after UV-induced breaks. Most of the sampled cells are quiescent, non-cycling keratinocytes in G0/G1. A student correctly predicts NHEJ will dominate, since HR requires a sister chromatid that only exists after S-phase DNA replication — a resting G1 cell simply has no homologous template available, regardless of how accurate HR would otherwise be.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'why does the cell choose HR here and NHEJ there?' to test whether a student understands that this is a template-availability constraint, not a preference. A weak answer says one pathway is simply 'better' than the other. A strong answer explains the cell-cycle restriction on HR, states the accuracy/speed tradeoff correctly, and — if the topic is cancer therapy — can walk through why PARP inhibition selectively kills HR-deficient BRCA-mutant cells rather than all dividing cells.

questions.prompt: Why is homologous recombination restricted mainly to S and G2 phases?

options.text: DNA-PKcs is only expressed during S/G2
HR requires an intact homologous template, and a sister chromatid only exists after DNA has been replicated
Ku70/Ku80 blocks HR only during S/G2
RAD51 is degraded during G1

explanations.a: DNA-PKcs is part of NHEJ, not HR, and its expression is not what restricts HR's timing.
explanations.b: Correct — HR copies from a homologous template, most reliably the sister chromatid, which is only present after S-phase replication.
explanations.c: Ku70/Ku80 is an NHEJ factor; its activity is not what confines HR to S/G2.
explanations.d: RAD51's cell-cycle-limited role reflects template availability, not enzyme degradation in G1.

questions.prompt: In the RAD51 filament-loading step of HR, what is BRCA2's specific role?

options.text: It clamps directly onto the broken DNA ends before any resection occurs
It loads RAD51 onto RPA-coated single-stranded DNA, displacing RPA to form the active filament
It ligates the final nick after strand resynthesis
It phosphorylates H2AX at the break site

explanations.a: End clamping onto raw broken ends is a Ku70/Ku80 (NHEJ) role, not BRCA2's.
explanations.b: Correct — BRCA2 mediates the RPA-to-RAD51 handoff, which is why BRCA2 loss specifically impairs RAD51 filament formation and HR.
explanations.c: Ligation of the resynthesized strand is not BRCA2's role; it acts earlier, at filament formation.
explanations.d: H2AX phosphorylation is carried out by ATM/ATR, covered in the DDR lesson, not by BRCA2.

questions.prompt: Match each factor to its pathway.

right.text: NHEJ
HR
NHEJ
HR

questions.explanation: Ku70/Ku80 and ligase IV are NHEJ's end-clamping and end-sealing factors; RAD51 and the MRN complex (initiating resection) belong to HR.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of homologous recombination.

items.text: MRN complex detects the break and initiates resection
RPA coats the exposed 3' single-stranded overhang
BRCA2 loads RAD51, displacing RPA to form the filament
RAD51 filament searches for homology and invades the sister chromatid

questions.explanation: Resection must occur before there is ssDNA for RPA to coat; RPA coating must precede the RAD51 handoff; and the RAD51 filament must be assembled before it can search for and invade a homologous sequence.

lessons.label: The DNA-Damage Response & p53

sections.heading: Two sensor kinases for two kinds of damage
sections.body: Repair pathways fix the DNA itself; the DNA-damage response (DDR) is the parallel signaling system that senses damage and decides what the cell does while repair is underway. Two related kinases sit at the top of this system, each tuned to a different damage signature. ATM (ataxia-telangiectasia mutated) is activated by the MRN complex at double-strand breaks — the same MRN complex that also initiates HR resection. ATR (ATM- and Rad3-related) is instead activated by RPA-coated single-stranded DNA, the signature left by stalled replication forks or by the resection intermediates that HR itself generates, meaning ATR responds broadly to replication stress, not just to a discrete break. One of ATM's earliest actions is phosphorylating a histone variant, H2AX, on serine 139 at chromatin flanking the break; this phosphorylated form, gamma-H2AX, spreads over megabase-scale domains around each DSB and was characterized by Rogakou and colleagues in 1998 — it is now the standard way to visualize and count individual DSBs under a microscope, one focus per break.

sections.heading: Transducers relay the signal into checkpoint arrest
sections.body: ATM and ATR each activate a dedicated downstream checkpoint kinase — CHK2 downstream of ATM, CHK1 downstream of ATR — which amplify and carry the signal away from the break site to enforce cell-cycle checkpoints at three points. The G1/S checkpoint prevents a cell from entering S phase with damaged DNA, largely via p53-driven p21 induction. The intra-S checkpoint slows replication origin firing when a fork encounters damage mid-S-phase. The G2/M checkpoint blocks entry into mitosis with unrepaired DNA, chiefly by CHK1/CHK2 inhibiting the phosphatase CDC25, which otherwise activates the CDK1-cyclin B complex needed to start mitosis. Together these checkpoints buy the repair machinery time before the cell commits to replicating or dividing.

sections.heading: p53: the decision hub, not just an arrest switch
sections.body: p53, stabilized and activated by ATM/ATR/CHK1/CHK2 signaling, is the node that converts 'damage detected' into a specific cellular outcome, which is why it earned the label 'guardian of the genome' from Lane in 1992. p53 is not a single lever; it is a hub that transactivates different gene sets depending on damage severity, duration, and cell type. Modest, repairable damage typically induces p21 (CDKN1A), which inhibits cyclin-CDK complexes and produces transient arrest, giving repair pathways time to work before the checkpoint releases the cell. Damage that persists or exceeds a threshold can instead push p53 toward permanent cell-cycle exit — senescence, reinforced by p21 and p16 — or toward apoptosis via p53 transactivating pro-apoptotic genes like PUMA and BAX. Because p53 sits downstream of the sensors and gates the toxic outcome of unrepaired damage, TP53 is mutated in more than half of all human cancers — losing this single decision hub lets cells with damaged DNA keep dividing instead of arresting, senescing, or dying.

lessons.workedExample: A student exposes cultured cells to a low dose of a DNA-alkylating agent and a high dose of the same agent, then stains for gamma-H2AX foci and measures p53 target-gene expression at 24 hours. The low dose shows scattered gamma-H2AX foci, transient p21 induction, and cells resuming cycling by 48 hours. The high dose shows dense gamma-H2AX foci, sustained p53 activation, and a rise in PUMA/BAX expression consistent with cells committing to apoptosis. The student correctly concludes that the same sensor-to-p53 pathway produced two different outcomes because the severity of damage, not a different mechanism, tipped the decision.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about the DDR to see whether a student treats p53 as a single on/off 'tumor suppressor switch' or understands it as a graded decision hub. A weak answer says 'p53 stops cancer.' A strong answer names the specific sensor (ATM for breaks, ATR for replication stress), the checkpoint it enforces, and explains that p53's downstream choice — arrest, senescence, or apoptosis — depends on the severity and duration of the damage signal it is receiving, which is why TP53 loss is so broadly permissive for cancer across cell types.

questions.prompt: What specifically activates ATR, as distinct from ATM?

options.text: Double-strand breaks detected by the MRN complex
RPA-coated single-stranded DNA, generated by stalled replication forks or resection intermediates
Gamma-H2AX foci alone, independent of any ssDNA
CHK2 phosphorylation

explanations.a: MRN-detected double-strand breaks are the signal that activates ATM, not ATR.
explanations.b: Correct — ATR responds to RPA-coated ssDNA, which is why it is activated broadly by replication stress, not only by discrete breaks.
explanations.c: Gamma-H2AX is a downstream marker produced after ATM activation at breaks; it is not itself what activates ATR.
explanations.d: CHK2 is downstream of ATM, not an upstream activator of ATR.

questions.prompt: Why does p53 loss contribute to cancer across so many different cell types and damage sources?

options.text: p53 is the sole enzyme capable of excising bulky DNA adducts
p53 sits downstream of both major sensor pathways (ATM and ATR) and gates whether damaged cells arrest, senesce, or die, so its loss removes that checkpoint regardless of what caused the damage
p53 only responds to UV-specific lesions
p53 directly repairs double-strand breaks by end-joining

explanations.a: p53 is a transcription factor and signaling hub, not a DNA-excising repair enzyme.
explanations.b: Correct — because p53 is the convergence point downstream of both ATM and ATR signaling, its loss removes the decision hub for any damage type that would normally trigger arrest, senescence, or apoptosis.
explanations.c: p53 responds to signals from both ATM (breaks) and ATR (replication stress), not only UV-derived lesions.
explanations.d: p53 does not perform end-joining itself; that is carried out by the NHEJ machinery (Ku70/80, DNA-PKcs, ligase IV).

questions.prompt: Match each DDR component to its role.

right.text: Senses double-strand breaks via MRN
Senses RPA-coated single-stranded DNA
Phosphorylated histone marking break sites, used as a DSB readout
Checkpoint kinase transducing the ATR signal

questions.explanation: ATM senses breaks via MRN and phosphorylates H2AX to create the gamma-H2AX marker; ATR senses RPA-ssDNA from replication stress and signals through CHK1.

questions.prompt: Order the DDR signaling cascade from initial break to cell-fate outcome.

items.text: MRN complex detects the double-strand break
ATM is activated and phosphorylates H2AX
CHK2 is activated downstream of ATM
p53 is stabilized and selects arrest, senescence, or apoptosis

questions.explanation: Detection by MRN must precede ATM activation; ATM activates the downstream transducer CHK2; and the signal converges on p53 last, where the cell-fate decision is made.

lessons.label: Genotoxicity Testing

sections.heading: The Ames test: a bacterial reversion assay for mutagens
sections.body: Bruce Ames and colleagues developed the assay bearing his name in the mid-1970s, publishing the standardized protocol with McCann and Yamasaki in 1975. It uses several Salmonella typhimurium strains (such as TA98 and TA100) engineered as histidine auxotrophs — unable to synthesize histidine and so unable to grow without it in the medium. A mutagen that reverses this defect via a new mutation restores histidine synthesis, and the number of revertant colonies growing on histidine-free plates is a direct, countable readout of mutagenic potency. Because many chemicals are not mutagenic themselves but become so only after liver metabolism, the assay is run both with and without an S9 fraction — a rat liver microsomal extract supplying the cytochrome P450 enzymes that convert such promutagens into their reactive, DNA-damaging forms. McCann and Ames reported in 1976 that Ames-test mutagenicity correlated with rodent carcinogenicity in roughly 90% of chemicals tested, a striking claim; a larger, more systematic comparison by Tennant and colleagues at the National Toxicology Program in 1987 found the correlation considerably weaker, closer to 50-60%, showing that a positive Ames result is suggestive of carcinogenic risk but far from proof by itself.

sections.heading: Detecting breaks directly: the comet assay
sections.body: The comet assay, introduced by Singh and colleagues in 1988 as single-cell gel electrophoresis, measures strand breaks directly in individual cells rather than inferring mutagenicity indirectly through bacterial reversion. Cells are embedded in a thin agarose layer on a slide, lysed to strip away membranes and histones, and electrophoresed. Fragmented DNA, carrying breaks, migrates out of the nucleoid faster than intact supercoiled DNA, producing a comet-shaped fluorescent image: an intact 'head' and a 'tail' of migrated fragments. The tail moment (combining tail length and fluorescence intensity) quantifies how much strand breakage occurred. Run under alkaline conditions, the assay detects single-strand breaks, double-strand breaks, and alkali-labile sites (including abasic sites) all at once, and because it works on any single cell rather than requiring a growing bacterial colony, it can be applied directly to primary human cells or tissue biopsies.

sections.heading: Chromosome-level and modern quantitative readouts
sections.body: The in-vitro micronucleus assay detects chromosome-level damage that neither the Ames test nor the comet assay can see: after cell division, a whole chromosome or an acentric chromosome fragment left outside the main daughter nuclei forms its own small extra nucleus, a micronucleus, visible by simple microscopy. This distinguishes two mechanistically different classes of genotoxic agent: clastogens, which break chromosomes and generate micronuclei from acentric fragments, versus aneugens, which disrupt the mitotic spindle (as colchicine does) and cause whole-chromosome missegregation, also producing a micronucleus but by a completely different mechanism. Gamma-H2AX foci counting, introduced by Rogakou and colleagues in 1998 and covered in the previous lesson as a DDR marker, has also become a modern quantitative genotoxicity readout in its own right — each focus corresponds to one double-strand break, giving a dose-responsive, microscope-countable measurement of DSB burden without needing bacterial growth or metaphase spreads at all.

lessons.workedExample: A cosmetic-ingredient screening lab tests a new preservative compound. It comes back negative on the Ames test with and without S9 activation, but positive on the in-vitro micronucleus assay. A student interpreting this correctly notes that the compound is not a bacterial point mutagen (no reversion), but it does induce chromosome-level damage — likely acting as a clastogen or aneugen through a mechanism the Ames test, built to detect base-level mutation, cannot capture at all. This is exactly why regulatory testing batteries require multiple assay types rather than relying on any single test.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'which assay would you use, and why not the others?' to test whether a student understands that each genotoxicity assay detects a mechanistically different kind of damage rather than being interchangeable options. A weak answer picks one assay because it 'tests for mutations.' A strong answer matches assay to lesion type — Ames for bacterial point mutation with metabolic activation, comet for direct strand breaks in single cells, micronucleus for chromosome-level clastogenic or aneugenic damage — and can explain why a negative result on one assay does not rule out genotoxicity detectable by another.

questions.prompt: Why is the Ames test run both with and without an S9 liver-microsomal fraction?

options.text: S9 protects the bacteria from being killed by the test compound
Some chemicals are only mutagenic after metabolic conversion by liver enzymes into a reactive form, which S9 supplies
S9 is required for the histidine auxotroph strains to grow at all
S9 increases the bacteria's mutation rate nonspecifically as a positive control

explanations.a: S9 is a source of metabolic enzymes, not a protective agent against toxicity.
explanations.b: Correct — many promutagens require cytochrome P450-mediated activation, which the rat liver S9 fraction provides, to become DNA-reactive.
explanations.c: Histidine auxotroph growth on histidine-free media depends on reversion, not on S9 presence.
explanations.d: S9 activates specific promutagens metabolically; it is not a generic mutation-rate booster used as a control.

questions.prompt: How does the McCann and Ames (1976) estimate of Ames-test/rodent-carcinogenicity correlation compare to the later Tennant and colleagues (1987) NTP analysis?

options.text: McCann and Ames reported roughly 90% correlation; the later NTP analysis found a considerably weaker correlation, closer to 50-60%
Both studies reported essentially the same near-100% correlation
McCann and Ames found no correlation at all; the later study found near-perfect correlation
Neither study addressed correlation with rodent carcinogenicity

explanations.a: Correct — the original striking claim was later revised substantially downward once a larger, more systematic chemical set was analyzed.
explanations.b: The two estimates diverge considerably; they are not the same figure.
explanations.c: McCann and Ames reported a strong, not zero, correlation in their original comparison.
explanations.d: Both studies specifically addressed the Ames test's ability to predict rodent carcinogenicity.

questions.prompt: Match each assay to what it directly measures.

right.text: Histidine-reversion mutation frequency in bacteria
Strand breaks and alkali-labile sites in single cells
Whole-chromosome or fragment loss after division
Individual double-strand break count via microscopy

questions.explanation: Each assay reads out a different damage level: bacterial point-mutation reversion (Ames), strand breaks in single-cell electrophoresis (comet), chromosome-level loss (micronucleus), and quantitative DSB counts (gamma-H2AX).

questions.prompt: Order these events in a positive comet assay from sample prep to readout.

items.text: Cells embedded in a thin agarose layer on a slide
Cells lysed to remove membranes and histones
Alkaline electrophoresis run
Tail moment measured from the comet image

questions.explanation: Cells must be embedded before lysis can expose the nucleoid, lysis must precede electrophoresis so fragmented DNA can migrate, and the tail moment is measured only after the comet image has formed.

lessons.label: From Damage to Mutation: Translesion Synthesis & Signatures

sections.heading: When repair loses the race: damage tolerance
sections.body: Every repair pathway covered so far removes or reverses a lesion before replication reaches it. But if a replication fork arrives at an unrepaired lesion first, the replicative polymerase — built for speed and fidelity on undamaged template, not for reading past a distorted base — typically stalls. Rather than repair the lesion, the cell can instead tolerate it: specialized translesion synthesis (TLS) polymerases from the Y-family are recruited to the stalled fork, insert a nucleotide directly opposite the lesion despite the distorted template, and let replication continue. TLS does not remove the lesion; it lets the fork survive past it, at a cost to accuracy that depends entirely on which TLS polymerase does the inserting.

sections.heading: Pol eta: an accurate specialist, and the disease that proves it
sections.body: DNA polymerase eta (Pol eta) is the clearest example of how specific a TLS polymerase's accuracy can be. Its active site is unusually spacious, letting it accommodate a cyclobutane pyrimidine dimer (CPD) and insert two adenines directly opposite the thymine-thymine dimer — the correct bases, restoring accurate sequence despite bypassing a lesion no ordinary polymerase could read through. Two research groups independently identified the gene encoding Pol eta in 1999 by showing it was defective in xeroderma pigmentosum variant (XP-V), a form of xeroderma pigmentosum with normal nucleotide excision repair but still an elevated skin-cancer risk — proof that NER alone is not sufficient protection against UV, and that accurate lesion bypass by Pol eta is doing real protective work of its own downstream of NER.

sections.heading: Pol zeta/Rev1: the error-prone extenders, and how tolerance becomes mutation
sections.body: Not every TLS polymerase is accurate like Pol eta. Pol zeta (built around the catalytic subunit REV3L) and Rev1 specialize in extending primers from a mismatched or distorted terminus that other polymerases, including some TLS polymerases, cannot extend from — a step that is inherently more error-prone, since extension proceeds from an already-imperfect base pair. This is the molecular moment a DNA lesion becomes a permanent mutation: as long as the lesion sits in the template unread, it is potential damage; once a TLS polymerase (accurate or not) has copied past it and the fork has moved on, whatever base ended up opposite the lesion is fixed into the genome at the next round of replication. A mutation, at the mechanistic level, is simply unrepaired damage that got replicated before it was fixed.

sections.heading: Mutational signatures: reading the cause from the mutation spectrum
sections.body: Because different damage sources and different bypass polymerases leave characteristically different base-change patterns, large-scale cancer genome sequencing can work backward from a tumor's mutation spectrum to infer what damaged it. Alexandrov and colleagues formalized this in a landmark 2013 Nature paper, cataloging COSMIC mutational signatures such as the UV signature (C-to-T transitions concentrated at dipyrimidine sites, reflecting CPD formation and bypass), the tobacco-smoking signature (G-to-T transversions, consistent with bulky PAH adducts on guanine), and a clock-like signature attributed to spontaneous deamination of 5-methylcytosine accumulating with age. The three excision-repair pathways covered earlier in this unit — base excision repair, mismatch repair, and nucleotide excision repair — were recognized by the 2015 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, awarded jointly to Tomas Lindahl, Paul Modrich, and Aziz Sancar respectively; the prize covered those three repair mechanisms specifically, not the DNA-damage-response signaling, translesion synthesis, or mutational-signature analysis discussed elsewhere in this unit.

lessons.workedExample: A whole-genome sequenced lung tumor shows a mutation spectrum dominated by G-to-T transversions, while a melanoma from the same biobank shows C-to-T transitions concentrated at dipyrimidine sequences. A student matches the lung tumor's pattern to the tobacco-smoking mutational signature (consistent with PAH-adduct formation and its bypass) and the melanoma's pattern to the UV signature (consistent with CPD formation and Pol eta or error-prone bypass at unrepaired dimers) — correctly reasoning from base-change spectrum back to damage mechanism rather than simply citing 'sun exposure causes melanoma' without the molecular link.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'how does damage actually become a mutation?' to test whether a student can name the specific step where an unrepaired lesion is converted into a permanent, heritable change — replication past the lesion by a TLS polymerase — rather than treating 'damage' and 'mutation' as synonyms. A weak answer conflates the two. A strong answer explains that a lesion is only a mutation once a polymerase has copied past it and fixed a base pair into the daughter strand, and can connect a specific bypass polymerase (Pol eta's accuracy versus Pol zeta/Rev1's error-proneness) to whether that fixation is faithful or mutagenic.

questions.prompt: What specifically distinguishes Pol eta from an ordinary replicative polymerase when it encounters a CPD?

options.text: Pol eta skips the lesion entirely and resumes synthesis past it
Pol eta's active site accommodates the CPD and inserts two adenines opposite it, restoring the correct sequence
Pol eta excises the CPD before replicating past it
Pol eta only functions in bacteria, not in humans

explanations.a: Pol eta does not skip the lesion; it synthesizes directly across it, base by base.
explanations.b: Correct — its spacious active site lets it read a thymine-thymine dimer and insert the correct adenines, unlike a replicative polymerase that would stall.
explanations.c: Excision is an NER function; Pol eta's role is tolerance (bypass), not removal.
explanations.d: Pol eta is a human enzyme, and its loss specifically causes the human disease XP-variant.

questions.prompt: At what mechanistic point does an unrepaired DNA lesion become a fixed, heritable mutation?

options.text: The moment the lesion first forms in the DNA
Only after cell division produces two daughter cells
When a translesion synthesis polymerase copies past the lesion and the resulting base pair is carried forward by the fork
When the DDR checkpoint releases the cell to proceed with mitosis

explanations.a: Lesion formation alone is potential damage, not yet a mutation — it can still be repaired before replication reaches it.
explanations.b: The fixation event happens at replication, not at the later division step.
explanations.c: Correct — replication past the lesion by a TLS polymerase is what converts unrepaired damage into a fixed base change in the daughter strand.
explanations.d: Checkpoint release governs cell-cycle progression, not the specific chemical step of fixing a base pair opposite a lesion.

questions.prompt: Match each 2015 Chemistry Nobel laureate to the repair pathway they are credited with.

right.text: Base excision repair
Mismatch repair
Nucleotide excision repair

questions.explanation: The 2015 Nobel Prize in Chemistry recognized Lindahl for base excision repair, Modrich for mismatch repair, and Sancar for nucleotide excision repair.

questions.prompt: Order these mutational-signature reasoning steps from raw data to conclusion.

items.text: Whole-genome sequencing of a tumor identifies its base-change spectrum
The spectrum is compared to catalogued COSMIC signatures (e.g., UV, tobacco, clock-like)
A dominant matching signature is identified (e.g., C-to-T at dipyrimidines for UV)
The likely damage source is inferred (e.g., UV exposure driving CPD formation)

questions.explanation: Sequencing must produce the spectrum before it can be compared to reference signatures; a best-matching signature must be identified before a causal source can be inferred from it.

lessons.label: Protein Homeostasis Under Stress

sections.heading: A balance, not a state
sections.body: Proteostasis is the dynamic balance between protein synthesis, folding, and degradation that keeps a cell's proteome functional. A newly synthesized polypeptide is not automatically useful; it must fold into a specific three-dimensional shape, often with help, and it must eventually be cleared once damaged or no longer needed. The proteostasis network — ribosomes making the chain, chaperones folding it, and two degradation machines removing it — has finite capacity. Push protein production, oxidative damage, or unfolding faster than the network can keep up, and misfolded proteins accumulate and expose hydrophobic patches that are normally buried. Those patches drive aggregation: misfolded chains stick to each other and to other proteins, forming insoluble clumps that clog cellular machinery and can seed further misfolding, as seen in amyloid diseases.

sections.heading: How stressors break the balance
sections.body: Heat destabilizes the weak, non-covalent bonds — hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions — that hold a folded protein's tertiary structure together, so even modest temperature increases above a protein's melting threshold unfold it. Oxidative stress is more targeted: reactive oxygen species oxidize cysteine and methionine residues and can carbonylate side chains, altering local structure and often marking a protein for degradation. Toxicants add further mechanisms — heavy metals like cadmium and mercury bind cysteine thiols and displace structural zinc, electrophilic toxicants such as reactive drug metabolites covalently adduct nucleophilic residues, and some xenobiotics directly inhibit the proteasome. Because these three stressor classes converge on the same downstream problem — a rising burden of misfolded protein — proteotoxic stress is considered a convergent toxicity endpoint: chemically unrelated toxicants can produce the same cellular emergency.

sections.heading: The first responders and the two disposal arms
sections.body: Molecular chaperones are the proteostasis network's first line of defense. Rather than adding folding information, most chaperones prevent aggregation by transiently binding exposed hydrophobic surfaces (holding), give a misfolded client repeated ATP-driven chances to refold correctly (refolding), and when a protein is damaged beyond repair, hand it off to degradation (triage) instead of protecting it further. When chaperone capacity is exceeded, misfolded proteins are cleared by two degradation arms: the ubiquitin-proteasome system, which tags individual soluble proteins with ubiquitin chains for rapid destruction by the 26S proteasome, and autophagy, which engulfs bulk cargo — aggregates, damaged organelles — in a membrane and delivers it to the lysosome. Both arms are covered in depth later in this unit; here, the key point is that chaperone triage decides which disposal route a doomed protein takes.

lessons.workedExample: A cell line is treated with a low, sub-lethal dose of cadmium chloride for 24 hours. Cadmium binds cysteine thiols on many proteins, displacing structural zinc and causing widespread misfolding — the same functional outcome a heat pulse would produce, despite a completely different chemical trigger. Chaperones initially hold the misfolded proteins, buying time; as the cadmium dose is not cleared, holding capacity is exceeded, chaperones triage the worst clients to the ubiquitin-proteasome system, and researchers observe rising poly-ubiquitinated protein levels on a western blot as direct evidence that proteostasis capacity has been overwhelmed rather than simply engaged.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes proteostasis to see whether a student understands that 'stress' is not one thing but a shared downstream consequence of many different insults. A weak answer says heat or a chemical 'damages proteins' with no mechanism. A strong answer names the specific bond or residue disrupted (hydrogen bonds for heat, cysteine thiols for cadmium, disulfide-forming oxidation for ROS) and explains why unrelated stressors converge on the same aggregation problem — showing the student grasps the proteome as a capacity-limited system, not a list of independent parts.

questions.prompt: Why is proteotoxic stress considered a 'convergent' toxicity endpoint?

options.text: Because only heat can cause it
Because chemically distinct stressors (heat, oxidants, metals) all raise the burden of misfolded protein
Because it only occurs in the mitochondria
Because the proteasome is the only structure affected

explanations.a: Heat is only one of several distinct stressor classes that cause misfolding.
explanations.b: Correct — heat, oxidative stress, and toxicants act through different chemistry but all increase the pool of misfolded protein, overwhelming the same proteostasis network.
explanations.c: Proteotoxic stress affects the whole proteome, not one organelle exclusively.
explanations.d: The proteasome is one clearance route, not the only structure implicated.

questions.prompt: Match each stressor to the specific molecular target it disrupts.

right.text: Weak non-covalent bonds (hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions)
Cysteine and methionine side chains via oxidation
Cysteine thiols and structural zinc sites

questions.explanation: Heat destabilizes the weak bonds holding tertiary structure; ROS oxidize sulfur-containing residues; cadmium binds cysteine thiols and displaces structural zinc.

questions.prompt: Order a misfolded protein's fate from initial detection to final clearance under manageable stress.

items.text: Hydrophobic patches become exposed on the misfolded protein
A chaperone holds the protein to prevent aggregation
ATP-driven refolding attempts are made
The chaperone triages an unsalvageable client to a degradation arm

questions.explanation: Misfolding exposes hydrophobic surfaces, a chaperone holds the client to block aggregation, refolding is attempted, and only a persistently misfolded protein is triaged for degradation.

questions.prompt: What is the functional consequence of exposed hydrophobic patches on a misfolded protein?

options.text: They make the protein resistant to degradation
They drive aggregation by sticking to other exposed hydrophobic surfaces
They increase the protein's solubility
They have no effect on protein behavior

explanations.a: Aggregated proteins are not inherently degradation-resistant; aggregation is a separate problem from degradation susceptibility.
explanations.b: Correct — hydrophobic patches that are normally buried stick together when exposed, nucleating aggregates that can seed further misfolding.
explanations.c: Exposed hydrophobic patches decrease solubility, not increase it, since hydrophobic groups avoid the aqueous cytoplasm.
explanations.d: Exposed hydrophobic patches are the direct physical driver of aggregation.

questions.prompt: Which best distinguishes a chaperone's 'holding' function from its 'refolding' function?

options.text: Holding uses ATP to correct structure; refolding is passive binding
Holding passively blocks aggregation; refolding actively drives the client toward its correct structure using ATP cycles
They are the same function with different names
Holding only occurs in mitochondria, refolding only in the cytosol

explanations.a: This reverses the two functions; refolding, not holding, is the ATP-dependent process.
explanations.b: Correct — holding is a passive, protective binding to prevent aggregation, while refolding is an active, ATP-driven attempt to restore native structure.
explanations.c: They are mechanistically distinct steps in chaperone action, not synonyms.
explanations.d: Both functions occur in multiple compartments; the distinction is mechanism, not location.

lessons.label: The Heat-Shock Response

sections.heading: An accidental discovery in fruit-fly chromosomes
sections.body: The heat shock response was found by accident. Ferruccio Ritossa, working with Drosophila melanogaster in 1962, noticed that when larvae were exposed to elevated temperature, a small, reproducible set of 'puffs' — locally decondensed, transcriptionally active regions — appeared on the giant polytene chromosomes of the salivary gland, and regressed again once the larvae recovered at normal temperature. Puffing was the visible signature of intense local transcription, so Ritossa had shown that heat rapidly and specifically switched on a small set of genes. It took over a decade to connect the puffs to protein products: in 1974, Tissières, Mitchell, and Tracy showed by radioactive labeling that heat shock induced synthesis of a small number of new proteins while suppressing most others — the heat shock proteins, named for the discovery method rather than a unique biological role, since related chaperones function under many kinds of stress.

sections.heading: HSF1: the switch that senses stress
sections.body: In unstressed mammalian cells, heat shock factor 1 (HSF1) is held inactive, monomeric, and chaperone-bound, largely by HSP90. When misfolded proteins accumulate, they compete with HSF1 for HSP90 binding, freeing HSF1 to trimerize, translocate to the nucleus, become hyperphosphorylated, and bind heat shock elements — short repeated DNA sequences in the promoters of HSP genes — driving a rapid transcriptional burst. This is a classic negative-feedback loop: the newly made HSP70 and HSP90 that result from HSF1 activation eventually re-bind HSF1 and shut the response back down once the misfolded-protein load falls, so the system self-limits rather than running continuously. The chaperone pool that closes this loop is itself a small ATPase cycle: an HSP40/DNAJ co-chaperone first delivers a misfolded client to HSP70 and stimulates HSP70's otherwise slow ATPase, driving ATP hydrolysis and locking the client into a high-affinity, ADP-bound state. Release only happens once a nucleotide-exchange factor (NEF) displaces the bound ADP and lets fresh ATP rebind, which lowers HSP70's affinity and frees the client — either to fold on its own or to re-enter the cycle. That same ATP/ADP cycle governs how much free HSP70 is available to re-sequester HSF1, so the DNAJ-stimulated hydrolysis and NEF-driven release steps are what set the pace of both client folding and the negative feedback described above.

sections.heading: A division of labor among chaperone families
sections.body: HSP70 is the workhorse refolding chaperone, cycling ATP-driven binding and release of exposed hydrophobic segments on misfolded clients with the help of HSP40 co-chaperones. HSP90 does not fold nascent chains from scratch; it matures specific 'client' proteins — many signaling kinases and steroid hormone receptors — into their final active conformation, making it a hub connecting proteostasis to cell signaling. HSP60, a barrel-shaped chaperonin related to bacterial GroEL, encloses a single unfolded client inside its central cavity to fold it in isolation, largely in mitochondria. Small HSPs act as ATP-independent holdases, binding misfolded clients on contact and preventing aggregation until ATP-dependent chaperones become available. Repeated mild heat exposure also produces thermotolerance, a transient, HSP-dependent resistance to a subsequent, otherwise lethal heat challenge.

lessons.workedExample: A student exposes cultured cells to a mild 42°C heat pulse for one hour, then lets them recover at 37°C before challenging them with a normally lethal 45°C heat shock. Cells given the mild pre-treatment survive the lethal challenge at much higher rates than naive cells — this is thermotolerance. Explaining the result requires the full chain: the mild pulse frees HSF1 from HSP90, HSF1 trimerizes and drives HSP70/HSP90 transcription via heat shock elements, and the elevated chaperone pool built during recovery is what buffers the subsequent lethal challenge, not any permanent change to the cells themselves.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe HSF1 activation because it tests whether a student can explain a stress response as a regulated circuit rather than a vague 'the cell responds to heat.' A weak answer states that heat shock proteins are made without saying what triggers or turns off their production. A strong answer names the HSP90 sequestration-and-release mechanism, describes trimerization and heat-shock-element binding, and recognizes the negative feedback that makes the response self-limiting and testable by thermotolerance experiments.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of HSF1 activation from resting state to gene transcription.

items.text: HSF1 is held monomeric by HSP90
Misfolded proteins compete with HSF1 for HSP90
Free HSF1 trimerizes and enters the nucleus
HSF1 binds heat shock elements and activates transcription

questions.explanation: HSF1 starts HSP90-bound; rising misfolded protein outcompetes HSF1 for HSP90; released HSF1 trimerizes and translocates to the nucleus; it then binds heat shock elements to drive transcription.

questions.prompt: Match each chaperone to its primary job.

right.text: ATP-driven refolding of misfolded clients
Maturation of signaling kinases and hormone receptors
Enclosed-cavity folding, largely mitochondrial
ATP-independent holding to prevent aggregation

questions.explanation: HSP70 refolds clients using ATP cycles; HSP90 matures specific signaling clients; HSP60 is a chaperonin that folds inside an enclosed cavity; small HSPs are ATP-independent holdases.

questions.prompt: What did Ritossa's 1962 observation in Drosophila directly show?

options.text: That heat directly denatures the proteasome
That heat induced a specific, reproducible pattern of chromosome puffing indicating localized transcriptional activation
That HSP70 physically binds misfolded proteins
That heat shock proteins are exclusive to insects

explanations.a: Ritossa's observation concerned chromosome puffing, not proteasome structure.
explanations.b: Correct — Ritossa saw that heat reproducibly induced puffs at specific chromosomal loci, showing a specific set of genes was being transcriptionally activated.
explanations.c: That mechanistic detail came from later biochemical work, not Ritossa's cytological observation.
explanations.d: Heat shock proteins were later found to be highly conserved across essentially all organisms.

questions.prompt: What did Tissières, Mitchell, and Tracy add in 1974 that Ritossa's 1962 work had not shown?

options.text: That the puffs corresponded to synthesis of a specific small set of new proteins
That heat shock only affects Drosophila
That HSF1 exists
That chromosome puffing does not require transcription

explanations.a: Correct — using radioactive labeling, they connected the cytological puffs to actual synthesis of a defined set of new proteins, the heat shock proteins.
explanations.b: Neither study made a claim restricting the phenomenon to Drosophila; it was later found broadly conserved.
explanations.c: HSF1 as a specific transcription factor was characterized in later molecular work, not this 1974 study.
explanations.d: Puffing is itself a visible sign of active transcription; this was not challenged.

questions.prompt: Why does the heat shock response shut itself off after the newly made HSP70/HSP90 pool grows large enough?

options.text: Because HSF1 is degraded permanently after one activation
Because the rebuilt chaperone pool re-binds and re-sequesters HSF1, forming negative feedback
Because heat shock elements mutate after use
Because ATP is exhausted

explanations.a: HSF1 is not permanently destroyed; it is reversibly sequestered again once free chaperone is available.
explanations.b: Correct — as free HSP70/HSP90 levels recover, they re-bind HSF1, restoring the monomeric inactive state and closing the feedback loop.
explanations.c: Heat shock elements are stable DNA sequences and do not mutate as part of the response.
explanations.d: ATP depletion is not the mechanism described for turning off HSF1 activity.

lessons.label: The Unfolded Protein Response (ER Stress)

sections.heading: Why the ER needs its own alarm system
sections.body: The endoplasmic reticulum folds and quality-checks every secretory and membrane protein a cell makes — a huge, continuous folding load carried out in an oxidizing environment specialized for disulfide bond formation. That environment is fragile: nutrient shifts, calcium disturbance, viral infection, or a burst of client demand can outpace the ER's folding chaperones, and misfolded proteins accumulate in the ER lumen faster than they can be cleared. This is ER stress, and it is distinct from the cytosolic heat shock response because the sensors sit in the ER membrane itself, reading lumenal folding status directly rather than relying on chaperone competition in the cytosol. The response the ER mounts is called the unfolded protein response (UPR), and it runs through three independent sensor branches that act on different timescales and targets.

sections.heading: Three sensors, three mechanisms
sections.body: PERK is a kinase that, once activated by misfolded protein in the ER lumen, phosphorylates eIF2-alpha in the cytosol, which broadly attenuates new protein synthesis — an immediate way to stop adding to the folding backlog while the ER catches up. IRE1-alpha is unusual: it has both kinase and RNase activity, and its RNase performs unconventional cytoplasmic splicing of XBP1 mRNA, removing a 26-nucleotide intron to shift the reading frame and produce XBP1s, a potent transcription factor that upregulates ER chaperones and ER-associated degradation components. ATF6 takes a third route entirely: ER stress triggers its trafficking to the Golgi, where site-1 and site-2 proteases cleave it, releasing a cytosolic fragment that travels to the nucleus and activates transcription of chaperone genes. The three branches are not redundant — PERK acts within minutes via translation, while IRE1-alpha and ATF6 act more slowly via new transcription, giving the cell layered, temporally staggered defenses.

sections.heading: When adaptation fails: the switch to death
sections.body: All three branches are initially adaptive, aiming to restore folding capacity by reducing the client load and boosting chaperone supply. But if ER stress is severe or prolonged and folding capacity is never restored, the same signaling arms — chiefly sustained PERK-driven translation of the transcription factor ATF4, reinforced by ATF6 — induce CHOP (also called DDIT3), a transcription factor that tips the balance toward apoptosis. CHOP represses the anti-apoptotic protein BCL2 and promotes pro-oxidant and pro-death gene expression, converting what began as a protective, adaptive program into a terminal one. This adaptive-to-terminal switch is a recurring theme in toxicology: whether a cell survives a chemical insult can depend less on whether stress pathways are activated and more on how long they stay activated.

lessons.workedExample: A cell is treated with tunicamycin, a chemical that blocks N-linked glycosylation and causes massive protein misfolding in the ER. Within minutes, PERK phosphorylates eIF2-alpha and global translation drops sharply. Within a few hours, IRE1-alpha-mediated XBP1 splicing and ATF6 cleavage boost chaperone and ERAD gene transcription, and the cell's folding capacity partially recovers. If the tunicamycin dose is low and transient, the cell survives via this adaptive UPR. If the dose is high and sustained, CHOP accumulates, BCL2 is repressed, and the same cell undergoes apoptosis — the same three sensors driving opposite outcomes depending on stress duration and intensity.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about the UPR's three branches to see whether a student can distinguish sensors by both mechanism and timescale rather than lumping them together as 'ER stress response.' A weak answer says 'the ER detects unfolded proteins and fixes them.' A strong answer names each sensor's distinct biochemistry — PERK's kinase action on eIF2-alpha, IRE1-alpha's unconventional RNase splicing of XBP1, ATF6's Golgi-cleavage route — and explains that unresolved stress, not stress itself, is what flips the response from adaptive to apoptotic via CHOP.

questions.prompt: Match each UPR sensor to its mechanism of action.

right.text: Phosphorylates eIF2-alpha to attenuate translation
Splices XBP1 mRNA via its RNase activity
Is cleaved in the Golgi to release a transcription-activating fragment

questions.explanation: PERK is a kinase acting on eIF2-alpha; IRE1-alpha has RNase activity that unconventionally splices XBP1 mRNA; ATF6 traffics to the Golgi for proteolytic cleavage that liberates its transcription-factor fragment.

questions.prompt: What is the immediate functional consequence of PERK-mediated eIF2-alpha phosphorylation?

options.text: Global attenuation of new protein synthesis
Immediate destruction of the ER
Direct splicing of XBP1 mRNA
Permanent shutdown of all transcription

explanations.a: Correct — phosphorylated eIF2-alpha reduces cap-dependent translation initiation broadly, easing the flow of new proteins into the overloaded ER.
explanations.b: PERK signaling does not destroy the ER; it is a protective, adaptive response.
explanations.c: XBP1 splicing is performed by IRE1-alpha's RNase activity, not PERK.
explanations.d: The attenuation is broad but reversible and does not eliminate transcription; select mRNAs like ATF4 are even preferentially translated.

questions.prompt: What role does CHOP play when ER stress is prolonged and unresolved?

options.text: It boosts BCL2 to prevent apoptosis
It is a transcription factor that represses BCL2 and promotes pro-apoptotic gene expression
It re-glycosylates misfolded proteins
It has no role beyond the adaptive phase

explanations.a: CHOP represses BCL2 rather than boosting it, pushing cells toward apoptosis rather than away from it.
explanations.b: Correct — CHOP is induced under sustained ER stress and drives apoptotic gene programs, marking the adaptive-to-terminal switch.
explanations.c: CHOP is a transcription factor, not an enzyme involved in glycosylation.
explanations.d: CHOP's defining role is specifically in the terminal, non-adaptive phase of the UPR.

questions.prompt: Order these events from onset of ER stress to a terminal, unresolved outcome.

items.text: Misfolded proteins accumulate in the ER lumen
PERK, IRE1-alpha, and ATF6 are activated
Translation attenuation and chaperone gene induction attempt to restore folding capacity
Sustained signaling induces CHOP and apoptosis if stress is not resolved

questions.explanation: Misfolded protein buildup activates the three sensors, which first drive an adaptive attempt to restore folding capacity; only if that fails does sustained signaling induce CHOP and apoptosis.

questions.prompt: Why does the ER need sensors distinct from the cytosolic HSF1-driven heat shock response?

options.text: Because the ER cannot make any proteins of its own
Because the ER's folding environment and lumenal status must be read directly at the ER membrane rather than inferred from cytosolic chaperone competition
Because HSF1 is only expressed in muscle cells
Because ER stress and heat stress are chemically identical

explanations.a: The ER is highly active in protein folding and modification; the issue is about sensing, not synthesis.
explanations.b: Correct — ER-membrane-spanning sensors read the lumenal folding environment directly, which the cytosolic HSF1 mechanism cannot access.
explanations.c: HSF1 is broadly expressed and not restricted to muscle tissue.
explanations.d: ER stress and heat stress arise from different physical insults and are read by distinct sensor systems.

lessons.label: The Integrated Stress Response

sections.heading: One phosphorylation site, four different alarms
sections.body: The integrated stress response (ISR) is the convergence point where four structurally distinct kinases, each tuned to a different type of cellular emergency, all phosphorylate the same residue: serine 51 of eIF2-alpha. PERK, already introduced as an ER-stress sensor, is one of the four. GCN2 detects amino-acid starvation by binding uncharged tRNAs that accumulate when amino acid supply cannot keep pace with translation demand. HRI was first characterized in red blood cell precursors, where it senses heme deficiency, but it also responds to oxidative and osmotic stress more broadly. PKR is activated by double-stranded RNA, a structural signature of many viral infections, making it part of the antiviral interferon response. Despite sensing four unrelated conditions — ER misfolding, starvation, heme/oxidative imbalance, and viral infection — all four kinases converge on the identical molecular output.

sections.heading: What phosphorylated eIF2-alpha actually does
sections.body: eIF2 normally delivers the initiator methionine tRNA to the ribosome as part of assembling the ternary complex needed to start translation; each round requires eIF2 to be recharged with GTP by its exchange factor, eIF2B. Phosphorylated eIF2-alpha binds and inhibits eIF2B rather than being recycled by it, so ternary complex formation falls and cap-dependent translation initiation drops globally — a rapid, energy-conserving brake on protein synthesis during an emergency.
