questions.explanation: The antioxidant response element reporter reads out Nrf2-driven oxidative stress signaling, the p53-response-element reporter reads out genotoxic stress, and the heat shock element reporter reads out general proteotoxic (protein-folding) stress.

questions.prompt: Order the components of an adverse outcome pathway from the molecular level to the whole-organism level.

items.text: Molecular initiating event (e.g., receptor binding)
Cellular key event
Organ-level key event
Adverse outcome at the organism/population level

questions.explanation: An AOP is built as a chain moving from a single molecular interaction, through intermediate cellular and then organ-level effects, to an adverse outcome observable in the whole organism or population.

questions.prompt: What is the main blind spot of the adverse outcome pathway framework identified in this lesson?

options.text: It cannot describe any molecular mechanism at all
It does not by itself account for toxicokinetics, so an in vitro hit concentration may not be physiologically achievable in vivo
It requires a new animal study for every chemical tested
It only applies to pharmaceuticals, never environmental chemicals

explanations.a: The AOP framework is specifically built to make molecular mechanism explicit through the molecular initiating event.
explanations.b: Correct — an AOP links mechanism to outcome but does not itself model absorption, metabolism, or clearance, so a hit concentration in a dish may never be reached in real tissue without added IVIVE analysis.
explanations.c: Part of the AOP framework's purpose is to reduce reliance on new animal studies by combining in vitro evidence into a weight-of-evidence case.
explanations.d: The AOP framework and programs like Tox21/ToxCast are applied broadly across industrial, environmental, and pharmaceutical chemicals, not pharmaceuticals alone.

lessons.label: From IC50 to a Defensible Claim: Designing a Toxicology Project

sections.heading: Choosing a model: cell line, primary cells, or organoid
sections.body: Every toxicology project starts with a model choice that shapes what the results can honestly claim. Immortalized cell lines, such as HepG2 for liver studies, are cheap and reproducible but often express drug-metabolizing enzymes like CYP2E1 at much lower levels than real tissue, which can hide bioactivation-dependent toxicity like the acetaminophen mechanism covered earlier in this unit. Primary cells isolated directly from an organ better reflect real physiology and metabolism but come with donor-to-donor variability and a limited usable lifespan in culture. Three-dimensional organoids or spheroids sit between the two: they rebuild tissue-like architecture and diffusion gradients that flat 2D culture cannot, at the cost of longer culture time and higher expense. None of these is the 'right' choice in the abstract; the right choice is whichever one keeps the pathway you are testing intact.

sections.heading: Matching the endpoint to the hypothesized mechanism
sections.body: A generic viability assay, such as MTT or resazurin reduction, tells you cells are dying but nothing about how, and pairing it with a mechanism-specific endpoint is what turns a viability curve into evidence. If the hypothesis is mitochondrial toxicity, oxygen consumption rate or a membrane-potential dye like JC-1 is the relevant readout, not a generic viability stain. If the hypothesis is genotoxicity, a comet assay or gamma-H2AX staining for double-strand breaks is appropriate; if the hypothesis is membrane lysis, LDH release fits; and if the hypothesis is ferroptosis or another regulated death mode covered in this unit, a rescue panel with the matching pathway-specific inhibitor is the right test. Choosing the assay before running the experiment, rather than after seeing a viability drop, keeps the project mechanistic rather than descriptive.

sections.heading: A real dose-response, and reporting the number honestly
sections.body: A defensible IC50 requires a proper dilution series, commonly half-log or two-fold steps spanning several orders of magnitude, run with technical replicates within a plate and biological replicates across independent experiments, alongside vehicle and positive controls. Fitting the resulting data to a four-parameter logistic (Hill) curve yields an IC50 with a confidence interval; reporting a single-replicate IC50 with no interval is one of the most common and most avoidable weaknesses in student toxicology projects. The strongest reports go further and pair the number with a death-mode finding, an IC50 of 12 micromolar rescued by ferrostatin-1 is a mechanistic claim, while '12 micromolar' alone is just a number. Finally, every in vitro IC50 needs an honest in vitro-to-in vivo caveat: cultured cells sit in serum-free or low-protein medium with no metabolic clearance, so concentrations easily achieved in a dish, tens of micromolar, may be far above anything a real tissue ever sees, and a strong project explicitly compares its IC50 to a known achievable exposure level, such as a compound's reported peak plasma concentration, rather than leaving that comparison for the judge to wonder about.

lessons.workedExample: A student screens a candidate nanoparticle in HepG2 cells using an 8-point half-log dilution series, in triplicate wells, repeated across 3 independent experiments, with vehicle and a known cytotoxic positive control on every plate. Fitting a four-parameter logistic curve gives an IC50 of 45 micromolar with a 95 percent confidence interval of 38 to 53 micromolar. A rescue panel shows partial protection with ferrostatin-1 and partial protection with z-VAD-fmk, suggesting a mixed ferroptotic and apoptotic death mode rather than one dominant pathway. The student then compares 45 micromolar to the highest concentration reported in relevant exposure literature and reports that it exceeds that level by roughly tenfold, explicitly flagging that their finding demonstrates a real biological effect at achievable laboratory concentrations but has not been shown to occur at expected real-world exposure levels.
lessons.judgeFraming: This is the synthesis question every toxicology judge eventually asks: 'is your number meaningful?' A weak answer reports a single IC50 from one experiment with no replicate structure, no confidence interval, and no comment on whether the tested concentration is realistic. A strong answer reports the replicate design, the confidence interval, the death mode evidence tying the number to a mechanism, and an explicit, numeric comparison of the in vitro concentration against a real achievable exposure level, treating the in vitro-to-in vivo gap as a stated limitation rather than an unstated hope that no one asks.

questions.prompt: Why might a HepG2 cell line understate acetaminophen-type bioactivation toxicity compared to primary hepatocytes?

options.text: HepG2 cells cannot be cultured for more than a few hours
HepG2 cells often express CYP2E1 and other metabolizing enzymes at much lower levels than real liver tissue
HepG2 cells are more expensive than primary hepatocytes
HepG2 cells cannot be exposed to any chemical at all

explanations.a: Culture duration is not the limiting factor described for this model-choice issue.
explanations.b: Correct — lower CYP2E1 (and other drug-metabolizing enzyme) expression means less bioactivation to a reactive metabolite, which can mask toxicity that depends on that metabolic step.
explanations.c: Cost runs the opposite direction: immortalized lines like HepG2 are typically cheaper than primary cells, not more expensive.
explanations.d: HepG2 cells are routinely used in toxicity screening; the limitation is metabolic capacity, not usability.

questions.prompt: Match each hypothesized mechanism to the endpoint that actually tests it.

right.text: Oxygen consumption rate / JC-1 membrane potential
Comet assay / gamma-H2AX staining
LDH release assay

questions.explanation: Mitochondrial toxicity is best captured by respiration or membrane-potential readouts, genotoxicity by DNA-damage-specific assays like the comet assay or gamma-H2AX, and membrane lysis by extracellular LDH release, each matched to what the hypothesized mechanism actually produces.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of building a defensible dose-response study, from design to final claim.

items.text: Design a multi-point dilution series with technical and biological replicates
Run the assay with vehicle and positive controls included
Fit a four-parameter logistic curve to obtain IC50 with a confidence interval
Compare the IC50 to a known achievable exposure level and state the in vitro-to-in vivo caveat

questions.explanation: A defensible claim starts with proper replicate design, runs with the controls needed to validate the plate, produces a curve-fit IC50 with uncertainty, and only then is interpreted against real-world achievable exposure, with the translation gap stated explicitly rather than assumed away.

questions.prompt: In the worked example, why does the student compare the 45 micromolar IC50 to reported exposure literature rather than simply reporting the IC50 alone?

options.text: Because a confidence interval makes the comparison unnecessary
Because an in vitro concentration achievable in a dish may not reflect what is physiologically achievable in real tissue, and a defensible claim states that explicitly
Because IC50 values are always identical to in vivo effective doses
Because journals require exposure comparisons only for FDA-approved drugs

explanations.a: A confidence interval describes the precision of the IC50 itself; it says nothing about whether that concentration is ever reached in a real organism.
explanations.b: Correct — cultured cells lack the metabolism, clearance, and protein binding that limit real tissue concentrations, so an honest project explicitly checks its in vitro number against a known achievable exposure rather than implying real-world relevance by default.
explanations.c: In vitro IC50 and in vivo effective dose routinely diverge, which is exactly why the comparison step matters.
explanations.d: This comparison is good scientific practice for any compound being evaluated for toxicity, not a rule limited to approved drugs.
